en: The Vinaya-saṃgraha of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume One.
Compiled by the Venerable Jayamitra;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.

Preface to the First Explanation of the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* I pay homage to the One who is tamed and has eliminated afflictions, Who is the primary cause for extinguishing the delusions of sentient beings;
Like the sun that shines broadly to benefit the boundless, He is able to utterly destroy all darkness.
The Buddha taught the extensive explanations along with the various matters, the Nidānas and the Muktakas;
from the Ekottarika up to the sixteen sections, these are what the Venerable Upāli inquired about.
The *Maṇavikā* presents an essential commentary, Along with the *Vinayottaragrantha* and the *Mātṛkā*;
I shall now condense these extensive texts in their proper sequence, So that those who delight in brevity may swiftly attain realization.
The Prātimokṣa Sūtra is difficult to hear even after the passage of immeasurable koṭis of kalpas;
likewise for its recitation, study, and upholding. Yet one who practices according to what is taught is even more difficult to encounter.
The meaning of the first verse here clarifies that both the teaching and its practice are difficult to encounter.

Regarding the term *prātimokṣa* (individual liberation): because one practices according to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, one gradually abandons the nine grades of afflictions—beginning with the lowest of the low—and attains permanent non-retrogression; thus, by attaining liberation from all afflictions, it is called *prātimokṣa*.

Furthermore, one observes that the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation are numerous in their various categories; the ability to relinquish them individually is called "individual liberation" (prātimokṣa).
Since sentient beings are swept away by delusions within the three realms, one should first diligently seek liberation for their sake.
"Sūtra" refers to the words of the Buddha, distinguishing them from the teachings of non-Buddhist schools.

"Hearing" means that with respect to what is spoken by another, one understands both the text and its meaning, because it is apprehended by the auditory consciousness together with the subsequent mind of discernment.

Regarding the term "difficult to encounter": it is because one meets with the appearance of a Buddha only once in a great while, and because rebirth in the higher realms and so forth is extremely difficult to attain.

Regarding the phrase "immeasurable koṭis of kalpas": this refers to *mahākalpas*; although the Dharma of the precepts is difficult to encounter even after passing through such vast numbers of eons, it would be even more difficult to meet with it were one to exceed these limits. This demonstrates the ultimate extremity of its rarity.
Regarding "reciting and reading," it means receiving [the teaching] through wisdom, whether by way of the text or its meaning.

Regarding "upholding," it means repeatedly recollecting and maintaining those two over a long period so as not to forget them, due to being diligently engaged in practices such as mindfulness and recitation.

Regarding the phrase "one who acts according to what they have spoken": this refers to one who, in the actions performed through body, speech, and mind, accords with the words of the Great Master without transgression. As for the phrase "even more difficult to encounter":

while hearing, reading, and upholding [the teachings] is still relatively easy to obtain, one who acts according to what they have spoken is extremely difficult to encounter. It is only through courageous exertion and diligent effort that the practice of the precepts can be perfected; it cannot be attained by those of inferior resolve. Thus, the word "more" is used to manifest its extreme difficulty.

In this context, it is explained that the teaching and its practice are difficult to encounter: hearing, reading, reciting, and upholding it constitutes the teaching, while honoring and cultivating it constitutes the practice.
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is joy; The proclamation of the subtle, sublime True Dharma is joy;
The Sangha being of one mind and shared vision is joy; Being harmonious and practicing together with courageous diligence is joy.
The meaning of this verse is to clarify that all the activities of the Three Jewels appearing in the world are causes of happiness.

Regarding the statement that "the appearance of the Buddhas in the world is happiness," this refers to the time of entering the womb and the time of manifesting birth; these are designated as the "appearance of a Buddha in the world" based on the principle of what is about to be accomplished. Thus it is said.

Although it is said that a bodhisattva receives the title of Buddha, or that a Buddha appears in the world at the moment of attaining perfect enlightenment, it is because at that time one achieves all-knowledge and obtains the designation "Buddha. Since this is the cause for the joy of sublime liberation, it is called "bliss," just as people in the world call fire "bliss."
The "joy of expounding the subtle and sublime True Dharma" refers to the twelvefold division of the teachings, such as the sūtras and so forth.
The "Saṃgha" refers to the eight types of great beings and others.

Regarding the phrase "unified mind and common view," this means that the assembly collectively adheres to the same precepts, views, deportment, and right livelihood; furthermore, it clarifies that because they share a unified mind and common purpose, they are difficult to break apart.
"Practicing in harmony and together" means that they collectively purify their ethical discipline (*śīla*) with a unified mind.

"Vigorously advancing" refers to diligently practicing the three trainings; or, it means exerting the mind with courage so that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are ultimately exhausted; furthermore, it means the mind is resolute and advances without retreat in whatever task is being practiced—all of these are causes for happiness.
To see a person of noble character is joy; to dwell together with them is also joy.
To never behold those who are foolish and deluded—this is what is called constantly experiencing happiness.

The meaning of this verse clarifies that associating with virtuous people and distancing oneself from evil companions is likewise a cause of happiness; thus, the first half and the second half should be understood respectively.

Regarding those called "precious persons," they distance themselves from and abandon sinful matters; such precious persons possess superior and wholesome virtues, and both seeing them and dwelling together with them can give rise to happiness.

If one does not cultivate wholesome qualities and is frequently deluded regarding the correct principle by means of evil conduct, this is called ignorance; one should not associate with such a person but should quickly abandon them.
To see one who possesses ethical discipline (śīla) is joy; to see one who is learned (bahuśruta) is likewise called joy;
to see an Arhat is true joy, because of the non-arising of future existence (punarbhava).
The meaning of this verse clarifies the distinctions among virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Now, there are two kinds of such "jewel-like persons":
first, the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), and second, the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
The mundane [path] is further twofold:
first, abiding in the portion of concentration;
second, abiding in the portion of wisdom.

Regarding "endowed with ethical discipline" (*śīla*), this refers to abiding in the factor of concentration; although it is a mundane treasure, it is also capable of distancing one from evil, as this clarifies that concentration is generated through the power of morality.
Regarding "much learning" (*bahuśruta*), this refers to abiding in the factor of wisdom, because wisdom is generated by means of concentration.

The second half clarifies that by operating the mind with equanimity toward the two dharmas of meditative concentration and wisdom, one abides in the ultimate state; this is the supreme, true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

As for the term "Arhat," it refers to one who has realized the dharma of non-arising amidst the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), meaning they have attained permanent liberation from the fetters of afflictions and manifold sufferings.
There is joy in the delightful stairway at the river crossing; there is joy in conquering enemies through the Dharma.
When the fruit of right wisdom is realized, there is the joy of being able to eliminate the conceit of "I" entirely.
The first half of this verse clarifies the cause for attaining happiness, while the second half clarifies that the arising of wisdom severs delusions.

Regarding the term "river crossing" (*nadī-tīrtha*): it refers to the river of liberation, which is free from the faults of the two extremes; because one can only attain it through the Eightfold Noble Path, it is called a "wondrous staircase. This is metaphorically like a river crossing with a wondrous stairway, as it serves as the cause for the joy of travelers.

Regarding the statement "the joy of victory in battle through subduing enemies by means of the Dharma," this clarifies that one employs the Dharma of correct practice as a defensive weapon against adversaries; because it subdues the afflictions (kleśa) so that they do not arise again, it is called "victory in battle."
The second half of the verse clarifies that by means of the sword of wisdom one cuts down the banner of self-conceit, destroys the army of Māra, and manifests supreme bliss.
If there is one who can form a resolute intention, Who well subdues the senses and desires and possesses great learning;
From youth until old age dwelling in the forest, They find joy in the tranquility of living in seclusion within an araṇya.
This verse describes how the practitioner who previously cultivated the dhūta qualities attains their perfection, as these are the causes of happiness.

Regarding "resolute intention": it refers to first generating a pure mind for the practice of contentment; it means making a firm decision to exert diligence without seeking fame or profit, restraining the body and mind, and guarding against external objects, because the supreme fruit of liberation is accomplished on this basis.
The phrase "having well-subdued the faculties and desires" indicates that the accompanying factors are pure and can coexist with ethical discipline (*śīla*).

The phrase "possessing great learning" clarifies that the attainment of superior fruits necessarily relies upon extensive study; it is through wisdom (*prajñā*) that one can discern and thereby sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).

A person of dull wit is not capable of dwelling in an araṇya; therefore, a bhikṣu should first study extensively. Even if one is not extensively learned, provided they clearly understand the characteristics of the precepts, they may likewise dwell in an araṇya.
The phrase "from youth until old age" and so forth clarifies that the resolute mind remains without regression from beginning to end.

The phrase "the joy of dwelling in tranquility and seclusion in an araṇya" means that only by departing from clamor and distraction can one approach the principle and cause the mind to dwell in happiness.
The six verses above were compiled by the Arhats during the council; the introductory text below generally expounds ten meanings:
first, clarifying the Buddha’s teaching;
second, censuring those who did not assemble together.
3. Not gathering [the assembly] but listening accordingly;
4. The ritual for making offerings;
5. Clearly explaining the formal admonitions.
Sixth, the admonition for the benefit [of the assembly];
seventh, the arising of faults due to the absence of such an admonition;
eighth, the formal announcement of the matter.
9. Exhorting them to listen with a sincere mind;
10. Purifying the assembly.
"Venerable sirs!..."
"So much of the spring season has passed, and so much remains;
as old age and death have already encroached and the life-faculty gradually diminishes, the Great Master’s Teaching shall soon perish."
Venerable sirs!

You should strive to illuminate [the Dharma] and not be negligent; through non-negligence, you will surely realize the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—how much more so the other wholesome dharmas belonging to the category of enlightenment?
“Venerable Saṃgha, what has been done first?
“The Buddha’s community of śrāvakas seeks little and has few concerns.
Those bhikṣus who have not arrived have declared their *chanda* and *pariśuddhi*.”
First, regarding the clarification of what was taught by the Buddha: this refers to the passage beginning with "Venerable Ones, such a portion of spring has passed," and so forth.
"Passed" (*atīta*) carries the meaning of having already gone by.

As for the term "spring season" (*vāsā*), it means that within the three seasons, whichever time it may be, one speaks of the *Prātimokṣa* while referring to that specific occasion; here, we provisionally rely upon the spring season as our basis.
The "three seasons" refer to spring, summer, and winter.
The phrase "that many" indicates a specific limit, meaning the number is taken according to the days remaining until the next *Poṣadha* (confession) ceremony.
As for the statement "there remain that many," it should be understood by calculating based on the remaining days at that particular time.

Regarding the statement "old age and death having already invaded," the intent is to clarify that old age and death are constantly present before one. Aging and dying are termed "old age and death" (*jarāmaraṇa*).

However, among the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), only this one is mentioned because its influence is most powerful amidst sorrow, lamentation, and so forth; it is intended to show that those who practice for purification lose their perfect accomplishments. This is the first cause.
However, there are briefly two kinds of causes for the perfection of a practitioner:
first, the basis; second, the root of practice. Regarding the loss of the basis:
due to the pressure of old age and death, one lacks the capacity [for practice], and the life-faculty is severed and destroyed in successive order.

Regarding "the fundamental loss of speech and conduct": this refers to the fact that the Great Master’s teaching will soon perish, because with the extinction of the Buddha-dharma, one falls away from and loses correct practice.
The World-Honored One of Great Compassion transforms all sentient beings through unerring meaning; therefore, he is called the "Great Master."

"Dharma" refers to the twelvefold division of the teachings; by means of these, the World-Honored One guides and benefits sentient beings, so that all who possess the necessary conditions undergo transformation.
Because of these two matters, one loses the practice of perfection.
The instruction "do not be negligent" is an exhortation to non-negligence, for through a diligent mind and courageous resolve, one brings glory to the holy teaching.
The reason it specifically says "non-negligence" is to show that among all categories of wholesome qualities (*kuśala-pakṣa*), non-negligence is the most preeminent.

Regarding the statement "one should be diligent," this is an exhortation to practice heedfulness, as it serves as the basis for the application of the supramundane noble path; that is to say, by practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā in tandem and with equal momentum, one attains the noble path.

Regarding the phrase "by means of heedfulness one shall certainly realize," this indicates that the Blessed One established the various rules of training (*śikṣāpada*) so that those members of the renunciant community seeking liberation might realize the fruits of the path.
"Speaking as one who knows" means that one’s knowledge of objects corresponds exactly to reality.
"Worthy of offerings" means that one is worthy of receiving offerings from all sentient beings.
"Perfectly and Fully Awakened One" (Samyaksaṃbuddha) refers to one who possesses non-erroneous, universal, and thorough knowledge.

As for the statement, "How much more so the other wholesome dharmas belonging to the category of enlightenment," this also corresponds to what precedes it: because non-heedlessness leads to enlightenment, all wholesome dharmas whatsoever are termed "wholesome dharmas belonging to the category of enlightenment."
Next, the refutation of not assembling as a whole is clarified.

Regarding the statement, "Venerable Saṃgha, what business has been undertaken previously?", this clarifies that there was no prior separate business [requiring absence], and thus one ought to come and assemble together.
The following passage states: "The Buddha’s assembly of śrāvakas seeks little and has few affairs; since they have no other business, why do they not come?
Furthermore, another explanation says: "At the time of the *poṣadha*, one sweeps and cleanses, making pure and solemn preparations, such as arranging lamps and flowers."
Because of previous actions, one must ask:
"Venerable Saṃgha! Have the matters previously to be performed already been completed?"
Regarding the terms "few desires" and "few affairs": "few desires" refers to having few cravings, while "few affairs" refers to being content.
Furthermore, "few desires" refers to the mental faculty (*manas-karma*), and "few affairs" refers to the physical and vocal faculties (*kāya-vāk-karma*).

As for the term "śrāvaka," it means "hearing from others"; because they listen and hear by following the sounds of others, and because they form a community through this, they are called the "community of śrāvakas.
A "community" (saṃgha) refers to those who have gathered together with a common mind that cannot be destroyed.
Next, the non-assembly and subsequent listening are explained.
Regarding the phrase "not coming" and so forth: at the time of the *poṣadha*, not participating in the assembly is termed "not coming.
The address "Venerable One" (*bhadanta*) is a term of mutual respect.
As the Blessed One said:
"Among the bhikṣus, whether they be junior or senior, one should not address them by name, clan, or surname;
rather, one should say, 'Venerable Sir'."
Or one may say, "Virtuous One. If the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, is to be addressed by his title of honor, failing to do so constitutes an offense against the Dharma.

Regarding the expression of *chanda* (consent) and *viśuddhi* (purity): if a bhikṣu is afflicted by illness or is engaged in the cultivation of superior wholesome qualities and thus unable to attend the assembly, he should express his consent and purity; this may be done either through verbal communication or through physical gesture (*kāyavijñapti*).

One should give it in this manner: having bared the right shoulder, removed one's leather sandals, and performed the appropriate acts of respect, one should squat down with palms joined and speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me!
Today, on the fourteenth day, the Saṃgha performs the poṣadha; I, the bhikṣu [Name], likewise perform the poṣadha on the fourteenth day.

I, [Name], declare myself to be completely pure and free from all obstructing dharmas. Due to the circumstance of illness, regarding this dharma-accordant matter of the Saṃgha, I now grant my consent and purity. May this declaration be communicated by you for my sake.
The second and third [proclamations] were likewise spoken.
If a bhikṣu is so seriously ill that he cannot give his consent (chanda), if he is able to be carried away, he should be taken into the assembly;
if he is unable, they should all go to the sick person to perform the poṣadha.
If it is not done in this way, the ritual act will not be accomplished and one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
If it is not a *poṣadha* but another *karma*, one simply gives the consent (*chanda*) and does not declare purity (*śuci*).
Once the bhikṣu holding the *śuddhika-icchā* has entered the midst of the assembly, he should address the bhikṣu seated beside him as follows:
"Venerable one, please attend!

In such-and-such a room, the bhikṣu named so-and-so is afflicted by illness and suffering; today, on the fourteenth day, the Saṃgha performs the *poṣadha*, and that bhikṣu so-and-so likewise performs the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day."

That bhikṣu, so-and-so, has declared himself to be completely pure and free from all obstructing dharmas; for the sake of the cause and condition of illness, he has granted his consent and purity for the legal affairs of the Saṃgha.
I now relate in full that which he has stated.
If there are other circumstances, one should speak accordingly according to the situation at hand.

The reason for declaring one's *kāyacitta-śuddhi* (purity of body and mind) before an individual rather than informing the entire assembly is to prevent various faults such as protracted delays and the arising of fatigue.
If a bhikṣu, out of negligence or for the sake of a base practice, gives his consent (chanda), he incurs the offense of duṣkṛta.

If one is performing a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), or is currently ill, or fears that illness is about to arise, or has recently recovered from an ailment, or is attending to a patient, or is exhausted, or is afflicted by hunger, thirst, cold, or heat; or if one’s nature is prone to excessive drowsiness and seeks to dispel lethargy by practicing other wholesome qualities; or if one is privately reciting the *Prātimokṣa* in a quiet room, or receiving instruction on the meaning of the precepts from another; or if one is a person committed to the literal text who concentrates the mind on its meaning for fear of forgetting it; or if one has newly attained sublime insight (*vipaśyanā*) manifesting before them in order to subdue the mind; or if one is engaged in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and does not wish to allow them to be interrupted—fearing that if distracted by other conditions, right mindfulness might be lost; or if at times one has seen the truths and attained the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*)—in all these cases, it is no offense to grant one's consent (*chanda*).
If one conveys the *chanda* (consent), those who have gathered together—whether they be young or elderly bhikṣus—should set aside other virtuous activities and proceed to the place of assembly.

Once the person conveying the *chanda* has received it, if they run swiftly, flee into a pit, stand on a precarious place such as a railing, travel through the air, go outside the boundary, step onto a double staircase, tread upon two ladders placed crosswise, fall asleep, enter meditative absorption, die, return to lay life, or say: [the following]: [The original text continues with a list of conditions under which the transmission of consent becomes invalid.]
If one says, "I am a śrāmaṇera, etc.," it does not constitute a properly maintained *chanda* (consent) or *śuddhi* (purity); one must take the *chanda* again.
If one person holds multiple *chanda* and *śuddhi*, they may be recited according to what can be remembered.
If [the recipient] is on the ground and [the giver] is in the air, or vice versa, neither is established; furthermore, one should not transfer the purity of desire (*chanda*) in such cases.
A person undergoing training (*śikṣamāṇa*) does not hold the desire of another, yet they should be given the desire by others because they are a bhikṣu.
Those residing within the boundary must grant their consent (*chanda*) to those also within the boundary; otherwise, it is not valid.
Regarding the request for instruction by a bhikṣuṇī, one may state whether such a person exists or not.
Due to the explanation of the rules concerning boundaries (*sīmā*), there are two types:
First, the small;
second, the large.

Within the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), in a place free from obstacles or difficulties, one establishes a small boundary field (*kṣudra-sīmā*). First, one observes the boundary markers (*nimitta*); for instance, in the eastern direction, these may be a wall, a tree, a fence, a hedge, a mound of earth, a standing stone, a driven stake, a cliff, or the like; the same applies to the other directions.

Once the assembly has recognized the signs, they announce it; then, having spread out the seats all around and struck the *ghanṭā*, they perform the preliminary preparations. When the great assembly has gathered together, there is no procedure for granting one's consent (*chanda*).
The resident bhikṣus together shall designate the boundaries, starting from the east, followed by the south, west, and north.
Once the boundaries are known, one bhikṣu shall perform the formal motion (jñapti-karman); the small boundary (kṣudra-sīmā) must be established first and not last.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now, all the resident bhikṣus here together designate the long-standing boundary markers for the four sides of the small boundary:
such-and-such a marker in the east, and so on, up to such-and-such a marker in the north."
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission: the Saṃgha shall now establish a small boundary (kṣudrasīmā) within this marked area.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now, all the resident bhikṣus here together proclaim the long-standing boundary markers for the four sides of this small boundary (*sīmā*):"
"Such-and-such a mark to the east, and so on, up to such-and-such a mark to the north.
Now, the Saṃgha shall establish a small boundary (sīmā) within this area defined by these marks.
If it is agreeable to the venerable ones to establish a small boundary within this area defined by these marks, let them remain silent; if it is not agreeable, let them speak."
“The Saṃgha has finished establishing this small boundary enclosure within these marked limits; the Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence. Thus do I now uphold it.”

Regarding this small boundary (sīmā), there is no fixed textual prescription; however, in every location in the West, it has a specific measurement, being only about one *zhang* or so. It is constructed by leveling the ground and encircling it with bricks, without any steps. A *caitya* is installed in its center, and the door faces one side. Next is the method for establishing the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*): the measurement of this great boundary is extremely large, reaching a width of two and a half *yojanas*. If there is no water, it extends downward likewise; if separated by water, the boundary extends up to the water's edge.
If there are trees or mountains within the boundary, the boundary follows those trees and mountains; upward, it reaches the water boundary, which is the same as the horizontal measurement.
If one wishes to establish the boundaries of a small *sīmā*, the matter may be settled according to one's preference.

When establishing a large *sīmā*, the boundary markers (*liṅga*) are established as before. The resident bhikṣus together observe the boundary markers at the four directions; then, having spread out the seats and struck the *gandī* gong, the entire assembly should gather, and the announcement should be made as before.
Next, one bhikṣu shall perform the formal motion with a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now, all the resident bhikṣus here together designate the long-standing boundary markers for the four sides of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*):"
In the east there is such-and-such a landmark, and so on, up to in the north there is such-and-such a landmark.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now establishes within these boundary landmarks a Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) for the *poṣadha* and the practice of dwelling together:
from the forest hermitage to this residence, excluding the village and its surrounding territory.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* is performed:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now, all the resident bhikṣus currently dwelling here together proclaim the long-standing boundary markers for the four sides of the great boundary:
such-and-such a marker in the east, and so on, up to such-and-such a marker in the north.
The Saṃgha should authorize the establishment of a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) for the practice of the Poṣadha and communal residence within this defined area:
from the forest hermitage to this dwelling place, excluding the village and its surrounding precincts.
Venerable sirs, if you approve of establishing within this marked boundary a single *poṣadha* zone for the communal residence of the Saṃgha as a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*),
extending from the forest hermitage to this dwelling— excluding the village and its surrounding precincts— then remain silent;
if you do not approve, please speak.

“The Saṃgha has completed the formal establishment of this great boundary for the Saṃgha’s common residence and the *poṣadha* ceremony within these marked limits. Since the Saṃgha has granted its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so.”

"If the Saṃgha has already established the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā), the bhikṣus therein must assemble in one place for the purposes of the Poṣadha and the Pravāraṇā, as well as for performing all *jñapti*, *jñapti-dvitīya*, and *jñapti-caturtha* karmas;
if the assembly does not gather, the ritual act is not accomplished, and one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma."

If one wishes to establish a "boundary for not losing robes" (*acīvarāsaṃsargamaṇḍala*) upon this [great] boundary, it should be established by relying on the characteristics of the great boundary itself; it should be done in this manner, having a single bhikṣu perform the formal motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
Having first performed the formal motion (*jñapti*), one then carries out the ritual act (*karman*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

At this residence, the harmonious Saṃgha has already together established a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) for the shared practice of the *poṣadha* and communal dwelling. If the Saṃgha deems it timely and grants its consent, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now establish within the limits of this great boundary a 'boundary for the non-loss of robes' (*acīvara-nāśana-sīmā*) for the bhikṣus."
The motion is thus made: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

In this residence, the harmonious Saṃgha has already together established a great boundary for the Saṃgha—a single *poṣadha* and common residence—by means of a formal act. Now, within the limits of the marks of this great boundary, the Saṃgha intends to establish a 'bowl-and-robe non-separation' boundary for the bhikṣus."

Venerable sirs, if you approve of establishing the *cīvarāstapatti-sīmā* (the boundary where monks do not lose their robes) within the limits of this great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), remain silent; if you do not approve, speak.

“The Saṃgha has completed the formal establishment of the ‘boundary for not losing one’s robes’ for bhikṣus within the limits of this great boundary. Since the Saṃgha has granted its approval by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so.”

If the Sangha has already established the *acelaka-sīmā* (the boundary where one is not separated from one's robes), then by carrying only the two robes—the upper and the lower—one may move about within the boundary without the fault of being separated from one's robes.

If there is a reason to dissolve either the small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*) or the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*), it should be dissolved by means of a formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

Having spread out the seats within the small boundary (sīmā), the ghaṇṭī is then struck. If the assembly has not gathered, and there are at least four persons within the small boundary, one bhikṣu should first perform the formal motion (jñapti) before proceeding with the ritual act (karmavācanā):
"Listen, venerable Saṃgha!

In this dwelling place, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a small boundary field (*kṣudrasīmā*). If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now together dissolve this small boundary field.
The motion is thus stated. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
At this dwelling place, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a small boundary (sīmā). The Saṃgha now together dissolves this small boundary."
"If the Venerable Ones approve of this small boundary field, they should remain silent; if they do not approve, they should speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [proclamations] are likewise spoken.
"The Saṃgha has finished dissolving the small boundary enclosure; the Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by its silence. Thus do I now uphold this.

Alternatively, if there was previously a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) but no small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*), and one now wishes to establish a small boundary, one should first dissolve that great boundary through a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal motion followed by three proclamations).
It should be dissolved in this manner: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
In this dwelling place, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) for the purpose of a common residence and the performance of the Uposatha (poṣadha).
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha allow that the Saṃgha now dissolve this great boundary.
[The motion] is thus stated. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

At this residence, the harmonious Saṃgha has previously together established a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) for the practice of the *poṣadha* and communal dwelling. The Saṃgha now dissolves this great boundary."
"If the Venerable Ones approve of the dissolution of this great boundary, let them remain silent; if they do not approve, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [proclamations] are likewise spoken.
"The Sangha has completed the dissolution of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā). Since the Sangha has granted its consent by remaining silent, I now hold it to be so.

Once the boundary has been dissolved, one should first establish a small boundary (kṣudra-sīmā) and subsequently establish the great boundary; furthermore, one should not lose one's robes, as prescribed above.
If one does not dissolve the old boundary before establishing a new one, the subsequent establishment will be invalid, and one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

If one wishes to establish both a small boundary (*sīmā*) and a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) simultaneously through a single formal act (*karmavācanā*) with one motion and two proclamations (*jñaptidvitīya-karman*), or to dissolve them simultaneously through a single motion and three proclamations (*jñapticaturtha-karman*), one should assemble the two Saṃghas upon the two boundaries. One should press the seating mats over the two boundaries, and the presiding officiant, standing there, should perform the formal act.

Furthermore, it should be known that when performing the formal act of binding, the small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) comes first; when performing the formal act of releasing, the small boundary comes last.
If one wishes to perform both the releasing and the binding simultaneously, the procedure for reciting the text should be understood according to the specific circumstances.

When establishing a boundary, one should not allow that boundary to enter another boundary, nor extend it over a place where water currently stands, nor include a small boundary area, nor even cross over a nuns' residence by means of that boundary.

In other realms, there are five locations that must not be transgressed: namely, the boundary of bhikṣus, the boundary of bhikṣuṇīs, a small boundary enclosure, a place where water collects, and the intermediate space between two boundaries.
Nor is it the case that by understanding this realm, one understands other realms; even a single great tree may constitute the characteristic of many realms.

When the boundaries are being established, once the directions and characteristics are known and the majority of the *karmavācanā* has been recited, if the officiant suddenly dies, the establishment of the boundary is nonetheless accomplished.
If one uses illusory arts or supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to create boundary markers, the demarcation of the boundary is not established.
Furthermore, one should not use things such as ripples on water, stars, or the moon to serve as boundary signs.

If visiting bhikṣus arrive at an empty dwelling and do not wait for seven or eight days for the resident monks before performing the formal boundary-delineation (sīmā-bandha), they incur an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta); they should rely upon the previous boundary and not rely upon the subsequent one that was established.
If there are bridges over rivers or mountain torrents, it is permissible to establish a boundary across them; otherwise, it is not.
If a bridge over a river or torrent has collapsed, one may spend up to seven nights repairing it; if the eighth night arrives, the legal efficacy of the boundary is lost.
If one originally had no intention of repairing it, then once the bridge has collapsed, the boundary is likewise lost.
There are five circumstances by which the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) is lost:

when the entire Saṃgha undergoes a change of gender; when the entire Saṃgha collectively abandons it and departs; when the entire Saṃgha simultaneously returns to lay life; when the entire Saṃgha dies at the same time; or when the entire Saṃgha performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to dissolve it.
If it is in an araṇya or within a village where no formal boundary has been established, to what extent is it called a "boundary"?
In an araṇya, it extends for one krośa; in a village, it extends to the walls or fences and their surrounding influence zone; this is termed a "boundary."

When bhikṣus from these two boundaries have assembled together within a space where their hands can reach one another, all formal acts (karmas) may be performed according to their will as described above; those who act in violation of the teachings shall all incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma (vyatikrama).
With palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas;
Regarding this Prātimokṣa for self-discipline, I shall speak—listen well, O virtuous ones.
This verse clarifies the ritual for making offerings.
Regarding the phrase "joining the ten fingers in reverence," it means joining both hands to manifest the gesture of respect.
Generally, there are two ways to make offerings to the Great Master: the first is to pay homage;
[the second is to offer material gifts].
2. Expressing Praise. Joining the palms in reverence is the manner of paying homage; "Śākyasiṃha" (Lion of the Śākyas) is the praise of his virtues.
The term "Śākya" clarifies that during his time as a layman, his clan was noble and eminent, not of low origin.
The term "Lion" signifies that after one has left the household life, all those classes of non-Buddhists who were previously feared and intimidated are struck with terror.

The term "Prātimokṣa" (Individual Liberation) refers to generating reverence for the Dharma of the Great Teacher; when one applies skillful means, it enables liberation from afflictions and delusions, and because it possesses supreme excellence, it is named Prātimokṣa.
Because he is able to subdue sentient beings who are currently entangled by afflictions such as passion and are fully bound by fetters, he is called "the Subduer.
When I say, "Listen well, O virtuous one," I am exhorting you to listen to the Dharma.
Having heard this, one should practice correctly as the Great Sage has taught;
regarding even minor transgressions, one should guard oneself with courage and diligence.
The horse of the mind is difficult to restrain; it must be governed with constant and resolute effort.
The Prātimokṣa is like a bit, with a hundred needles of extreme sharpness.
This verse clearly elucidates the admonition.

Regarding the statement "having heard it, one should practice correctly," this means that after hearing [the teachings], one acts without error; being free from indolence and always diligent and courageous, one is exhorted to practice and abandon all that is unrighteous, just as the Great Sage personally delivered his instructions which are all to be upheld.

The "Great Sage" refers to the Bhagavān; he is called the Great Sage because he is the most venerable and supreme among worldly beings, and because he is superior to the sages who are Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.

Minor offenses refer to those that are prohibitive (pratikṣepaṇa-śīla) rather than natural transgressions (prakṛti-sāvadya). Regarding these minor offenses, one should guard them with vigor and without indolence.
In this context, it is also stated that by analogy one should understand that once natural faults have been restrained, one must likewise apply mindfulness toward the minor offenses.
Regarding the variant reading:

"The valiant should diligently protect," this follows the principle of omitting the particle *api* when summarizing the prevention of natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). This statement is intended to express that one must not be lax or negligent regarding any point of transgression, but should maintain them with the utmost earnestness.
"Sin" refers to base and evil dharmas, because they are objects of disdain and shame for those of superior character.
"Diligent protection" refers to the arousal of vigor within virtuous dharmas.
Regarding "courageous resolve": it refers to the diligent and courageous determination to subdue attachment to various sensory objects, for they are truly fearsome, like a galloping horse.

Regarding "constant continuity": it refers to the uninterrupted racing toward objects that are extremely difficult to restrain when in close proximity. These terms reveal that the mind is a master that is difficult to tame; therefore, one must discipline the mind, for if the mind is well-tamed, body and speech will follow what is correct.

Since afflictions arise from this root of the mind, one should be exhorted solely to focus one's mindfulness on washing them away to achieve thorough purity; one should constantly contemplate impermanence and non-self.
Those who cling to a self as permanent are like space, whose essence is without change; therefore, the principle of severing delusions does not apply to them.
As for the term "bit," it refers to the mouths of those who are unsubdued and violate the precepts; it means applying a bridle to their mouths.
"Truthfulness" (*yathā*) means being in accordance with principle and being well able to distance oneself from the faults of the two extremes: attachment to pleasure and self-inflicted suffering.
Furthermore, it is called "truthful" because it accords with their faculties, inclinations, and dispositions; moreover, "truthful" carries the sense of a metaphorical illustration.

Regarding "those with a hundred needles": this refers to those who have violated the precepts, who in this present life experience various kinds of burning afflictions, remorse, and heartache that are comparable to the pricking of needles.
This is a rough enumeration of the general number, stated here as one hundred.

Regarding the term "extremely beneficial": it is so called because it can sever the causes for future transgressions by cutting them off; thus, two meanings are established regarding the "bit" of the precepts. These are: first, giving rise to remorse in the mind and confessing the committed offense; and second, ensuring that wrong views never arise again.
If a person violates the rules of conduct, they are able to cease immediately upon hearing the teaching;
like a noble steed, such a Great Being shall emerge from the battle array of afflictions.
This verse clarifies the benefit of admonition and instruction.
"Contravention" refers to an offense.
"Rules of conduct" refers to the various training precepts (*śikṣāpada*).
"Being able to desist upon hearing the teaching" means that one is restrained not by means of weapons such as knives or clubs.
The term "Great Being" (mahāsattva) refers to one who has received full ordination (upasampadā).
As for the "noble steed," it refers to a virtuous and wise horse.
Regarding the phrase "one who shall emerge from the battle array of afflictions": the afflictions (kleśa), being difficult to destroy, are likened to a military formation.
The Great Being’s essential resolve is to emerge from birth-and-death; he exerts himself in the cultivation of pure precepts to shatter the army of afflictions.
To say "he shall emerge" means that he shall attain the fruit of Arhatship and so forth.
If a person lacks this bit, they will never find joy;
submerged in the fray of afflictions, they wander deluded through birth and death.
This verse clarifies that the fault of not being cautioned gives rise to suffering.
If a person lacks this bridle, those such as the various non-Buddhists whose minds race toward erroneous objects, as well as those who are addicted to desire, will be muddled by sensual pleasures.

The statement that they "never take delight even in speech" reveals their lack of the nature for *nirvāṇa*; it means they have no heart of love or joy toward the principle of perfect quiescence (*parinirvāṇa*).

Regarding "those who have perished in the battle against afflictions": this refers to those who, due to false teachings, engage in combat with the afflictions; because they lack the bridle of virtue, they are defeated by them, which is termed "perishing in the battle."

Those who wander in delusion through birth and death lack the distinct bit of liberation; thus, they cycle through the five destinies without rescue, turning according to their karma and losing the correct path.
Next, the formal announcement (*jñapti*) is made to inform the assembly:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
Today, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the Saṃgha shall perform the poṣadha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha consent that the Saṃgha now perform the poṣadha and recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
"Thus it is announced.

Regarding the phrase "Venerable Saṃgha, please listen," etc., it is intended so that [the assembly] will not harbor divergent thoughts but will listen with single-minded attention, and so that they may correctly remember and maintain what is heard.
Regarding the term "saṃgha," there are five types:
namely, a group of four, a group of five, a group of ten, a group of twenty, and a group of many.

Among these, as for a saṃgha of four persons, with the exception of the *pravāraṇā* (invitation to point out faults), the *āpattivyutthāna* (expiation of offenses), and the *upasampadā* (full ordination), all other *karmas* (formal acts) may be performed.

Regarding the *pañcavargīya-saṃgha* (a community of five): with the exception of the full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the central region and the formal rehabilitation from an offense (*āpattivyutthāna*), all other [formal acts] should be performed by it.
Regarding the *daśavargīya-saṃgha* (a community of ten): with the exception of the formal rehabilitation from an offense, all other [formal acts] should be performed by it.
Regarding the *saṃgha* of twenty persons and the *saṃgha* of many persons, all [monastic] dharmas are performed by them.

As for the mention of the "fourteenth day," this indicates the time for the *poṣadha*; based on the three seasons of spring, summer, and winter, within each four-month period, one takes the end of the third fortnight and the end of the seventh fortnight—these are always the fourteenth day for the *poṣadha*, while all other days are the fifteenth day.
It should be known that within one year, six months have fourteen days and eighteen months have fifteen days.

Furthermore, during each day of the bright and dark fortnights, the number of days must be announced to the assembly so that all may know it; either the Elder, or the administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*), or another person shall say:
"Venerable sirs!..."

Today is the [day] of the [black/white] fortnight; for the sake of the donor who has established this monastery, the protective deities of the monastery, and the four classes of benefactors, each person shall recite a verse on the merit of giving.
The reason one must perform the confession at this time is twofold:
first, to know the proper time for the *poṣadha*;
second, to prevent laypeople from coming and questioning [the monks].
Furthermore, the calculation of days should follow either the lunar cycle, the constellations, or royal law, according to whether the months and days are long or short.

As for the term *poṣadha*: *poṣa* has the meaning of "nourishing" (*dīrgha-poṣa*), and *dha* has the meaning of "holding" (*dhāraṇa*). It is called *poṣadha* because when the assembly gathers to recite the precepts, they are thereby able to nourish wholesome dharmas and maintain their own minds.
Furthermore, *poṣadha* is as explained before; *dha* has the meaning of "purifying and removing," referring to the increase of wholesome dharmas and the purification and removal of unwholesome ones.
As for the phrase "the time has arrived," it means that it is the time for the *poṣadha*, free from all other obstacles or hindrances.
"Listen" means to ask the assembly of disciples present at that time whether they grant permission.
It does not mean "the Saṃgha should permit," as in "the Saṃgha should permit me to recite the precepts for the assembly."
"To state it thus" means to inform others by referring specifically to the matter at hand.

The reason why the entire assembly does not recite it together is that not everyone is able to memorize and uphold the precepts; furthermore, even if some can recite them, they may not have mastered them thoroughly.
Moreover, from the perspective of the principle of listening to the Dharma, such a practice would be inappropriate.

The reason one does not perform the *poṣadha* by speaking individually within separate rooms is that, in doing so, it would no longer constitute a *poṣadha* for the great assembly; furthermore, gathering together in one place brings greater benefit.
Moreover, performing it individually would entail the fault of some not hearing the True Dharma.
Whenever there is a virtuous bhikṣu who has mastered the recitation of the Prātimokṣa on the day of the Uposatha, one should not have a person under training (śikṣamāṇā) recite it.
Even if there are only four monks at the residence, they should all assemble together; they must not stay apart, nor should they take formal consent (chanda).

If one performs the *poṣadha* (observance of purity) in a crowded *caitya*, or in a layperson’s dwelling, or in an exposed place, or in an impure place, or in a noisy and bustling place, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
There is certainly no other place [where this applies] than these four cases where there is no offense; one must not perform the *poṣadha* in the presence of laypeople.

Furthermore, if one performs the *poṣadha* while sleeping, while in meditative absorption, while begging for food, while attending to bodily needs, or while making offerings, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
At other times, if there are obstacles, being in such a state is not a transgression.

If there is a bhikṣu within the boundary who, being detained by government authorities, does not come to assemble for the poṣadha, he incurs the offense of separate residence (pārivāsika), and the poṣadha is not validly performed.
If one is detained, others should go to the authorities on their behalf to seek his release; if they do not do so, they incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
For a monk who is insane, the "method for the insane" (*unmattaka-vidhi*) should be granted, in order to prevent him from being subject to separate residence (*pārivāsika*).
Whenever bhikṣus reach the day of the poṣadha, they should first carefully examine themselves: "Have I committed any offenses during this half-month?"

If one recalls an offense, one should confess it according to the Dharma. One should go before a pure person, assume the appropriate dignified posture, squat with palms joined, recall the name of the previous offense, and speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me!..."

I, the bhikṣu [name], have committed such-and-such an offense. Regarding this offense committed, I now, before the Venerable One, confess and disclose it all from a state of purity; I do not conceal it.
"By confessing and declaring one's offenses, one attains peace and happiness; by not confessing and declaring one's offenses, one does not attain peace and happiness.
A second and third time, he spoke thus.
He should be asked:
"Do you see your offense?
He should answer:
“I see it. “Will you be able to well protect all the precepts in the future? He replied:
“Very well,” the monk being addressed should reply: “So be it.”
The one confessing the offense should reply, "Virtuous one.

If there is doubt regarding the offense, one should seek a definitive resolution from a master of the Vinaya; once this is known, one should subsequently disclose it. One should confess the offense before a bhikṣu and not before a bhikṣuṇī or others; if one confesses before a bhikṣuṇī or others, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

One should not confess a transgression to another person who has committed a transgression of the same category; that is, a *pārājika* offense is of the same category as a *pārājika*, and so on, up to a *duṣkṛta* offense being of the same category as a *duṣkṛta*.
The term "sabhāga" (having a common portion) means similarity; it refers to those who share the same offense.
If, at the time of the *poṣadha*, one recalls an offense committed, one should then maintain it through mental recollection, saying:
"Today, on the fourteenth day, the Saṃgha performs the *poṣadha* ceremony. I, the bhikṣu [Name], recall an offense within the Saṃgha."
"I, [Name], having taken upon myself the offense committed, shall, after the Sangha has performed the Poṣadha ceremony, confess it according to the Dharma before a pure Bhikṣu.
The same applies by analogy to offenses regarding which one feels doubt.
If the person reciting the precepts remembers or suspects an offense, they should act accordingly in these cases.

If the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense, they should encourage one virtuous bhikṣu to go to another residence, confess and eliminate the offense before a pure person, and then return to the original location; there, all those who have committed offenses shall confess their offenses before this bhikṣu.
If there is no one capable [of acting as a witness], a *jñapti* (sole announcement) may be made as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Today the Saṃgha observes the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day; all members of the Saṃgha have committed offenses. However, not a single person is able to go to another place before a pure bhikṣu to confess their offense according to the Dharma, so that we might confess our offenses before him and thereby purify them."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now perform the Poṣadha; later, when proceeding to another location, the offenses shall be expiated according to the Dharma.
"I declare it thus.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has doubts regarding an offense, he should say:
"I have doubts regarding the offense."
It should be performed according to the preceding procedure.
If among the assembly there is one bhikṣu who is pure and free from offense, that pure bhikṣu should go to a like-minded bhikṣu and speak with a virtuous mind, causing him to remember [the matter].

One should confess one's offense before the bhikṣus, so that when all those present have heard it, they may likewise speak of the transgression; certainly none will remain silent in agreement with it.
If one knows that another bhikṣu is unwilling to confess, yet persistently interrogates him to force a recollection, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmāpatti*).

If one does not know whether the person before one has committed an offense or is innocent, and proceeds to have them confess based on a mere estimation while regarding them as pure, the confession is not validly established.
If one performs the *poṣadha* while harboring the thought or suspicion that they are living separately, they incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).

If one performs the *poṣadha* with the intention of causing schism, this constitutes a preliminary act for breaking the Saṃgha (*saṃghabheda-prayoga*) and incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; they must reunite and perform the *poṣadha* again.

If, at the time of the *poṣadha*, the resident bhikṣus have already performed the *poṣadha* while the number of newly arrived guests is small, they should earnestly seek the harmony of the assembly and perform the *poṣadha* once again.
If they are unwilling to do so, they should go to a small boundary enclosure (*kṣudrasīmā*) and perform the *poṣadha* themselves.
If the number of visiting monks is greater than those of the resident monks, the resident monks should harmonize with them and perform the *poṣadha* once again together.
If the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) has concluded, the time for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation ceremony) is itself termed the *poṣadha* (confession and purification);
there is no further need to perform it separately. Furthermore, a *bhikṣu* and a *bhikṣuṇī* should not perform the *poṣadha* in the same location.
If a bhikṣuṇī comes to request instruction, one should converse with her and must not avoid her.
On each upoṣadha day, the instructor should sit beneath the gatehouse and wait for the bhikṣuṇīs to come and request instruction, making arrangements as the occasion requires.
To say there is a "place of residence" means that in that place there is a person capable of performing the *karmavācanā*.
To say there is no "place of residence" means that in that place there is no person capable of performing the *karmavācanā*.

Regarding the terms "having a place of residence" and "not having a place of residence," this means that one portion [of the community] understands the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual), while another portion does not.
If the location where the bhikṣus reside is suitable for communal living, they should proceed to that place on the day of the *poṣadha* (confession ceremony) to perform the *poṣadha*.
If one goes to a place where there is strife and people are quarreling, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
Even if there is no monastery where monks reside, if there are companions with whom one can dwell happily, it is permissible to go there without fault.
If a difficult situation is imminent, one should depart according to one's inclination.
However, when the day for the Poṣadha ceremony arrives, disciples and attendants must not follow their own inclinations by permitting [the preceptor] to go elsewhere.

If there is no one to recite the precepts at that location, one should go to another place and perform the *poṣadha* (purification) in the presence of those who recite the precepts; if one does not go, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

If one sits where there is no one to recite the *Poṣadha*, one must not let the first *anuvassa* (rainy season retreat) pass beyond the second *poṣadha*; one should instead go to a place where the *Poṣadha* is recited. In all cases, one must not perform the *Poṣadha* recitation in the presence of laypeople.

During the period of the rains retreat (*varṣā*), one should perform the *poṣadha* (confession and purification) together with those who are in agreement, pure, free from transgressions, and share the same view.
If there are monks who are deaf or lack understanding, they may perform the *poṣadha* ceremony in the same location; they shall likewise count toward the required quorum.

If one arrives on the day of the *poṣadha* ceremony alone, one should, at the place where the *poṣadha* is to be held, smear it with fresh cow dung, sweep it, sprinkle water, spread out seats, and strike the wooden gong; having thus completed the preliminary preparations.
Having recited a small portion of the sūtras, he should observe the visiting bhikṣus from a high and distant place.
If three or more have come to perform the *poṣadha* together, or if none have arrived, that bhikṣu should remain in his own seat and, with mental reflection and verbal expression, speak as follows:
"Today is the fourteenth day; it is the *saṃgha-poṣadha*. I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall also perform the *poṣadha* on this fourteenth day."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], declare myself to be completely purified of all obstructing dharmas; I now perform the poṣadha for the sake of maintaining it.
Should I later encounter a harmonious assembly, I shall perform the poṣadha together with that harmonious assembly in order to fulfill the aggregate of precepts.
The second and third times should also be spoken in this manner.
If one or two persons come, they should perform the *poṣadha* face-to-face (*pratimukha*), acting according to the rules for a single person.

If a bhikṣu encounters a village while traveling on the road, or enters a village, or stays outside a village, and it is the day for the Poṣadha ceremony, he should perform the Poṣadha individually for each person.
Those residing within a village must not perform the *poṣadha* separately from the boundaries of the village;
those outside the village should perform the *poṣadha* outside the village boundaries.
If traveling together with a caravan, provided that the caravan members do not object, one should perform the *poṣadha* wherever they stay or wherever they travel.
If others should find fault with this, one should maintain it through mental recollection.
There are six matters for maintaining the *poṣadha* through mental recollection; if maintained thus, all are accomplished without offense:
first, the maintenance of the three robes (*tricīvara*).
2. Relinquishing the three robes;
3. Designating extra robes;
4. Relinquishing special invitations.
5. To perform the *poṣadha*; 6.
To perform the *pravāraṇā*. One ought to perform the *poṣadha*, yet if one does not do so, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
To perform the *poṣadha* (confession and purification) when it is not the proper time is also a transgression of the Dharma.
This excludes the "Auspicious *Poṣadha*," which is performed because the community, having been divided, has regained its harmony and the assembly rejoices in performing the *poṣadha*.

If there is a bhikṣu who was previously subject to the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (the act of suspension) by the Saṃgha, and later obtains release from it, he should request the great assembly to grant him a separate time for the *poṣadha*.
There are five ways of reciting the *Prātimokṣa*:
first, reciting the introduction (*nidāna*), while informing the others that the remainder has been heard regularly.
2. Having finished reciting the introduction along with the *pārājika* rules, the remainder is announced as being "as commonly heard";
3. the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; 4. up to the two *aniyata* rules.
5. Up to the conclusion.
Who should recite the Prātimokṣa?
It is the senior monk (sthavira) within the assembly.
If [the first person] is unable, one should have a second or a third;
or they may take turns in succession, or one may separately invite another person.
If the Elder can recite the introduction (*nidāna*) but the others cannot recite it, the other persons should recite the *pārājika* rules and so forth.
If one who is insane can speak, it also constitutes the recitation of the precepts. "Venerable sirs!
I shall now perform the *poṣadha* and recite the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*."
Venerable sirs, listen attentively and reflect well upon this.
If anyone has committed an offense, they should disclose it; if you have not committed one, remain silent. By your silence, it shall be known that all the venerable ones are pure.
As when questioned otherwise, one answers according to reality, so too now,
within this assembly of superior bhikṣus, even after being asked up to three times, one should answer according to reality.
If a bhikṣu remembers having committed an offense and does not disclose it, he incurs the offense of intentional lying.
Venerable sirs!
The Buddha has declared that intentional lying is an obstructive dharma. Therefore, a bhikṣu who seeks purity should disclose it.
To disclose it brings peace and happiness; not to disclose it brings no peace or happiness.
"Venerable sirs!
I have recited the introduction to the Prātimokṣa Sūtra. Now I ask the venerable sirs: Are you pure in this regard?
Thus he asks three times: "Venerable sirs!"
"In this matter, we are pure, for we remain silent; thus it is now with me.
Next, the exhortation to listen with a sincere mind is clarified.

Regarding the phrase "Venerable Sirs," as the time for reciting the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* approaches, if one does not revere [the teaching], the water of the Dharma will not moisten one's heart; therefore, he exhorts them to collect their minds and not give rise to distraction.
The phrase "listen attentively" generally instructs one to apply the mind.
The phrase "reflect upon it well" specifically clarifies three meanings.

To clarify the three types of listeners, they are compared to three kinds of vessels: namely, those that are turned upward, those that are intact, and those that are clean, as these are capable of containing and utilizing [the teaching].
If [a vessel] is covered, leaking, or foul, it is incapable of receiving things; this should be understood in that order.
Next, the purification of the assembly is explained.
Regarding the phrase "if there is an offense," etc.: if one has previously committed an offense and now remains silent without speaking of it, one incurs further guilt.
Just as one answers truthfully when questioned by others at other times, so it is here.
"I am now among this assembly of superior bhikṣus" praises the congregation listening to the precepts at that time.
Regarding "recollection and knowledge": even if one has committed an offense, if one does not recollect or know it, there is no offense of false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*).
Although one may remain silent and say nothing, such silence is still termed false speech.
Because verbal action is manifested through bodily gestures,
some say: "These are offenses committed solely by the mind."
Regarding these obstructive dharmas, they act as obstacles at two times:
first, in the present life, they obstruct all wholesome dharmas;
second, in the future, they hinder rebirth in the happy realms.
For one who seeks purity, "purity" refers to nirvāṇa.
It is for the sake of seeking nirvāṇa that one speaks of transgressions, and not out of fear of being censured or punished by others.
Regarding the statement that disclosure leads to peace and happiness, there are five aspects:
first, by means of diligent exertion, one remedies all forms of indolence;
second, by means of being free from transgression, one remedies all faults.
Third, by means of reverence, one remedies pride;
fourth, by means of freedom from regret, one remedies remorse;
fifth, by means of tranquility and meditative concentration, one remedies a distracted mind.
Regarding the "Preface to the Precept Sūtra" (*Śīlasūtra-nidāna*): "Sūtra" refers to a concise exposition of meaning.
It is intended to clarify a brief presentation of the characteristics of the precepts and to explain their essential outlines, rather than providing an extensive commentary.
As for the term "preface" (*nidāna*), it signifies a beginning or introductory sequence.
This means that when the precepts are recited, this serves as the prerequisite, enabling the subsequent recitation to arise.
The reason only three questions are posed is to avoid being either too brief or too prolix.
If it were overly concise, those who are dull-witted would find it difficult to understand at once;
if it were overly extensive, I fear it would take too much time and cause the assembly to grow weary.
Nevertheless, for each of the three questions, one incurs a separate offense.
"Upholding" (dhāraṇa) means "to fully comprehend.
*Vinaya-saṃgraha* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume One;
*Vinaya-saṃgraha* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume Two.
The Venerable Jayagupta compiled this work, which the Dharma Master Yijing translated by imperial decree.

This general exposition of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) consists of two parts: the first clarifies the introduction and reveals the origins of the recitation of the precepts; the second describes various categories to identify and explain the training rules.
Furthermore, each individual training rule (*śikṣāpada*) consists of twenty-one sections.
Regarding these twenty-one:
first, the origin (*nidāna*) of the offense;
Second, the person capable of committing the offense;
third, the offense committed;
fourth, the object or circumstance of the offense.
5. The underlying afflictions;
6. The benefits of the established precepts;
7. Transgressions and non-transgressions.
Eight, the completion of the offense through its constituent factors;
nine, the causes for the arising of transgression;
ten, the explanation of the names of the offenses.
11. The essential nature of the expiation of offenses;
12. Whether they are curable or incurable;
13. Whether the offenses possess the nature of prohibitions;
14. Action performed and not performed;
15. The presence or absence of skillful means; 16. Grave offenses.
Seventeen, light offenses;
eighteen, mutual non-differentiation;
nineteen, differences in the expiation of offenses.
Twenty: With defilement and without defilement;
Twenty-one: The origins of committing offenses.

Regarding the "place where the origin of an offense occurs," this refers to a specific country or city where a particular training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established; that very location is termed the place where the origin of the offense occurs.
Regarding the term "person who has committed an offense," it refers to the individual on whose account a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established.
Regarding the term "the offense committed," it refers to the transgression produced by means of body and speech.
Regarding the objects and matters of the offenses, there are generally two types:

sentient and non-sentient. These should be examined and reflected upon as they apply within each individual precept; to summarize, there are sixty-five matters, namely: matters of sexual defilement, matters of appropriation, matters of intolerance, matters of seeking profit, matters of dwellings, matters concerning fellow practitioners of the holy life (*sabrahmacārin*), matters concerning the Saṃgha, matters of using base things, matters of using requisites, and matters concerning female lay disciples (*upāsikā*).

The ten matters concerning extra robes (*atireka-cīvara*): the matter of being apart from one's robe, the matter of anticipating the completion [of the robe season], the matter of seeking [robes] due to a cause, the matter of accepting impure wealth, the matter of bedding and furniture, the matter of traveling on a journey, the matter of possessing alms bowls, the matter of seeking fine things, and the matter of taking robes.

Twenty matters: the matter of receiving robes, the matter of storing robes, the matter of robes, the matter of diverting another's property, the matter of requisites for medicinal needs during illness, the matter of contravening the mind, the matter of going forth, the matter of disciples, the matter of instigating disputes, and the matter of preaching the Dharma.

The thirty matters: the matter of one under thirty years of age not having received full ordination; the matter of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra; the matter of destroying seeds; the matter of the village of spirits; the matter of contemptuous disparagement; the matter of causing distress; the matter of using water; the matter concerning bhikṣuṇīs; the matter of eating; and the matter of visiting householders.

The forty matters concerning non-Buddhist practitioners; observing military affairs; forming alliances; using fire; granting consent (*chanda*); sleeping and lying down; failing to examine carefully; dyeing robes; following one's own whims; and the matter of animals.

The fifty matters concerning jesting, matters concerning women, matters concerning full ordination (*upasampadā*), matters concerning the destruction of ground, matters concerning repeated invitations, matters concerning minor training rules (*śikṣāpada*), matters concerning censure, matters concerning disputes, matters concerning accepting invitations, and matters concerning entering a village.
The sixty matters concerning the needle-case, the dimensions of the bed, the dimensions of the robes, the formal procedures, and the interrogation.
Regarding the sixty-five points concerning the origins of affliction, there are two types:
first, those that are innate (*sahaja*); second, those that arise from conditions (*pratyaya-ja*).

The various types of karma created according to the mind differ, as do the afflictions (*kleśa*); these are explained according to their respective matters within the training rules (*śikṣāpada*). There are twenty-seven kinds, namely:

the affliction of greed, the affliction of hatred, the affliction of delusion, the affliction of lust, the affliction of grasping, the affliction of intolerance, the affliction of seeking gain and offerings, and the affliction of contention and resentment.
The affliction of dwelling places; the affliction of base actions; the affliction of false wisdom; the affliction of stinginess regarding one's home;
the affliction of seeking mastery; the affliction of transgressing limits; the affliction of neglect and deficiency; the affliction of depending on conditions;
the affliction of reproach and suspicion; the affliction of concealment; and the section on appropriation.
The affliction of mere vexation; the affliction of arrogance toward the Dharma; the affliction of lack of compassion; the affliction of contemptuous disparagement; the affliction of a frivolous mind;
the affliction of failure to acknowledge and rectify faults; the affliction of lack of tranquility; the affliction of disrespect;
and the affliction of intolerance toward the censure of others.
Regarding the benefits of establishing the precepts: it means that the Great Teacher, the Buddha, observed ten advantages and thereby established the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
As for what constitutes an offense and what does not: if one intentionally violates a precept, it is called an offense; otherwise, there is no offense.

Regarding the phrase "the offense is established through the completion of constituent factors": for each training rule (*śikṣāpada*), an offense is only established when all the constituent conditions are fulfilled.
Regarding the phrase "the causes that give rise to transgressions," there are six types:
first, those arising from the body; [and so forth].
2. by speech; 3. by mind; 4. by both body and mind.
5. By means of speech and mind;
6. By means of body, speech, and mind.
Regarding the explanation of the names: this refers to the different designations such as *pārājika* and so forth, which will be explained in detail below.
Regarding the essence of the offense: in general, all committed offenses have as their essence the intentional engagement of body and speech.
"Those who may be disciplined" refers to those undergoing training (*śikṣamāṇa*).
"Those who cannot be disciplined" refers to those characterized by a lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*).
"Nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to that which is inherently sinful; "prohibition" (*pratikṣepa*) refers to that which arises only because of a specific regulation.
Furthermore, another explanation states:
"Natural sins (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are committed only within a defiled mind, whereas prohibited sins (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*) apply to both defiled and non-defiled minds."
Regarding the terms "acting" and "not acting": "acting" refers to performing an action with one's own body or speech; "not acting" refers to accomplishing a matter through restraint.
Therefore, to act intentionally is called "having the means," while to commit an offense unintentionally is called "lacking the means."
Regarding what are called "grave offenses," there are six distinct characteristics within them:
first, by way of the formal precept;
second, by way of the objective act.
Third, by reason of afflictions;
fourth, by reason of transgressions;
fifth, by reason of persons.
Sixth, by way of time.
Regarding "by way of prohibition," this means that because the World-Honored One has established a training rule (*śikṣāpada*), there is a grave offense.

Regarding "by way of the matter," for example, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for taking the life of an animal; even among the offenses of the communal instruction (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*), it cannot exceed this.
Regarding "by way of affliction," it means that because it arises from afflictions such as disrespect for the teachings, it is grave.
Regarding "by way of transgression," it means that because one repeatedly commits the offense, it is grave.
Regarding "by way of the person," it means that because one has not planted roots of goodness and is by nature dull-witted, the offense consequently becomes grave.

Regarding the factor of time: it means that if one conceals the offense for a long duration, it becomes grave; this is like a small amount of water which, when dammed by an object and allowed to stagnate for a long time, forms great waves. Conversely, if the opposite of the aforementioned six factors is the case, it is considered light.

Regarding the statement that "the common characteristics are without difference," this means that both the positive injunctions and prohibitions of the training rules (śikṣāpada) all share the body, speech, and mind as their common characteristics.
Regarding the statement that "there are differences in the expiation of offenses," there are four types:
first, those from which one is exonerated only through extremely severe disciplinary measures, namely the *pārājika* offenses;
2. By means of intermediate punishment, namely the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
3. By means of minor punishment, namely the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
4. Without punishment, namely the remaining offenses.
"Being defiled" means having greed and so forth as its cause; "being undefiled" is the opposite of this.
Regarding the reasons for committing an offense, there are five causes by which one commits an offense:
first, due to a lack of shame.
Second, due to a lack of respect for instruction;
third, due to a disposition toward negligence;
fourth, due to an inherently dull and obtuse nature.
V. Due to the loss of right mindfulness.
Part One: The Four Pārājika Dharmas. First of the Four Pārājika Dharmas in Part One. A summary verse says:
If one commits an impure act, takes what is not given, or kills a human being, [one is defeated].
