3. The Training Rule on Taking Human Life. The Third Section: The Remainder of the Four Pārājika Dharmas. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in the country of Kaliṅga. Then, the bhikṣus heard the Buddha teach the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Having practiced it, they developed a profound sense of revulsion toward the body, which is like a mass of pus and blood. Consequently, they sought out the heretical śramaṇa Mṛgāra to have their lives taken, and they also killed one another.

All acts of killing arise from an inability to endure circumstances or an inability to endure afflictions, resulting in the severing of another’s life-faculty; therefore, this training rule is established:

"If a bhikṣu, whether it be a human being or a human fetus, intentionally takes its life with his own hand, or provides a weapon, or wields a weapon himself, or seeks one who wields a weapon, or encourages death, or praises death, saying: 'Ho, man!'"
"What use is this burdened, impure, and evil life?
You would be better off dead now; death is superior to life.
Thus, according to his own thoughts, he used various words to exhort and praise [the person], urging them toward death.
If that person dies because of it, this bhikṣu also incurs a pārājika offense and shall not live in community with others.
This constitutes an offense when, based on a human being as the object, with the intent to kill, the perception of a human being, and the employment of means to take life, the life is ended.
In this context, "object" refers to humans and human fetuses.
A "human" is one whose six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are fully developed.

A "human fetus" is one that has entered the mother's womb and possesses the faculties of body, life, and mind; by virtue of this, it is subsumed within the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) of humans.
Whether female, male, or *paṇḍaka*, and whether their physical faculties are complete or incomplete, all constitute the object of killing.
The term "intentionally" (*saṃcintya*) indicates that the taking of another's life was not due to error.
The object must be a human being, and the intention must correspond to that object. There are two types of preliminary effort (*upakrama*): [text continues].
This refers to the body and speech.
Regarding the body: it means committing killing with one's hands and so forth;
or providing a weapon, such as when one knows another intends to commit suicide and thus places a knife or similar instrument nearby.
"Or holding a knife oneself" means that, perceiving one's own lack of strength, one merely grasps a knife and causes another bystander to assist by supporting the hand while committing the killing;
or it means requesting another person to hold a knife and kill.
Speech refers to acts such as exhorting or praising others with the intent to cause them to die; if they do not wish to die, one exhorts and persuades them to do so.
If they desire death, one praises it, saying:
"What use is this burden of sin and the like?"
This means it is said:
"While life exists, transgressions are heavy; after death, blessings are many.
As for the term "impure," it refers to being accomplished by relying upon the impure.
They are called those who live impure and wicked lives because they are abandoned by superior persons.
Their statement that "death is better than life" is intended to cause others to rejoice.
Following their own mental inclinations, they think: "By encouraging another to die, I shall acquire merit."
Regarding "by other words": this does not refer only to what has been stated here, but further refers to exhorting and praising [suicide] by means of other expressions.

To say "he died because of that" clarifies that it was not due to any other matter; rather, by exhorting someone to death and thereby causing the life of another to be cut off, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If the person does not die, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one first employs skillful means to dispatch another person to death, but later gives rise to a remorseful mind and does not desire their death, then even though the person dies, one incurs only a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Regarding the statement that "taking life constitutes an offense," this refers to cases where death results from such an act.

Regarding the offenses herein: it refers to a bhikṣu who, by means of his own body or external objects such as bricks, or by using both together like a sword, or by means of poison, or by setting traps and pits, or by providing various liquors and other drugs to cause mental derangement, or by performing incantations to induce delusion, or by setting mechanical devices, or by pushing someone off a precipice, a moat, a tower, a pavilion, or any dangerous place, or by employing deceptive means to send another toward fire, water, or other fearful and perilous locations, or by leaving someone in the open air on a cold night to freeze.
If a woman, a man, or a *śaṇḍha* (eunuch), etc., perceives them as being alive, or conceives doubt, yet initiates the means of harm and thereby causes death, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense;
if they do not die, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
One may raise a whole corpse or a half-corpse to cause harm to a living being; the gravity of the offense incurred should be understood as corresponding to the nature of the object harmed.
There is a distinction here: if those two [corpses] instead harm a bhikṣu, one incurs a sthūlātyaya due to the prior preparatory effort.
If a bhikṣu harms that corpse-demon, he incurs two grave offenses (sthūlātyaya).
If he harms a manifested form, he likewise incurs a grave offense.
If he has no intent to harm the mother but intends to kill the fetus, and by trampling the mother’s womb the fetus dies while the mother does not, he incurs a pārājika offense.
If the mother dies but the fetus does not, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; if both die, it is a *pārājika*;
if neither dies, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
It should be understood in this way: if one has the intent to kill the mother and not the fetus, it may be recognized by analogy with what precedes.
If there is a fetus of an animal or a non-human being in a human woman’s womb, one who intentionally causes an abortion incurs a grave offense (sthūlātyaya).
If one knows that there is a human fetus within the womb of an animal, or knows that a human being has transformed into an animal, one incurs the full offense when taking its life.
If one transforms one's own body into the form of an animal and harms another person while perceiving them to be a bhikṣu, one likewise incurs the full offense.
If one intends to harm another person but mistakenly harms one's father, mother, or an arhat, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is because there was no intent to kill the father and so forth;
likewise, it applies when one perceives a non-arhat as an arhat, or an arhat as a non-arhat, and the same holds true for one's parents.
If one employs the means of killing toward one's mother or others, yet dies before them, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) in both cases.
If a woman miscarries and another woman picks up the fetus and places it in her own womb, if one kills the latter woman, the *ānantarya* (heinous) offense is not incurred;
however, when she goes forth into the religious life, she should ask the latter woman [for permission].
If one perceives a human being as a human, or harbors doubt regarding it, one incurs the full offense.
If one kills a non-human being while perceiving them as a human or doubting their status, one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
If one perceives a human being as an animal, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If one perceives [the victim] as a non-human being, one also incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
When a sentient being is being pursued, if a bhikṣu sees them and informs another with the intent to kill, he commits an offense according to the specific circumstances of the act.
If, among a large group of people, he harbors malice toward one but mistakenly kills another, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
In a state of neutral mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), one incurs only the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If one strikes another with a mind of mere playfulness and, as a result, causes death, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.

If the preparatory effort was initiated before full ordination (*upasampadā*) and the person only dies after having been fully ordained, the two sets of four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be applied accordingly, as previously described.
If one employs skillful means and dispatches an agent to commit a killing, even if the agent subsequently changes gender to become a bhikṣuṇī, the perpetrator still incurs the fundamental offense.
If two sexual organs arise [in the victim], the perpetrator incurs the preceding grave offense (sthūlātyaya).
To retreat and become a *śrāmaṇera* (novice) also constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
The subsequent rules of training should be understood according to their respective cases; there is no need for further elaboration here.

If one sees sentient beings being swept away by water, burned by fire, or oppressed by thirst, and does not take them by hand or give them water; or if one sees someone about to die who can be saved if one has the strength to do so, yet fails to rescue them—either because they do not wish to die or because one adopts an attitude of indifference (*upekṣā*)—if that person subsequently dies, in all such cases one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (*duṣkṛta*).
If a person is harmed by another and dies as a direct result of that cause, one incurs a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) for killing if the victim's life was not yet at its end;
if death was not certain, one incurs a defeat offense (pārājika).

If one encounters an urgent danger and flees for one's own life, and in doing so, with no feeling of compassion, pushes or strikes another person but lacks the intent to kill them: if the other person dies, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense);
if they do not die, it is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If, however, there is the intent to kill, one incurs the root offense (*mūlāpatti*).
Those who have left the household life out of reverence for the Dharma preserve their lives in pursuit of liberation; if one commits suicide, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

However, if one originally lacked the intent to kill and strikes a wall or similar object, and a person is killed by mistake due to that action; or if one moves a patient against their wishes, or the patient dies as a result of medical treatment, in all such cases there is no offense.

If one has no intention to kill the patient, yet the words spoken cause them to desire death; or if one holds a knife or a rope without careful consideration and places it near the patient; or if one places poison—these all constitute a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

One who lacks wisdom should not be entrusted with attending to the sick; however, if there is an urgent matter that necessitates care, one should provide thorough instructions and ensure they maintain the utmost attentiveness.
The patient should say:
"Do not help me to rise."
If one forcibly supports another to make them rise, and that person dies as a result, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

One should understand that other modes of conduct are to be treated in the same manner; for instance, when carrying a sick person along a road, it should be understood according to this same principle.
He told the sick person, "Wash first before you get up. Consequently, the person passed away.

Although there was no offense in this case, one should not carry a seriously ill person away together in a litter; while there is no offense if death results from such an act, one likewise should not carry them away in haste or recklessly.
Or, while tending to the sick, one may feel weary and exhausted; or harbor ill intentions, hoping for the patient's wealth; or utter words of anger, saying:
"Let them die as they please; I will not tend to them."
If one causes death as a result [of such actions], one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense in all cases.
If suitable food is available but one gives that which is unsuitable, the caregiver also incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
however, if no other food is obtainable, there is no offense.
If one dies from an unripened abscess [after being lanced], it constitutes a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*);
if it was a ripened abscess, there is no offense.
It is not a transgression to lance it with a knife or a needle; however, if one is not skilled in medicine beforehand, one should not perform such lancing.
If one uses a blade to perform surgery for oral ailments, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
however, there is no offense if one performs the incision because no physician can be found.
One who suffers from hemorrhoids should not undergo surgical excision; rather, they should eliminate the condition through the application of medicine, mantras, and skillful means.
Whenever treating an illness, one should consult a physician;
if no physician is available, one should consult a bhikṣu who understands medicine;
if there is no such person, one should consult someone who has previously suffered from that same illness.
One who has never been ill should consult senior practitioners before hastily administering medicine; to do so would constitute a transgression of the Dharma.

If one understands medicine and others come to seek counsel, one should give rise to a compassionate mind and bestow prescriptions and remedies; provided there is no intention to seek profit, there is no offense.
However, to do so for the sake of seeking profit is improper.
If one observes a wound or injury, one should bandage it in a secluded place so as not to allow laypeople to see and deride one's medical skill.
One should not abandon another to whom one has administered a purgative; however, there is no offense if one departs after having properly instructed them on what is appropriate.
Seeing another bhikṣu who was ill and about to die, he did not attend to his own robes and bowl; thinking, "When he passes away, I shall rightfully obtain all his clothing and property."
This is the intent of a caṇḍāla; one incurs a transgression against the Dharma.
Furthermore, one should not administer medicine to others with the intent to kill, but should instead cultivate a benevolent mind wishing for the illness to be cured.
If one sees another administering medicine with the intent to cause an abortion and fails to intervene to prevent it, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (dharmātikrama).
When a bhikṣu walks with his head bowed and accidentally kills someone before him without intention, there is no offense.

One should not walk with the face cast downward while harboring a mind of malice or affliction; this constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense, and if done with the intent to kill, it is a grave transgression (*pārājika*).
If a bhikṣu on the road is afflicted by the suffering of illness, he should not be carried on a stretcher, but must instead breathe regularly.
If the patient has personal requisites, one should carry them on his behalf; he should proceed in such a way that he arrives there by the time of the meal.

If he fears arriving late, he should go ahead himself, enter the monastery, wash his bowl, and arrange his seat. He should then request food on behalf of the patient and wait for him, or he may meet the patient on the road carrying the food.
If one does not act thus, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
In general, one must not give vinegar to a person who has been wounded. If one sees another choking on food and strikes them out of compassion, there is no offense even if they die as a result.
When striking with a mallet, one should exercise mindfulness.
One should ask the patient:
"Where shall we seek the medicine?"
One should seek out materials as instructed to provide for them.
When performing construction work, if a brick thrown by a bhikṣu should injure another bhikṣu’s head and cause his death, there is no offense.
In all cases of transporting bricks and the like, one should hand them from hand to hand; one must not throw them from a distance so that they break.
There will certainly be tearing or bursting; inform [the recipient] before handing it over.
When ascending a ladder or working while on top of it, one should tie the lower garment so as not to expose the body; at other times, the garment need not be tied.
Whenever construction work is undertaken, bhikṣus should assist; they should work for a single session and not all day long.

If it is during the spring season, they should work before midday; if it is during the winter months, they should work after midday. They should anticipate the time and cease their tasks so that those who go on almsround may wash their hands and feet, and so that those traveling between villages do not miss the proper time for a meal.

If there are monks who are constantly free from the toil of begging for alms, the administrative officers (vaiyāvṛtyakara) should provide them with well-prepared food and drink using other resources; the meal thus provided is called "pleasing food" (manāpa-bhakta).
If the Saṃgha is impoverished, one should exhort and convert others to provide timely offerings, whether as light meals, non-time beverages, or oil for anointing the hands and feet.
If one does not do so, the person in charge incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.

If a bhikṣu lifts a heavy object and, when his strength fails, lets go, thereby killing a craftsman, he commits no offense; however, one should not lift a heavy burden by oneself. If it must be moved, a layperson must be interposed between the lifter and the load. One should lift and lower [the object] simultaneously; if one lets go without looking after the other, one incurs an offense.
Ordinary people may carry one load, while bhikṣus may carry two; if it exceeds this, they should not lift or bear it.
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs should not hold objects upon their heads or on the tops of their shoulders; if they do so, they incur a duṣkṛta offense.

If bandits should come, you should manifest fear and alarm, display gestures of shouting and rebuking, and cast away jars, pots, pestles, wooden clubs, and the like—whether they be near your person or behind you—without giving rise to any intent to harm or causing them injury.

Whenever discarding objects, one should cause others to move far away; if someone is struck, although there is no offense for this, if one discards them without giving notice, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If a cow, startled by something, runs off and accidentally pushes over a child, resulting in the child's death, there is no offense as it was not intentional.
One must apply careful mindfulness when avoiding cattle.
If one binds a person with ropes, or reports them to the authorities so that their hands or feet are severed, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one calls upon others to dwell together in a place where tigers and wolves are present, there is no offense if they are subsequently killed or wounded.
Nevertheless, one should carefully examine the dwelling place.
When a bhikṣu struck his own genitals, the Buddha said:
"It is proper to strike this one and then strike others; those who lack wisdom commit the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

The venerable Udayin sat down negligently in the house of a layperson; failing to observe carefully, he crushed another's child. Whenever one sits down without looking, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

4. The Training Rule on Falsely Claiming to Have Attained Superhuman Qualities. The fourth training rule concerning falsely claiming to have attained superhuman qualities was established when the Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī by the side of the Markaṭahrada River. At that time, some bhikṣus, for the sake of food and drink, praised one another before their relatives, falsely claiming to have attained superhuman qualities.
Desiring that the assembly know [the truth] regarding the pursuit of gain and the afflictions of seeking profit, this training rule was established:

"If a bhikṣu, being actually without knowledge and without thorough understanding, and knowing for himself that he has not attained the state of a superior person—the peaceful, noble, and sublime realization, wisdom, vision, and dwelling in bliss—should nevertheless say: 'I know; I see.'"
At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, desiring to purify himself, he speaks thus: "Venerable sirs!
It is true that I neither knew nor saw, yet I said that I knew and that I saw."
"Deceptive and false speech.
With the exception of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), this bhikṣu also incurs a *pārājika* offense and should not be lived with.
"Ignorance" refers to the lack of understanding regarding the objects of knowledge, such as impermanence and the nature of what is to be reviled.
Lack of thorough knowledge means that regarding the presence or absence of impermanence and so forth in an object, one does not examine it thoroughly according to its actual state;
thus, being unable to know reality as it is regarding what exists or does not exist, one falsely produces erroneous explanations and speaks of what is not the Dharma.
Furthermore, "lacking knowledge" means that one has never known the qualities of a superior person (*uttara-pudgala*).
"Lacking pervasive knowledge" means that one is unable to fully comprehend the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
"Knowing for oneself that [the goal] is not attained" means that one knows for oneself that [realization] has not yet been realized within one's own being.

The "Dharma of Superior Persons" refers to the Dharma of the Victorious Stream; that is to say, in comparison to all the base, inferior, and evil phenomena such as the five hindrances of ordinary fools, it is superior and preeminent.
"Quiescence" refers to that which is most sublime.
"Noble One" (ārya) refers to one who is able to distance themselves from and avoid unwholesome dharmas.
"Exalted realization" refers to that which is attained not through physical strength or intellectual cleverness, but by other means.
Another explanation states:
"Quiescence" refers to *nirvāṇa*, because it is free from all afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Exalted realization" refers to the noble ones (*ārya*) of the four fruits.

Regarding the terms "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "vision" (*darśana*): these correspond respectively to the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).
Furthermore, another explanation states:
"Knowledge refers to the thorough understanding of [the truths] such as suffering and impermanence; vision refers to seeing [beings] such as devas and nāgas."
"Abiding in peace and happiness" means being able to dwell securely in all the virtues inherent within the various meditative stages (*samāpatti-bhūmi*).
"I know" refers to knowing the principles of the Truths (*satya*) and so forth.
As for "I see," it refers to seeing the various devas and so forth.
If one has previously committed the offense of lying, even if one does not speak of it oneself, how could one possibly avoid committing a *pārājika* offense?
Why is it necessary to state the phrase "at another time" and so forth?

Even if one has committed a transgression of the precepts and the offense itself is established as a full guilt (*mūlāpatti*) without needing to confess it, others may merely harbor doubts regarding that person and cannot yet treat them as one who is not in communal residence (*asāṃvāsika*). Therefore, the phrase "at another time" and so forth must be present for the status of non-communal residence to be fully established.
If it is "questioned," it refers to speaking in response to another's inquiry;
if it is "not questioned," it refers to speaking of the three grave offenses (tīrthika-crimes) without being asked.
Since there is no difference in principle [between these two cases], why is it that the discussion of "questioning" and so forth is presented specifically within the section on falsehood?
If one relies on the preceding three [cases], this matter also exists;
however, it is mentioned only here because it pertains specifically to dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
The term "false" (*mṛṣā*) indicates that what is stated therein lacks any real meaning.
A deceiver is one whose original resolve was to seek food and drink, yet makes such false statements for the sake of some superior purpose.
A liar is one who first gives rise to a deceitful mind and then articulates what is said.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu says, "I have seen devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, pūtanas, piśācas, kumbhāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas."
"I approached him at that time, or heard his voice, or he came to me, and we conversed together"—
thus, conceiving a false notion, he informs the person before him.
If he understands [the meaning], he incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If he says that he slandered him by claiming he had engaged in such acts with a *sūpiśāca* demon, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one says: "I have already attained twenty kinds of perceptions: namely, the perception of impermanence; the perception of suffering in what is impermanent;

the perception of emptiness in what is suffering; the perception of non-self in what is empty; the perception of revulsion toward food; the perception of lack of delight in all worldly things; the perception of danger; the perception of abandonment; the perception of dispassion; the perception of cessation; the perception of death; the perception of impurity; the perception of a livid corpse; the perception of a bloated corpse; the perception of a festering corpse; the perception of a worm-infested corpse; the perception of a blood-smeared corpse; the perception of a scattered corpse; the perception of a bleached-bone corpse; and the perception of contemplating emptiness."
When each of these is spoken, one incurs the original offense.
Or, one might say:
"I have attained the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, the four immeasurables, and the six supernormal powers."
Furthermore, those forest-dwelling bhikṣus who are not troubled by non-human spirits are indeed noble ones;
even when I dwell among them, I am not troubled.
Moreover, in their dwellings, if a noble one sits upon an excellent and sublime seat, I too shall accept that excellent and sublime seat.
"All such [cases] constitute an offense of *pārājika*.
As for the statement, 'When I was in right mindfulness, I attained the specific characteristics of dharmas and suppressed the afflictions,' this constitutes a grave offense."
"I have regressed from the three fruits before attaining them, or I have regressed after attaining them"—this may be a cryptic expression meaning: "I am a learner (*śaikṣa*), for I study the Vinaya;
I am one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), for I have mastered the Tripiṭaka;
I have attained 'nothingness,' for I possess no extra robes or alms bowl."
I am one in my final birth, speaking in relation to previous births;
I am a stream-enterer, having entered the river of the Dharma;
I have attained the fruit, meaning I have attained the fruit of recitation, or I have attained the *āmra* fruit.
I am free from the five fears because I have no fear regarding the past;
I have severed the afflictions because I have no delusion regarding the past;
and I have already attained that which is to be obtained by the Buddha’s assembly of śrāvakas—namely, the teachings of the Āgamas and so forth, as well as the thorough cultivation of the faculties.
I am the Great Teacher because I explain the Dharma;
I am the Buddha because I have well awakened to evil matters;
I am a śrāvaka disciple of the Buddha Vipaśyin because I have taken complete refuge in all Buddhas.
When speaking such words, if one harbors deceitful intentions and speaks with artifice or secrecy, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one speaks without ulterior motive exactly as stated, saying,
"I have attained the state of a superior person" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), one incurs the primary offense (*mūla-āpatti*).
Some say: "I have attained the state of stream-entry, yet it is not that fruit. Others say:
"In whichever house they are all sages, I am in that same house, yet I am not a sage.
However, since all those sages receive robes from there, I too receive robes, though I am not of their kind."
If others say that I have attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), I truly have not; they speak of other fruits and so forth.
One should understand it in this same way:
"Today I have not attained worldly concentration (*laukika-samādhi*), nor have I yet attained the supramundane sublime concentration (*lokottara-praṇīta-samādhi*) beyond it."
"I have attained the first dhyāna at such-and-such a place, yet it is truly not associated with the factors of enlightenment.
He then wrote his own name, saying:
"I have attained the fruit of the Path."
He then replied to him, saying,
"The scribe who wrote this said that I have attained the fruit of sainthood.
Those who say such things all incur a sthūlātyaya offense.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, as previously described,

commits a pārājika offense by employing various means to manifest himself as possessing extraordinary virtues, claiming that there are bhikṣus who have attained such fruits, seen celestial beings, or achieved superior meditative concentrations;
yet he does not say, "I am that very person."
When speaking such words, they all constitute a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*) and result in a *sātisāra* matter; it is said that all are *duṣkṛta*.
If the person before one does not understand the speech, the gravity of the offense is determined accordingly.
"If you are a sage, you should take this seat. He then remained silent, accepting the invitation.
The other asked him, "Are you a brāhmaṇa?"
He replied: "Because I am able to eliminate all transgressions;
or because I am well-restrained regarding the six sense faculties."
"If he is an Arhat, he should accept and eat the food.
If he accepts it in silence, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense; the same should be stated for cases involving going away, returning, and so forth.
Furthermore, another commentary states:
"When one expresses the matter at hand through bodily gestures, and remains silent when questioned, one incurs the offense of *parājika*.
If one perceives the person as such, or harbors doubt regarding them, one incurs the full offense (*mūlāpatti*) at the moment the other understands."
When speaking to a non-human being while perceiving them as a human or harboring doubt about it, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Likewise, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense if one speaks in haste when there is no person present but one perceives a person to be there; or when one is in a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*); or when the other person is asleep; or when one is speaking to someone who is ignorant; or when the other person does not understand what is being said.

There is no offense in cases such as when the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana prophesied the victory of the Vaiśālī army, or prophesied the falling rain and the birth of a son, or entered the *ākiṃcanyāyatana* concentration and heard the sound of the elephant king; in all such instances, there is no offense.

For what reason are the first three *pārājika* offenses taught in the order of sexual misconduct followed by killing and then matricide (and so forth), rather than following the sequence of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying as found elsewhere?
This is explained according to the chronological order in which these transgressions occur.
Furthermore, they are arranged in sequence because each preceding factor induces the succeeding one:
through unwholesome conduct, one proceeds to theft; having committed theft, one then kills an enemy; and when questioned after the killing, one utters false speech.
Furthermore, whichever affliction is most powerful is to be restrained first.
What are the characteristics of these four defeats (*pārājika*)?
They are lack of disenchantment, lack of forbearance, and lack of realization; however, among these, lack of disenchantment being the most powerful, it is established as the first two.
First, regarding sexual desire;
second, because of intolerance toward wealth, one commits killing and tells falsehoods for the sake of gain.
"Venerable sirs!..."

I have already explained the four *pārājika* dharmas; if a bhikṣu commits any one of these offenses, he shall not dwell together with the other bhikṣus. As it was before, so it is after: having incurred a *pārājika* offense, he should not dwell in communion.
Regarding the phrase "O Venerable Ones," this is intended to clarify the four *pārājika* dharmas; if one commits even one of them, it is not permissible to dwell together [with the Sangha].
Question:
"The former individual was a layperson and lacked the status of a bhikṣu; when he later commits a transgression, is his physical nature different from that of the former layperson?"

Answer: "Just as he was previously a layperson and not a bhikṣu, so too when he later commits a transgression, it is no different from before; therefore it is said, 'as it was before, so it is afterward.'"
It is not that one looks for [the offenses] among the four *pārājika* [offenses], as it was said regarding "before and after.
The concluding text follows the above; one should know that the resulting offense is as previously stated.
**The Second Section: Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas** **The First of the Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas of the Second Section** A summary verse says:
Emission, touching, disparaging, offerings, and matchmaking; Small rooms, large monasteries, and slandering;

1. The Training Rule on Intentionally Ejecting Semen (Śukravisṛṣṭi-śikṣāpada). The first training rule, on intentionally ejecting semen: When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Udāyin, out of a defiled mind, manually stimulated his organ and emitted impurity. Based on this matter of sexual misconduct and the underlying affliction of lust, the Blessed One established this training rule.
"If a bhikṣu intentionally emits semen, except in a dream, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The four subsequent precepts are all likewise. This first training rule lacks the objective condition of a female; although that specific object is absent, one still experiences pleasure.
The next two training rules refer to performing preliminary preparations through body and speech.
The fourth involves contriving deceptive means to seek sensual pleasure.
The fifth involves performing preparatory acts for the sexual misconduct of others.
There are five kinds of semen:
that of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) and his consecrated crown prince is blue; that of other sons is yellow.
That of a Wheel-Turning King’s minister is red. It is thick when the organ is fully developed and thin when it is not yet developed; this is stated according to their inherent nature.
If one is injured by a woman, or damaged by other circumstances, these five kinds of semen may occur in a single person.
Regarding the phrase "excepting in dreams," this means that apart from dreaming, one incurs an offense in all other cases.
Although there is consciousness within a dream, no fixed, real entity can be found therein; therefore, one does not rely on this to clarify an offense.
Even if one has a mind of emission during the waking state, the emission that occurs in the dream is not a primary offense.
Regarding the term *saṃghāvaśeṣa*: first, the matter depends upon the community;
second, its nature is residual, as it can only be removed through the community, indicating that it is not a primary grave offense.
The *saṃgha* is the assembly, and *āpatti-śeṣa* (remainder) is the instruction; it is only through following the instructions of the assembly that the offense is extinguished.
Furthermore, while the substance of the first four precepts is "without remainder" (*anavaśeṣa*), this one is "with remainder" (*sāvaśeṣa*) because it can be remediated.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, for the sake of pleasure, or for medicine and the like, or desiring to test his strength, causes impurity to flow from his own internal body or from an external sentient being, he incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Other texts state that even if the object is an external thing not classified as a sentient being, emitting semen constitutes an offense of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* class.
If one applies the means—whether by grasping or squeezing—with the intention of experiencing pleasure and desiring to emit semen, if it is emitted, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not emitted, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one employs preparatory effort while awake and then discharges [semen] in a dream; or conversely, forms a mental intention for pleasure;
or initiates preparatory effort first and later ceases the mental intent;
or performs preparatory effort such that as the semen is about to move, one immediately restrains the mind—in all these cases, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).

Regarding the statement "about to move," this means that although the semen has not yet departed from its original location, it is immediately prior to the flow of the impurity; even though the semen has not yet flowed, there is already a state of transformation.
Regarding those instances where [the emission] occurs within the body and is discharged: this refers to when the semen has already moved and departed from its original location.

Whether it be through intentional dancing or music, shaking the body in the air, striking or pounding, massaging or pressing, rubbing with medicine to relieve itching, causing the organ to flow upward against its natural direction, rubbing against a woolen rug, or against stones, wood, jars, and the like, or intentionally discharging impurity upon a mass of flesh—in all such cases, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If there is no discharge, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense in every instance.
If one discharges [semen] from the head, neck, ears, nose, or other parts of the body, or from a place where it is blue-swollen and oozing with pus, it constitutes the fundamental offense.
To what extent is it defined as "discharging impurity"?
This refers to the emission from within the body.

If one causes impurity to be discharged by grasping another's generative organ, or at times measures one's own generative organ, or grasps and squeezes it with the hand for the sake of pleasure or tactile stimulation such that arousal occurs, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense in each case.
If one looks at one's own generative organ with a defiled mind, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
There is no offense in the following cases: if, while scratching an itch or a scab, it subsequently flows out;

if while jumping over a pit; if while running swiftly; if while rubbing the thighs; if while touching clothing; if while recollecting a former partner; if upon seeing an object of desire; if while entering a bathhouse to receive massage and friction; or if, due to sudden agitation, one touches a woman's body and, because of intense afflictions, it immediately flows out.
For example, when the bhikṣu Nanda encountered his mother and unconsciously embraced her, there was no offense in either case.

However, those with excessive desire are permitted to possess leather bags made from the skins of sheep, deer, or similar animals; these should be tanned until soft, filled with sand or other materials, and fastened around the waist with a strap.

One must not wear them when entering the midst of the assembly, nor at the incense altar, nor during the circumambulation of the *caitya*. They should be washed clean, dried in the sun, and kept from becoming foul or spoiled.
If the necessary items are lacking, one should further keep an additional [screen] in a secluded place to hold it up.

**The Second Training Rule on Touching a Woman** When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Udāyin had a woman come with him to view the rooms. Because he preached the Dharma to her, a defiled mind arose within him, and he touched her body to take pleasure as he pleased. As the circumstances of the offense were the same as before, this training rule was established.

"If again a bhikṣu, with a mind entangled in lust, makes physical contact with a woman—whether grasping her hand, grasping her arm, grasping her hair, or touching any part of her body—with the intent of experiencing pleasure, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
Regarding "one whose mind is bound by defilement" (*saṃkliṣṭa-citta*): there are cases where the mind is defiled but not bound; thus, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) should be established.
The first permutation refers to the arising of a mind of defiled attachment.
The second permutation refers to the arising of a mind bound by craving toward a preceding object.
The third case refers to the presence of both conditions;
the fourth case refers to the exclusion of the aforementioned characteristics.
"A woman" means one with whom sexual intercourse may be engaged, and whose body parts are not damaged.
The hand refers to the area from the wrist forward;
the arm refers to the area from the wrist backward.
Hair refers to the hair on the head as well as the cloth used for binding the hair.

Regarding the offenses herein: if one has a defiled mind and approaches a woman capable of sexual intercourse, and her various body parts are not separated by clothing, there is an offense for each of the nine acts, namely: touching, intense touching, leaning against, grasping, pulling, dragging, lifting up, lowering down, and embracing all over.
"Touching" (*sprśana*) refers to the initial contact with the hand;
"intense touching" (*atisprśana*) means repeated rubbing and stroking;
"leaning" (*niṣadyā*) refers to the mutual physical leaning against one another.
"Grasping" means to hold with the hand;
"pulling" means to draw from a distance;
"dragging" means to pull near.
"Upper" refers to lifting the upper part from below;
"lower" refers to supporting the lower part from above.
"Embracing all over" means holding [the body] tightly and completely.
If a bhikṣu, with a mind seeking pleasure, engages in these nine matters with a woman, he incurs the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* in every case.
If he intends to commit an impure act, even if there is no garment intervening and he merely touches her body, he incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.

If one touches a body that has decayed, or if both bodies have decayed; if the body is covered in many scabs or sores; if, intending to touch this person, one mistakenly touches that person; if one touches hair, fur, nails, teeth, or dry, withered bones with one's own hair, fur, nails, or teeth; if one further entertains doubt as to whether it is this person or that person; if one touches a bhikṣuṇī who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti); or if one touches a corpse that is discolored (vinīlaka) up to a skeleton (asthisaṃkalika)—in all these cases, one commits a sthūlātyaya offense.

If a bhikṣu, with a defiled mind, makes physical contact with a woman who subsequently transforms into a man, or if he himself transforms, or if both transform simultaneously, he incurs a sthūlātyaya offense or a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣu makes physical contact with a man who subsequently changes into a woman, he incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Whether the change occurs spontaneously or both parties change simultaneously, the offense incurred is the same as before.

Regarding whether the perception of the gender has changed or not, and the cases of a bhikṣuṇī making contact with a woman or a man, the gravity of the offense—whether heavy or light—is explained in detail according to the specific circumstances.
It should be understood accordingly: if there is no physical barrier between a woman incapable [of sexual intercourse], a man, or a paṇḍaka, it constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense for all.
If there is a physical barrier or if the parties involved are animals, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If one perceives a human female as a human female, or if one has doubt regarding her, yet touches her with a defiled mind, one incurs the full offense.
If one perceives a non-human female as a human female, or has doubt regarding her, it is a thullaccaya.
If one perceives a human woman as not being a human woman, it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If the person has both sexual organs and the female organ is predominant, one incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
if it is otherwise, one incurs only a sthūlātyaya offense.

When a mother and daughter, or sisters, touch each other's bodies with a mind seeking pleasure, they incur a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), because the perception of pleasure does not arise due to the presence of shame;
however, if there is no shame, they incur the full offense (pārājika).
If one kicks the female organ with a toe or strikes it with earth or a tile, in all such cases, one incurs a *thullaccaya*.
Furthermore, no bhikṣu should paint the form of a woman or any other sentient being; to do so constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one sketches white bones; if one paints a skull; if one uses scented mud to draw various flowers on the ground; if one touches a mother, daughter, or sister without a defiled mind; if one perceives others as being one's mother or so forth; if at the time of touching, the mind is the same as when touching the earth; or if one has a wholesome intention to observe the coldness, heat, hardness, or softness of a woman’s body.

If one sees a woman falling into fire, or consuming poison, or attempting suicide with a blade, or falling into a pit, or being swept away by water, one must rescue her in every case; the ritual for rescuing those drowning shall now be explained.

If one sees a woman being swept away and drowning in water, and one has the physical strength to do so, one should rescue her; however, one must not give rise to defiled thoughts, but rather regard her as a mother or a daughter and pull her out.
If the person who has been submerged is unable to move, one should place them face down upon the sand or soil; however, they must be watched over and not abandoned.
A bhikṣu should not remain standing too close by; when he must leave for some reason, he should entrust someone else with the task of watching over them.

Those engaged in recitation should recite the sutras; those practicing meditation should collect their mindfulness. Alternatively, they may entrust the cattle to a herdsman for watch and protection before going out to seek food. After eating, they should return to inspect whether the animals are alive or dead, ensuring that this matter is examined with thorough scrutiny.
There are five kinds of animals that may be relied upon to cross a river: namely, the elephant, the horse, the ox, the buffalo, and the yak.

One should not rely on a female animal to cross; however, if one carries a float-bag for the purpose of crossing safely, the bag must be dyed and processed, and should not be painted with colorful designs.

If a mother comes to embrace him, or a daughter sits upon his lap, or he suddenly falls to the ground and lands atop a woman, or he brushes against a woman's shoulder at a narrow pass—none of these constitute an offense.

When entering for alms, one must exercise mindfulness: if a woman has lustful intentions and drinks water by pressing her hand to her mouth, the bhikṣu should not pour the water in a continuous stream; rather, he should have her drink from cupped hands, pouring more only when she has finished.
If one acts otherwise than this, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense if a woman speaks continuously with a mind free from passion. **The Third Training Rule:

On Speaking Vulgar and Evil Words** When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Udāyin saw several women entering the monastery to look about. With a defiled mind, he engaged them in vulgar speech and mocked them. This led to public censure and disgrace. As the circumstances of the disturbance were the same as before, the Blessed One established this training rule.

"If again a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by defilement, engages in vulgar, wicked, and improper speech with a woman that corresponds to sexual desire, such as the talk of husband and wife, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
The meaning of "defiled entanglement" is as explained above.

Regarding "a woman," this refers to a human female who understands speech concerning good and evil. In this context, it is for the purpose of revealing the fault, the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), the specific characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), and by means of an analogy.

Regarding the fault: it refers to the fact that the nature and cause of speaking base and evil words are both defiled, because they are currently loathsome and will lead to rebirth in the miserable realms.

Regarding the common characteristic: it refers to the fact that establishing improper speech as a standard of conduct is rejected by superior persons, and is universally recognized as being contrary to the Dharma.
The "specific characteristic" refers to speech associated with sexual desire.
The "analogy" refers to that of a husband and wife.
Regarding the offenses herein, there are nine types; by speaking [of them], one incurs the full offense in each case.

If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, addresses a woman who understands his meaning, whether speaking of good or evil, directly begging or begging by means of an artifice, asking directly or asking indirectly, citing an example, praising her, or reviling her—with any one of these nine matters, if he speaks them in conjunction with vulgar and wicked words, he commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If the person does not hear [the words], or hears them but does not understand them, yet there are no vulgar or evil syllables present, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If such a woman approaches a bhikṣu and speaks these nine matters, and he, with a defiled mind, accepts her words and responds accordingly, engaging in improper conversation together, he also incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
To say "well-spoken" means: "Your three sores are truly lovely.
To say "ill-spoken" means: "Your three sores are not good things.
To say "direct begging" means: "Come and do such-and-such things with me."
"Indirect solicitation" means manifesting a heart of affection by saying, "I shall conceive the utmost love for you.
"Direct questioning" means: "If a woman performs such an act, that woman will certainly be cherished by men; you too may now perform such an act, and I shall love you."
Regarding "indirect questioning" (*ku-maṇḍala-praśna*): if there is a woman who performs such an act and is loved by a man, one asks, "Are you now capable of performing this act?
Because one does not ask about the specific details of the matter, it is called indirect questioning.
Regarding "citing an example": [One says,] "A certain woman previously engaged in such an act with me; you too should now do so with me.
Regarding "praising": "Sister, if you can engage in such an act with me, it will bring about celestial bliss."

Regarding "speaking with anger and abuse," this refers to reviling by uttering vulgar and evil words; that is, when one actually speaks vulgar words concerning sexual union, one incurs the full offense.
If there are other words spoken that are intermingled with words concerning the practice of sexual desire, one likewise incurs the full offense.
If one utters base and evil words toward another—whether by sending a messenger, by oral transmission, by letter or seal, by hand gesture, or by saying:
"Your faculties are impaired; you are a sinful object; you may consort with me, lie down with me, and share what you hold dear."
However, this is not to be spoken using the vulgar term *yavā*; rather, one should address a nun who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or say to her: "Sister!"
"Give me some leaves.
The woman understood her meaning.
If she sees a bhikṣuṇī wearing fine clothing, she speaks these words:
"Sister, you are dressed in amorous attire, seeking a man.
If she says, "Young girl!..."
"If you cannot endure the act of desire, why do you not insert your burning head into the female organ?
Or if he further says:
"You may perform such an act with a beast; you should give me that which is below your waist, and you ought to bestow upon me whatever object you cherish."
The woman understood his meaning and replied,
"I shall prepare it now. If he says:
"Please give me some water," he said.
The woman replied,
"There is no water."
The bhikṣu replied: "You yourself are water.
In this same way, even until the point where you may give me a cake, you yourself are the cake."
However, that woman understood his intention and asked,
"For what reason are you unhappy? He replied:
"I desire to obtain you.

If a person is by nature prone to vulgar speech, and in the presence of a *mahānagna* or a *mahācāṇḍāla*, speaks such foul and evil words while perceiving a non-existent woman as being a woman, these all constitute the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
If one perceives a young boy, a young śrāmaṇera, or an animal as being an actual woman, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
If the mind makes no distinction, one incurs the fundamental offense (mūlāpatti) whenever there is an actual woman present.
If one intends the mind to be restricted such that one does not speak to that person but speaks only to this one, and that person is present, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If the speech is indeed vulgar, yet one perceives it as non-vulgar, there is no offense.
If one suspects a human male to be a human male, or suspects a human female to be a human female, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one suspects a non-human to be a human, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one perceives a human to be a non-human, it is an offense of wrongdoing (*duṣkṛta*).

In other places it is said that if a woman speaks vulgar and evil words, and one accepts them through speech with a heart of pleasure in the matter, even if one does not personally utter those vulgar and evil words oneself, one still incurs the fundamental offense.
If, when saying "yava," one intends "barley" (*yavaka*), or if one says the word "yava" or other vulgar expressions,
there is no offense provided that such words are not considered offensive in the local customs of the region.

4. The Training Rule on Soliciting Offerings. Regarding the fourth training rule on soliciting offerings: While the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Udāyin again solicited offerings from other women. As the circumstances causing offense were the same as before, he established this training rule.
"If again a bhikṣu, with a mind bound by passion, in the presence of a woman, should praise his own person, saying:

'Sister! If there were a bhikṣu similar to me—one who is fully endowed with moral discipline (śīla), possesses superior wholesome qualities, and practices the holy life—he should be honored with this dharma of sexual desire.'"
"If a bhikṣu speaks in this manner, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
In this context, "seeking offerings" refers to providing for the body.
"Possessing śīla" refers to the perfection of the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha).

That which possesses superior wholesome qualities refers to the perfection of the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*); because all pure virtues are thereby brought to fulfillment, it is like fine gold.

As for "holy life" (*brahmacarya*), it refers to being endowed with the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*). "Brahman" refers to *nirvāṇa*; because this practice leads toward it, it is called "holy life," and because it is the practice of Brahman, it is named "holy life."
Furthermore, "wholesome qualities" (kuśala-dharma) refers to being endowed with virtues such as fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) and so forth.

Generally speaking, there are eighteen types of transgressions regarding these characteristics. They are as follows: one says of oneself, "I am the most," "the superior," "the distinguished," "the exquisite," "the virtuous," "the excellent," "the worthy of offerings," "the beloved," "the vast," "the most supreme," "the most superior," "the most distinguished," "the most exquisite," "the most virtuous," "the most excellent," "the most worthy of offerings," "the most beloved," and "the most vast. This is intended to manifest that one's own wholesome qualities are perfected, such that among all offerings, one is the most eminent;
it is because one extols the superior virtues of the Tathāgata’s disciples, which are distinct from other forms of worship.
Because it arises from a mind of straightforwardness;
because it is produced from the nature of wisdom;
because it is initiated by a mind that delights in the Dharma.
Because those who possess this Dharma are worthy of offerings from kings and others;
because they possess a good reputation that pervades all directions;
and because they are the dwelling place of supreme merit—these correspond respectively to the preceding nine [qualities].

Regarding these nine matters, there are further distinctions that, when expressed with superlative terms, constitute another set of nine; thus, these eighteen matters are detailed as in the extensive text.
If one speaks these words with a defiled mind and the other person understands them, one incurs the full offense for each instance.

The three [precepts] beginning with *śīla* may be taken either collectively or individually; the rest is as stated in the text. When [the offense] is spoken, it constitutes a fundamental transgression (*mūlāpatti*).
If the words "sexual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) are absent, one incurs only a gross offense (*sthūlātyaya*).
If one lacks the words "similar to me," one incurs a grave offense (sthūlātyaya).
If one lacks both the words "similar to me" and the word "sexual desire," one incurs only a minor offense (duṣkṛta).
If one engages with a woman capable of sexual intercourse, one incurs the root offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If she is incapable, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
This same *sthūlātyaya* applies when engaging with a man or a *paṇḍaka* who is capable.
Incapable men, *paṇḍakas*, and various species of animals all incur an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*); other corresponding cases should be considered according to the above principle.

The Fifth Training Rule on Matchmaking. When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, Kālo Mṛḍgāraputra acted as a matchmaker for an old acquaintance. At that time, laypeople either praised or criticized him, and the non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners likewise gave rise to derisive talk.
The circumstances are the same as before; this training rule was established due to the afflictions of contention and resentment.

"If a bhikṣu acts as a matchmaker, conveying a man’s intentions to a woman or a woman’s intentions to a man, whether for the purpose of formal marriage or secret liaison, even for a mere moment, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
There are three determinations that constitute the offense of matchmaking: determination regarding the parties, determination regarding the matter, and determination regarding the time.
As for "determination regarding the parties," it means conveying the man’s intention to the woman and conveying the woman’s intention to the man.
Regarding "certainty of the object," this refers to matters concerning men and women, wives, or the act of acting as a matchmaker for illicit unions.
Regarding "certainty of time," this refers to even a brief moment.
Regarding "acting as a matchmaker," this refers to going back and forth to convey messages.
Regarding the duties of a wife, there are seven types.
What are these seven? They are:
marriage by water-offering, marriage by purchase, marriage by royal decree, marriage by mutual consent, marriage for sustenance, marriage by cohabitation, and momentary marriage.
"Water-giving" refers to when one's parents give water to another and hand over their daughter.
"Betrothal by wealth" refers to when one's parents take wealth as a bride-price for the betrothal.

Regarding the "royal banner": it refers to when a king personally leads his army to invade another country, or when other bandits plunder a village, taking the women they have captured as wives or concubines.
Regarding "seeking one's own pleasure," it means that one’s own mind harbors the aspiration to become another's wife.
Regarding "food and clothing," it means that one comes to become a wife specifically for the sake of seeking food and clothing.

Regarding "living together," it means that both parties possess their own wealth with which they sustain their lives, yet they enter into a covenant as spouses and bind themselves in intent to dwell together.
The term "for a brief moment" means that she does not engage in the affairs of a husband and wife for a long duration; she is also called a "woman without entanglement.

She is called "without entanglement" because, although she has a husband, she maintains the precepts and dwells in purity, being unlike those of ordinary character. Thus, she is termed "without entanglement."
Regarding "private intercourse," this refers to a woman who is either unmarried or whose husband has died, and who wishes to engage in illicit relations.
There are ten types of protection that may prevent such acts:

namely, protection by her father, protection by her mother, protection by her brother, protection by her sister, protection by her paternal grandfather, and protection by her paternal grandmother; if these six are absent, she is protected by other relatives, which is termed "protection by kin."
If one belongs to the Brahmin caste, it is called protection of the lineage (*gotra-rakṣā*);
if one belongs to a Brahmin clan, it is called protection of the family (*kula-rakṣā*).
When neither such lineage nor clan exists, it is collectively termed protection by royal law (*rāja-dharma-rakṣā*).
If there is a woman who abides by the Dharma with a chaste mind free from impurity, this is called protection by the Dharma (*dharmarakṣā*).

If a bhikṣu, whether seven or ten times, acts with the intent of matchmaking—receiving a message from one party, conveying it to the other, and reporting back—this constitutes three instances of mediation.
Whether he goes in person, dispatches a messenger, or sends someone through a series of intermediaries, all such cases are included within this category.

If one acts for oneself as one [act] and dispatches another to act as two, or if one acts for oneself as two and dispatches another to act as one—provided they achieve union—it is in all such cases a formal communal instruction (saṃghāvaśeṣa).
If one acts for oneself as one or two, or if they do not achieve union, one incurs only the preparatory offense of a sthūlātyaya.

In all cases of acting as a matchmaker, people are categorized as either "honored" or "lowly. Those who are "honored" refer to the heads of households; their word is taken as final, whereas the opposite constitutes being "lowly.
If one accepts the proposal, goes to inquire, and returns with a report—these three stages are all considered "honored," and at that point, one commits the fundamental offense.
If one person is superior and two are inferior, or two are superior and one is inferior, it should be understood that for those in the superior positions, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
for those in the inferior positions, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
One must not respond to a superior person with inferior speech, as this also incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
There are three matters by which a response is established even without verbal reply:
first, the appointment of a place;
second, the fixing of a time.
Third, manifesting signs (*nimitta*).
If one sees me residing in a certain place, one knows that the matter will be accomplished; this is called the designated location (*sthāna*).
If one sees me at a certain time, it indicates that the matter will be accomplished; this is called the fixed time (*kāla*).
If one sees me holding an alms bowl or wearing new robes, they will know that the matter is appropriate; this is called "indicating a sign.
When the other person understands through these three actions, it constitutes a "reciprocal response."
Furthermore, there are three things that also constitute the act of matchmaking:
first, speech; second, writing; [and third, gestures].
3. Hand Gestures (Mudrā).

By means of these three factors—receiving the words, questioning the other, and returning the reply—or by using one factor to constitute all three, or by mixing them at different times, one incurs the full offense.
The preceding section has clarified the case of being together; next, the case of being apart shall be distinguished.
There are seven different types of separation from the object:
first, separation at the time of actual combat;
2. Separation after a fight;
3. Breaking off blades of grass as a token of agreement;
4. Throwing a tile to set a time.
Fifth, she spoke in the presence of witnesses;
sixth, she declared, "She is not my wife";
seventh, she cried out in a loud voice so that her neighbors and associates would all know.
Regarding the first three types of separation, if a go-between mediates to bring about reconciliation, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding the next three types of separation, reconciling them incurs the offense of *thullaccaya*.
Regarding the final type of separation, reconciling it constitutes a formal act of the community (*saṃghādisesa*).

Regarding the four types of inferior women and the ten cases of illicit intercourse, these follow the seven types of separation; if the union occurs, all constitute a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. This includes:

acting as a matchmaker for those who have conceived (referring to the fetus), or for those who have given birth to a son or daughter, or for those who have given birth to both a son and a daughter, or for a *paṇḍaka*; acting as a matchmaker for non-humans or animals; or again, acting as a matchmaker for a *bhikṣuṇī* or a *bhikṣu*, or for one practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), or for oneself, or for a young girl; or when acting as a matchmaker, the gender of one party changes during the process, or both change; or during the three stages of the matchmaking process, one remains in their natural state while the other two are mentally disturbed, or one is mentally disturbed while the other two are not—cases such as these all result in a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If laypeople come to invite the Saṃgha to act as intermediaries for marriage, and they collectively dispatch a messenger, all involved incur the fundamental offense.
If one person alone acts independently as a matchmaker, then that single individual incurs the offense.

Whether one has already received full ordination (*upasampadā*) or is in the process of receiving it, there are two sets of four permutations regarding these three matters, which should be understood as being the same as above.
If one performs these three matters after having already received full ordination, one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
The remaining two pairs of lines constitute a *sthūlātyaya* offense due to the act of ordination;
the other two pairs constitute three [offenses], all of which are *duṣkṛta*.
If one informs another:
"If one asks, 'Why do you not seek a wife?
one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
Furthermore, if one says:"
"If that family has a daughter, why not seek her in marriage?
Thinking thus as a go-between, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Having performed the three acts of matchmaking for another, if the parents subsequently change their minds, or if the boy or girl dies, or if one encounters illness, or if one meets with famine—due to such causes that prevent the match—all these constitute *sthūlātyaya*.
If there is a woman who instructs a bhikṣu to tell the head of another household:
"All the people and property of my family belong entirely to you," and the bhikṣu,
knowing this to be the case, transmits the message, or consents to it for the purpose of providing food as an offering for the Saṃgha.
If a woman and a man have previously made an appointment and the woman instructs a bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!
If you see that certain man, please inform him:"
"I shall wait for you at such-and-such a place.
When one says such things, a coarse offense (sthūlātyaya) is incurred.
However, if one does not know the other's intention and acts as a messenger of communication, there is no offense.
If a woman causes a bhikṣu to go and strike a man on the shoulder with his fist, because she lacks a malicious intent, he incurs a light offense.
If she says, "Why does this man not become a son-in-law who enters the household? [the bhikṣu incurs no offense].
If one asks: "Why does this woman not serve her mother-in-law?
or if one says:
"Why does this man not live in a separate room?"—
even a single word such as this that corresponds to the work of a matchmaker constitutes an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) for all such speech.
A disciple says to a teacher:
"If I wish to act as a matchmaker for others," should the teacher hear these words and grant permission by remaining silent, he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
All other rules of training (*śikṣāpada*) should be understood accordingly.
In all matters of matchmaking and marriage, one incurs the full offense only when the man and woman actually engage in sexual intercourse.
For what reason are the four trainings arranged in this sequence?
Generally, when a man does not yet know a woman's intentions, he first takes her hand to test her feelings.

If she consents, one should next take hold of her arm, and so on, gradually touching her throat and abdomen and other parts; if she does not consent, one should speak vulgar words to entice her feelings. These two methods are employed toward a woman who lacks faith.
If she is a woman of faith and reverence who knows the joy of merit, one should encourage her with various virtuous words.
These three cases concern her own defiled desires; the next one concerns acting as a matchmaker for others out of a desire for food and clothing, thereby uniting men and women.

6. The Training Rule on Constructing Small Dwellings. This sixth training rule concerning the construction of small dwellings was established when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣus were occupied with so many tasks in constructing dwelling places that their minds became distracted, and they neglected all wholesome qualities.
Furthermore, by repeatedly begging and thus harassing various donors, he incurred reproach and disgrace.
Due to disputes and resentment arising from matters concerning his dwelling, as well as the afflictions associated with such base conduct regarding his residence, this training rule was established.
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu himself solicits materials to build a small hut for his own use when there is no patron, it must be built according to the prescribed measurements.
Herein, the measurement is twelve spans of the Buddha’s hands in length and seven spans in width."
That bhikṣu should lead a community of bhikṣus to inspect the site.
That community of bhikṣus should inspect the site to ensure it is a place that is in accordance with the Dharma, a pure place, free from disputes, and suitable for spiritual progress.

If a bhikṣu, at an improper place, an impure place, a place of contention, or a place lacking access, should personally solicit materials to build a cell for himself without an owner, and without having other bhikṣus go to inspect the site, and should he construct it there exceeding the prescribed dimensions, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Seeking for oneself" means that according to one's own desire, one personally searches for and seeks out either grass or wood.
"Constructing a small hut" means either doing it oneself or having others do it.
"Without an owner" means there is no other person who acts as its master.
"Made for oneself" means it is not for the sake of the Saṃgha.

"It should be of the proper measure" means that because excessive labor would cause one to neglect their duties, it must not be so large as to cause harm; yet, fearing that a cramped space might lead to distress, it must not be too small.

Regarding the statement that it is twelve *tāla*-spans long and seven *tāla*-spans wide: calculating the Buddha’s twelve *tāla*-spans in terms of the standard human measure, it equals eighteen cubits (*hasta*) for a person of average height, since three *tāla*-spans of such a person constitute one *tāla*-span [of the Buddha].

Regarding the statement that "this bhikṣu should [consult] the community of bhikṣus," this is for the purpose of preventing three matters: namely, if one does not consult with the bhikṣus when inspecting the site before undertaking construction in violation of the Dharma; or if there are holes inhabited by insects, ants, snakes, scorpions, and the like, it is termed an "impure site."

Furthermore, one should observe that places near a royal palace, or the residence of a householder, or the dwellings of non-Buddhists, or a bhikṣuṇī convent, or where large trees are being cut down, are known as sites of contention.
Furthermore, one should observe that if within a fathom’s distance from the edge of a house there is a well or a path, or if it is near a precipice, it is called a place where one cannot proceed.
In all these cases, the matter should not be granted; it should be granted only when circumstances differ from these.

A bhikṣu who is constructing a dwelling should go to the original site and request the assembly to inspect it. Whether the entire assembly goes together or a designated individual is sent, one must not rely on hearsay and fail to personally verify the site.
Having observed that there is no hindrance, one should address the assembly in their presence, saying: "Virtuous ones!
You should know that I have finished observing the site for that dwelling; it is in accordance with the Dharma and pure. It is fitting that you know the time has come."
One should first perform the formal announcement (jñapti) and subsequently carry out the ritual motion (karmavācanā).
If all matters are contrary to the rules, yet the construction of the dwelling is completed and fit for use, one incurs the offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If the site is impure, if there are grounds for dispute, if there is no progress toward the goal, if the community does not observe or grant permission, if the measurement exceeds one cubit (*hasta*), or if any one of these faults is present; or if at some point the work is begun and then abandoned; or if it is seized by another; or if, after labor has already been undertaken, one passes away; or if one becomes a layperson (*avadātavasana*); or if one becomes a novice (*śrāmaṇera*); or if one uses one's own property—in all such cases, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu, "Build a dwelling for me,
but do not let it violate the Dharma," and that bhikṣu builds it in violation of the Dharma, he incurs the offense himself.
If one sends another person, saying:
"This place is excellent and suitable for building a hut; I shall beg for wood and other materials to provide for you," yet the site is actually impure, both parties incur an offense.
If ten people together construct one dwelling, and they all collectively initiate the preparatory effort, all ten incur the offense.
If one causes another to construct a dwelling, yet harbors a doubtful mind as to whether it will be built or not, one incurs a sthūlātyaya.
There is no offense in the case of a house already completed, a room previously accepted for use, or a large mosquito net; in all these instances, there is no offense.
