2. The Two Indeterminate Rules (Aniyata-dharma). A summary verse says:
If in a screened place, a location capable of sexual intercourse, [one sits or lies down with a woman].
"And in a place free from obstruction, there was no third person present.

At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Then the bhikṣu Udāyin sat with his knees pressed against those of the woman Gupta in a secluded spot, preaching the essentials of the Dharma to her.
At that time, the female lay follower (upāsikā) Viśākhā, having witnessed this matter, was unable to bear it in her heart and went to inform the World-Honored One.
Due to this incident involving the female lay follower and the affliction of sexual desire, the first *aniyata* rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu should sit alone with a woman in a secluded place, screened from view and suitable for sexual intercourse,
and a faithful upāsikā should charge him with one of three matters:
either a pārajika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika offense."
If that seated bhikṣu confesses his own matter, he should be disciplined according to one of the three rules as appropriate:
either a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*;
or else, he should be disciplined by means of the matter as stated by the *upāsikā*.
"This is called an indeterminate rule (*aniyata-dharma*).
In this context, the indeterminate rules take as their essence the matter, the location, the intention, and the evidence:
"If a bhikṣu is alone with a single woman" refers to the matter.
That which acts as a barrier is the "place";
that which is capable of engaging in sexual intercourse is the "sentient being";
and if any upāsikā endowed with right faith should speak [to this effect], she is the "witness."
"Monk" (bhikṣu) refers to one who has received full ordination and whose sensual desire is manifest.
"Alone" means being without other monks or other men.
"One" means being without bhikṣuṇīs or other women.
"A woman" refers to a human female capable of engaging in sexual intercourse.
"A secluded place" refers to a concealed location, capable of shielding one's form so that sexual intercourse may be performed.
There are five such types:
a wall, a fence, a garment, a thicket, and darkness.
In such places, either a man approaches a woman or a woman comes to a man.

Regarding the phrase "a place capable of sexual intercourse": within a distance of one fathom (*vyāma*), they may occupy the same seat with their bodies in close contact, such that they can sit or lie down together; however, this depends on whether that woman consents or does not consent.
A "rightly faithful upāsikā" refers to one who has realized the truths (dṛṣṭasatya).
Some say that even if she is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), provided she possesses loyalty and faith such that her words and deeds do not diverge, one may likewise trust her speech.
Regarding "speaking according to one [party]": either a woman, unable to bear seeing what has occurred, speaks;
or, because that bhikṣu protects himself and refuses to speak for himself, she speaks according to the facts only when it is time for him to provide testimony.
"Pārājika" refers to any one among the four grave offenses;
"Saṃghāvaśeṣa" refers to any one among the thirteen [offenses].
"Or a *pāyattika* (offense entailing expiation)" refers to any one among the ninety [offenses].
"Speaking for oneself" means speaking in accordance with the facts regarding the matter committed.
"If" means either it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) or it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) confessed face-to-face.
In this context, the term "sound" is not definitive. If the original intention was to engage in sexual misconduct while seated together on the same seat, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Alternatively, regarding the matter described by the *upāsikā* for the purpose of disciplining that bhikṣu, it is intended to show that the *upāsikā* lacks clear understanding of the intrinsic nature of the offense and the causes from which it arises; nevertheless, seeing a bhikṣu sitting with a woman, eating from the same vessel, or drinking from the same cup—such matters as these should all be subject to disciplinary punishment.

Regarding the term "indeterminate offense" (*aniyata-dharma*): it is said that because the essence of this transgression lacks a fixed characteristic, it may involve multiple offenses such that they cannot be definitively specified.

As for the characteristics of the violation herein, it refers to sitting together with [a monk] in a place of activity or a place of residence; one should discipline him according to what he himself has stated.

Regarding these three cases, if one does not speak for oneself, one should undergo the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to seek the nature of the offense.
Once this *karman* has been performed, all the rules of conduct must be observed as previously described: one is not permitted to ordain others, grant them the ten precepts, or perform similar acts.
If one does not act in accordance with this, all incur an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
Furthermore, one should question the woman who reported the matter regarding her complexion, appearance, gait, and location;
if there is a second person, one should also question them about the matter, and if the accounts correspond, one should deal with the case as described.

If the case does not correspond, one should follow the words of the bhikṣu; whether he speaks at random of another offense, or claims there is an offense where there is none, or perceives this offense as being another, in all such instances, one must administer discipline according to the words of that bhikṣu.
Regarding the distinction within the second indeterminate case: the setting was in Rājagṛha, caused by the bhikṣu Śrīgupta sitting together with the woman Sthūlanandā.
This is because it was spoken by the Upāsikā Upavāsā; in an unsecluded place, one is incapable of engaging in sexual intercourse, as there is no possibility of committing a *pārājika* offense.
"If a bhikṣu should sit alone with a woman in a place that is not screened off and is unsuitable for sexual intercourse,
and a faithful upāsikā should charge him with one of two rules—
either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*."
If that seated bhikṣu confesses his own matter, he should be dealt with according to one of two rules:
either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*;
or else, he should be dealt with according to the matter as stated by the *upāsikā*.
This is called an indeterminate rule.
**The Third Section: Thirty *Niḥsargika-pāyattika* Rules** The first summary verse states:
Holding, separating, storing, and washing robes; Taking robes, begging, and receiving in excess.
"Of equal value and from different owners, sent by messenger with the price for robes.

1. The Training Rule on Having Extra Robes Without Distinguishing Them. This first training rule concerning having extra robes without distinguishing them was established by the Buddha while he was at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in Śrāvastī. At that time, many bhikṣus accumulated numerous robes and neglected their wholesome practices. This rule was formulated due to the matter of extra robes, the transgression of limits, neglect, and the underlying afflictions.

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the kaṭhina robe has been suspended, and he obtains an extra robe, he may keep it for up to ten days without having formally designated it."
"If one keeps [the robe] beyond that limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the phrase "having finished making the robe," it was because the physician and elder Jīvaka offered robes that the Blessed One, on this account, permitted the keeping of robes.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:

"My body is now extremely supple; I can still sustain myself with only three robes. How much more so for the bhikṣus, whose bodies are not supple, yet who find even three kinds of robes insufficient."
"Therefore, it was ordained that each bhikṣu shall possess three robes (tricīvara), sufficient for maintaining the body without exceeding the limit of surplus.

Beyond these three robes, he is permitted to accept and keep ten kinds of articles; however, anything other than these robes that is not in accordance with the Dharma should not be kept. This includes: garments of wild hemp, blankets of camel hair, garments made of leaves, leopard skins, deer skins, or small bathing cloths; or those dyed blue; or those who go naked or pluck out their hair; or those who wear garments of owl feathers, human hair blankets, or those who adopt the vow of silence."
All of these are the dress and deportment of non-Buddhists (tīrthika) and do not constitute the dharma of those who have gone forth; whoever practices them incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
Furthermore, if one wears any other garments belonging to non-Buddhists, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense in every such case.

If one wears a robe with trailing ends, or ties up the robe, or wears a tunic and trousers; or at times binds the hair in an uṣṇīṣa, or wraps the head, or wears the upper and lower garments of a layperson; or adorns oneself with painted patterns, various necklaces, or the sacred thread of a brahmin; or wears a string of beads bound upon the arm.
All such improper garments as these are the attire of laypeople;
if one wears or uses them, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
However, there is no offense if a physician places a consecrated thread on an arm for the sake of treating an illness.
It should be tied behind the elbow; if it is cured, one should not discard it lightly, but should place it within a hole in a wall or a wooden post.

One should know that the three robes have distinct uses for consumption: when performing manual labor, when traveling on the road, or while inside the monastery, one should regularly use the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*).
When performing acts of reverence, eating, or consuming food, one should wear the seven-strip robe (*saptaka*).
To ward off the cold, when entering a village to beg for food, when eating, or when paying homage to a *caitya*, one should wear the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*).
The latter two robes should be made by cutting and piecing together patches.
If one is poor, they must nevertheless be cut for the purpose of entering a village.
Why is it that one does not enter a village wearing uncut robes?
However, there are two aspects of a bhikṣu’s robe that differ from those of laypeople: namely, their color and their shape.
Laypeople wear robes that are purely white and uncut, whereas bhikṣus wear robes of dyed (defiled) colors and cut [patches].
If one obtains new cloth for making a saṃghāṭī or a niṣīdana, it should be made double-layered.
An uttarāsaṅga and an antarvāsaka should be made single-layered.
If the first two [layers] are triple-layered and the latter two are double-layered, it is likewise permitted.
If one applies a second layer over an undifferentiated object, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; by the eleventh day, one commits the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Or, one might think:
"I shall seek another garment to serve as a lining.
Thereupon, one removes the second layer, incurring an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); by the eleventh day, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If one thinks, "After it has been washed and dyed,
I shall take this material back and re-sew it onto this garment," there is no offense.
If one does not affix [the patches] by the eleventh day, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If one obtains old cloth to make a *saṃghāṭī* or a *niṣīdana*, the seven-strip robe should be made with four layers, and the five-strip robe should be made with two layers; alternatively, one may remove and reattach [the strips], following the previous instructions as appropriate.
Regarding rag robes (*pāṃśukūla*) and old, tattered garments, their weight may be adjusted according to one's preference.
As for the method of arranging the strips and the partitions: according to the rules for the arrangement of the *antarvāsa*, there is one long strip and one short strip;
for the *uttarāsaṅga*, there are two long strips and one short strip.

If there is no possibility of cutting and patching, or if it is the robe of a person with few desires or a poor person who lacks sufficient cloth for such work, one is permitted to keep it even if it is not cut and patched with patches;
or if one currently lacks the leisure for tasks such as sewing and stitching, there is no offense in maintaining it even if it is merely a plain strip of cloth.
The saṃghāṭī has nine different numbers of strips:
namely, nine, eleven, thirteen, fifteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty-one, twenty-three, and twenty-five.
Regarding the patchwork of the robe: the first three [patches] consist of two long strips and one short strip;
the next three consist of three long strips and one short strip;
the final three consist of four long strips and one short strip. Beyond this, it becomes a "torn rag" (*pāṃśukūla*) and is unfit for wearing.
In total, there are three grades of *saṃghāṭī* robes:
namely, superior, medium, and inferior.
The superior is three cubits in height and five cubits in width; the inferior is each reduced by half a cubit; those between these two are called medium.
The *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) also has three grades:
the superior consists of three or five [patches]; the small is each reduced by half an *hasta*; those between these two are called the medium.
The five-strip [robe] is the same as this.
Furthermore, there are two types of five-strip robes:
those with two vertical and five horizontal strips, and those with two vertical and four horizontal strips.
Provided they merely cover the three wheels [of the body], these are said to be the minimum dimensions for a robe that may be formally maintained.

If one’s body is tall but the cubits are short, one should measure according to the body and not according to the cubit; if the opposite is the case, one should likewise measure according to the body.
If the body is exceptionally large, one should sew the lower garment (*śīrṣaka*) into a *guḍuluka* and use it.
If one makes a robe exceeding or falling short of the aforementioned measurements, or fails to follow the prescribed dimensions, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) in each case.
Regarding the method of washing robes: a bhikṣu should not have a guest washerman wash his clothes, for fear that they may be damaged.
One should not go to the homes of laundrymen; rather, one should wash one's own clothes.

Place the lye-water in a washing vessel and wash slowly with either the hands or the feet. If the clothing is stained by fragrant mud or other oily substances, it should be washed using hot water, ash, and the like.

Regarding the method for dyeing robes: first take tree bark, wash away the dust and dirt, and beat it with a mallet until it is crushed. Dry it in the sun, then boil it three times, setting each decoction in a separate location.
First use the first decoction, next use the second, and finally use the third.
When wishing to dye, one should take a small amount of the liquid and place it in a vessel; only then may one hold the garment and adjust the quantity until the cloth is thoroughly saturated.
One should not place the robe inside a vessel containing much liquid, nor should one wring it out too forcefully so as to damage the fabric.
Once the liquid has been wrung out, one should soften it by massaging it several times before spreading it out to dry in the sun.

Regarding the method for drying clothes: stretch a thin cord horizontally and drape the edges of the garment over it; split bamboo strips to serve as clothespins, using as many as desired. If the moisture flows toward the bottom edge, turn the garment back upward so that no drops fall; one should check it frequently.
If the robes are heavy, they should be hung on wooden stakes or branches and turned over frequently.
New robes should be dried in the sun using a fresh tree-bark decoction, while old robes should be dried in the shade using an old tree-bark decoction.
Once it has dried, moisten it with a small amount of water to soften it; this will make the color even more brilliant and ensure it does not fade.
If one is dyeing inside a monastery, if the ground is stained by the dye, it should be wiped clean with cow dung; if the ground is lime-plastered, it must be washed with water.

As for the method of sewing and stitching, one should cut and trim according to the pattern of a rice paddy field; the leaves should face both sides and must not lean toward only one. There are three distinctions among the leaves:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
The upper width is four finger-breadths, or like the outstretched feet of a crow; it narrows evenly to two finger-breadths at the bottom. The space between these two is called the middle.
Generally, for a small altar, one should use half the size of a large altar, marking its location with bamboo splinters or needles and the like.

However, when cutting the small altar to correspond with the large altar, one must further increase it by half a leaf; only after the single seam is completed will the light and dark be properly aligned. Any other way is incorrect.

The four sides are provided with borders slightly narrower than the petals; at the shoulder corners, four finger-widths from the border, patches are placed, and within these patches small holes are pierced to accommodate fine cords and loops approximately two finger-widths in length.
When folded back and tied together, it forms two loops; a button should be placed along the edge at the front of the chest.
It is folded into three pleats at the location where the loops and button are to be secured, or according to the size of the body.
There are three kinds of knots:
first, those resembling the fruit of the *yǎngwù*;
second, those resembling the seeds of the *kuí* plant.
Third, it resembles the fruit of the *tánglí* (Chinese crabapple).
Just as with the upper portion, the same applies to the lower hem; when worn inverted, it may be donned at will without constituting an offense.
When going outside, fasten the inner ties together, drape it over the neck, and let the corners rest upon the shoulders.
There are five kinds of items that should not be cut or hemmed:
first, the *saṃkakṣikā* (upper robe);
second, the *uttarāsaṅga* (outer robe).
Third, woolen rugs; fourth, thick felted cloaks;
fifth, tattered items.

Whenever one intends to cut and sew garments, a mat must be spread beneath; if no mat is available, one may smear the ground with cow dung, spread various leaves, or sweep and clean the area before performing the cutting and tailoring.

When sewing or stitching, one should use bamboo or wood to fashion a frame for the cloth according to the size of the garment; having secured the four edges upon this frame, one should then sew and stitch as previously prescribed.
If one does not follow this, all incur an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
Alternatively, if one sews or stitches by relying on other methods, there is likewise no offense.
There are five kinds of robes:
1. Robes with a donor: this refers to when one knows for certain that there is a person who intends to give those robes.
2. Robes without a donor: this refers to when one does not know for certain the location of the donor.
3. The "returned robe" refers to a robe that was taken to a cemetery and then brought back.
4. The "cemetery robe" refers to a robe discarded in a charnel ground.
Fifth, the paṃsukūla (rag-robe); this has five distinctions:
first, the paṃsukūla from the road;
second, the paṃsukūla from the riverbank; [and so forth].
Third, refuse rags from an empty place;
fourth, refuse rags from a heap of refuse;
fifth, tattered refuse rags.
Furthermore, there are five types: namely, those chewed by oxen, gnawed by rats, bored through by ants, burned by fire, and those discarded by nurses.
As for the substance of these robes, there are seven types in total, distinguished by their specific circumstances and origins.
What are the seven?
First, woolen garments;
second, kusha-grass garments; [and so forth].
3. The śaṇaka robe; 4. the kambala robe; 5. the dukūla robe;
Sixth, the *kocava* robe; seventh, the *apalānduka* robe.

Regarding the statement that the *kaṭhina* robe is "again brought forth," it is because of this that the matters concerning the *kaṭhina* must be clarified: namely, the method of its spreading, those who may jointly receive the robe-material, as well as the benefits obtained and the ritual for the removal of the robe.
First, the matter of spreading the *kaṭhina* robe shall be explained.
The assembly must be in harmony, and on the fourteenth day of the eighth month, they should collectively address the *saṃgha*, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Tomorrow, the assembly should gather together to spread the *kaṭhina* robe.

When the time came for the assembly to convene, they performed the formal procedure consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to appoint a person endowed with five virtues to act as the one who spreads the *kaṭhina*.
Next, one should perform the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) to entrust the robe to him.
Once he has received the robe, he should, together with the other bhikṣus, carry out tasks such as washing and dyeing; even those who can handle two or three stitches should all assist in the work.
When those who are making the robe—whether two or three people—form this thought:
"I am giving this robe to the Saṃgha; it shall be spread as the kaṭhina, it is currently being spread as the kaṭhina, or it has already been spread as the kaṭhina."
Regarding these three types of mind, it suffices to employ the latter two as the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*).
If one does not do so, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

If someone who has spent the rains retreat elsewhere comes here and requests that the procedure be performed, the person who spreads the cloth (*cīvara*) also fulfills the requirement for spreading the cloth.
On the fifteenth day of the eighth month, the person who spreads the *kaṭhina* robe shall inform the Saṃgha, saying:
"Tomorrow, I shall spread the *kaṭhina* robe for the venerable Saṃgha."
"Virtuous ones, each of you must relinquish your own three robes and bring them together into the midst of the assembly.

When the following day arrives, the person responsible for displaying the robes should adorn and make offerings to the *kaṭhina* robe with ointments, incense, and various flowers and colored fabrics, and then place it upon a clean tray.
Holding it up before the assembly, he stood before the senior monk (upādhyāya) holding the robe and made this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This robe has been authorized by the Saṃgha to be spread as kaṭhina."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am now appointed by the Saṃgha to serve as the kaṭhina-spreader for [Name].
I, [Name], being the kaṭhina-spreader for [Name], shall use this robe to spread the kaṭhina for the Saṃgha.
A second and third time he spoke in this same manner.
He then spread out his robe before the Elder. The Elder said:
“Excellent! The robe-cloth is being spread; it is most excellently spread.
This will bring me gain and benefit, which I shall surely obtain.”
In this manner, it should continue down to the last member of the assembly.

The person who spreads the *kaṭhina* cloth must not take this *kaṭhina* robe to places for defecation or urination, nor to houses where there is smoke or fire; he must not stay in the open air, nor go outside the boundary. Even if he has a reason to travel, he must not spend the night away. If the day for the *pravāraṇā* ceremony arrives and the King has added an intercalary month, the bhikṣus should simply rely on their own *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) to receive the *kaṭhina*; they do not follow the king’s legal system.
If the Saṃgha is divided, the faction of the Dharma should act;
if both groups together perform the *kaṭhina* ceremony, the faction of the Dharma should receive the resulting offerings.
What kind of cloth-material is suitable for performing the *kaṭhina* ceremony?
If one obtains many robes during the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), one should take one of them as the *kaṭhina* robe and distribute the remainder according to one's wish.

It must be a new robe that has already been washed and dyed, one that has never been worn, and not a robe given as an urgent offering; it must be one of these: a *saṃghāṭī*, an *uttarāsaṅga*, or an *antarvāsa*. Among these, at least one must be fully completed.
If one has not yet mastered the technique, it is improper to stretch [the cloth]; five cubits or more shall constitute what is in accordance with the Dharma.

If the material is coarse or thin; if it is used for covering a corpse during transport; if it is made of leaves, bark strips, or similar materials; if it has been worn previously; if it is an object subject to the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if it is torn, softened by wear, or has been patched—none of these should be stretched.
If it is obtained on the fifteenth day and has already been completed, one may also make it into the *kaṭhina* robe.
Who are those who together spread the *kaṭhina*?
They are those within the same boundary (*sīmā*) who are virtuous bhikṣus, who collectively accept the robe, as well as those who have granted their consent (*chanda*).
There are ten kinds of persons with whom it is not appropriate to share the *kaṭhina* robe:
first, those who have not completed the summer retreat;
second, those who have broken the summer retreat.
3. Those who enter the later retreat;
4. Those who enter the retreat in another location;
5. Those who are not present at the time of the spreading of the robes.
Sixth, one who practices the *parivāsa* probation;
seventh, one whose *parivāsa* probation is completed;
eighth, one who practices the *mānāpya* penance.
9. One who has completed the stage of mental joy;
10. One undergoing training (*śaikṣa*).

Furthermore, there are ten persons who receive material benefits but do not obtain spiritual benefit; that is, by substituting the previously mentioned fourth person with one who is a *śrāmaṇera*, these constitute ten persons.

There are five kinds of persons who obtain neither benefit nor advantage: namely, the three types of persons subject to suspension, those who observe the rains retreat elsewhere, and those belonging to the faction of illegality when the Saṃgha is schismatic.
What constitutes benefit? There are ten kinds:
first, one may keep an extra robe for more than ten days;
2. One may keep extra robes for more than one month;
3. One may stay overnight separated from one's robes;
4. One may travel to various places while possessing only the two upper and lower robes.
5. One may possess many sets of the three robes;
6. one may accept food from a separate group;
7. one may accept food by passing it around;
8. One may go and eat by oneself without having been invited;
9. One may enter a village at improper times without announcing one's intention;
10. One may receive food at will from a family whose wealth has been exhausted by the Dharma.

From the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the first month is the period for the distribution of robes; however, one obtains the full benefit simply by spreading out the robe, and it does not constitute a violation of the training rule.
How should this *kaṭhina* robe be relinquished?
On the fifteenth day of the first month, the person who spread the robe should address the assembly, saying:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Tomorrow I shall bring forth the *kaṭhina* robe; each of you, venerable sirs, should maintain your own robes.
When the following day arrived, the entire Saṃgha assembled, and they brought it forth by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
If one hears that bandits are approaching and fears being plundered, one may take out the *kaṭhina* robe even if the time limit has not yet arrived.
If there are valuable items, they should likewise be distributed immediately.
There are eight fundamental reasons for taking out the *kaṭhina* robe.
What are the eight? The summary verse says:
First, departing after resolving; departing while undecided; being certain of departure; and losing one's robe.
"Having heard [of] departure, one departs from the boundary with doubt; when hope is severed, those of like mind depart together.

Regarding the phrase "one who has definitely departed and lost the robe," this refers to a bhikṣu who has no lingering attachment to this place, desires to go to another region with no intention of returning, and has made a firm resolve to leave the boundary.

This refers to the indeterminate loss of robes: that is, if a bhikṣu goes beyond the boundary to seek robes, whether he has not yet made them, or has already made half of them; and regarding these acquired materials and his place of residence, whether he feels attachment or lacks attachment, or whether he has expectations or lacks expectations, intending to return again to make the robes, or if he gives rise to such a doubt.

Regarding those who have definitely lost their robes, it is as previously described; however, the distinction here is that one who says, "I am now going away and will not return, nor can I make a *cīvara*," is one who has lost the robes through departure. This refers to one who goes outside the boundary to make a *cīvara*, and while beginning the work, the robes are subsequently lost.

Regarding "one who hears [the robe] being sent out and loses it": this refers to one who has gone outside the boundary to seek a robe and hears from afar that the community is sending out the *kaṭhina* robe, and thus feels sympathetic joy.
Regarding "one who goes outside the boundary and suspects losing it":
this refers to a bhikṣu who thinks to himself, "If my robe is not finished, shall I return or not?"
If one gives rise to such a thought and then crosses the boundary, the [robe] is lost.

Regarding "losing the robe through the severance of hope": if one originally intends to go beyond the boundary to obtain cloth for making a robe, but upon reaching that place, fails to find any cloth and the hope for obtaining it is completely severed, the robe is thereby lost.

Regarding "those who share the same intention in giving out the robe": this refers to when a bhikṣu goes outside the boundary to seek a robe and later returns to the monastery; those with the same intention then collectively give it out. This is explained briefly here; the details are clarified extensively in the section on the *kaṭhina* robe.
If the community has been split, this group must spread the *kaṭhina* robe and then emerge together with that group in harmony.
Generally, for a community of *bhikṣus* who spread the *kaṭhina* robe, they obtain its benefits for five months;
for those who do not spread the robe, the benefit lasts for one month.
For what reason is this robe called *kaṭhina*? It signifies that which is firm, solid, and exquisite.

However, because the great assembly relinquishes and maintains the robes and so forth, it is able to bear [the burden] such that no transgression occurs; since it possesses this functional power, it is called "firm and solid. Alternatively, it is so named because the substance of this robe is exquisite.

Regarding "extra robes" (*atireka-cīvara*): this refers to any robes obtained in addition to those formally maintained, provided their substance is pure and they are subject to formal distribution (*vibhaṅga*).
Regarding "up to ten days": this sets the limit at ten days.
Regarding the "keeping of robes," this refers to the thirteen types of requisite robes: first, the *saṃghāṭī*;
second, the *uttarāsaṅga*; [and so forth].
3. The *antarvāsa*; 4. The *niṣīdana*; 5. The lower garment (*śāṭī*).
6. The inner robe; 7. The saṃkakṣikā; 8. The uttarāsaṅga for the saṃkakṣikā.
9. A towel for wiping the body;
10. A towel for wiping the face;
11. A garment for shaving the hair.
12. The wound-covering cloth;
13. The medicine-value cloth.
These various cloths are each to be formally designated by name and maintained by speaking thus to a single bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir, please take note!
I, the bhikṣu [name], now formally accept this saṃghāṭī robe; it has been made into a finished garment and is for my personal use."
Thus he said a second and a third time; even regarding robes purchased with the price of medicine, it is the same.
If one obtains an unwashed, undyed, or uncut material to temporarily count as a robe, one should maintain its status in this way:
"Venerable one, please attend to me!..."
I, the bhikṣu [name], now take formal possession of this robe-cloth; I shall make it into a nine-panel saṃghāṭī robe with two long panels and one short panel.
If no obstacles arise, I shall wash, dye, cut, and sew it, and it shall be for my personal use.
Thus it was repeated a second and a third time; the same applies to the other two [robes].
If no bhikṣu is present, the formal maintenance [of the robes] is accomplished by addressing the other four assemblies.
If one has a reason to relinquish the three robes, one should relinquish them before a single bhikṣu in this manner:
"Venerable sir, please take note!
I, the bhikṣu [name], this saṃghāṭī robe was previously my formally maintained robe; I now relinquish it.
Thus one should say three times; the other two robes are to be treated accordingly.
If long-haired garments or heavy, bulky items cannot be properly maintained, those with short hair should be maintained and used.

If the hair is long and the item is heavy, one should use it by maintaining the mental resolve that it has been entrusted to another. When obtaining such heavy items, one should mentally reflect and verbally say:
"This is the property of the donor so-and-so; I use it for his sake."
"There is no need for such discrimination.

To ward off the suffering of cold and to remove the heat, it is permitted to keep coarse and thin materials such as wool, kṛmuka, linen, cotton, and woolen carpets; as well as seats and mats, and all other garments including silk threads and waistbands."

If the three robes become stained with grease or filth on the shoulders, one should replace the fabric at the shoulder area with a patch one and a half cubits long and one span wide, sewing it on along all four edges; when it becomes soiled, it should be removed and washed.
If blood flows from the body, one should provide a garment for wiping the body, which should be washed and dyed frequently;
likewise, it is permitted to keep a rain-bath robe if necessary. Regarding the method for the bag for the three robes:

it should be three cubits in length and one and a half cubits in width. Fold the cloth double and sew it into a bag; stitch both ends closed with an opening in the center. Insert the robes inside the lengthwise fold and drape them over the shoulder; fasten a toggle-strap at the opening to prevent insects from entering.

Whenever one places robes, the three principal robes (tricīvara) should be on top and the other robes below. One should guard them with care as if protecting the skin of one's own body, so that the donor may obtain abundant merit and those who use them may lack for nothing.

As for the method of making the pillow case: it should be four cubits long and two cubits wide, sewn together as a single-layered bag; one may also fill the interior with cotton wool, sheep’s wool, or similar materials, and then sew it closed to be used for supporting the head.

The method for making a mosquito net is as follows: it should be twelve cubits in circumference, with a canopy fixed at the top; four corner poles are erected according to the height of the body and secured with straps.
Those who possess only the three robes are permitted to keep a washing skirt; even if it is not formally consecrated through ritual possession (*dhāraṇa*), there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu possesses any extra robes that ought to be formally designated—whether they be finished garments or unfinished ones—he should designate them by forming the intention of entrustment before his ācārya or upādhyāya.

Whether it be another person of high standing or a fellow practitioner of the holy life, it is virtuous to entrust [one's belongings] to someone whose observance of the precepts, learning, and virtuous qualities exceed one’s own.
It should be stated as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me!
I, the bhikṣu [name], possess this extra robe which has not yet been formally designated; it is appropriate that it be so designated."
"I now make this distinction before my upādhyāya; since the upādhyāya acts as the trustee, I now hold it.
A second and third time, he spoke thus.
Even if the person to whom one entrusts [the robes] should happen to be beyond the great ocean, it is not an offense to perform the formal distribution (*vibhāga*) on their behalf from afar.
When performing the distribution, one should not do so in the presence of that entrusted person; rather, one should perform the distribution together with others.

The person to whom the items have been entrusted should not take those separately designated objects; furthermore, after the death of the person who made the entrustment, they should not see the community taking the robes and dividing them as the property of the deceased—this is the prescribed procedure.
This act of entrustment is not a formal ritual; even if the person to whom it is entrusted has passed away, the entrustment remains valid and distinct until one hears of their death.
Once one has heard of their death, one should designate another person as the trustee. The original trustee should not say "I request [this]," nor should they inform anyone of this.
If there are extra lengths of five-piece or seven-piece robes, they must all be distributed.
However, an extra *saṃghāṭī* should not be distributed; it may be kept as it is for the sake of benefiting others.
This means that if one sees a person receiving full ordination who lacks a *saṃghāṭī*, one should give it to them.
The reason the Buddha commanded the bhikṣus to distinguish [and allocate] robes was to prevent two kinds of faults:

the fault of surplus and excess if they were not distinguished, and the fault of deficiency if their possession were not permitted. This is so as to distinguish them from laypeople and non-Buddhist practitioners.
In keeping extra robes, one must understand five matters:
first, clarifying the person who keeps them;
second, clarifying the place from which they are received.
Third, explaining avoidance and pursuit;
fourth, explaining relinquishment;
fifth, explaining enjoyment.
Regarding those who may keep [extra robes]: whom did the Buddha permit to keep long-term extra robes?

It refers to those with few material gains; or those who have been accustomed to pleasure since birth; or those who have fallen from the heavens of their own inclination; or those whose bodies suffer much illness; or those with much grease and grime; or those with many lice; or those living in places of much cold or heat; or those engaged in manual labor; or those who by nature have a great fondness for playing with clothing.
Because the practice of keeping an extra robe (*aticīvara*) enables one to maintain mindfulness, such a person is called a "keeper.
Regarding the phrase "the place of receiving":
even if one is a renunciant or a householder who, though currently poor, is by nature inclined toward generosity, one should not beg from them.
Even if someone brings an offering to give, one should not accept it, for fear that they will fall into want.
One should not accept the gift of a person who is insane; however, if one knows that the parents are still living, one may accept it.

If persons who are deceitful, addicted to gambling, fond of fighting, thieves, butchers, or *caṇḍālas* should come with offerings to give, one must not accept them; for such acts invite much censure and ruin pure faith.
What kind of clothing and garments should a bhikṣu accept?
As for expensive fur robes (*kambala*), the Saṃgha should possess them; other fur robes, cloaks, and mantles may be accepted by a bhikṣu.
However, if he is in a central land, various leather garments, furs, and skins such as those of bears and brown bears must not be possessed.
There is no offense in using items belonging to others.
One may use mats made of processed leather; furthermore, in frontier regions, it is permitted for bhikṣus to use various types of leather.
When making leather footwear, the sole should consist of only a single layer; if the sole becomes worn through, it should be repaired.
Where exactly are the border regions?
To the east they extend to the Bhaṇḍagāra forest; to the west, to the two villages of Sūtunnu; to the south, to the Carmaṇvatī River; and to the north, to Mount Uśīra.
The summary verse says:
To the east, the Bhaṇḍagāma forest; to the west, the two Tuna villages;
to the south, the Vārakārī river; to the north, Mount Usīra.
That which lies outside these boundaries is called a borderland (*pratyantaka*), while that within is called the central region (*madhyadeśa*).
If one obtains bear skin from a hunter in a borderland, it may be accepted without offense.

It should be placed beneath the door of the Buddha hall for the bhikṣus to sit upon, or it may be used regularly by treading upon it to improve one's eyesight; thus the Noble One has permitted its use.
If one obtains a leather bedding in a layperson’s home, for the sake of benefiting the donor, one should sit upon it but not lie down.
However, if one suffers from hemorrhoids or blurred vision, it is permitted to take a bear skin; one should sit upon its fur, as this can alleviate the ailment.
Originally, for the sake of the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, single-layered leather sandals were permitted in the Middle Kingdom;
however, because of the mahallaka bhikṣus, they were again prohibited;
and now, for the purpose of protecting bedding, they are once more permitted.
If the soles are multiple layers thick, it is not an offense to have laypeople wear them before using them oneself.

However, if leather sandals have thick soles that make a sound when stepped upon, or if they are shaped like ram’s horns or various flowers and leaves, or if they are embroidered with colorful patterns—these were all prohibited while at Vaiśālī.
Furthermore, one should not use the hides of elephants, horses, lions, tigers, leopards, jackals, or wolves; nor is it appropriate to use the sinews of these animals for sewing objects.
Regarding all footwear, whether it be sandals with a cloth covering at the front or back, none are permissible;
nor should one wear leather shoes that expose the toes.
However, in countries of cold snow, one should wear *puṭra* (boots).

In cold countries where ice freezes into glacial ridges, one may wear wooden clogs when in the monastery at places for the large and small needs; if wearing them in a layperson's home, there is likewise no offense.
If they are coarse straw sandals or sandals made of bamboo leaves, one should not wear them at all.
However, if a bhikṣu suffers from a disease involving heat or blood in his thighs or legs, he may wear sandals of grass.

If a skillful bhikṣu wishes to mend his own shoes, he should do so in a secluded place so as not to be seen by others; he is permitted to keep tools such as awls and knives for this purpose without offense. This is called the "scope of acceptance."
Regarding "avoiding and resorting": if one possesses the three robes as well as other garments, they should be properly protected.

One must not place these robes in locations where they might be eaten by insects or ants, chewed by cattle, gnawed by rats, where cliffs are about to collapse, or where they might be consumed by fire, blown away by wind, soaked by water, or stolen by bandits. In such places, one should never leave the robes.
If the *āraṇa* (woolen cloak) is of high value or of middling quality, one should not keep it; rather, it should be kept within the village and dried in the sun upon bitter leaves from time to time.
One should not stay overnight in a room that lacks door panels or where no other bhikṣus are present.
If one does not take the *saṃghāṭī* (outer robe), one should not go outside.
There are five causes and conditions by which it is permitted to leave the *saṃghāṭī* behind:
first, when there are bhikṣus present at the location and the door has panels.
2. Doubting that it will rain;
3. Fearing capsizing while crossing a river;
4. Being during the period of the *kaṭhina* robe.
5. The Method for Being Separated from One’s Robes.
If the seams or edges of a robe are torn or damaged, one should patch them with cloth or bind them with thread.

When wearing robes, one must not let the body fall heavily while sitting on rough, hard ground, wood, stone, or refuse heaps where there is no seating material. Instead, one should prepare a wooden block and rub it smooth, or fashion a bundle of grass wrapped in cloth; using these as seats of appropriate size according to one’s convenience.
When performing manual labor, one must carefully protect oneself so as not to let mud or dirt soil the robes.
When walking through places with thorns and brambles, one should lift the hems of the robes to prevent them from being torn or damaged.
If one fails to wash what should be washed, or fails to sew or dye what should be sewn or dyed, in each case one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

One should not perform manual labor while wearing the *saṃghāṭī*; one should not walk on a road while wearing it; one should not sit with it wrapped around the body nor lie down while wearing it; and one should not wear it while naked.
When prostrating, do not let the robes brush the ground.
Do not wrap the knees, nor sit or lie upon the two lower garments.
If no other object is available, it is permitted to use them as a cushion for sitting or lying; there is no offense.
However, when lying down to sleep, one should sleep little and remain awake much; furthermore, one should not lie down haphazardly in any place.
If there is frequent involuntary discharge during dreams, one should cover the body with clothing and fasten it so that it does not slip off.
One should not leave one's robes in an impure place.
If there are laypeople present, a bhikṣu should not carry his own clothing; furthermore, he must not casually wear a long-haired woolen cloak (*kambala*).
If there are many lice and nits, one should replace them with another garment.
One should frequently inspect the clothes one wears and entrust one's garments to a place where they can be safely kept; this is called "avoiding and resorting."

Regarding "renunciation": if a person by nature is fond of many robes, they should discard everything beyond the three robes (*tricīvara*). Because the craving for fine garments disturbs the mind and because it increases attachment that obstructs the eye of the Path, one should wear rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*).
Those who are fond of fine, smooth garments should wear felt and woolen robes.

Those who wear rag-robes (pāṃśukūla) and those who dwell in charnel grounds (śmaśāna) should not make use of excellent items belonging to the Saṃgha, such as fine cloaks, variegated rugs, and the like.
Anyone wearing a shroud must not enter a monastery nor prostrate before a caitya.

If they wish to circumambulate and pay homage, they should remain at a distance of one *vyāma*. Furthermore, they must not use the bedding of the Saṃgha, nor join the assembly, nor preach the Dharma to laypeople, nor enter the homes of the laity.
If it is necessary to go there, one should remain outside the gate until the host calls one in, and should say to them:
"I dwell in the charnel ground. If they say:
"You may come. One should enter at will; however, unless invited to sit, one should not take a seat.
A bhikṣu who does not wear patched robes or fasten them with buttons and loops should not enter a village, except in cases of unavoidable circumstances.
If one enters the dwelling of a renunciant from a non-Buddhist sect, there is no offense provided the garment is not cut.
Furthermore, one must not enter a village or the house of a layperson with a skirt that is not fastened with a cord; this is termed "abandonment."
Regarding "enjoyment," at the time of placing [the robe] and while using it, one should give rise to this thought:
"In relation to this robe, my mind delights in reducing conditions; I shall sustain this physical life and cultivate all categories of wholesome qualities."
"This is not something accomplished by my own power; it is the robe of a donor. For the benefit of both myself and others, I shall guard and use it.
This is called "enjoyment.
As stated above, those who do not act in accordance with this will all incur an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

It is said that one may possess an extra robe for up to ten days without having formally designated it; if one possesses it beyond this period, it means that a bhikṣu has obtained an extra robe and neither designated nor consecrated it, such that when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, this is called "possessing it beyond the limit."
Regarding the term *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*: the object must be relinquished and the offense must be confessed.
What constitutes the offense?
It means that if on the first day of the month one obtains a single robe or many robes, by the tenth day they must be formally assigned, formally maintained, or discarded.
If it were not so, then upon the appearance of the dawn on the eleventh day, one would incur the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one obtains a robe on the first day of the month, and again obtains a robe on the second day, continuing in this manner until obtaining a robe on the tenth day.

If one does not perform the formal distribution (*vibhaṅga*) of a robe on the first day, then any robes subsequently obtained, as well as miscellaneous items—even down to alms-bowl bags, waist-straps, and so forth—will all constitute an offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) by the eleventh day, because the continuity of defilement from the previously acquired robe persists;
this should be understood to apply analogously for the second, third, and subsequent days.
What is defined as the minimum measure for a *naiḥsargika* robe?
It is that which measures one cubit in both length and width.

If one has already made a formal determination (*vibhakta*) regarding a robe but then perceives it as not yet determined (*avibhakta*), one incurs only a *pāyantika* offense and need not relinquish the robe, because there is no matter requiring disciplinary action in this case.
If one keeps robes for the sake of the Triple Gem, there is no offense.
Or, at times, a donor may say: "This is my property;
you, O virtuous one, should make use of it."
Although one does not perform the formal distribution (*vibhāga*), there is no offense in using it.
However, if one forms this thought:
"This robe shall remain until a certain day, at which time I shall perform the distribution," or "I shall perform the distribution by the tenth day," [there is no offense].
Regarding this, there is no offense in the interim.
If one does not form the intention to set a limit, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) every day.
There is no offense for one who does not remember [the transgression].

Whether one's mind is entangled by many afflictions and lustful attachments, or is characterized by ignorance, or lethargy, or by mental negligence such that one fails to exercise discernment—all such persons incur the fundamental offense.
If a garment contains a mixture of woolen threads and camel hair, after ten days have passed, one incurs only a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) because it is impure.

In all cases where an object subject to *naiḥsargika* forfeiture has already been forfeited, or has been eaten by insects or ants, or has been blown away or burned, or has otherwise been lost or destroyed, one need only confess the offense; there is no substance remaining to be relinquished.
In other training rules (*śikṣāpada*), one should understand it by analogy with this.
There is no offense if a garment among those kept for ten days is lost;

or if at times the material is so small that it does not measure even one cubit (*hasta*); or if one is deaf or blind and thus does not hear or see [the lapse]; or if it is one's own property entrusted to another; or if one has the perception that it has not yet been obtained.
In all these cases, there is no offense.
If one becomes insane immediately after obtaining the robe, the five-day period is extended once the mind is restored.
Other points regarding their application or non-application should be considered according to the specific circumstances.

2. The Training Rule on Being Separated from the Three Robes. This second training rule was established when the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣus entrusted their robes to others and wandered about as they pleased wearing only their upper and lower garments; thus, they failed to properly protect themselves, and those who received the entrusted robes became preoccupied with many affairs.
Because the underlying affliction regarding the separation from one’s robes is the same as before, this training rule was established:

"If a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the *kaṭhina* robe has been suspended, and he stays overnight—even for a single night—outside the boundary separated from any one of the three robes, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

"If, moreover, a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the kaṭhina robe is then suspended, is it possible that there be a bhikṣu who, although he has finished making his three robes, the kaṭhina is not suspended?"
This should be formulated as four propositions, as fully detailed in the extensive text.

Regarding the three robes—namely the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, and the antarvāsaka—one incurs an offense only if one separates oneself from these after having formally undertaken their custody; as for the other ten items, although they are likewise formally undertaken, there is no offense in staying apart from them overnight.
Regarding the specific details therein: if one does not carry a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), one should not go to stay overnight at another monastery.
If there are obstructing circumstances, one should borrow one to lie upon, or otherwise use an *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe) as a proper substitute for lying down.
If one goes to a secluded place during the day, or goes out for alms, or intends to return on the same day, there is no offense.

An offense here occurs when one goes outside the boundary without taking the robe and does not return, such that the appearance of dawn (the *abhilakṣaṇa*) passes; one incurs the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
There are three ways of being separated from one's robe:
first, separation by means of depositing it elsewhere;
second, separation through loss of mindfulness.
Third, separation through use.

Regarding "separation by being lifted from its place," this refers to when one's robe is lifted while in a location with obstructions or difficulties such that it cannot be re-examined, or due to loss or misplacement.
Regarding "separation through loss of mindfulness," it refers to no longer recollecting the location where one's robes were placed.
Regarding "separation through use," it means that as soon as the robes have been temporarily set aside, one encounters circumstances that create an obstacle, preventing their use.
Even if one is separated from one's robe, there is no offense provided that the robe is recovered before the appearance of dawn.
When a bhikṣu has a reason to enter a village, he should carry a robe made of cut pieces;
however, if he does not enter a village, there is no offense if he does not carry one.

Regarding the exemption from the formal ritual (karmavācanā): by virtue of the noble Śāriputra and Mahākāśyapa, the Great Assembly permitted those who are separated from their saṃghāṭī robes due to the Dharma, or those who, being physically weak, aged, or ill, lack the strength to wear them, to depart without committing an offense.

Regarding the locus of offense herein: it refers to a single house, a village, and so forth. This means when mountain-dwellers or forest-dwellers live together in a single row of houses, the entire interior of these rooms, together with an area extending one fathom (vyāma) outside, constitutes its "sphere of influence" (sīmā).
This is based on the common practice;
as for other specific cases, they shall be described below.
If there are two rows of dwellings, the procedure is likewise the same.

Regarding "a village of many houses" (*bahugrha-grāma*): this refers to a place where houses are scattered without order at their entrances; the boundary is determined according to each individual house, as there is no common area.
Regarding "an enclosed village" (*prākāra-grāma*): up to what point does its boundary extend?
This refers to the area where a bamboo cart drawn by six oxen can turn around, or the distance from which a chicken can fly and drop its dung.
As for an enclosed village with fences and hedges, up to what point does its sphere of influence extend?
This refers to the places reached by the dust kicked up by the hooves of cattle and sheep when they enter, or the areas where people of conscience perform their bodily functions.
As for a village with moats and ditches, how far does its jurisdiction extend?
This refers to places reached by a twelve-fathom ladder, or places reached by coarse bricks or stones when refuse is being discarded.
If a bhikṣu resides within the jurisdiction of a village and his robe is worn within the village, or conversely, it constitutes no offense.
If it were otherwise, and the body and the robe were in different locations, one would incur a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) before the appearance of light;
at the moment the appearance of light occurs, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding "one village having one *sīmā* (boundary)": this refers to a case where within that village there is a single grove, a single assembly hall, and a single temple site.
The case of many villages sharing a single *śakti-bhāga* (boundary division) is also the same as before.

Regarding one village having many *śakti-bhāgas*, this refers to a village that has many gardens, groves, and so forth, where the gates serve as common points of access; the case of many villages having many *śakti-bhāgas* is likewise the same as before.
Among these, the specific distinctions refer to places that are not shared.
One should understand that there are twelve such places:
homes, shops, stalls, towers, courtyards, halls, as well as the dwellings of non-Buddhists, venues for music and performance, vehicles, boats, or groves of trees; these should be understood.

Regarding the following twelve matters, they are to be assigned in sequence to their respective locations: the door, the seat, the bed, the ladder, the pillar, the gate, the temple, the banner, the place, the carriage-seat, the rudder, and the well; these, along with the base of a tree, constitute the common sites.
Each of these has four propositions that should be considered according to the specific circumstances.

If there is a single head of the household, or if brothers have not divided their property, this location is termed a "single jurisdiction" (*ekasīmā*); if it differs from this, it is termed a "multiple jurisdiction" (*anekasīmā*).
If those of external paths view a single entity as having one spatial extent (*ekādhikaraṇa*), then by reversing this, it becomes many.
When tree branches intersect, they are said to have one spatial extent; by reversing this, they become many.
Regarding the distinction between the extent of a threshing floor and that of a tree: the area reached by the chaff during winnowing constitutes the extent of the threshing floor.
The area covered by the shadow at midday on the summer solstice, the area where leaves fall in the absence of wind, and the area reached by raindrops constitute the extent of the tree.
A "stall" (*pū*) refers to a place where various incense and goods are sold.
A "shop" (*dian*) refers to a place where merchandise and goods are stored; the rest is as explained in the extensive text.

If a bhikṣu resides in two places while his robes are on both sides, or if his robes are in two places while he resides in a different location, one should understand—according to the sequence—that there may be no offense, or there may be an offense, and that it may be light or heavy, based on the specific circumstances.

If one is within the boundary for ritual robes (*karmabhūmi-cīvara-sīmā*) but the body and the robe are in different locations, or if they are situated on opposite sides of an open space, these are all termed "separation from the robe" (*cīvara-vipravāsa*).

If there is no robe-boundary at the residence of a bhikṣu, the area extending up to the walls, fences, and so forth constitutes the "sphere of influence" (*pradeśa*). When traveling on a road, this extends to forty-nine *vyāma*; when standing, sitting, or lying down, it is one *vyāma* in circumference. This is its sphere of influence.
If one lies down across two boundaries, provided that even the corner of one’s robe does not leave the body, it is not termed "losing the robe.
