**The Training Rule on the One-Month Garment (Māsa-cīvara-śikṣāpada), the Third.** At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, many bhikṣus kept extra robes for a month or even longer than that, thereby neglecting their cultivation of the primary practice. Because of the matter of fulfilling expectations, the afflictions were the same as before, and thus this training rule was established.

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and the kaṭhina robe has been suspended, and he obtains an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara), he may accept it if he needs it; having accepted it, he should quickly have it made into a robe. If there is a source from which he hopes to obtain more to complete it, and it is insufficient, he may keep it for up to one month."
"If one exceeds [this limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the acquisition of out-of-season robes: the five-month period and the one-month period are called the "robe season"; anything other than this is termed "out of season."
If one obtains a robe during the proper time, there is no offense provided it is not subject to formal distribution.
During the improper time, if the robe is insufficient and there is another source from which more may be expected, one should seek it so that it becomes sufficient.
"One who should receive" refers to one who is permitted to keep [the robe] at the appropriate time.

"One who has expectations" means one who thinks, regarding friends, preceptors (*ācārya*), and so forth, or at a quinquennial assembly (*pañcavārṣika*) and the like, "I shall obtain a robe," or "I may exchange it at some time."
If it is insufficient, one thinks, "I am short by this much clothing; I shall seek to fulfill it.

If a bhikṣu, on the first day of the month, obtains cloth of blue, yellow, or other colors that is sufficient according to the Dharma, yet does not make a robe because he gives rise to a further hope, thinking, "When I obtain another similar item, I shall then complete the robe."
Alternatively, if there is no expectation [of obtaining more], there is no offense during the ten-day period; however, upon reaching the eleventh day, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If the requirement is not yet fulfilled, one may continue until the end of the month.
If one exceeds this limit, one incurs a *naiḥsargika* offense.
If, within ten days, one’s hope for obtaining the expected garment is completely severed, then upon exceeding ten days, one commits an offense.
There are two kinds of robes:
1. Unworn clothing: this refers to new clothing. 2. Worn clothing:
this refers to clothing that has already been used at any one of the three [seasonal] periods.

If one has obtained these two types of robes but their full measure has not yet been reached, and one keeps them for more than one month without performing the formal distribution (*vibhāga*), one incurs an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

**The Fourth Training Rule: On Having an Unrelated Nun Wash a Used Robe** The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the bhikṣu Udāyin had his lower garment stained with semen; he gave it to two nuns, Guptā and another, who were unrelated to him, and ordered them to wash it. They took the impurity and placed it inside their female organs and even into their mouths. With the same causal events and afflictions as before, the Buddha established this training rule.
"If a bhikṣu should have a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or beat a used robe, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
This was established to eliminate the affliction of sexual desire and to prevent her from neglecting her proper duties; therefore, it is permitted for a relative bhikṣuṇī to perform the washing.

Furthermore, it was to prevent the fault of public censure and because frequenting women repeatedly causes one's own afflictions to increase and intensify; for these various faults, he established the rule prohibiting [contact with] those who are not relatives.
Regarding the term "non-kin," it refers to those who do not belong to one's own kinship group.

Regarding the term "kin," it refers to all members of one's family lineage tracing back seven generations from one's grandparents; these are all designated as kin, while anyone other than these is considered non-kin.
Regarding the term "bhikṣuṇī," it refers to one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*), and not to other lower classes of the community;
all other training rules (*śikṣāpada*) should be understood in this same way.

Regarding the term "old garment," it refers to a garment that has already been worn and is maintained as such; the offense is incurred only when the substance of the garment conforms to the pure dharma.

If one is old or sick and lacks strength, or if a bhikṣuṇī out of respect for their virtue and seniority is willing to wash them, or if it is their own disciple, there is no offense in any of these cases.
However, if one causes [a bhikṣuṇī] to wash woolen rugs or bedding, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
Regarding "washing": even dipping it once in water constitutes what is called washing.

Regarding having it washed or dyed when it is soiled with mud: even a single immersion in dye or a single strike with the hand constitutes the act. If one who is not a relative is perceived as such, or if there is doubt about their status, and one has them wash, dye, or strike the garment, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one actually is a relative but perceives them as not being a relative, or is in doubt about it, and causes them to wash, dye, or beat [the robe], one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) in each case.
If, after the robe has been given, the nun undergoes a change of gender or returns to lay life, she incurs a *sāmantaka-dukkaṭa* (preparatory wrongdoing).
If one causes a nun who is not a relative to wash by means of a nun who is a relative, one also incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one intends to wash this garment but mistakenly washes another garment instead, one incurs only a *pāyattika* offense; there is no rule for forfeiture in this case.
Whenever one observes a disciple committing an improper act and fails to stop them, the teacher also incurs an offense because of failing to provide correct instruction.

Regarding those cases where there is no offense: if it concerns the property or robes of the Triple Gem; or if one causes a nun who is a relative to wash them; or if one washes them oneself at the appropriate time; or if the preceptor (upādhyāya) washes them; or if an upāsaka or upāsikā washes them; or if one causes a nun who is either a relative or not a relative to wash them—in all these instances, there is no offense.
There are four distinctions regarding having another person wash one's clothes:
first, not washing them at all; second, washing them only slightly; [third, washing them moderately; fourth, washing them thoroughly].
Third is washing well;
fourth is over-washing.
Thus, dyeing and beating likewise each have four distinctions; one should understand that the gravity of the offense follows the specific circumstances of the act.
There are five types of dyestuffs, namely: roots, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
However, there are two distinctions regarding improper colors:
the first refers to the eight kinds of primary colors.
What are these? The verse says: Realgar, madder, saffron, Cinnabar, indigo, and red lac.
The eight colors, including yellow ocher and *sūfaṅga*, are such that a bhikṣu should not use them to dye his robes.
The second category refers to deep crimson and light crimson.
If one wears these two colors out of a desire for ornamentation, it is entirely impure; one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

If there is a donor who gives rise to a mind of reverence and offers a robe of great color, the bhikṣu should use another dye to neutralize that great color; wearing it in this manner constitutes no offense.
When putting on clothes, one should abandon three kinds of thoughts and give rise to five kinds of thoughts.
As for the three kinds:
first, the thought of delighting in adornment;
2. A mind that treats [the requisites] with contempt;

3. A mind that seeks fame through hypocrisy—the latter refers to falsely wearing tattered robes, desiring others to know him as one of virtue and conduct, in the hope of attracting profit and reputation.

These three kinds of thoughts should all not be entertained; rather, one should seek only to change the color of the robes, obtain enough to sustain the body, comply with the Great Teacher’s instructions, and advance in the cultivation of wholesome qualities.
As for the five kinds of thoughts, they are: first, knowing the proper measure;
second, knowing the intervals.
3. Knowledge of reflection;
4. Knowledge of time;
5. Knowledge of number.

Regarding "knowing the proper measure": when using clothing, one should know its degree of newness or wear and use it accordingly; one should pull gently and slowly so as not to cause damage, for such items are difficult to obtain later.

Regarding "knowing the intervals": one should not constantly wear the same garment repeatedly, for it will become foul-smelling and quickly torn; rather, one may use them in alternation. Regarding "reflective examination":

one should constantly reflect that the origin of this robe was extremely difficult to obtain; since it did not come from the strength of one's own arms but was bestowed by others, one should cultivate a mind of gratitude and ensure that when using it, one does not engage in unrighteous conduct.

Regarding "knowing the proper time": when cold or heat are appropriate to the season, one should enjoy them in moderation. If one acts contrary to the seasons, one harms both oneself and others. To harm oneself means to fail to benefit one's own person; to harm others means that merit will not increase.

Regarding "knowing the measure": one obtains the thirteen requisites sufficient to sustain the body; to store them in great quantities or seek them out increases greed and causes the abandonment of one's practice.
The summary verse says:
Know the measure, know the intervals, Reflect and examine, and recognize the proper time.
Knowing the number [of robes], one should use them in a way that benefits both oneself and others.

If a robe requires washing, one may wash it oneself, or have a disciple, a layman (*upāsaka*), a laywoman (*upāsikā*), or a trustworthy washerman do so; one must not be careless, causing damage to the robe.
There are five benefits to washing and laundering clothes:
they eliminate foul odors; lice and nits do not breed; the body is free from itching; they can properly take dye; and they are fit for long-term use.
To not wash one's robes results in five disadvantages.
There are likewise five benefits to wearing dyed robes:

because they accord with the physical appearance and deportment of the Noble Ones; because they cause one to abandon arrogance; because they do not receive dust and grime; because lice and nits do not breed upon them; and because they are soft to the touch and easy to maintain.
There are five kinds of faults in excessively washing clothes:
they cause them to wear out quickly; they become unfit for hard work; they involve mental toil in their use; they are a useless burden of labor; and they obstruct various wholesome qualities.
Wearing well-dyed robes also involves five faults:

because it increases one's own arrogance and indulgence while giving rise to envy in others; because it causes others to perceive one as having a cultivated appearance and beautiful complexion; because it causes much toil and hardship when seeking them; because it obstructs the cultivation of wholesome qualities; and because excessive dyeing damages the robe, rendering its use unreliable.
If one beats [the cloth] excessively, there are likewise five faults: four are the same as before, and the fifth is that beating it too much damages the cloth so that its utility is not durable.
Because the bhikṣu Nanda beat his robe excessively, the Buddha said:
"One who uses a robe should not beat it, nor should they beat it excessively."
If one receives clothing from a donor that has been severely beaten [in the weaving process], and it possesses a fine luster and texture, one should use it after softening it;

yet if it still does not soften, one may place it in the open air and rub it until the luster is lost, or sprinkle it with water and soak it before using it. If using property belonging to the Saṃgha, one should act in the same manner.
Some commentators, based on this, maintain that striking is not permitted at all. Others, however, say:
"If that were so, one would merely prohibit striking; why then specify 'striking excessively'?"
Thus, we know that the prohibition concerns beating [the robe] with a fault, not the act of beating itself.

Furthermore, since it is permitted to send [a robe] for washing, dyeing, and beating, yet prohibits [doing so] with a nun who is not a relative while not obstructing others, we know that there is a sense in which beating the robe is allowed, as previously explained.
Those who do not act accordingly shall all incur the offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) through confession.

The Fifth Training Rule: Taking the Robe of a Nun Who Is Not a Relative. While the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Upānanda took a robe offered by a thief from the bhikṣuṇī Utpalā. As the circumstances were the same as those previously described—namely, the underlying afflictions of public censure and dependence on external conditions—the Buddha established this training rule.
"If a bhikṣu should take a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika. Regarding the term "not a relative":

because one takes a robe from a non-relative bhikṣuṇī for one's own benefit regardless of whether she has them or not, whereas one would harbor a sense of consideration toward a relative, this rule was established to prohibit taking from a non-relative.

Except for trade—whether exchanging robes, whether of the same substance or different substances, whether paying the full price, half-price, less, or more, whether of inferior quality, superior quality, or similar items—one may engage in such trade according to the donor's intention; or, observing their intent and out of compassion, one may accept them.
Whether for the sake of repaying kindness, for the sake of merit, or out of a spirit of devotion, receiving [gifts] in these cases constitutes no offense.
Furthermore, even if it is not a formal trade, if one forms the intention, "I shall pay the price," this is likewise termed trade.
If one engages in trade for the sake of ornamentation, with a mind of contempt, or with a deceitful intent, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) in all such cases.
However, if one lacks upper and lower robes, one should accept [the trade].
If one accepts more than this, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the perception of the object and doubt, it is the same as in the preceding training rule (*śikṣāpada*).

Alternatively, if one takes [the robe] without being face-to-face, or takes it by means of a letter or the like, or if the robe is not present before one, in all such cases one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if it is a śrāmaṇerī or a śikṣamāṇā; or if she offers it to the Saṃgha; or if she has developed a sense of deep reverence while listening to the sublime Dharma; or if it is an offering made at the time of her full ordination (upasaṃpadā); or if it is given as payment for goods; or if it is obtained through trade; or if one knows that the nun is a person of great merit and she places the robes and articles before the bhikṣu, saying:
"I have other robes and currently lack nothing; I pray that you will accept these."
Having spoken these words, he leaves the robe and departs.
Whether thinking of it as belonging to a friend or relative, or thinking of it as something for temporary use—receiving such robes in this manner constitutes no offense.

6. The Training Rule on Begging for Robes from Householders and Housewives Who Are Not Relatives. The sixth training rule concerning begging for robes from householders and housewives who are not relatives: When the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Śrāvastī, Upānanda was skilled in preaching the Dharma. Many laymen and laywomen developed deep faith and respect for him; desiring to make offerings, they promised to give him robes.

Having heard these words, he went to that person's house and immediately offered a blessing; however, he then forcibly demanded a robe from him, which gave rise to affliction. This caused the other to become unhappy and led to his own long-term greed. As the circumstances were identical to those previously mentioned, this training rule was established due to the faults of exceeding limits, neglecting duties, and the affliction of being subject to reproach.
"If a bhikṣu should beg for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except at the proper time, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The 'proper time' refers to when a bhikṣu's robes have been snatched away, lost, burned, blown away, or carried off by water; this is the proper time."
Regarding the terms "layman" and "laywoman," these distinguish them from other eunuchs; it means that only when they are men or women does one incur a grave offense (pārājika).
If they are of the class of non-males, those with dual sexual organs, or followers of external paths (tīrthikas), one incurs only a minor offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding "begging," it means either begging for oneself or having another person beg on one's behalf.
Regarding "having one's robe taken away," this refers to being robbed by thieves, or having a robe given by another and subsequently demanding it back.
Regarding "losing one's robe," this refers to its being lost, forgotten where it was placed, or damaged by insects or rats.
Regarding "burning one's robe," this refers to its being consumed by fire or ruined by alkaline ash.
To say "the robe is blown away" means it has been carried off by the wind.
To say "the robe is drifted away" means it is being carried off by water.
There are three different factors regarding a robe: its price, its color, and its dimensions.
Value refers to a price such as five *kārsāpaṇas* and so forth.
Color refers to blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth.
Dimension refers to five cubits (*hasta*) and so forth.
Regarding the offenses herein: if the value and quantity are complete, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of begging, and upon acquisition, the primary offense (*pārājika*).
In cases where one suspects or is uncertain that the person is not a relative, the same principles as stated above should be applied.

Whether manifesting bodily signs, sending letters and the like, reducing the quantity, begging for warp or woof threads, changing the gender at the time of taking possession, uttering flattery, deceiving others, displaying strange appearances, or seeking by means of harsh words—all such acts constitute an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

There is no offense in the following cases: when [the robe] is lost or stolen; when another person offers a robe; when begging for cloth one obtains only a small fragment; when begging for a small fragment but another gives a large piece; when begging for a rain-cloak; when begging for a mosquito net; when begging on behalf of the Saṃgha; or when begging from non-humans or animals. In all such instances, there is no offense.

7. The Training Rule on Begging for Excessive Clothing. This seventh training rule concerning begging for excessive clothing was established by the Buddha while he was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī. Because the six groups of bhikṣus were repeatedly robbed by bandits, they began to beg for upper and lower robes in excessive amounts. As the circumstances of the disturbance were the same as those previously described, this training rule was promulgated.
"If a bhikṣu, having had his robes taken away, lost, burned, blown away, or carried off by water, should beg for robes from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative."
If that person offers many robes and a bhikṣu requires them, he should accept two robes at most—one for the upper body and one for the lower body.
If he accepts more than that, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.

Regarding "giving," this refers to repeated giving, earnest giving, giving with a sincere mind, giving with a deceitful mind, giving with a superior mind, giving with an inferior mind, giving with a specific intention, giving in accordance [with circumstances], giving not in accordance [with circumstances], giving one's own wealth, giving another's wealth, giving in common with others, giving when departing, giving when returning, giving with a mind of anger, giving with a joyful mind, giving through habitual practice, giving without habitual practice, giving by signaling, giving by speaking oneself, giving by sending another, and giving with one's own hand. These various aspects of giving differ according to the state of the donor’s mind.
Giving with compliance, giving with a deceitful mind, or giving with a mind of anger—when one receives [the gift] at such times, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing);
in all other cases, it is the fundamental offense (*pācittiya*). Regarding "upper and lower robes," there are two kinds:
first, the upper and lower robes of a bhikṣu.
The superior [robe] is the *saṃghāṭī*, measuring five cubits in width and three cubits in length;
the inferior is the lower garment (*nivasana*), measuring five cubits in width and two cubits in length.
Second, the upper and lower garments of laypeople.
The superior [measure] is eleven cubits in length and three cubits in width;
the inferior is seven cubits in length and two cubits in width. Some say:
"The lower garments refer to the *nivasana* (skirt) and the *saṃkakṣikā*; the upper garments refer to the three Dharma robes (*tricīvara*).
If one requests upper and lower garments for a bhikṣu, or upper and lower garments for a layperson, there is no offense provided that each is obtained according to the prescribed measurements.
If one seeks more than the proper measure, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of begging;
once it enters one's hand, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one begs for a layperson’s upper and lower robes, even if they are slightly insufficient, one should not beg for more.
If one begs for more than this, one incurs an offense.
If there is any surplus, it need not be returned to the owner.
If the robes for the upper and lower garments requested by a bhikṣu are insufficient, he must beg for more.
If it exceeds [the prescribed length], it must be returned; if it is not returned, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. **The Eighth Training Rule:

Begging for Clothing from a Layperson Who Has Granted Permission.** The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, Upānanda forcibly demanded the price of clothing from a layperson. The donor, feeling constrained and having no choice, purchased the goods and gave them to him. The details of this matter are the same as those previously related.
Out of concern for the afflictions of criticism and resentment arising from exceeding limits and waiting for conditions, this training rule was established:

"If a monk has a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative, and they together provide the price for a robe, intending to buy such a pure robe to give to a specific monk for him to use at the proper time."
This bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation, upon being informed by another, goes to that person's house and speaks thus:
"Excellent, worthy sir!
For the sake of the price for robes prepared for me, you may purchase such pure robes and give them to me at the proper time, so that they may be of good quality."
"If one obtains the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding "the price of the robe," this refers to cowries, gold, or silver.
"Purchases" refers to items obtained through buying, not those obtained by begging.
Regarding the phrase "such a robe," it refers to one worth five *kārsāpaṇas* up to fifty *kārsāpaṇas*, or one that is blue in color and so forth, or five cubits in length up to fifty cubits.
"Pure" refers to items such as camel-hair blankets and the like, because their substance is unfit for use as clothing.
"At the proper time" means either in accordance with the time when a bhikṣu has need of it, or in accordance with the time when a bhikṣu is permitted to keep it.
"Having not previously accepted an invitation" means that one has never before spoken of being invited.
"Excellent, O virtuous one! is a phrase used for praise and exhortation.
"To be fine" means to seek what is superior and grand; that is to say, the price, color, and dimensions are all exquisite.
If one begs for more than the permitted amount, it constitutes an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing); once it enters one's possession, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

If one has already initiated the preparatory effort before full ordination (*upasampadā*), but only acquires the wealth after having been fully ordained, it should be explained according to the preceding rule.
There is no offense if one begs from gods and the like, or if one begs for thread, silk floss, small pieces of cloth, and so forth.

The Ninth Training Rule on Encouraging Others to Make a Robe: "If again a bhikṣu, there are a householder or a householder’s wife who are not relatives, each having prepared the price for a robe, intending to buy such a pure robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu."
This bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation, upon being informed by another, went to that person's house and spoke these words:
"Excellent, worthy sir!
For the sake of the price for robes prepared for me, you may purchase such pure robes and give them to me in a timely manner, so that they may be of good quality."
"If he obtains the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

The basis for this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) and the offense are the same as before; however, the distinction is that while a husband and wife had separately provided the price for two robes, intending each to purchase a superior garment to offer to a bhikṣu, the bhikṣu urged them to combine them into a single robe.

10. The Training Rule on Soliciting Robes Beyond the Limit. This tenth training rule concerning soliciting robes beyond the limit was established when the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī. At that time, a minister of Rājagṛha named Bṛhaspati, having encountered some merchants, sent the price for a robe to Upānanda.
Having heard this, he went to retrieve it and handed it over to another person, yet he continued to demand it back by force.
That person had business requiring him to attend a public assembly; the bhikṣu refused permission, so the man immediately took the price and returned it to him.
Because he departed at an improper time, he violated the communal regulations and was fined sixty *kārsāpaṇas*.

Since taking impure wealth disregards the intentions of others and causes distress, and because the underlying affliction regarding the act of accepting such impure wealth is the same as before, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) is established.
"Furthermore, if a king, a great minister, a brahmin, a householder, or others should send a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to a bhikṣu."
The messenger, carrying the price for the robes, went to the bhikṣu and said:
"Venerable One!
This item has been sent by such-and-such a king, minister, brahmin, or householder, and I have brought it here; Venerable One, out of compassion, please accept it."
The bhikṣu said to that messenger:
"O worthy one!
I ought not to accept this price for robes; however, if I obtain a pure robe appropriate for the season, I shall accept it."
The messenger said: "Venerable sir,
are there any attendants?"
The bhikṣu who needs robes says: "There is;
whether it be a monastery attendant or an upāsaka, this person is the bhikṣu’s steward.
That messenger goes to the steward, gives him the price for the robe, and says:
"You may use this price for robes to purchase a timely, pure robe and give it to the bhikṣu so-and-so, so that he may wear it.
After that messenger has properly instructed the attendant, he returns to the bhikṣu and says:
"Venerable One!..."
"The person in charge you indicated has already been given the price for the robe; you should accept it once you have obtained a pure robe.
If a bhikṣu requires a robe, he should go to the person in charge and, after reminding them two or three times, say:
"I require a robe."
"If he succeeds, it is well. If he does not succeed, he may go to that person up to four, five, or six times, remaining silent wherever he stands.
If he obtains the robe after four, five, or six visits, it is well.
If he does not obtain the robe, and he seeks to obtain it beyond that number of times, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
If, in the end, the robe is not obtained, that bhikṣu should go to the place where the robe-price was sent, either going himself or sending a trustworthy person, and inform them, saying:
"You sent the price for a robe for the sake of such-and-such a bhikṣu, but that bhikṣu did not obtain the robe; you should know this so as not to let this opportunity be lost."
"King" refers to an anointed monarch (*abhiṣikta-rāja*).
"Minister" refers to one who personally assists in the administration of state affairs.
"Brahmin" refers to one of noble lineage.
"Householder" refers to persons of noble rank.
"And so forth" refers to those both inside and outside the city.
As for the statement, "I should not accept this price for the robe," what does "should not" mean?

That is to say, bhikṣus should not perform such actions themselves; nor should they accept or possess gold, silver, jewels, and the like, nor grain, millet, rice, beans, villages, gardens, slaves, cattle, sheep, or vehicles. While the Saṃgha may accept these items such as gold and silver, an individual person should not.

If there are fields or gardens, they should likewise be held collectively; they ought to be entrusted to the monastery’s *kappiyakāraka* (pure men) and other laypeople, who shall calculate the shares, collect the taxes, and provide for the Saṃgha.
If a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) or a hired laborer cultivates the field themselves, all the rice, wheat, vegetables, fruits, and seeds therein are impure; a bhikṣu should not eat them.
Furthermore, copper basins, copper bowls, cauldrons, pots, and jars—all these belong to the Saṃgha and are not for the private possession of individuals.
If they require protection, one should appoint a person to oversee the utensils, who should polish and wipe them from time to time so that they do not become blackened or damaged.
If monastic utensils are distributed to an individual, there is no offense in their use.
However, if any bhikṣus possess private copper vessels, they incur an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
Spoon and drinking vessel, as well as a salt dish, robes and bowl, bedding, and whatever is required for medicinal needs during illness—these should be kept by an individual.
As for the term "monastery attendant (*śrāmaṇera*) of the Saṃgha," it refers to the monastery’s own attendant.
An *upāsaka* is one who has received the three refuges and the five precepts.
Regarding the phrase "remaining silent," there are four modes of remaining silent, which serve as the basis for the six types of interrogation.
What are the four abodes?
First, the abode of the workshop;
second, the abode of the house.
Third, the place of fields;
fourth, the place of shops.
"Factory" refers to places where earthenware and the like are made, as well as places for shaving hair.
"House" refers to a dwelling;
"field" refers to sugarcane;
and "shops within the fields" refers to places where goods are sold.
Regarding the "six interrogations," it refers to when the person in charge of robe-funds sees a bhikṣu coming and speaks these words:
"Why have you come, Venerable Sir?
You are most welcome!"
"You should sit upon this seat; you should eat this cake; you should consume this rice; you should drink this gruel.
Having heard this, the bhikṣu immediately replied in a loud voice, "I have come for the sake of robes."
When each word is spoken, if one answers so swiftly as to leave no opportunity for the other to utter further speech, it is called an "incomplete interrogation.
If one answers slowly, allowing the other to speak further words, it is called a "complete interrogation."
Regarding the instruction to "send a trustworthy person," this refers to disciples or attendants.

In this context, an offense occurs if a king or his minister sends the price for a robe and one accepts it oneself without entrusting it to a *kappiyakāraka* (a person authorized to handle such items); this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If, after three verbal requests and six silent reminders, one does not obtain the robe and then seeks it again, there is an *duṣkṛta* offense at the initial request; if the robe is obtained through such speech, there is a *pāyattika* offense; and once the robe is obtained, there is an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
It is said: "Even if one does not personally employ expedient means, if others request [it] and one believes them and does not refuse, one incurs the same offense as mentioned above.
If the person in charge replies:
"You may now take the price for the robe.
The bhikṣu should say:
"I have already relinquished it; you should return it to its original owner."
If one says, "Venerable sir,
you may take the robe; I shall inform him," there is no offense at the time of taking it.
If a bhikṣu seeks clothing without following this sequence, he commits an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
If he interrogates the other with false or similar matters to extort the price for the clothing, or if he fails to inform the owner, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in each case.
If one obtains a robe by soliciting from three places where people exceed the prescribed number, one commits an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
If one obtains a robe by soliciting from three places where people do not exceed the prescribed number, one commits an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta).
If one considers the cases of humans mixed with non-humans, there are eight permutations in total; the gravity of the offenses is detailed as in the extensive text.
The summary verse says:
"Three instances where humans constitute one [permutation], and three instances where humans constitute two [permutations] each."
Three cases where it is not a human constitute one [category], and three phrases where two are not humans constitute another;
these are all to be understood according to their meaning. Together they form eight phrases:
when acting in accordance with the teaching, no offense is committed; yet if the transgression is sought, guilt immediately arises.
If a bhikṣu begs for the price of a robe from a human, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense; upon obtaining it, he incurs a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If he begs for the price of a robe from a non-human or a nāga, he incurs a duṣkṛta offense; upon obtaining it, he commits a naiḥsargika offense.

If one sends a messenger with a letter and seal to request the price for robes, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if the robes are obtained, one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

If a layperson deposits the price for robes intended for a bhikṣu with a non-Buddhist or a non-human being—and this applies even to cases where they expect to receive them from one another—if one requests it after the [stipulated] time has passed, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if the robes are obtained, it is an offense involving forfeiture.
There is no offense if one obtains [the item] by counting it out, or by seeking it through skillful means.
When requesting the price for a robe, one should speak as follows:
"The items previously given may be returned; I currently have a deficiency in my robes."
The summary verse says:
*Kauśeya*, pure black, the sixfold division of the *niṣīdana*,
carrying wool, washing, gold and silver, pledging as collateral, and buying and selling.

11. The Training Rule on Using Wild Silkworm Silk for Bedding. The eleventh training rule concerning the use of wild silkworm silk for bedding was established when the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣus were using *kośeya* (wild silkworm) silk to make bedding. This resulted in the killing of living beings, increased their greed and acquisitiveness, caused them to neglect their own wholesome qualities, and damaged the right faith of others.

Because of the excessive neglect and deficiency regarding bedding and seats, and due to the affliction of being subject to reproach and dependence on external conditions, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu makes a bedding or seat using new *gośīrṣa* silk-cotton, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
Regarding the term "new," there are two kinds of new:
first, that which is newly manufactured; second, that which is newly acquired.
This refers to newly manufactured *kauśeya*, meaning pure *kauśeya* silk from silkworms.
Regarding the term "reclining equipment," it refers to bedding and cushions.
There are two types: first, stuffed cushions;
[second, spread-out cushions].
Second is "completion by patching.
Regarding the term "reclining mat," both types are included.
The three subsequent precepts all rely on completion by patching as their basis.
Regarding the maker: first, making it oneself;
second, having another make it.

Whether for the sake of seeking excellence, for the sake of durability, or for the sake of exchange—whether it be a single cocoon, a small ball, or a large mass; whether it be torn, split, or spun with a bow—even if it is not yet finished, one incurs a light offense (dukkaṭa); once completed, one incurs the offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If one suspects that it is *kauśeya* (silk) when it is indeed *kauśeya*, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If it is not *kauśeya* but one perceives it as such or suspects it to be so, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense, but it need not be relinquished.
There is no offense if one perceives what is not *koseyya* (silk) as not being *koseyya*.

If the work is abandoned before completion, or if it is for another, or if two people work together, or if it consists of wool, hemp, or jute, or if it is mixed with impure substances—whether done by oneself or commissioned through another—one incurs a minor offense (*duṣkṛta*) in all such cases.

There is no offense if the garment is already completed; or if it has been used by another; or if one repairs an old item; or if another person offers a *koseya* (silk) robe; or if another person offers *koseya* thread and has someone else weave it; or if *koseya* thread and cotton are easily obtained at that location.
Or if another says to him,
"I shall make a *kauśeya* robe for you," and he remains silent out of a desire to obtain it,
then due to that greedy mind, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).

12. The Training Rule on Using Blankets Made of Pure Black Sheep’s Wool. This twelfth training rule concerning the use of blankets made of pure black sheep’s wool was established when the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣus were frequently seeking out black sheep’s wool to make new blankets.
Because one becomes attached to beautiful colors and further seeks out fine textures, thereby neglecting one’s duties, prolonging greed, and obstructing what is beneficial;
since the causes of affliction are the same as before, this training rule is established:
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding using pure black wool, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
Regarding "pure black wool," there are four types of color:
first, naturally black;
second, naturally blue.
Third, dyed with mud;
fourth, variegated in color.

Regarding "new," this refers to something newly made that is pure black—whether in a patch, a lump, a cluster, or whether it is draped, split, or struck with a bow—and while it is not yet finished, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); once completed, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture). The rest is the same as before.

13. The Training Rule on Making Bedding with Improper Proportions. The Thirteenth Training Rule on Making Bedding with Improper Proportions: “If a bhikṣu makes a new woolen bedding, he should use two parts of pure black wool, one-third part white, and one-fourth part coarse.”
If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat without using two parts of pure black wool, a third part of white, and a fourth part of coarse wool, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
The conditions are the same as before.
Regarding the "third portion of white," this refers to the hair on the flanks, the neck, and the back.
Regarding the "fourth portion of coarse," this refers to the hair on the head, feet, and belly; because the head, feet, and belly are the sites of movement, the hair there is coarse and rough.
Regarding "not following the prescribed proportions": if one does not rely on the two-part calculation, one incurs the fundamental offense.

There is no offense if, for example, one makes a wool rug weighing ten *jin*, consisting of five *jin* of pure black wool, two and a half *jin* of white wool, and two and a half *jin* of coarse wool; if the proportions are increased or decreased further, it should be explained according to this principle.
Whenever one wishes to make a mattress, one should divide the wool into four parts:
two parts black, one part white, and one part coarse. Within the black portion, it is further divided into two;
thus, the three and four meanings are established.

When making a mat, if one subsequently reduces the weight by one ounce, or even half an ounce, from the latter two parts, or uses pure black [wool], having already applied the necessary effort, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); if it is completed, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
Regarding the offense herein, it is based on the use of black wool because it is difficult to obtain.
However, if two-thirds of the material is used for making a mattress, there is no offense regardless of the quantity.

If it is not for one's own sake, or if it has already been completed by another, or if black wool is easily obtained while the other types are difficult to find, then whether the weight is reduced or increased, it constitutes no offense.

14. The Training Rule on Making New Bedding Before Six Years Have Passed. The fourteenth training rule concerning making new bedding before six years have passed: the circumstances are the same as those previously mentioned; it was established because [the Buddha] prohibited the useless discarding of items by those who cherish what is new and fine.

"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat, even if his heart is not inclined toward it, he must use it for six years. If he discards it before six years have passed and makes another new one, except by means of a formal act of the Saṃgha, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense."

Regarding the statement "maintaining for six years," even if one does not wish to keep it, the full period must be completed; for example, if one makes a mat in this year, or again makes another mat in this year, continuing in this manner until a mat is made in the fifth year.
If one makes a second mat for the first time, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; once it is completed, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

The substance of the first mat itself does not constitute an offense. If, in the sixth year, one makes another new mat—whether by discarding the previous one to make the subsequent one, or by making it for someone else—there is no offense.
Or, having already initiated the preparatory effort, one subsequently returns to lay life and undergoes full ordination (*upasampadā*) again to resume the construction;
or, having first undergone a change of gender and later returning to the former state to complete the construction again—one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

Or, if one makes a new mat before six years have elapsed, the community should grant the formal authorization (*dharmakarma*), or the community should go to inspect it; this must be requested three times.
One should not grant the Dharma immediately according to their wishes.
Or, if they bring a mat into the assembly, if it is too long it should be cut;
if it is too short or too narrow, it should be patched and reinforced.
If it is slightly worn, one should apply a patch;
if it is completely ruined and beyond repair, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one proclamation) and provide him with a separate rug.

The Fifteenth Rule: On Making a New *Naiṣadika* Without Using the Old Patch. While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, there was an elderly bhikṣu who, for the purpose of making a new *naiṣadika*, obtained five hundred large woolen cloths from merchants from the north and discarded all his old *naiṣadikas*.
When the Blessed One saw this, he had it readjusted, desiring to prevent the monk’s sense of contempt; as the circumstances of the offense were the same as before, he established this training rule:

"If a bhikṣu makes a new *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), he must take a piece from the worn portion of an old one, measuring one span of the Buddha’s hand in length and breadth, and patch it upon the new one for the purpose of discoloring it."
If a bhikṣu makes a new *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) and does not patch the old one onto the new one for the purpose of discoloring it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Niṣīdana" refers to a lying mat. "Length and breadth" means it is square.
"One should take an old one" refers to an old bedding cloth.
If a complete [piece] is not available, one should collect old materials and patch them together.
Regarding what is called "a Buddha-span" (*vitasti*): three spans of an average person constitute one span of a Buddha, which corresponds to one and a half *cubits* (*hasta*).
To patch with a piece of cloth of a ruined color (bad color) signifies durability; because of this heavy patching, it becomes durable for long-term use.

If one patches new cloth with old cloth such that it is less than one finger-width or half a finger-width of a Buddha-span, this does not constitute a valid patch, and one incurs the offense of *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one possesses an old [robe] yet forms the perception or harbors doubt that it does, the cases are all as explained above.
Alternatively, if one has forgotten about the old one, or if it is completely ruined and unfit for repair, there is no offense provided that only a newly made one exists.

The method for making a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) is as follows: it should be made in two layers, colored either blue, mud-colored, or red; various mixed colors are not permitted. It may be folded into three parts, and the bottom third should be cut to form fringes, which are sewn along the four edges in the same manner as the fringes of the three robes (*tricīvara*). One who does not follow this rule incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

16. The Training Rule on Carrying Wool Over Three *Yojanas*. The sixteenth training rule concerning carrying wool over three *yojanas*. The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus traveled toward the country of Nepāla. On the road, they encountered a wool cart whose axle had broken; they then begged for and obtained a great quantity of wool, which they carried away themselves.
Because of the circumstances of traveling on the road and the afflictions being the same as before, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu obtains wool while traveling on the road and has need of it, he should take it."
"If there is no one to carry it, one may carry it oneself for up to three *yojana*s.
If one exceeds this distance, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"While traveling on a road" refers to while on a dangerous road.
"Obtained" means acquired by begging from others.
"Required" means that one may take whatever is needed according to one's purpose.
"No one to hold it" means there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person).

Regarding the transgression herein: seven *paramāṇus* (extreme atoms) constitute one *rajas* (dust particle); seven of these constitute a *vāri-rajas* (water-dust); seven of these constitute a *loha-rajas* (gold-dust); seven of these constitute a *śaśa-rajas* (hare-hair dust); seven of these constitute a *aviraja* (sheep-hair dust); seven of these constitute a *goraja* (cow-hair dust); seven of these constitute a *chidra-rajas* (window-mote); seven of these constitute a *likṣā* (nit); seven of these constitute a *yūka* (louse); seven of these constitute a *yava* (barley grain); and seven of these constitute one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). Twenty-four fingers constitute one cubit (*hasta*); four cubits constitute one bow (*dhanus*); five hundred bows constitute one *krośa*. At this distance, it is designated as an *araṇya* (wilderness) location.
If a bhikṣu carries wool on his own back while traveling along a road in a place where there are no villages, and he travels more than three yojanas, he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If there are villages along the road—specifically, if there are seven villages with one *krośa* between each—and the bhikṣu travels through these intervals between the villages, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* for half a village and a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* upon passing the village.
If the path between villages is half a *krośa*, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if it is a full *krośa*, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one carries it away while traveling through the air, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one carries away a *pātra* (alms bowl) for the purpose of making a hat, or a waist-belt (*kaṭīsūtra*), or a *sthapuṭaka* (a type of pouch), there is no offense.
In general, bhikṣus should not carry burdens.

17. The Training Rule on Having a Non-Relative Nun Clean Wool. This is the seventeenth training rule. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the Venerable Upānanda had Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī clean wool. Because of this, her formal practice was neglected. With the cause being the pursuit of gain and the affliction being as previously described, he established this training rule.
"If a bhikṣu should have a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
Regarding "wash": it includes even soaking it once in water.
"Staining" refers to dyeing even down to a single immersion in dye.
"Beating" refers to beating even down to a single layer.
Regarding having a nun who is not a relative wash, dye, or perform similar tasks, the application of the object and the mental perception are as explained above.

If one sends a letter ordering it to be made, or does it for another, or for the Three Jewels, or if two people make it together, or if the wool is impure, in all such cases one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The rest is all as explained above in the precept concerning the washing of old clothes.

**The Eighteenth Training Rule: Handling Gold, Silver, and the Like** When the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, some bhikṣus handled gold, silver, and other such valuables. The people then discussed this, saying:
"If the sons of Śākya are permitted to handle gold, silver, and the like, why do they not accept the five worldly sensual pleasures?"
The Buddha said:
“If a bhikṣu requires firewood, grass, or the like, he should seek firewood, grass, and such; he must not, on that account, seek gold or other such items.

Furthermore, at Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus personally took hold of gold and other valuables, or caused others to take them. Consequently, laypeople and non-Buddhists gave rise to criticism and disdain. Because of the affliction of accepting impure wealth, as in previous cases, this training rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu, with his own hand, takes hold of gold, silver, coins, or the like, or instructs another to take hold of them, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
Regarding the phrase "with his own hand," it means that he personally grasps or holds them.
"To instruct another" means to cause a person to take hold [of it].
"Gold, silver, and so forth" refers to gold, silver, or cowrie shells, or various types of currency.

Regarding the offense herein: if it is the property of another, or if one accepts as a deposit gold, silver, and so forth, as well as various coins and cowries, or if one picks up what has been lost, one incurs only a *pāyattika* (downfall) offense; however, the items need not be relinquished.

If one obtains one's own property and does not perform the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*), whether one holds it oneself or causes another to do so, it constitutes an offense of abandonment (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

If others offer gold or other valuables and one has already formed the intention to accept them, provided that neither oneself nor another has yet physically grasped or touched them, there is no primary offense.
If one instructs another to take [an object], there are eighteen ways in which the offense is fully established.
These are: telling that person, "Take this object," "Take it from this place," or "Take such a quantity of it."
"Take this object," "Take it here," "Take this much.
"Place this object," "Place it here," "Place this much."
These nine phrases are all direct instructions.
Within these three sets of three, each consisting of a beginning, middle, and end, they should be understood according to the sequence of the number of vessels for the recipients.

Furthermore, there are three sets of three [categories] based on teaching not face-to-face; that is, by substituting "this" for "that" within the preceding nine, they likewise become nine phrases, totaling eighteen.
If one causes another to take [an object] from a place where it can be obtained, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; if one seizes it oneself, one incurs the primary offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If it is from a place where it cannot be obtained, both incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Regarding gold, silver, and other such items, whether they have been processed or not, touching them constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If they are not standard currency, or if they are deficient, obsolete, or only partially resemble it, grasping them constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one finds lost or discarded items on land or in water, they should be placed in a conspicuous location; whoever recognizes them as theirs may take them.
Treasure-trove without an owner should be taken and used for the benefit of the Three Jewels as appropriate.
If one discovers a treasure trove belonging to an owner, one should inform the owner and inquire about its identifying marks; if it corresponds to those marks, it should be returned.
If it does not correspond, it may be used for the benefit of the Triple Gem.
If one grasps it with a disrespectful mind, one also incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If it is gold and one perceives it as such, or if there is doubt about it, one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If it is not gold but one perceives it as such, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If one does not relinquish doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If it is gold that is not gold, and one perceives it as not gold, there is no offense.
The same applies to silver and other such items.
This refers to one's own property; if one obtains it, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one takes another's property into one's own possession, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense without forfeiture.
If it is brass, copper, iron, lead, or tin, there is no offense when taking hold of them.
If one’s money, jewels, or other property is stolen by bandits, there is no offense in taking it back for oneself.

If one hears that a calamity is about to arrive and no *kappiya-kāraka* (pure person) can be found, one may personally dig a pit to secretly conceal property belonging to the Saṃgha, property belonging to a *stūpa*, or property belonging to the Dharma, and having done so, should depart.
If he returns at a later time, he should personally go out and retrieve it;
if there is no difficulty in doing so, he incurs the full offense.

If, during the summer retreat, a donor gives the price for robes to the community of bhikṣus, they should accept them while maintaining the mental attitude that this gift is being entrusted to them by the donor.
The bhikṣus should seek out a person of faith and respect, or a temple attendant (śrāmaṇera), or an upāsaka to serve as a pure donor.
When a bhikṣu obtains gold or other such items, if he perceives them as the property of the donor and takes hold of them, there is no offense.

Even if one is far removed from the object and receives an impure thing, if one holds it with the mental intention that it belongs to the donor, there is no offense whatsoever as long as the donor remains alive.
If no donor can be found, one should take gold, silver, or other such items and, standing or remaining before a single bhikṣu, speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me!
"I, the bhikṣu [name], having obtained this impure wealth, shall take this impure wealth and exchange it for pure wealth.
Having said this twice or thrice, he should personally take possession of it, or cause another to take possession of it.

If a bhikṣu, while on a journey, obtains gold, silver, or the like, he may carry it himself for the sake of provisions for the path, or have a *kappiyakāraka* (a lay attendant) or a *śrāmaṇera* (novice) carry it away.
It should be understood that regarding gold, silver, and the like, the śrāmaṇera is only prohibited from personally possessing them;

he is not forbidden from handling them. **The Nineteenth Training Rule: On Making Profit from the Sale of Goods.** While the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, Upānanda engaged in trade with a non-Buddhist. He exchanged his own coarse woolen blanket for the other’s fine woolen blanket. Because the circumstances of the trouble were the same as in the previous case, this training rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu, moreover, seeks profit through various forms of lending and borrowing, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the term "various," it refers to employing numerous methods of seeking gain through lending and borrowing.

“Interest and profit” refers to seeking gain through money and the like; or by means of gold, silver, pearls, shells, jade, various threads, or by amassing grain and wheat; or by driving carriages and horses for the sake of profit; or by exchanging finished goods for unfinished ones.
This should be treated as four cases: when the item has not yet been acquired, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*; once it is acquired, it becomes a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.
The same applies to the interest generated from the object.

If another person uses a bhikṣu’s property to generate interest, and the bhikṣu, out of greed for profit, remains silent and does not stop him, he incurs the root offense (*mūlāpatti*) at the moment the profit is obtained.
Regarding other objects of perception—whether for another person, or in cases where one's faculties have been transformed—all such phrases should be explained according to the preceding rules.

If the goods are for the purpose of managing the assets of the Triple Gem, or if they are being given by a donor as an inexhaustible treasury, even if one goes about seeking them, it does not constitute an offense.

However, when lending out such items for profit, one should take a double deposit and seek reliable guarantors; a formal contract must be drawn up specifying the date at the end of the year, and this should be announced to the Elder (sthavira) and the administrative officer (vaiyāvṛtyakara) so that they are all made aware, or alternatively, it should be announced to those faithful lay devotees (upāsaka).
If a bhikṣu has made a profit from lending out capital and wishes to relinquish it: if the item is a type of wealth that a bhikṣu is permitted to possess, he should give it to a trustworthy bhikṣu;
if it is impure wealth, he should give it to a layperson of faithful heart.
This refers to a formal transaction; it is not a case of something not yet given.
If the item is not returned, one should go and demand it forcefully; it must not be allowed to go to waste.

**The Twenty-first Training Rule on Buying and Selling** The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī. Due to the various acts of buying and selling committed by the group of six bhikṣus, the circumstances of the disturbance were the same as before, and thus this training rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu again engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Regarding the term "various kinds," this refers to engaging in many types of trade: either accumulating goods in large quantities at low prices and in times of scarcity to resell them at high prices and in times of abundance for profit; or observing the seasonal trends to anticipate periods of plenty or famine, thereby seeking livelihood by speculating on market fluctuations to gain profit.

Regarding "buying and selling," this refers to such items as cotton cloth, thread, kusha grass, white cotton, ghee, oil, sugar, honey, rice, beans, paddy, hemp, copper, iron, gold, silver, pearls, shells, jade, and various types of currency.
If one purchases with the intent for profit, one incurs a light offense.
If one sells without the intent for profit, there is no offense.
If the situation is reversed—meaning one initially has no offense but later acts with the intent for profit—one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If both possess a malicious intent, it is light at first but grave later;
if neither possesses it, there is no offense. Some say:
"If one first purchases for profit, one incurs a grave offense immediately; only after subsequently selling it for profit does one perform the formal relinquishment and repentance.
This purchase and sale of wealth should be relinquished according to the preceding rules; the gravity of the offenses regarding the object and one's perception thereof may be inferred by analogy.
If, at the time of buying or selling, one does not speak according to reality, or uses false measures and scales to deceive another, one incurs the offense of lying (*mṛṣāvāda*).
At the moment the goods are obtained, one commits the offense of stealing (*steya*).

Whenever one intends to buy or sell goods, one must first resolve the mind to have no desire for profit; thus, whatever profit is obtained in the course of the transaction is entirely without offense.
However, even if monks are acting for the sake of their three robes, they must not engage in trade with the intent of seeking profit.

Furthermore, at a marketplace where laypeople conduct trade, one should not personally negotiate the price; rather, one should have a layperson who possesses faith or a *śrāmaṇera* purchase it on one's behalf, and there is no offense.

If such a person is not present, one should personally reimburse the value, returning the price either twice or thrice; it should not exceed this, nor should one engage in bargaining over high and low prices.
When communal property is about to be sold, the Elder (Upādhyāya) should first establish the base price, but he must not immediately announce the sale based on that alone.
One should take the final bid that is of the highest price and only then give it to him.
If one does not actually wish to buy but falsely increases the price of another, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one puts on the robe immediately after the auction has concluded, before the price has been paid, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
If a donor, out of faith, offers their wife and children as a gift, one should ask them both what they desire.
If they say, "We shall be sold; we will accept the price," [then one may proceed].
Regarding this, one should sell [the goods] according to the donor's intention; the bhikṣu should not increase the price, for if he increases it, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
Furthermore, he should not inquire as to the value; he should accept whatever price the donor provides.
If parents, with faith, offer a young child to a bhikṣu, he should accept him for their sake.
If they later demand him back, he should return him;
if they offer a price, he may accept whatever amount they give, and there is no offense.

This young boy was at the side of the bhikṣus, with a fragment of a kāṣāya tied around his neck, being nourished and sustained by them from time to time. Later, when he had grown up and, desiring to repay their kindness, brought an object as an offering, you should accept it as you please.
