The summary verse says:
Two bowls, two weavers, Taking away robes, and urgent offerings.
Rain-clothing for forest-dwellers; diverting seven-day medicine to the Saṃgha. 21.

The Training Rule on Possessing an Extra Alms-bowl Beyond Ten Days Without Distributing It. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the bhikṣu Upānanda, out of greed to purchase alms-bowls, urged sixty people, each of whom gave him sixty *kārsāpaṇas*.

Furthermore, the six groups of bhikṣus went about begging for fine bowls from others in many places; out of greedy attachment, they accumulated them, neither using them themselves nor giving them away to others. This increased their afflictions and obstructed the cultivation of the right practice. Because of these excesses regarding bowls—namely, neglecting one's duties and the affliction of public reproach—the Buddha established this training rule (śikṣāpada).
"If a bhikṣu, moreover, keeps an extra bowl for more than ten days without making a formal distribution of it, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
Regarding the term "extra bowl" (dīrgha-pātra): this refers to when one already possesses a bowl that has been formally accepted and maintained, yet keeps another; this is called "extra."
If one does not make a formal distinction, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) offense day by day;
after ten days have passed, it becomes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If one currently lacks a bowl, the bowl obtained later is not considered "extra."
If one does not maintain [the bowl] properly, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) every day.
There are two kinds of bowls:
first, iron; [second, clay].
2. Clay. By this it may be inferred that stone bowls belong to the category of clay.
If this were not the case, how could the World-Honored One have accepted the stone bowl from the devas, knowing it was not pure, yet used it himself?
There are four kinds of bowls:
namely, those made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. If these have not yet been formally accepted, they should not be accepted; if they have already been accepted, they should be discarded.
Furthermore, there are four other kinds of bowls:
Brass, red copper, white copper, and wood—if these have not yet been formally accepted, they should not be accepted;
if they have been accepted, they may be used as medicinal bowls at one's discretion.
If it is a bowl that is in accordance with the Dharma and should be formally maintained, place the bowl in the left hand, cover the opening of the bowl with the right hand, and speak as follows:
"Venerable one, please attend to me!..."
I, the bhikṣu [name], hold this pātra; it is the vessel of the Great Sage, the vessel for alms-gathering. I now maintain it for the purpose of using it for food at all times.
The second and third [times] are to be stated in the same manner.
If one wishes to relinquish them, it should follow the procedure for relinquishing robes.
If there are two bowls, one should keep the better one, while the other should be disposed of according to the rules.
A small bowl for a bhikṣu is considered large for a bhikṣuṇī; the measurements of these bowls shall be explained later. There is no offense in the following cases:

if the bowl is smaller than the prescribed measure, or larger than it; or if one keeps an extra bowl intending to give it to another person, or to provide for the needs of one who has gone forth and received full ordination—even if one does not formally designate it as such, there is still no offense.
If one keeps two small bowls for storing soup and vegetables or for drinking water, as well as a salt dish with a spoon, there is no offense in any of these cases.

Furthermore, within a large bowl, one may keep as many small bowls as can fit; if it accords with one's needs, keeping many is not an offense. However, one should additionally keep one more large bowl to prevent the occurrence of deficiencies.

This differs from the non-Buddhists who sew leaves together to make vessels or eat by cupping their hands; such practices are difficult to maintain and difficult to provide for, and do not possess the characteristics of a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
The World-Honored One permitted only one [alms bowl], neither too many nor too few, which is well-suited to the Middle Way for sustaining the body and cultivating one’s practice.
Is there a case where a bhikṣu, by keeping an almsbowl for even one night, incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense? Yes;
that is to say, if he acquires an almsbowl and his gender changes to become a bhikṣuṇī, after the lapse of one night, he incurs the original offense.

Regarding the method of holding the alms bowl: one should not have a person who has not yet received full ordination wash it; however, if they are able to preserve and protect it, washing is permitted.

One should never write one's own name upon the bowl; if it is written for private record-keeping, there is no offense. All items belonging to others should be treated according to this same principle.
If one writes down the name at that time, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
When a person offers an object to the Triple Gem, they should engrave the donor's name upon the offered object, stating: "This is the meritorious gift of so-and-so."

One should mark the bedding and requisites belonging to others with one's own sign. When taking the bowl out of or putting it into its bag, one should not stand while washing or drying it in the sun, nor should one place it on the ground; rather, one should support it with an object. One should not remove impurities from it, nor place it where it will become defiled; furthermore, cow dung containing sand should not be used for washing.
If it is damp, do not place it inside a bag; if it is already dry, one should not leave it out in the sun for too long.
One should use it with moderation, guarding it as one would one's own eyes.
When traveling on a road, one should not carry it uncovered or wrap it in the corner of a robe; rather, it should be placed in a bag and carried over the shoulder.
There are three kinds of bags:
first, the alms-bowl bag;
second, the medicine bag.
3. Regarding the miscellaneous pouches:

when hanging them over the shoulder, they should be placed one on each shoulder in their proper order; they must not be crossed over, nor should they be hung level with the sides so that they protrude from the corners of the shoulders like the shape of a jar or a drum.
As for the method of making the loop: sew the inner felt of the strap and bind it with thread so that it does not curl or shrink.

Regarding the place where the bowl is kept: if one is in a monastery, one should construct a niche or cave; if one dwells in an araṇya (hermitage), one should weave a basket from bamboo or reeds and coat both its interior and exterior with clay and cow dung.
If one intends to travel elsewhere, one should not take it with one; at whatever destination one arrives, one should make another according to the occasion.
If a bhikṣu knows how to make a bowl himself, he should do so in a secluded place and not allow laypeople to see him.

**The Training Rule on Begging for a Bowl, the Twenty-second.** When the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the time came for Upānanda to go out for alms. Upon arriving at the place of some merchants, he begged for a second bowl because of his greedy desire for something fine. This increased his afflictions and invited the reproach of others. As the circumstances of the trouble were the same as before, the Buddha established this training rule.

"If a bhikṣu has an alms bowl with fewer than five mends that is still fit for use, yet seeks another bowl for the sake of desiring something better, and obtains one, it is an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
That bhikṣu shall relinquish this extra bowl in the midst of the assembly; he shall take the lowest-quality bowl and give it to that bhikṣu, saying:
"This bowl is returned to you; you should not keep it as your own possession, nor should you treat it as a special item, nor should you give it away to others."
"One should examine it carefully for oneself and use it slowly; even when it is worn out, one should maintain it—this is the Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "fewer than five patches," it means not yet having reached five patches.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who used a bowl with five patches to beg for alms; because he had to repair it every day, he neglected his primary spiritual practice.
Whether the bowl had five patches or more than that, [the Buddha] permitted him to keep an additional bowl.
There are five kinds of molten or moist substances that should not be used to mend a bowl:
namely, brown sugar, yellow wax, lead, tin, and lacquer.
There are five methods for mending an iron bowl:
1. Stop the hole with a fine nail;
2. Fix a small iron plate and drive it in until firm;
3. Like fish-teeth, cut notches on all four sides so that the inner and outer parts clamp together.
Fourth, cover the circumference of the hole with iron sheets and nail them down;
fifth, use filings, of which there are two kinds:
first, crushed iron filings, and second, powdered whetstone.
First repair the iron bowl, and next repair the earthenware bowl.

When using powdered material for the patch, mix the powder with oil in an iron bowl and grind it thoroughly with an iron hammer; only then apply it to fill the hole, and immediately heat it over a low flame to make it hard.
If it is coarse or rough, apply oil again and fumigate it according to the prescribed method.
If there are cracks or pores in an earthen bowl, fill them with a mixture of sugar and clay, and dry it by heating over a fire.
If it is cracked or broken, one should carve out the waist of the bowl and fill it with an iron drum-shaped patch; this should then be coated with clay and fired for use.
Generally speaking, there are four kinds of perfection regarding an almsbowl:
first, perfection of substance, which refers to it being made of iron.
2. Perfection of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-sampat*): that is, it is sturdy, without holes, without seams, and does not retain grease or grime.
3. Perfection of measure (*pramāṇa-sampat*): that is, it is a large bowl (*mahā-pātra*). 4.
Perfection of the source of acquisition (*lābha-sthāna-sampat*): that is, obtained through distribution among the assembly, obtained from a donor, or it is a bowl that was previously cherished.
If a bhikṣu already possesses this bowl and seeks another that is superior, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense upon obtaining it.
Regarding "in the midst of the community": this bowl should be relinquished within the community; first, one should request that the bowl which was obtained through an offense be distributed.
A bhikṣu who possesses five qualities should be appointed; beginning from the arrangement of the seats, up until the inquiry:
"Are you, so-and-so, able to conduct the distribution of the bowl for transgressions for the Saṃgha?"
He replies, “I can. Then,
one bhikṣu should perform the formal act of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* to appoint him.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to distribute the bowl that has been found guilty of an offense to the Saṃgha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now appoint so-and-so as the distributor of the bowl found guilty of an offense."
"O Bhikṣus, this so-and-so now offers to the Saṃgha his bowl for transgression.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
Next, perform the karmavācanā:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! ... [and so forth] ...
I now maintain it thus. This should be performed according to the formal announcement (jñapti).
The Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus, you shall practice the rite for the bowl that has been forfeited. I shall now establish the rule for practicing this rite for the forfeited bowl.
When the community is in harmony, one should make a formal announcement, saying: "
"Venerable sirs! Tomorrow I shall perform the distribution of the bowl for transgressions for the Saṃgha.
Venerable sirs, each of you should bring your bowl and assemble."
When the next day arrived and the entire Saṃgha had assembled, that bhikṣu stood before the Elder holding his bowl that was subject to forfeiture, praising its excellence and saying to the Elder:
"This bowl is radiant, pure, and complete; it is fit for use. If you require it, you should take it."

If the senior monk accepts it, he should give it; then, taking the senior monk’s bowl, he should go and give it to the second senior monk. If the second does not want it, he should give it to the third.

When it is the turn for the third senior monk to receive [the offering], if the first senior monk requests it again, it should not be given at the first request, nor should it be given at the second request; however, at the third request, it should be given.
The Elder commits an *dukkaṭa* offense and must confess it.
This applies likewise down to the last person in the line; if anyone subsequently demands [the bowl back], it should be understood accordingly.
When the alms-round has been completed in this manner, the bowl finally obtained should be given to the monk who committed the forfeiture offense, saying:
“Bhikṣus! This bowl is not fit to be kept as a personal possession, nor should it be discarded; one may use it gradually until it breaks.
Any bhikṣu who uses a bowl that has been declared faulty and does not comply with this instruction commits a *vyatikrama* offense.
When a bhikṣu who possesses an *āpatti-pātra* goes for alms, he should place the *āpatti-pātra* in a fine bag and the *dhāraṇīya-pātra* (the bowl he is authorized to use) in another bag.

If he obtains fine food, he should place it in the *āpatti-pātra*, and if the food is coarse, he should place it in the *dhāraṇīya-pātra*. He should set the *āpatti-pātra* aside and always eat from the *dhāraṇīya-pātra*.
Whether washing, drying, lifting, or fumigating it, or when traveling on a road, one must always keep the bowl properly placed until it breaks.
If a bhikṣu does not abide by these rules of conduct, he incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

"This is your bowl which you should not keep as a formal possession" means that although he previously possessed a bowl kept as a formal possession, this bowl is given to him for the purpose of undergoing disciplinary penance, requiring him to use it.
That which should not be discriminated, one likewise should not discriminate as being pure and then keep it.
Regarding "not giving to others," one should not take this and bestow it upon another person.
One should use [the object] with careful deliberation; one must not allow it to be damaged by suddenly giving rise to a mind of weariness or indolence.
If one deliberately damages it, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

If one obtains many bowls, they all constitute the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; from among these bowls, one should select a good one and perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for it within the assembly, while all remaining bowls may be distributed as one pleases.

Regarding the offense herein: when a bhikṣu’s bowl is broken, from the first mending up to the fifth, if it is still fit for use yet he fails to mend it and instead seeks another bowl for the sake of its excellence, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of searching; once he obtains it, he incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If one perceives what is not excellent as excellent, one incurs only a *pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense for one who perceives what is excellent as not excellent, or what is not excellent as excellent.

Furthermore, if one seeks it on behalf of another, or seeks it jointly with two people, or sends a letter to obtain it, or obtains it from a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), in all such cases, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one acquires [the cloth] by purchase, or obtains it from another because it is not available, or receives it through exchange, there is no offense in any of these cases.

**The Twenty-third Training Rule: On Begging for Thread and Having an Unrelated Weaver Weave a Robe** When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the bhikṣu Upānanda requested thread from a spinner and had the weaver Kākaṇḍaka weave a fine upper robe for him.

Furthermore, relying on a king or a minister to have a bolt of cloth woven for them causes distress to others and gives rise to censure; because they seek after such worldly matters, the afflictions are the same as before, and thus this training rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu should himself beg for thread and have a weaver who is not a relative weave it into a robe,
and if he obtains the robe, it is an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

Regarding the phrase "begging for thread oneself," it refers to obtaining half a *liang*, one *liang*, or more; namely, cotton thread, or *koseya* (silk) thread, or domestic silk, or wool, or *śāṇaka* (hemp), or *kṣauma* (flax), or wild hemp, or *kṣaumika* (linen) thread, or *koñcika* thread, or *avalantaka* thread.

If one begs for *koseyya* (silk) and has a non-relative weave it into a bedding mat (*śayanāsana*), one incurs two *pāyattika* offenses and one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, because the substance of the garment is a single unit.
If one has it woven into other garments or for items such as waistbands (*kaṭibandhana*) and the like, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense in every instance of the weaving.

Whether obtained by begging from a relative, begging from a non-relative, or purchased for oneself—regardless of the means by which the thread was acquired—if one causes a single non-relative weaver, or many, to weave it, or causes a relative to assist in the weaving, or assists in the weaving oneself, in all such cases, one commits an offense of forfeiture and transgression (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).

Regarding what is called "no offense": if one begs from a relative and has that relative weave it, or if a relative acts with the perception that they are a relative, and so forth—the phrasing is as above.
Furthermore, there is no offense if the donor themselves possesses faith and has another person weave it for them, or weaves it for a price.
If one, with a deceitful mind, proclaims one's own superior virtues, there is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of receiving the gift;
if the other person is superior, both [the giver and receiver] incur it simultaneously.
If one actually possesses such virtues, there is an *āpatti* (offense) of *duṣkṛta*.
Even if one is a relative of the weaver, if one causes them distress by not knowing the proper time, or displays strange signs, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense.
If one mixes impure fibers—such as camel hair and the like—with [pure wool], or weaves for another person, these are all *duṣkṛta* offenses.

24. The Training Rule on Urging a Non-Relative Weaver to Weave a Robe. The twenty-fourth training rule concerning urging a non-relative weaver to weave a robe: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the bhikṣu Upānanda, for his own sake, had a weaver weave a large white woolen cloth (śvetakaṃbala). He gave a bowl full of food to that weaver, which invited public reproach and suspicion. As the circumstances of the offense were the same as before, this training rule was established.
"Furthermore, if a monk has a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, and they have an unrelated weaver weave a robe for that monk;
if this monk, having not previously received an invitation, conceives a different thought and goes to that weaver’s place and speaks thus: 'Do you know this?'"
"Please weave this robe for me. Excellent weaver!

You should weave it well, combing it thoroughly, selecting the fibers carefully, and beating it until it is extremely firm. I shall provide you with sustenance by means of a small portion of alms-food, or a full measure of alms-food, or even the monetary value of such food."
"If a bhikṣu, having provided such materials to a weaver, obtains a robe [thereby], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Without having previously accepted an invitation" means that he has not first given his consent for the other to request or take [the materials].
Regarding "conceiving a different thought," there are four kinds of thoughts:
first, the thought of density, meaning it should be well-woven;
second, the thought of brightness, meaning it should be thoroughly cleansed and combed.
Third, mindfulness of fineness, which means skillful discernment.
Fourth, mindfulness of luster, which means thorough beating.
The initial mention of "well-woven" also implies being broad and extensive.
"Food from a bowl" refers to the five kinds of *khādaniya* (solid foods) or the five kinds of *bhojaniya* (soft foods).
"Types of food from a bowl" refers to raw grains, rice, and so forth.
Regarding the term "value of food," it refers to the price paid for food.

In this context, the offense consists of everything from the initial exhortation to have it made, up until the garment has not yet entered one's possession; in all these stages, one commits a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one has obtained the robe, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If it is an impure robe, or if one encourages a eunuch or a hermaphrodite to make a robe, in all such cases one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

**The Training Rule on Taking Back Robes, Number Twenty-Five** The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣu Nanda gave his saṃghāṭī robe to the bhikṣu Dharma. Later, due to a dispute arising from anger, he took the robe back from him.
Because of an inability to endure [criticism], one gives rise to the slander and censure of others.
Due to the matter of taking up robes, this training rule was established to prevent the afflictions of intolerance, negligence, and reproach.

"If again a bhikṣu has previously given a robe to another bhikṣu, and at a later time, becoming vexed, angry, and abusive, giving rise to a mind of contempt and disdain, he either seizes it himself or instructs another to seize it, saying:
'Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.'"
"If one uses a robe that has been separated from that person's body for one's own enjoyment, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The phrase "gives a robe" is the general heading.
If, at the time of giving him a robe, one says,
"You may serve as my messenger," and then seizes the robe back if he does not perform the service, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Later time" refers to a different occasion.
"Annoying" refers to manifesting signs of irritation through bodily action.
"Anger" refers to the binding of resentment and malice within the internal mind.
"Abusive speech" refers to uttering intolerable words out of harbored resentment and hatred.
"Contemptuous speech" refers to manifesting signs of anger and indignation for the sake of an unbeneficial matter.
"Seizing" means that based on an original intention to expect something, when one's desires are not fulfilled, one instead seizes it back, conceiving of it as one's own property.
If it is otherwise, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding "using" [the object], it means forming the intention that it belongs to oneself.

As for the transgression herein: if a bhikṣu, whether by body, speech, or both body and speech, or by himself or through another, should seize or snatch [an object] away—even if only until the corner of a robe has not yet left the body—one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in every instance.
Once it has been separated from the body, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If laypeople seize the robes of a bhikṣu, they can generate immeasurable unwholesome karma.
Regarding the cases where one has not actually seized them but forms the perception that one has, and so forth, these should be explained as previously stated.
If one knows that the previous owner is not careful with the requisites of a śramaṇa and fears they might be lost or damaged, there is no offense in taking them up with a virtuous intention.

The Twenty-sixth Training Rule: Regarding the Retention of an Urgently Offered Robe Beyond the Prescribed Time. While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the six groups of bhikṣus divided the distribution of robes during the rainy season retreat. Because of this, discord and resentment arose. Due to the matter of receiving robes, they exceeded the time limit and neglected their duties, leading to public censure and affliction. Consequently, this training rule was established.

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, during the first three months of the rainy season retreat, when ten days remain before its completion, receives an urgent offering of robes (ātyayika-cīvara), he who needs it should accept it and may keep it until the time for distributing the robes."
"If one keeps [it] beyond this limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
At that time, the border regions of King Prasenajit rebelled; he issued an edict to the Great General Bhadrapāla, commanding him to lead the army to punish those who were disloyal.
At that time, the general entered the monastery and addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the midst of clashing weapons and battle, life itself is difficult to preserve; I now offer these robes, wishing to bestow them with my own hands."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to accept them; the general then left the robes behind and departed. They were gathered in one place and were largely damaged by insects.
When the bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"You should accept them."

"Having received [the robes], one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion with one subsequent proclamation) to appoint a person endowed with five virtues as the custodian of the robes.
Regarding the phrase "less than ten days remaining," it means that there are still ten days left before the fifteenth day of the eighth month.
Regarding "robes given in urgency," there are five types of robes given during urgent circumstances:

namely, giving when one has fallen ill oneself; giving for the sake of a sick person; giving at the time of impending death; giving for the sake of a deceased person; and giving when about to depart on a journey.
Furthermore, another commentary states:
"To give robes in times of urgent distress refers to robes given outside of the prescribed season.
To say "should receive" means it is appropriate to receive them at the proper time for receiving robes.
Regarding the statement "should be kept," this refers to a period of five months or one month.

If the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, the limit is until the middle of the ninth month; if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread, it extends until the middle of the first month. These are the matters permitted by the World-Honored One for the sake of benefit; to keep [the robe] beyond these limits constitutes an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If there are five kinds of urgent robe-offerings (*ātyayika-cīvara*), one should accept them and distribute them accordingly.
If the donor says,
"I wish to give with my own hands," [one should comply].
Regarding the phrase "one who has not yet reached the limit," one should also accept [the robe] from such a person.
There is no offense if one has already been appointed as the custodian of robes.
Or, if the donor speaks as follows:
Regarding the statement, "You may keep this robe; when I return, I shall offer it with my own hands," it should not be divided.
If one has not actually made a formal distribution, yet forms the thought that it has been distributed, or harbors doubt about it, the categories of cases are as stated above.
After the *yathā-sukham* (end of the rainy season retreat), regarding the intercalary month, the King should maintain it in accordance with the date of the previous *varṣā* (rainy season) retreat.

**The Twenty-seventh Training Rule: Regarding Staying in an Āraṇya for More Than Six Nights Separated from One’s Robes.** While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, some bhikṣus living in forest hermitages (*āraṇya*) were plundered by bandits. The World-Honored One then permitted bhikṣus in forest hermitages to leave one of their three robes (*tricīvara*) behind in a village dwelling; thus, while residing in the forest, they would incur no fault of being separated from their robes.

If there is business for the Saṃgha, or business concerning a stūpa, or personal business or business on behalf of others, one may go to another place and stay away from one's residence for up to six nights; it should not exceed this.

At that time, the group of six monks stayed away from their lodgings for seven nights; because of the complications arising from leaving their robes behind, as with the previous case, this training rule was established:
"If many bhikṣus are dwelling in an araṇya (forest hermitage) and observe the later retreat, and there is a place of fear, terror, or danger..."
If a bhikṣu wishes to leave one of his three robes behind in a village dwelling,
and he has a reason to go outside the boundary of the araṇya, he may stay apart from that robe for up to six nights.
"If one exceeds this limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the term "araṇya" (wilderness), it refers to a distance of one *krośa* from a village.

Regarding the "later retreat" (*paścimikā varṣā*), it refers to those who observe the summer retreat later; because their previous retreat site was subject to defects such as overcrowding, they go to the Forest of No-Contention (*araṇyavihāra*) to avoid these and observe the later retreat.
"Being startled" means knowing that a thief intends to come to this place.
"Being terrified" means being wounded or killed upon seeing a thief arrive.
"Being fearful of difficulty" means that thieves frequently come.
Furthermore, lions, tigers, wolves, and non-human beings should be assigned respectively [to the four types of fear].

Moreover, the perils of bandits, or the perils of lions and the like, or the perils of mosquitoes, gadflies, snakes, and scorpions, or the perils of cold and heat, should be assigned respectively to the preceding four phrases beginning with "fear."
The "three robes" refers to the robes that one maintains through formal possession (*dhāraṇa*).
"Placing them in a village house" means there is a place with lanes, streets, or thoroughfares suitable for walking;
"placing" means leaving them as a deposit with another person.
Regarding "having a reason," this refers to matters concerning the Three Jewels or individual persons.
Regarding "must go forth," this means departing from the boundary of one's forest hermitage (*araṇya*) dwelling.
As for the offense herein: if one exceeds six nights and reaches the seventh night, yet the dawn has not yet appeared, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense.
If the light of dawn appears, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Furthermore, another explanation states:
"If one leaves with the original intention of returning immediately, but is delayed by circumstances and fails to reach the location of the robe, there is no fault of being separated from the robe."

Regarding those who are exempt from offense, there are eight difficult circumstances (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*), as well as cases such as obtaining the formal authorization of the community (*saṃghakarma*) or the perception of six nights, which should be understood as explained above.

The Twenty-eighth Training Rule: Regarding the Use of a Rain-Bathing Robe After Seeking It in Advance. While the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the group of six bhikṣus greedily sought material gain; they frequently begged for rain-bathing robes, thereby contravening the practice of renunciation.
This was established as a training rule due to the same underlying afflictions regarding robes as mentioned previously:
"If a bhikṣu has one month remaining of the spring season, he should seek a rain-bath robe; until the final half-month arrives, he should wear and use it."
If a bhikṣu, when less than one month remains until the end of spring, seeks a rain-bathing robe and continues to wear it during the final fortnight, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.

"Only one month of spring remains" means that three months of the spring season have already passed and one month remains, from the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month; during this period, one should seek the rain-clothing, but prior to reaching these dates, one should not seek it in advance.
When the rainy season arrives, one should not go searching for [new lodgings].
Regarding the duties that ought to be performed within the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat), they shall now be explained.
Once the fifteenth day of the fifth month has arrived, the official in charge (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*) shall sweep and plaster the dwellings to make them clean.
When the assembly has gathered, one should announce:
"Tomorrow the bhikṣus shall enter the rains retreat; all matters pertaining thereto should be kept in mind.
If the assembly wishes to divide the rooms and bedding after the retreat has begun, it should be done as previously prescribed in the rules concerning the construction of monasteries.

On the sixteenth day, the administrator should observe the number of people and prepare tally-sticks (*śalākā*). He should wash them with scented water, coat them with fragrant clay, and place them in a clean tray; fresh flowers are spread upon them and they are covered with a clean cloth. Then, having struck the *ghanṭā* to assemble the great assembly, the tally-sticks are placed before the *sthavira*.
Next, the rules for the retreat (varṣā) should be proclaimed, and the person appointed to oversee the assembly should go on patrol and announce:
"Venerable sirs! Those who are of one mind and desire it, may you observe the retreat here."

The community of bhikṣus should not, during the summer retreat, interrogate one another regarding their offenses, nor should they establish unlawful regulations that cause the bhikṣus to dwell in discomfort; whoever violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma (dharmāpatti).
The one who distributes the counting sticks (*śalākā*) holds a tray of sticks before him, while the one who collects them follows behind with an empty tray.

The Great Master and Teacher first places a single stick; then the entire assembly, rising from their seats and squatting in a respectful posture, carefully examines the matter. Having received the sticks, they hold them with both hands and place them upon the empty tray.
If there are novices, their preceptors or instructors should take the voting sticks on their behalf.
Next, the voting stick for the deity who protects the monastery should be taken.
Once the total number has been ascertained, one should announce:
“At this present dwelling place, there are this many individuals who have received the voting sticks.
The donor is so-and-so, and the administrator is so-and-so; such-and-such a village district is the place for alms-seeking.”
At that time, all the bhikṣus should conduct an inspection.
Having inspected the place where they will beg for alms, they should reflect to themselves:
"I am fit to observe the rains retreat in this place; it shall not give rise to suffering, and should such arise, I shall be able to eliminate it."
If I should fall ill, there shall be attendants to care for me and provide me with medicine.
From such-and-such a village or ward, I shall seek alms as my place of begging; there, the food and drink required will be sufficient for my sustenance.
Having formed this thought, he should enter a secluded place, stand before a single bhikṣu with full observance of dignified deportment, squat down with palms joined, and speak as follows:
"Venerable one, please attend to me!
Today, on the sixteenth day of the fifth month, the Saṃgha enters the summer retreat; I, the bhikṣu [Name], also enter the summer retreat on the sixteenth day of the fifth month.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall observe the three-month summer retreat within the boundary of this residence; with [Name] as my patron, [Name] as my steward, and [Name] as my attendant for the sick, I shall repair whatever parts of this residence are dilapidated, cracked, or broken throughout its duration. I now enter the summer retreat here.
The second and third [times] should also be spoken in this same manner.

Whether before or after, one should act according to one's preference. If one has committed a *pārājika* offense, one must first undergo formal exclusion (*pravāsanīya*) before performing the *pravāraṇā*.

When interrogating someone regarding their offense, if the person’s statements shift or change, there is no need for further interrogation.

If one has doubts regarding the gravity of an offense, one should consult those well-versed in the Tripiṭaka to obtain a definitive judgment, and then administer the disciplinary action according to the facts.
If factions involved in a dispute arrive, one should employ skillful means to have them depart, and only afterwards perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony.

Regarding the offenses herein: if one is observing the earlier retreat (*pūrvavārṣika*), one should seek and store [requisites] according to the aforementioned seasons; to do otherwise constitutes an offense.

If one perceives it as the wrong time when it is indeed the wrong time, or if there is doubt regarding it, it constitutes *naiḥsargika* [offense].
The two cases of minor offenses and the two cases of no offense should be explained according to the above principles.
If the object is not a substance that should be purified, or if it is coarse and thin, or if two people together beg for it or use it, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) offense.

**The Twenty-ninth Training Rule: Regarding the Misappropriation of Community Property for One’s Own Use** When the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Śrāvastī, a donor offered a fine piece of white cotton cloth to the Saṃgha. The bhikṣu Upānanda then diverted it for his own personal use.
Because the matter of diverting another's property and the underlying afflictions are the same as before, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object intended for the Saṃgha has been given, should divert it for himself, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
"Knowing" means either knowing by oneself or being informed by another.
"The Sangha" refers to the disciples of the Buddha.
Even if the donated object has not yet reached the assembly, when it is diverted into one's own possession, it is still termed "diverting the object."
There are five kinds of saṃgha:
first, the shameless saṃgha, referring to those who have broken the precepts;
second, the mute sheep saṃgha, referring to those who cannot understand the Tripiṭaka.
3. The Saṃgha of concordant assembly refers to those who perform the *karmavācanā*.
4. The conventional Saṃgha refers to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who are pure and virtuous.
5. The ultimate Saṃgha refers to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "benefiting sentient beings," there are two kinds of benefit:
first, the benefit of clothing;
second, the benefit of food.
All clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, and the value of vessels and bowls are obtained from others; therefore, they are called "beneficial things" (*liwu*).
Here, "benefit" (*li*) refers specifically to the benefit derived from clothing and utensils.
Regarding "giving," it means that the donor forms a resolute intention:
"Now I give this object to the Saṃgha.
Whether by body or by speech, one manifests the act of giving; up to this point, it is termed "giving."
"To appropriate for oneself" means to take possession as private property.

Regarding the offense herein: whether it be one person, two persons, many persons, or a communal object that is diverted into one's own possession, at the time of the preliminary effort (*prayoga*), one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); once the object is acquired and belongs to oneself, one commits the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
Some say: "If one knows that another intends to give to a different person, yet diverts it into one's own possession, one commits only a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Or, if one knows that another intends to give to one specific person, yet diverts it to one, two, or many people, or to the Saṃgha; or likewise, if intending to give to two, many, or the Saṃgha, one diverts it to the other four [categories of recipients]—since it does not enter one's own possession, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Or, knowing that [the gift] was intended for the Saṃgha of this location, he instead diverted it to the Saṃgha of another location or to the community of Bhikṣuṇīs;
or again, knowing it was intended for the Saṃgha of these Bhikṣuṇīs, he instead diverted it to that [other] Saṃgha of Bhikṣuṇīs or to the community of Bhikṣus;
or he gave it to two assemblies and diverted it to one, or perhaps the reverse of this.

If the Saṃgha is split, and one diverts property belonging to the faction that follows the Dharma to the faction that does not follow the Dharma—or conversely—one incurs an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in all such cases.

If one diverts the construction of rooms, corridors, eaves, doors, rafters, beams, and so forth, against the original intention of the donor, or builds them in an inappropriate location, this also constitutes an *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one moves these [images] from a representation of the Honored One to make something else or for decorative purposes, there is an offense in every such case.
However, if they are borrowed temporarily, there is no offense.

One should understand it thus regarding stūpas and the objects belonging to a stūpa: the walkways, steps, floral arches, eaves, multi-storied pavilions, the *caitya* wheels and canopies, the tiers of placement, and so forth, down to the precious vases—if these are used interchangeably, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense.
If one informs the donor and acts according to their permission, there is no offense.

However, if at times one intends to give food to the poor and destitute or to animals, but instead bestows it upon others, this deviates from the original intention and constitutes an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one seeks it but does not obtain it, there is no offense.
One should understand that the same applies by analogy to other realms of existence.
If one actually returns [the property] while having the thought or doubt that one is returning it, one incurs an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
If one does not divert [the property] but has the thought that one is diverting it, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one diverts or does not divert [the property] but has the thought that one is not diverting it, there is no offense.
If one knows that communal property is being diverted into one's own possession, even down to a single thread sewn onto one's robe, this robe must be entirely forfeited.
Furthermore, another explanation states:

"If one sees others about to give property to a group of shameless people, and observing that one's own merit is superior to theirs, one redirects the gift into one's own possession for the benefit of the donor, there is no offense."
If one intends to give clothing or requisites belonging to one’s parents to the Saṃgha, but then diverts them for one’s own use, one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).

If someone offers an object to the present Saṃgha, one should first announce it, then strike the *gandī* bell; once the assembly has gathered—whether consisting of several individuals or by means of counting sticks—one should then distribute the items equally.
If a person observing the rains retreat has a reason to travel and departs after having entrusted their portion to another, that other person should take the share;
if it was not entrusted, then it should not be taken.
If the person who received the entrustment does not take it on behalf of the absentee, they should compensate by returning an equivalent amount from their own property.
However, there are eight types of gains when profit is obtained:
first, gain acquired through the territory;
second, gain acquired through established regulations; [and so forth].
3. Benefits obtained through reliance;
4. Benefits obtained during the rainy season retreat (vassa);
5. Benefits obtained by the Saṃgha.
Sixth, the gains obtained by bhikṣus;
seventh, the gains obtained face-to-face;
eighth, the gains obtained from a fixed location.

Regarding the term "benefits obtained within a boundary" (*sīmā-labdha-lābha*): this refers to the fact that there is a fixed jurisdiction for a single boundary, or for two boundaries, or for many boundaries; according to these distinct locations, the benefits acquired are each allocated to their respective boundaries, and those who have resided there since the beginning shall divide them together.

Regarding what is called "the benefit obtained through establishing a regulation," this refers to when various bhikṣus—whether belonging to the same faction or not—jointly establish a formal agreement and then enter the rains retreat, stipulating within a certain village, ward, or street: "In such-and-such a house, we entrust you; in such-and-such a dwelling, we entrust you."
If one receives material gain in accordance with established regulations, it is called "gains based on regulations.

If, at a residence belonging to a faction, an invitation is extended to both members of that faction and those who are not, and after food has been provided to all, the gains are given to the members of the faction while the water of auspiciousness (*maṅgalodaka*) is given to those who are not, then the faction alone is entitled to receive the gains.
If, at a residence belonging to a faction, one invites both members of that faction and those who are not, the benefit should accrue to the members of that faction.

If, at a residence belonging to a faction, one invites both members of that faction and those who are not, and after providing food for both, places the object of merit between the two senior seats and offers auspicious water to both senior seats, then the benefit should accrue to the members of that faction; this is how it should be understood.

If one invites both members of one’s own faction and those of the opposing faction to a dwelling place that belongs to neither faction, and after providing offerings to both, one presents the gift and water before the *upādhyāya* (senior elder) at either one of the two locations, then the member of the opposing faction should rightfully receive the benefit; this should be understood accordingly based on the above principle.

Furthermore, it should be known that when one invites both those who are partisans and those who are not-partisans to a neutral location and provides food for all, if at any point an object or water is offered before the presiding elder (upādhyāya), then the partisans and non-partisans shall together receive and share it equally.

Regarding "benefits obtained based on dependence": this refers to depending upon men, women, and *paṇḍakas* for the purpose of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), and obtaining the requisite offerings from such donors based upon them.

Regarding the phrase "profits obtained during the rains retreat" (*varṣā-lābha*): this refers to the goods acquired during these two periods of the rains retreat, which are to be distributed according to the original intention of the donor.

Regarding the phrase "profits obtained by the Saṃgha": this refers to definitive profits for which no specific allocation has been made; since these items are definitively given to the Saṃgha, they have not yet been divided among them as to whether they are to be given to those who completed both rains retreats or to those currently present.
This property should be divided after consulting the donor.

Regarding the benefits obtained by the bhikṣus, this refers to the determination of specific shares; that is, those who reside in a particular dwelling or courtyard shall receive the benefits pertaining to it.
"Benefit obtained face-to-face" refers to the benefit acquired through direct encounter.
"Benefit obtained at a fixed location" refers to the place where the World-Honored One resided for a long period.
There are eight great *caityas*:
first, the place of the Buddha’s birth, located in the Lumbinī Grove at the city of Kapilavastu;
second, the place of his attainment of Buddhahood, located beneath the Bodhi tree on the Vajrāsana at the Dharma-āraṇya in Magadha.
Third, the place of turning the Wheel of Dharma is at the Deer Park in the Abode of the Sages near Vārāṇasī.
Fourth, the place of parinirvāṇa is between the twin śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara.
5. At Vulture Peak Mountain in the Bamboo Grove Monastery within the city of Rājagṛha;
6. In the High Hall by the side of the Monkey Pond in the city of Vaiśālī;
7. At the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in the city of Śrāvastī.
8. The place where he descended from heaven was the village of Pāṭaligāma.
Of these, the first four places are called fixed locations, while the latter four are called non-fixed locations.
If there is a gift intended for a particular realm of rebirth, that object should be offered solely within that realm and must not be diverted elsewhere.
If one lacks the power to send it there, one should offer it as a substitute for any one of the three [types of offerings].
The other three locations should be understood by analogy with this.
The other four *caityas* are different from these.
If the Saṃgha is split during the summer retreat, one should grant the benefits to the faction that adheres to the Dharma, and not to the faction that adheres to what is contrary to the Dharma.
If one abandons the precepts after the summer retreat has passed half its duration, they should be granted their share of the benefits; otherwise, they should not.

If a bhikṣu dies, there shall be a distribution of food and drink, down to even a single leaf from a tree; as for the distribution of clothing and requisites, it extends even to spinning them into wicks for lamps—all of these may be divided equally.
If there is a garment of superior quality or high value, one should not cut it; rather, it should be sold for its price and the proceeds shared among them.
If the two communities of monks and nuns together receive a benefit in the form of clothing, it should likewise be divided equally.
To male novices (śrāmaṇera) and female novices (śrāmaṇerī), one should give one-third.
To female trainees (śikṣamāṇā) and those desiring full ordination (upasaṃpad), one should give one-half.
As for the benefit of food and drink, it should be divided equally regardless of seniority or juniority.
If the number of bhikṣus is large and the number of bhikṣuṇīs is small, the items should be divided according to the number of persons.
If the number of bhikṣus is small, they should be divided equally between the two groups.
Regarding the goods obtained from events such as the Buddha-mahāpariṣad, the five classes of the ordained community should share them together.

At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the Venerable Upānanda passed away, leaving behind clothing, wealth, and various goods worth three hundred million gold coins.
At that time, the assembly of bhikṣus from the six great cities all gathered together, each saying,
"I am entitled to a share of this property.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu arrives during the five periods, he should be given a share of the benefits. What are these five?
[The text continues with the list of the five periods]."
1. When striking the *gandī*;
2. when reciting the *Triśaraṇa-anityatā-sūtra*;
3. when paying homage to the *caityas*.
Fourth, the time for distributing the voting sticks;
fifth, the time for making the formal motion (*jñapti*).
The method for making the formal motion should be performed as follows:
Having spread the seats and struck the gavel, once the assembly has gathered, one should perform the *jñapti-karman* (motion) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu so-and-so has passed away here."
All robes, wealth, and miscellaneous items, whether currently present or not, are now being formally maintained.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and they grant their consent, may the Saṃgha permit this: the Saṃgha shall now collectively maintain all the robes, wealth, and miscellaneous items, whether currently present or not, belonging to the deceased bhikṣu [Name].
"Thus it is declared.
If the assembly is not gathered in harmony, or if there is no one to preside over the legal procedure, one should perform the "initial and final" rite (*pūrvāparavidhi*).

This means taking a small amount of the deceased's property—such as one or two cowrie shells—and distributing them individually to the foremost elder (*sthavira*) at the head of the assembly and to the lowest-ranking monk; these serve as the definitive record. Thereafter, the present monastic community (*saṃgha*) shall divide the remainder as usual, and no further formal ritual is required.
If the ritual has been completed from beginning to end, one should not give a share to anyone who arrives.
However, if [the property] was present during the first four periods and absent during the last two periods, one should still give a share.
If the announcement (*jñapti*) has been made, then all those currently residing within the boundary who are entitled to receive it shall receive their share.

If the announcement has not been made, nor the formalities of the beginning and end performed, then all who are disciples of the Blessed One’s voice-hearers (*śrāvaka*), whether currently dwelling in Jambudvīpa or in other locations, shall all have a share.
The summary verse says:
Striking the ghaṇṭā and reciting the three invocations, At the time of circumambulating the caitya,
And at the time of distributing voting sticks, Or when the assembly makes a formal announcement together.
If it is difficult to assemble the great assembly, one may provide a record of the beginning and the end;
one should take the property of the deceased and distribute small portions from time to time.
Question:
Regarding the relative weight of items to be divided, the verse says:
Fields, houses, shops, and bedding; Copper, iron, and various hides.
Razors, water-jars, robes, and the like; Clotheslines, poles, and various livestock;
Food, drink, and all manner of medicines; Beds, seats, and written contracts;
The Three Jewels, gold, silver, and so forth— These differ according to whether they are finished or unfinished.
Regarding such items as these, whether they are divisible or indivisible, one should distinguish them according to what is appropriate; this is what the World-Honored One has taught.
As for "according to what is appropriate," it means that fields, houses, shops, bedding, woolen rugs, and various vessels of copper and iron are not to be divided.

If there are an iron bowl, a small bowl, a small copper flask, a copper cup, door-keys, needles and awls, a knife, an iron ladle, a brazier, as well as an axe, and the bags for containing these various items.

If there are earthenware vessels—such as alms bowls, small bowls, water flasks for pure or defiled use, or any containers for storing oil—all of these should be divided; the rest should not be divided.
As for bamboo and wooden utensils, leather bedding, shaving implements, slaves, food and drink, grain, wheat, beans, and so forth, these shall enter the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions.
Any movable items should be stored in the monastic treasury to be used collectively by the Saṃgha of the four directions.
If fields, houses, villages, gardens, shops, or buildings cannot be moved, they shall be assigned to the Saṃgha of the four directions.

As for all other possessions, whether robes or clothing—be they monastic or secular, dyed or undyed—as well as items such as leather, oil-flasks, and footwear, these shall all be divided among those present.
Large bamboo poles may be used as flagpoles for the image of Jambudvīpa; those that are fine may be given to the bhikṣus to serve as staffs for their mendicant’s walking sticks (*khakkhara*).
Among the four-legged animals—such as elephants, horses, camels, mules, and donkeys—they should be given to the royal household.
Cattle and sheep belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions must not be divided.
Items such as armor and mail likewise belong to the royal house.

Miscellaneous weapons and the like may be forged into needles, awls, knives, and the heads of mendicant staffs (khakkhara), which should then be distributed from the senior monk (*sthavira*) to the Saṃgha present there.

Fishing nets and window screens should be used for such purposes; various superior colors, as well as items such as yellow, vermilion, blue, azure, and green, should be brought into the Buddha hall for use in painting images.
White earth, red earth, and inferior shades of blue should be distributed among those present.
If the wine has already turned sour, it should be buried in the ground; once it has finished fermenting into vinegar, it may be provided as food for the community.
If the wine has not yet spoiled, it should be poured away.
Various medicinal herbs and such should be placed in the Sangha’s clean storehouse to provide for the sick.
The precious gems and jade shall be divided into two portions:
one portion shall enter the Dharma;
the other portion shall enter the Saṃgha.
Dharma objects may be used to transcribe Buddhist scriptures and to maintain the lion throne; those that enter the Saṃgha shall be divided among those present.
If items such as beds and couches are made of precious materials, they should be sold, and the proceeds shared equally by the Saṃgha.
That which is made of wood shall enter the property of the Sangha of the four directions.
All sūtras and śāstras must not be divided; they should be stored in the scriptural library for the members of the Sangha of the four directions to read together.
Other books may be sold, and the proceeds should be distributed among those currently present.
Regarding all items involving deeds or contracts, if they can be recovered early, they may be divided among the community;
if they have not yet been recovered, the deeds shall be stored in the monastic treasury to be used for the needs of the Sangha of the four quarters at a later time.
If there are gold, silver, or items made or unmade from them, as well as cowrie shells or various coins, these shall all be divided into three portions:
first, for the Buddha; second, for the Dharma; and third, for the Sangha.
Buddha-property should be used for the repair of Buddha halls and for the stūpas containing hair and nail relics;
property belonging to the Dharma should be used for copying Buddhist sūtras and maintaining the lion throne;
and property belonging to the Saṃgha should be divided among those present.
If there are other items remaining, they should be divided according to this same principle.
If a bhikṣu dies while in a layperson’s house, all his clothing and belongings shall be given to the person who arrived first.
If they arrive at the same time, give it to the one who requested it first.
If they request simultaneously, one may accept it if a layperson offers it, or one may accept it according to the donor's inclination for giving.
If there are other bhikṣuṇīs at the place where a bhikṣu has died, they should not be given a share.
Likewise, if there are other bhikṣus at the place where a bhikṣuṇī has died, they also should not be given a share.
If there were none at all, they should be mutually inclusive.
If one dies in the space between two realms, one should receive the share corresponding to the direction in which the head is pointing.
If one lies across both realms, the two places shall share it together.
If there are many people present, they should be divided into groups of ten or similar numbers, and each group may divide its own portion as it sees fit.
If, within such a group, a share has been allotted but not yet divided, and one person dies, this becomes a deceased person's property and must be redistributed among the remaining ten.
If one who has been divided from the community dies, the property belongs to the entire assembly.

If a person who has been subject to the formal act of suspension (*pratisāraṇīyakarman*) dies while living together with those who desire purity, the property of the deceased shall be divided by those who are pure.
If there is no one who is pure, the items shall be divided among those being disciplined.
Regarding a *śrāmaṇera* who dies while residing in the quarters of a faction, all his robes and requisites shall be divided by that faction.

If one who does not delight in solitary possession relinquishes [the property] to enter the great assembly, this constitutes a proper relinquishment, and the great assembly should divide it; thus it should be understood. Regarding the place of residence of a partisan:

if a partisan dies at the place of residence of a partisan, it should be understood according to the principle of the case. Regarding the place of residence of a non-partisan: if a partisan dies at the place of residence of a non-partisan, it should be understood according to the principle of the case.
Devadatta preached five heterodox doctrines; those who mentally consented to them were called his followers, while those who relied upon the World-Honored One were called non-followers.

When a bhikṣu dies, whether the attendant was one of the five groups of renunciants or an ordinary layperson, wherever they may be, if that sick bhikṣu passes away, the six types of requisites should be used from among the deceased’s belongings to reward the caregiver as a repayment for their kindness.
Regarding the "six items," these are the three robes, the alms bowl, the sitting mat, and the water filter; these are to be bestowed according to the merit and capacity [of the recipient].
If a bhikṣu is ill, he may speak as follows:
"After my death, you may take these items and give them to that person."
Regarding the phrase "this is the way of laypeople," such an entrustment is invalid; these items should be divided.
If they are handed over face-to-face, it constitutes a proper gift.
The corpse should be cremated, and once the offerings and recitations of the sutras are completed, the items may then be divided. To act otherwise constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If a deceased person has left behind entrusted property, that property shall be divided among the Saṃgha at the very location where it is situated.

If, after the death of a *karmadāna* bhikṣu, his personal requisites have become so intermingled with the property of the Three Jewels that they cannot be distinguished, the property of this deceased person shall be shared between the Three Jewels and the Saṃgha.

If a person within the boundary conceives the thought that they are outside the boundary, or harbors doubt, yet participates in the distribution of robes, they commit a *vyatikrama* offense; all members must assemble.

If a bhikṣu entrusts property to another and both pass away, the custodian of the goods should perform the ritual of formal possession (*dhāraṇa*) and may then use it as he pleases; the remainder is as detailed in the extensive text.

If a single bhikṣu obtains the goods acquired during the communal rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*), he should accept them; however, at the time of acceptance, he should maintain them through mental resolve (*manasikāra*), saying:
"This robe has now arrived; it is the property rightfully belonging to the present Saṃgha and is an object to be divided. It shall be divided and used by the present Saṃgha."
"Since there is no great assembly, this robe should be received by me; I shall now maintain it.
If anyone arrives before it has been maintained, one should give them a share;
if one does not give it, they incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one obtains cloth within the boundary and carries it outside the boundary to divide it among others, if there is no intent to steal, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing);
if there is an intent to steal, one incurs the offense of theft (*steya*).
If it is property acquired during the summer retreat, those who have broken their retreat (*varṣā-bheda*) should not receive a share.
Even if the time for giving regular robes has passed, one should still accept the offering of summer robes (*kārttika-cīvara*).
If there is a face-to-face gift of robes during the robe season, even those who have not yet entered the summer retreat period should likewise accept it together.

If both monastic communities of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs have been provided with a meal, and the donor brings an item of property that does not go before the senior monk, one should question the donor before distributing it.

If the offerings were originally intended for the bhikṣus, once the food for both communities has been consumed, the items should be placed before the presiding elder; these should then be divided into two equal halves.
If a bhikṣu departs during the summer retreat on business for the sake of the community, although he is not physically present, he shall receive his share of the summer offerings.
If those observing the *varṣā* retreat—whether they have arrived early or late, or have already sat for more than half the period—are entitled to receive all the summer provisions (*varṣā-lābha*).

Whenever one serves as the head of the community, upon seeing the person distributing food—even at the very first moment when a single spoonful of salt is set down—one should instruct that person to kneel with palms joined and announce to the assembly:
"The time for the equal distribution of offerings has arrived."
The Elder, hearing the voice, replied:
"One may proceed with impartiality.
If the first person did not speak, the second should respond.
If this is not stated, the senior monks (sthavira) and others will incur an offense against the Dharma (dharmātikrama).

If a donor, at the time of making offerings, wraps the tree with various silks and brocades as an adornment, these items should be collected; whenever a festival or assembly arrives, they should be tied back to the tree or hung elsewhere for occasional worship.

If it is hung on a wall, it shall be used for painting the walls; if it is in a warm hall, it shall be used for the bathhouse; if it is by a well or pond, it shall be used for providing drinks at appropriate and inappropriate times.
If it is in the infirmary, it should be used for preparing fine food and provided as offerings according to the occasion.
If offerings are located on the ordination platform, under the eaves, beside the towers, or beneath the gatehouse, the bhikṣus should divide them among themselves.
However, if they are suspended or placed within the central courtyard of the monastery, these belong to the Saṃgha of the four directions and must not be divided for personal use.
There are five kinds of property whose substance should not be divided:
first, the property of the Saṃgha of the four directions;
second, the property of a stūpa.
Third, items for the infirmary;
fourth, items produced from the primary source;
fifth, food that should be consumed.
Regarding roots, fruits, sugarcane, and the like, although these are items fit for consumption, they should be distributed in one's presence.
As the text states:
"If there are many *āmra* fruits, they should be divided and given to the Saṃgha, from which one may then partake as one sees fit."

When these fruits are ripe, one should have a bhikṣu remain silent while guarding them; he must not engage in clamor or contention, for one who violates this incurs an offense of transgression (vayadharmāpatti).
When intending to distribute the fruits, one should first examine them for insects and subsequently purify them with fire.
"If there are no persons who have not yet completed their training, it is not an offense for a bhikṣu to accept [the items] and use them himself.

Regarding the benefits obtained at the stūpas of the Śrāvaka disciples, they should be used to repair and maintain those very stūpas; if there is any surplus remaining, it should be distributed among those present.
Regarding the rules for constructing a *caitya*: for a *caitya* of the Tathāgata, it should be constructed in its entirety;
for that of a Pratyekabuddha, there is no precious vase at the top;
for that of an Arhat, four *cakra* wheels are installed.
The remaining three fruits decrease by one in sequence accordingly.
If a bhikṣu who is an ordinary person of pure virtue [builds a stūpa], it is called a *píngtóu zhèdǐ* (flat-headed stūpa) as there is no wheel-shaft above.

If a donor provides wealth to construct a monastery, the donor’s intention should be followed by using those funds to create various implements, provide food and drink for the laborers, and supply oil for rubbing the feet, lamps, and miscellaneous necessities, ensuring that nothing is lacking.

If there is a donor who constructs a dwelling place and first bestows it upon one person, then further transfers it to another—one, two, three, or to the entire community—this is called an illegal gift.
Those who consume it are likewise called impure.

This applies even when giving to the great assembly—whether the community of bhikṣus or the community of bhikṣuṇīs—if one diverts it to another place, what was initially called "giving" subsequently becomes "non-giving"; both the giver and the receiver thereby commit an unrighteous act.
However, regarding bedding and other items given by a donor, one may only use them after having them prepared at their original location; one should not take these to give elsewhere.
There are five types of persons who enjoy [the fruits]:
first, those who enjoy as masters, namely those beyond training (aśaikṣa);
second, those who enjoy the wealth of their parents, namely those still in training (śaikṣa).
Third, enjoyment through permitted use, which refers to those who uphold the precepts.
Fourth, enjoyment like a debtor, which refers to those who are lazy and indolent.
Fifth, enjoyment like a thief, which refers to those who violate the precepts.
What is meant by breaking the precepts?
It refers to committing even one of the four grave offenses; as previously stated, such a person cannot digest a single mouthful of food or place a single foot upon the grounds of the Saṃgha.
One who does not act in accordance with this shall incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma.
*Vinaya-saṃgraha* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume Seven;
*Vinaya-saṃgraha* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume Eight.
