37. The Training Rule on Eating at Improper Times. The thirty-seventh training rule concerning eating at improper times: At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Then, seventeen groups of bhikṣus, having encountered circumstances that led them to abstain from food, went to the houses of laypeople to beg for alms.
Having already received the food, he ate it at an improper time.
As the circumstances of the offense were the same as before, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding what is called "improper time," there are two boundaries:
first, that which has passed noon;
second, that before the appearance of the morning light.
Regarding "food," this refers to *kālāhāra* (medicines taken at the proper time) and things that may be chewed or eaten.

If one has the perception of it being the improper time (*vikāla*) or harbors doubt about it, yet swallows it, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. If one perceives it as either the proper time or the improper time while harboring doubt, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one perceives it as the proper time when it is actually the improper time, there is no offense.

If there is a cause of illness, and a physician instructs one to eat non-time flour or meat, one should take grain or barley from within cow dung, grind it to make flour, and give it to him to eat; likewise, meat from within jackal dung may be consumed at improper times.
If such things do not alleviate the illness, and the disease can only be cured by eating wholesome food, one may provide whatever food is required in a private place.
When people of Jambudvīpa travel to the other three continents or go to the heavens, they should eat according to the time-measure of their original location.
"Is it possible for a healthy bhikṣu in Southern Jambudvīpa to eat at an improper time without incurring an offense?"
“There is; it refers to when bhikṣus from the eastern and western continents come here and eat according to their own local time.
One should know that regarding the rules of conduct for the mealtime, if the assembly is large and the time of day is difficult to discern, the Buddha said:
“When the mealtime is about to arrive, first strike the *gaṇḍī* once with a long roll, then strike it three times; these together are called the ‘three strikes.’”
Once the assembly has heard this, each person shall bathe and purify themselves; then the great multitude together bathes the sacred image.

Any bhikṣu who is ill should immediately request food, and the bhikṣus in charge of affairs are also permitted to eat first. Next, the bell is struck three times and then struck again three times; this is collectively termed the "long strike," after which the great assembly may then eat.
If the sound is too faint to be heard, one should strike a large drum or blow a pair of conch shells.
Whenever reciting scriptures, bathing an image, or performing a ritual bath, one should strike the drum three times.
Regarding the method for striking the *kenchi* (temple bell), there are five types:
if the assembly is constantly gathered, strike three long tolls followed by three heavy strikes;
if the monastery is engaged in construction work, strike three long tolls followed by two heavy strikes.
If a bhikṣu dies, one long strike of the gong should be made, which gradually becomes fainter until it ceases.
If he was in a place for seated meditation, one should shake the mendicant’s staff (khakkhara) to alert him.
If the community encounters bandits, one may strike as many times as necessary to wake the people.

Regarding the difficulty of distributing food when a large assembly has gathered: seats should be assigned according to the available space, and food and drink should be placed before each person, starting with the senior monk (*upādhyāya*).
If there is concern that the distribution of food may be uneven, the supervising official should observe the proceedings as they proceed.
If there are few people serving food, the bhikṣus receiving the food and drink should proceed together; two persons must not eat from the same dish.
If no vessels can be found while traveling on the road, eating together is not an offense, nor is it forbidden to eat together with a śrāmaṇera.
The bhikṣus should first receive the food and hold their vessels without setting them down, and only then eat together.
If there is a lay attendant (kappiyakāraka) with whom food must be shared, it should be thrown to them from a distance.
If members of one's retinue have been long separated and, upon meeting, feel joyful and wish to eat together, they may do so in a secluded place.
According to the rules for śrāmaṇeras, a bhikṣu who wears only the lower garment (antarvāsaka) with no upper garment should not consume food.
If one is ill, emaciated, or elderly, one should wear a small *saṃkakṣikā* over the upper garment or fasten a waistband, and eat in a secluded place.
If one is unable to wear even this, one should rest as appropriate for the time, wearing only the lower skirt and eating in a secluded place.
If there are vessels made of gold, silver, crystal, or lapis lazuli, one should not use them at all.
However, if one is in the abodes of devas, nāgas, or yakṣas where no other vessels can be found, one may eat as one pleases using them.

When the assembly has taken their seats for a meal and the signal that the time has arrived has not yet been given, one must not serve the food; nor should even a single spoonful of salt be accepted. Should anyone accept it, they incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
If the person serving the food does not understand the procedure, the Elder (sthavira) should instruct him by chanting; if the Elder forgets, the next seat in seniority should instruct him.

While eating, one should not arbitrarily request food or drink according to one's own whims. Those with weak digestive power may request cooked fruit, while those who are young and strong may take raw fruit as they please. If it is necessary to make a request, one should do so with a low voice.

When eating, one should sit in a squatting posture and maintain a dignified demeanor; one should not look about, but rather cultivate a sense of detachment, abide in right mindfulness, and remain free from agitation before partaking of food.
If one acts otherwise, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma.

When the meal is finished, any remaining food should not be discarded at will; rather, it should be given to one's parents or others. If laymen or laywomen come to beg for alms, one should guard one's own mind and bestow whatever is available.
If it is for animals, one should give only a single handful; one must not step upon the grass or leaves used to hold the bowl.
One should also not eat while wearing shoes or sandals.
However, if one is ill and fears injury to the body, one may step upon leather sandals.
When eating crisp or hard cakes and fruits, one should not make a sound; they should be moistened with liquid.
When drinking thin gruel, one must not slurp or make noise.
If radishes and the like are to be eaten, they should be split apart before consumption.
If one is in a layperson’s home, once the elder has finished eating and the washing and rinsing are completed, one should return to one's original seat and recite the verse on giving for them.
If one hears the sound of the verse being recited while eating, one should not continue to eat;
however, if there is concern that the time for the meal will expire, there is no offense in continuing to eat. Alternatively, one may listen to one or two gāthās and then eat again.
The senior monk should constantly observe those of the upper, middle, and lower seats, ensuring that no one eats in haste or remains unsatisfied.
When the meal is finished, he should take a handful of food, moisten it with water, and discard it as he pleases to give to the animals.

If a donor comes to invite the Sangha, one should first distribute counting sticks to ascertain the number before reporting it. Should another guest arrive just as mealtime approaches, or if someone from among the counted members has gone elsewhere, one must inform the donor.
If one wishes to go out at the time of a meal, one should remain and wait until the meal is finished; however, if there is a valid reason, one may leave as appropriate.
If many guests arrive but there is little food, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should ensure it is distributed equally.
If the food is abundant, one should distribute it according to the amount provided by the donor.

Once the assembly has finished eating and the verses for the dedication of merit have been recited, one should remain for a short while to observe the donor; if the donor wishes to hear the Dharma, one should preach it for them, but if they have no such intention, one may depart as one pleases.

After the bhikṣus have finished eating, they should all recite one or two gāthās to repay the kindness of the donors; furthermore, they should not make perverse or evil aspirations, but rather aspire for the permanent liberation from afflictions through their severance.
As stated above, those who do not act in accordance with this shall all incur an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

**The 38th Training Rule on Eating Food that Has Been Touched: The 38th Training Rule on Eating Food that Has Been Touched.** When the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Kara used to beg for food and eat it. He would then dry up whatever food remained, and when there was wind or rain, he would eat it after it had been soaked by the water.
The circumstances and the offense are the same as before; thus this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu eats food that has been previously handled, it is a pāyattika.
"Previously handled" means that it was previously grasped with one's own hand, or was set aside overnight intending to eat it oneself.
However, there are two types of "already tasted" [food]:
first, that which is received from another before midday and remains permissible until noon;
second, that which is received after midday and remains permissible until the first watch of the night. If one eats beyond these time limits, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one touches food that has not been formally accepted and consumes it within the permitted time limit, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; this is called "improper touching.
If one does so after the time limit has passed and the food has already been touched, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one has previously touched [an object] and then touches it again while suspecting that one has done so, it is a *pāyattika* offense; the next two cases are minor offenses (*dukkaṭa*), and the final two involve no offense.

If one is on the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru) and touches something that was previously touched—or touches it without having received it—there is no offense in either case, because those beings lack the sense of "mine" regarding objects.
If one takes it from there to another location, there is likewise no offense.

If a bhikṣu has committed the transgression of prior contact in three instances—namely, by means of the Saṃgha, by means of a bhikṣu, and by means of one undergoing training (śikṣamāṇā)—[he is not liable for further offense].
If a bhikṣuṇī has committed the offense of physical contact in four instances—with the śikṣamāṇā being the fourth—she is considered to have no such offense in relation to two kinds of persons:
first, those who lack a sense of shame, meaning they do not fear transgression; [and second, those who have already committed the same offense].
2. One who possesses a sense of shame and modesty may forget their right mindfulness.

If, while having a desire for a novice (śrāmaṇera) or similar person, one holds food and gives it to them, yet still maintains that desire at the time of eating, one incurs one *duṣkṛta* offense; if one then eats, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one gives with the expectation of a reward but eats without such expectation, one incurs only a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one gives without expectation but eats with expectation, one incurs only a *pāyattika* offense.
If there is no expectation [of gain] at all, there is no offense in eating from them.

However, if one has previously touched a bowl, spoon, cup, bowl-sack, or even a *cīvara*, water flask, or mendicant’s staff—even items such as door-keys that have come into contact with these—and then drinks or eats while the mouth or hands are still contaminated by such contact, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).

If a bhikṣu wishes to drink water or eat food, whether at the proper time or outside the proper time, he must rinse his mouth with water two or three times before drinking or eating; if he does not do so, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
If a sick person has no other place from which to obtain food, there is no offense even if they eat ghee or other substances that have been previously touched by others.

When water or milk is being poured and flows downward, if it is caught in a vessel and becomes connected with food that has been touched by others, a bhikṣu may hesitate and not dare to eat it. The Buddha said:
"If water and such flow downward, there is no transgression in eating it."

When traveling on the road, if there is food or provisions that śrāmaṇeras and others, being weak and incapable, cannot carry, one should tie them with a rope and have them hold the rope; only then may one lift them up or support them as they set them down. In all such cases, there is no offense.
Alternatively, one may have another person hold the cord and temporarily lift the food for them so that they may rest.
If, due to fear of bandits, that person discards the food and flees, one may carry it oneself; there is no fault of "touching overnight" (saṃsṛṣṭa-rātri) in this case.
If there is no other way to cross a river or a stream, one may also send someone to hold a rope while both lift it together to cross.
If these two people have no means to get across, one may carry them alone across; this also does not constitute an offense.
When transporting large quantities of rice or grain by means of carts, if a cart is about to overturn, one should assist in steadying it upright.
If a sick bhikṣu must ride in such a cart, he should avoid the area near the front rail.
If one travels by boat, one should avoid the area where the rudder is kept.
When drying grain, rice, or other supplies, if a danger arises and no one else is present, one should personally collect them and bring them inside.
If traveling on a dangerous road where no assistance can be found, if one has provisions for food, one should carry them oneself; upon reaching a destination, one may exchange them for sustenance.
If there is certainly no one to exchange with, divide the food into two portions: take one portion and give it to an unordained person, and take the remaining portion to eat together.

If even this is not possible, one should go without food for one day; on the second day, eat one "tiger-fist" portion; on the third day, eat two "tiger-fist" portions; and from the fourth day onward, eat as much as one desires until full.

If one's provisions should be exhausted along the way and one sees food and drink, yet there is no person who has not yet received full ordination (anupasampanna) to whom one may entrust it, then even if one does not perform the ritual purification (pariśuddhi) or formally accept it, or even if one climbs a tree oneself to pluck fruit for consumption, all such actions are permitted and do not constitute an offense.
If ghee, milk, or other substances are boiling over in a monastic cauldron or pot and there is no one available to assist, one should stir them oneself to prevent their loss.

If a bhikṣu is drying medicinal herbs or similar items and a danger arises when no one else is present, even if he must lift them himself, he incurs no offense for handling them after they have been left overnight.
Any exceptions permitted during times of difficulty must not be practiced once those difficulties have ceased.
However, there is no offense if one inadvertently touches a vessel such as a butter jar that is intended for boiling dye.

If one carries this vessel while intending to ascend to the upper gallery, it should be placed on the ground if one has not yet reached the midpoint of the path; however, once one has passed the midpoint, it should be carried out.
Whenever drinking non-timely liquids, one must first wash the hands and rinse the mouth to ensure purity before drinking.
If one acts otherwise, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.

However, because the mouth is constantly moistened by saliva and contact, seeking extreme purity therein is impossible; therefore, one should use soap powder (*cūrṇa*) and cow dung (*gomaya*) mixed with water to rub all around the lips until they are clean, rinsing the mouth with water two or three times. When drinking [after doing so], there is no offense.
If there are cracks in the bowl, one should wash it two or three times before using it.
If hot food has been placed inside and grease floats to the surface, there is no offense.

If there are grains of last night’s rice remaining in the cracks of the bowl, one should pick them out and rinse it with water two or three times; even if some residual moisture remains, there is no offense regarding the food.
If a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī each have food that has been touched overnight, it is permitted for them to eat it after they have exchanged their respective portions with one another.

If a bhikṣu takes up the food belonging to a bhikṣuṇī with the intention that it belongs to her, and the bhikṣuṇī subsequently offers it as a gift, he may eat it; the six permutations regarding the perception of the object should be considered according to the principles set forth above.

39. The Training Rule on Not Accepting Food: The Thirty-ninth Training Rule on Not Accepting Food. The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣu Kara frequently stayed in the śmaśāna (cemetery). There were some laypeople performing a sacrifice to their ancestors, and he took whatever food and drink was there for himself and ate it.
At that time, the common people mocked and slandered them, saying they ate human flesh; this evil reputation spread abroad, causing the monastic community shame and embarrassment.
Consequently, the World-Honored One established the rule that one must eat only after another has offered it, so that there would be a person to offer it who could serve as clear testimony.
At that time, the group of six monks ate whether food was offered to them or not.
As the circumstances causing offense were the same as before, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu, without having received it, places food in his mouth and swallows it—except for water and tooth-sticks—he commits a pāyattika."

"Not receiving" means not receiving [the precepts] from a person under training (śikṣamāṇa), a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a male novice (śrāmaṇera), a female novice (śrāmaṇerī), or any members of the laity.
If monkeys, bears, or brown bears possessed the intelligence to know what constitutes a formal undertaking (*samādāna*) and what does not, they too would accomplish such an undertaking.
There are four factors for the dharma of undertaking:
first, the necessity of mental attention (*manasikāra*).
2. There is a person who bestows it;
3. one receives it with one's own hands;
4. placing the bowl or similar vessel on the ground, one supports it with one hand.
Furthermore, there are five kinds:
first, giving from body to body;
second, giving from object to body; [and so forth].
3. Receiving by bodily offering and material acceptance;
4. Receiving by material offering and material acceptance;

5. Receiving by placing on the ground, which refers to those regions where bhikṣus are held in suspicion or dislike: [the donor] prepares a maṇḍala and places the bowl upon it, pointing from afar to instruct that [the gift] be placed therein.
Furthermore, there are five ways of receiving offerings:
first, receiving with palms upturned;
second, receiving by means of a bed.
3. Receiving with a wooden stand;
4. Receiving with a corner of the robe;
5. Receiving by placing it within the alms bowl.

There are five ways in which the formal acceptance (*pratigraha*) is not accomplished: namely, being outside the boundary, being at a great distance, being at one’s side, being behind one’s back, or joining the palms [at an improper time]. Contrary to these, the method of acceptance is duly accomplished.

At that time, there was a donor who had prepared various offerings of food and arranged them before the assembly with the sincere intention of giving them away. However, a fire broke out in his house; he abandoned the food to go and extinguish the blaze, and as no one was left to present the food, the time for the meal was about to pass.
The Buddha said:
"One should adopt the mental attitude of the inhabitants of Uttarakuru and take it up with one's own hand to eat.

If one has received food, and there is some that was not formally offered, one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) hand it over; if there is certainly no one to offer it, one may clear it away and eat it oneself.
If juice falls into it, one should eat only after removing most of it.
If one has already received food and a child touches it, one must receive it again before eating.
There are five kinds of dust:
Tangible objects, non-tangible objects, pure objects, impure objects, and even subtle particles—if these can be discerned, they must be further received.
Furthermore, there are five types of objects:
the objects of drink, food, clothing, flowers, and fruits; all of these must be received and consumed.

Whenever one wishes to receive food, one must first apply mindfulness: whether placing it in the bowl or receiving it on a leaf, if the food is dropped elsewhere after being told to place it here, one must receive it again before eating.

If the person serving food is unfamiliar with the proper rules and places it carelessly upon the tray, one should receive it all over again; furthermore, one should not take it oneself and give it to a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) to hand over for eating.
If it is a sick person for whom no one else can be found, there is no offense in not receiving [the food].
In general, when attending to a patient, one must first ascertain whether they are fit or unfit before giving them food.
Regarding the term "chewing and swallowing," it refers to that which is in the throat.
Furthermore, when irrigating the nose, one should first wash one's hands thoroughly and receive the liquid from another before pouring it;
this is because once it enters the mouth, it must inevitably be swallowed.
Regarding the exception for water and tooth-sticks: if the water is turbid such that one's reflection cannot be seen in it, one should have another person hand it to you.
However, for such turbid water, one should use grapes or jujube seeds, or else place a ball of flour into the turbid water; once the water becomes clear, it is fit for consumption.
If salt water or alkaline brine is fit for use as salt, these must all be formally received.
If there are discarded grains of rice within a pond or river, it is no offense to take the water and filter it for use.
If water is covered by a film of oil, curd, grease, or scum, one should stir it and then filter it for use.

If, while traveling on a road, one sees water being drawn with a pulley, or water contained in a curd-jar or a leather bag, there is no offense in filtering and using it at any time, whether during the permitted hours or otherwise.
Later, it will become difficult to open, so it should not be used regularly.
There are five types of jars and vases:
namely, those for containing feces and urine, as well as vessels for storing alcohol; these should not be used and should be discarded far away.

A vessel for storing ghee should be scorched with fire to remove its greasiness and thoroughly washed with cow dung; it may then be used at all times, whether during the proper hour or otherwise, or it may be purified by immersing it in pond water.
If a bird comes to peck at the rice in one's alms bowl, one should move its beak to the four sides and eat as desired; there is no offense if food is touched by flies or gnats from a defiled place.
All water jars used for storing water should have covers made of brick or wood to prevent insects from entering.
If there is an opening at the top of the mouth of the water jar, it should be plugged with a cover made of bamboo or wood.
If the water in the jar is scanty and one fears it will not suffice for washing the hands, one should drink from a leaf.

If no one takes the leaves, one should use those that have turned yellow and fallen; if these are unavailable, one may use even the branches and leaves. If even these are not available, one should squat in one place and drink from the mouth of the vessel as one pleases.
One should also understand the ritual for using the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*): when chewing it at dawn, five benefits are obtained:
first, it clears away heat;
second, it can eliminate cold-natured phlegm (*śleṣman*).
Third, it causes the mouth to be pure;
fourth, it brings a desire for food and drink;
fifth, it enables the eyes to see clearly.
There are three kinds of tooth-sticks:
the long ones are twelve finger-breadths, the short ones eight finger-breadths, and those between these two are called medium.
When using them for chewing, first wash the hands thoroughly with soap-powder or earth-dust; next, wash the tooth-stick, and then chew it.
Once it has been chewed, one should rinse it with water before discarding it.
If one is in a place where water is scarce, one should rub it on sand or soil before discarding it.
This was because in a previous life, this bhikṣu had once been a venomous snake; when he discarded his tooth-stick without rinsing it, insects nearby were poisoned and died.
For this reason, the World-Honored One prescribed that one should wash before discarding it.
However, when discarding tooth-sticks, mucus, saliva, and the like, one should first snap the fingers or cough two or three times in a secluded place, and only then discard them.

If it is a place where people constantly pass, if it is a consecrated ground (śuddhabhūmi), or if it is beside a fine tree, or if one is younger than the elders—none of these are suitable places for chewing.
There are three matters that should be done in a secluded place:
namely, defecating, urinating, and chewing the tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha).

If one is old or infirm, one should keep a water-receiving vessel; if this is lacking, one should bite off about an inch of the tip [of the tooth-stick] at the edge of a water drain to make it soft, and then slowly rub the teeth, the gums, and the jaw, ensuring that the entire area is thoroughly covered.
Next, use a tongue scraper; bend it to clean the tongue thoroughly, but do not make it excessively sharp so as to cause injury.
It should be made of bamboo, wood, brass, copper, or iron; with the exception of precious materials, all other substances are permitted for its construction.
If a toothpick cleaner is not available, one should split the toothwood into two pieces and rub them against each other; it should be used according to the previous method.
If no toothwood is suddenly available, one should use bean dregs or dry cow dung to thoroughly cleanse the mouth and lips before eating.
If one has finished eating, the rule is likewise; until one has rinsed the mouth with pure water, one must not swallow the saliva from the food. Regarding the offenses herein:

if one has not received [the food] and perceives it as such, or if doubt arises, one incurs a *pāyattika* (falling offense). The next two cases are minor offenses (*dukkaṭa*), and the final two involve no offense.
If there are few people serving food at a layperson's home and there are jars of ghee, honey, and so forth, once they have been received according to the Dharma, the bhikṣu should distribute them.
However, he should not touch vessels belonging to the Saṃgha.

Regarding baskets and containers containing cakes, fruits, and other such items, the bhikṣu should first receive them from the layperson and then hold them; if he wishes to set them down, the bhikṣu should go in front while the layperson follows behind.
When a bhikṣu is walking, that which has already been formally accepted is considered received; that which a layperson gives while he is walking is newly received.
Regarding various fruits, they are divided into three grades—superior, middling, and inferior.
While walking, one should not take them unevenly; if a fruit falls from the bowl into another place, one may take and eat it oneself provided it is within reach of the hand.

This has already been accepted; if it were further removed, one would have to accept it again. **The 40th Training Rule on Soliciting Delicate Food** The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.

At that time, the six bhikṣus of the group of six had accepted an invitation from the patron Mahānāman. Having arrived at his residence, they saw that what had been prepared there was not fit for consumption. They then went to other houses to beg for fine food. After obtaining milk, curd, and other delicacies and eating their fill, they returned to the house where they had first been invited, but could no longer eat. Consequently, this gave rise to public criticism.
The circumstances and the cause for offense are the same as before; thus this training rule was established.

**The Forty-first Training Rule on Using Water Containing Living Beings** When the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, the bhikṣu Chanda harmed the lives of many sentient beings while using water.
Out of a lack of compassion regarding the matter of using water, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that water contains living organisms, should use it, he commits a pāyattika offense."
Regarding "use," there are two kinds of use:
first, internal use, which refers to what is required for the sustenance of the body;
second, external use, which refers to washing robes, bowls, and so forth.
The previous training rule was restricted to the application of mud and straw for construction purposes;
this present one, however, generally concerns any kind of usage.

If a bhikṣu—with a mind of greed or hatred, or due to forgetfulness, or due to thirst—uses water containing insects, regardless of the quantity, whether he has observed it for the presence or absence of insects or not, yet perceives it as having insects, and without a sense of shame or remorse does not filter it, then by drinking even a single handful from a vessel or similar container, he incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Some say: "When taking water with a vessel or similar object, one incurs a downfall only when it has been completely used up.
If one merely forms the intention to take it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense of mental censure."
"Once the preparatory effort has been undertaken, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) through confession.

One should understand that the cases regarding the offenses of *pācittiya* (falling away) are similar. If one forgets the observation from beginning to end, one also incurs a *dukkaṭa*. Regarding the six permutations of the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), four constitute an offense and two do not.
Some say: "If one perceives water that is free of insects as containing insects, one also incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
There are five kinds of eyes with which one should not look at water:
1. Eyes afflicted by sores;
2. Eyes with cataracts over the pupils;
3. Wild and disordered eyes.
Fourth, the eyes of the aged and infirm;
fifth, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).
Because that divine eye differs from human faculties, it is not permitted to observe [with it].
For how long should one observe the water? It is said:

for the duration it takes for a bamboo cart drawn by six oxen to turn around; or, once the mind has become pure, one may observe and know that there are no insects, and even if one drinks without filtering, there is no offense.
If one does not inspect or filter [the water], it is in all cases unfit for use.
One should know that there are five kinds of filtering implements:
first, the square sieve;
2. The dharma-flask; 3. The kuṇḍikā; 4. The water-strainer.
5. This refers to the corner of one’s robe.
If a bhikṣu does not possess a water-strainer or similar implement, he should not travel to another village or monastery for a distance exceeding three *krośas*.

However, if he knows that at his destination there will be no lack of [clean water], it is not an offense if he does not take one with him; that is, if he knows that the monastic community (*saṃgha*) there always has pure water.

If one knows in advance that there are no insects in a river or a well, or if at least one companion among those traveling together carries a water-strainer, then while traveling with them, one should ask:
"Shall we share this strainer?"
"Shall we take a different path, or shall we turn back? Can you carry my bowl alone for me?
If he agrees, we may go together; if not, we should not go together.
If one does not inquire, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If traveling with the current for five *krośas*, or against the current for three *krośas*, there is no offense even if one departs without a water filter.

If one follows the current of a river and observes that there are no insects in the water at a single point, one may drink and use it as desired for a distance of one *krośa*, provided that no other river has entered between those points.
If it is neither flowing water nor water flowing upstream, when observed once, it may be used within a distance of one *vyāma*.
There are five kinds of purified water:
first, that which is purified by the Saṃgha;... [and so forth].
2. Purification by individual inspection;
3. Purification by means of a filter;
4. Purification by a spring.
5. Well water is pure.
If one knows that the person [who drew it] is a keeper of the precepts who preserves life, then even if one does not examine it, there is no offense in drinking the water when it is obtained.
Whenever one observes water, from the time the sun rises until the appearance of the dawn light has not yet emerged, one may use it as required.
If, when taking water, holding the filter with the hand causes fatigue over time, one should use a three-pronged stand to support the filter and tie its two sides to it.
If the water flows too rapidly and insects die of distress within it, one should place sand or powdered cow dung in the filter to slow its flow.

Alternatively, one may make a bowl of earthenware or copper with three holes pierced in its rim; attach cords to each hole and tie them to three poles. Place the corner of the water filter inside the bowl and catch the filtered water in a vessel below. One must observe for insects within the vessel until it is full.
When examining water for insects, if they are so minute as to be difficult to see, one should indicate them with a blade of grass or a stalk of straw, but not with a finger.

Once the water has been taken, place the filter in a bowl; if it is near a pond or river, pour the water there directly. If you must remain on dry land, release the water into a well. You must not hold the filter in the air and invert it over the well, causing the insects to suffocate or resulting in injury to living beings.
One should prepare a device for releasing living beings by making a small jar with two handles attached at both the top and bottom, secured with double ropes and covered with a fine mesh.

Pour clean water into it and inspect it with great care; once you know there are no insects, lower it straight into the well. Turn it upside down and pull it out, repeating this process several times until no insects remain in the mesh. You must wash it thoroughly, dry it in the sun, and ensure it is completely dry.

If the vessel is fragile, one should place a flower-hole at the bottom made of copper, iron, or earthenware; it should be three or four finger-widths wide and two or three finger-widths high, and it should be used after being secured with silk or layered cloth.

If a water jar for the Saṃgha is placed within the monastery, it should be situated in a convenient location; one should also provide a wooden stand or a brick seat for it. It must always be kept clean and pure, and should be scrubbed with *kuśa* grass from time to time so that it does not become defiled.
If there is a foul odor, it should be dried in the shade; if the hands are not clean, one should not touch it at all.
If there is a reason to take it away for the sake of drinking, one should carry it away using a copper or earthen bowl, or by holding it within a leaf.

The person who distributes water must wear clean clothing; they must not touch the jars or vessels with garments that have been worn overnight or are defiled. Young novices (śrāmaṇera) are also permitted to distribute water.
If laypeople come to borrow jars or vessels, one should give them old ones and not new ones;
however, when bhikṣus borrow them, they may be given as one pleases.
One room should be used for storing utensils; if copperware is few, it may be kept together with other items.
If there is much, it should be placed in a separate storehouse. As for the vase for releasing living beings (*mokṣa-ghaṭa*), even a single rope will suffice.
The bowl for receiving water may be placed upon a strainer.

**The Forty-second Training Rule: On Forcibly Sitting in a House Where Food is Being Consumed.** While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, Udāyin was skilled at interpreting omens and could anticipate people's intentions. Knowing that a certain man and woman intended to engage in unrighteous conduct, he immediately preached the Dharma to the woman, thereby causing them mutual agitation. Because of this incident involving visiting a household for food and the affliction of lust, this training rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a household is engaged in a meal, should sit down forcefully therein, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the term "knowing," it means being aware that the people of that household intend to engage in sexual intercourse.

Regarding "those who possess food": women are the food of men, and men are the food of women; this means that when men and women engage in sexual intercourse, they mutually enjoy one another, and thus they are called "those who possess food."
"To sit down forcibly" means to occupy a seat by one's own will without asking the host for permission; hence, it is called "sitting forcibly.

Regarding the offense herein: it refers to a situation where a man and a woman, each harboring lustful intentions, have reached a mutual agreement and are about to engage in sexual intercourse. At that time, if a bhikṣu, with a defiled mind, forcibly preaches the Dharma to them, thereby obstructing their activity and causing them resentment.
If one sits upon it while it is still occupied, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the six permutations concerning the presence or absence of food and the perception thereof, they are the same as previously described.
If it is a celestial maiden (*devī*) or a *khañjaka*, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense in all cases.
There is no offense for one who, being pursued by bandits and seeking refuge by concealing their form, has no mind of sexual desire.

**The Forty-third Training Rule: On Forcibly Standing in a House Where Food Is Being Consumed.** While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Udāyin entered a layperson’s house ahead of others and hid his body behind a door panel to observe them engaging in improper conduct. When the people there became aware of him, they reviled and scolded him.
The circumstances and the offense are the same as before; thus this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a household is engaged in a meal, stands insistently in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the term "a secluded place," it refers to a location where there are only two people.
In the preceding cases, whether in a secluded or exposed area, sitting was the prescribed posture;
here, however, it refers specifically to a secluded place, and standing is the required action—even for a very brief moment, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If there are difficult circumstances, as before, there is no offense.

The Forty-fourth Training Rule: On Giving Food to Naked Ascetics, Male or Female. While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the Bhikṣu Ānanda, having finished his meal, gave the remaining food to two naked female ascetics.
Of those two daughters, one was old and the other was young; without careful consideration, he gave one cake to the old woman and two to the young one.
The old mother said to the young one:
"He gave two cakes while harboring a specific desire; you should prepare them accordingly.
This training rule was established due to the faults of external paths, the censure of others, and the affliction of waiting for conditions.
"If a bhikṣu, with his own hands, gives food to a naked ascetic or to other male or female non-Buddhist practitioners, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the term "naked," this refers to the naked ascetics (nirgranthas).
Regarding the mention of "other non-Buddhists," this term collectively includes all other such classes.
"Giving with one's own hand" means giving with one's own hands, having made a firm resolve to bestow the gift.
In this context, the offense refers to male and female practitioners of non-Buddhist sects, such as the naked ascetics (nirgranthas).
When the recipient is present, if a bhikṣu hands it over, or it falls into their hand, or drops into their vessel, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it has not yet fallen [into the vessel], one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, because by giving with one's own hand, one gives rise to arrogance and a lack of shame toward the other.

If one does not have [the food] present before oneself, or if it has been placed on the ground, and one first sets aside a portion and only afterwards eats, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) in all such cases.
The six permutations regarding the perception of the object (*ālambana-saññā*) should be understood as explained above.
If it concerns close relatives or those suffering from illness, there is no offense if one accompanies them at the appropriate time.
If one wishes to go forth [into homelessness] and live together with them, it is as explained in the extensive text.

**The Training Rule on Observing an Army, the Forty-fifth.** When the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit arrayed his military forces, intending to launch a campaign.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went to observe [the army].
Because they observed military affairs and were not free from the afflictions of restlessness, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu goes to observe an arrayed army, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the phrase "arraying the army," it means intending to engage in battle.
There are four types of military forces:
namely, elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry.

Regarding the offense herein: if there is a great military force not far from a monastery, and they have arrayed their troops and banners with the intent to engage in battle, and a bhikṣu goes to watch—even if they do not actually fight, but watch as if they were fighting—at the very moment of first seeing them, he incurs a *pāyattika* (falling) offense.
If one employs such means, one incurs many offenses of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If one observes the armies of devas, nāgas, asuras, and so forth, one likewise incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
Even intentionally observing the fighting of quails and the like constitutes an offense of wrong-doing; the perception regarding the object is the same as previously stated.
There is no offense if: a hostile army is about to arrive and one must go to observe it to ascertain its distance;

or if one encounters it while begging for food; or if the military camp is on the path; or if the army enters the monastery; or if there are circumstances of distress—in these cases, observing even at length constitutes no offense.

46. The Training Rule on Staying Two Nights in an Army. This is the forty-sixth training rule. When the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit issued orders for his military forces; upon seeing this, the group of six monks remained there for an extended period.
The circumstances and the cause for affliction are the same as before; thus this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu has a reason to go into an army, he should stay for no more than two nights.
If he stays longer, it is a pāyattika."

Regarding the offense herein: if there is a military force drawn up nearby, and a bhikṣu, having a reason, accepts an invitation to go there, or if greed arises toward the gain of robes; [this constitutes an offense].
Whether that military camp is orderly or disorderly, if one stays to observe it with the intention of inspecting the troops, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense when the dawn appears on the third night.
When employing skillful means, there is also much regret.
There is no offense if one is restrained by a king or others, or if there are other difficult circumstances.

47. The Training Rule on Stirring Up Troops in Distress. This is the forty-seventh training rule. When the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the group of six bhikṣus went to a military encampment where the troops were in a state of agitation; they stirred up the weapons and caused the elephants and horses to bolt, leaving the army terrified.
The circumstances and the cause for offense are the same as before; thus this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu stays within an army for two nights and observes troops preparing for battle, sees the vanguard soldiers, or watches them arrayed in formation, it is a pāyattika."
"Equipping the army" refers to the preparation and mobilization when one is about to engage in battle.
"The leading banner" refers to whichever of the four types of banners is seen being drawn forward at the head.
What are the four banners?
First, the lion banner;
second, the great ox banner.
Third, the whale banner;
fourth, the garuḍa banner.
As for "military," it refers to the foremost among the four types of military forces.
Regarding the deployment of battle arrays, there are four types:
first, the spear-and-sword formation;
second, the carriage-pole formation; [third, the... [fourth, the...].
Third, the crescent moon formation;
fourth, the garuḍa-wing formation.
As for "scattered troops," this refers to miscellaneous military forces other than those cited previously.
Regarding the offenses herein: if one observes the army having already been arrayed, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If the army has not yet been arrayed, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
If one observes the army being arrayed, up to its being disbanded, in all such cases one incurs a *pāyattika*.
The rest is the same as before; there is no offense in cases of difficult circumstances.

**The 48th Training Rule: Striking a Bhikṣu** When the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, Udāyin struck the group of seventeen monks because they did not comply with his commands.
This training rule was established due to the affliction of intolerance arising from the act of consorting with others.
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."

Regarding "striking": whether it be snapping one's fingers, kicking with the toes, using bricks, tiles, or the like, or striking another with a blade of grass—if one strikes another with as many fingers as there are, or with as many mustard seeds or blades of grass as there are, one incurs that same number of *pāyattika* offenses.
If one does not harbor such an intent, one still incurs an equal measure of the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If one strikes with the intention to kill, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding the term "bhikṣu," whether he maintains the precepts or has broken them, if one perceives him as having the appearance of a bhikṣu and forms the thought that he is a bhikṣu, or if one entertains doubt [regarding his status], one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If one strikes another who is not a bhikṣu while perceiving them as a bhikṣu or suspecting them to be so, or if one strikes a pillar, a wall, or any other object with a distracted mind, in all such cases, one incurs an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
There is no offense if it is not done with a mind of anger, but for the sake of a beneficial purpose.

The Forty-ninth Training Rule: Threatening a Bhikṣu with the Hand. The circumstances for this forty-ninth training rule are the same as those previously mentioned; the difference lies in threatening with the hand, which led to the formulation of this rule.
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger and displeasure, makes a threatening gesture toward another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
This means that if one makes a threatening gesture with the intent to strike, at the very moment the hand is first raised, one incurs the full offense.
If one raises a hand toward many bhikṣus, the offense is incurred according to the number of persons involved.
When one is harboring resentment toward a bhikṣu, one should go to him and seek his forgiveness; one should not seek to offer an apology while the anger in one's heart has not yet subsided.
They likewise cannot emulate the conduct of a lion, for their hearts are hardened and they lack mutual forbearance.
If they are unwilling to endure it, one should dispatch a wise person to skillfully mediate and bring the dispute to a swift end.
When a junior [monk] arrives at the presence of an angry bhikṣu, he should prostrate as soon as he reaches the boundary of his sphere of influence;
the other should say, "Are you free from illness? If he sees bhikṣus engaged in quarreling, he should mediate and resolve it without taking sides.
One should not go to see where laypeople are fighting, for fear of being cited as a witness.
As stated above, those who do not act in accordance with these instructions all incur an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
**The Fiftieth Śikṣāpada on Concealing Another’s Gross Offense** While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, Upānanda committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The bhikṣu Dharmadatta saw this; fearing that it would be spread abroad, he spoke these words:
"I already knew that your preceptor had committed an offense, but in order to suppress evil and promote good, I never mentioned it to anyone."
"You have seen my fault; it is only right that you conceal it.
When Dharmadatta heard this, he told the bhikṣus, and the matter was as before.
Due to the affliction of concealment, this training rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, conceals it, he commits a pāyattika.
"Knowing" means either knowing through one's own perception or learning it from the words of another.
Regarding the term "bhikṣu": whether one maintains the precepts or has broken them, anyone possessing the characteristics of a bhikṣu is called a bhikṣu.
Regarding "grave offenses" (sthūlātyaya): this refers to the first two categories [of pārājika and saṃghāvaśeṣa] as well as their preliminary preparations.
"Concealment" (paticchādana) means to cover over one's transgressions.
Regarding the offense herein: if, having seen or heard [of another's fault], one conceives the intention to conceal it until the appearance of the dawn light, one incurs a *pācittiya* offense.
All other concealments of offenses are *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
Even if one confesses before a person who has broken the precepts, the confession is not valid; the perception of the object should be understood accordingly.

There is no offense if, when speaking of another, it would cause them distress; or if there is a threat to life or to the *brahmacarya*; or for the sake of protecting the Saṃgha from schism—if one conceals [the offense] for these reasons, there is no offense.
The sixth summary verse says: Companions, vexation,
fire, bathing, Sleeping together, the rule regarding non-obstruction,
Not having relinquished, a novice, defilement, Receiving jewels, and during extreme heat.

**The 51st Training Rule: Regarding Going Together to a Layperson’s Home and Not Being Given Food.** The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī. At that time, Upānanda had a prior animosity toward the bhikṣu Dharmadatta. He used flattering words to entice him and led him to a layperson’s home, where he then refused to give him food, causing him to suffer from hunger and exhaustion; the details of this matter are the same as before.
Out of intolerance for afflictions, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu speaks to another bhikṣu, saying:
'Venerable friend!'"
"Let us go together to a layperson's home; we shall give you delicious food and drink so that you may be fully satisfied.
When that bhikṣu arrived at the layperson's home, they gave him no food at all, but said to him:
"Venerable one!"
"Go away! I do not find pleasure in sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure in sitting and speaking alone.
If, by speaking these words, one intends to cause distress, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Households" refers to Brahmins and other lay families.
"Causing them to be satiated" means intending not to give them food or drink so that they suffer from hunger.

Regarding the offense herein: if one possesses the appearance of a bhikṣu and perceives another as a bhikṣu, and with a mind intent on causing disturbance, the other person understands the intent, one incurs a *pāyattika* (falling) offense.
If one disturbs a person under training (*śikṣamāṇā*) or any other person, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense.
If one causes disturbance in a nunnery, at a temple of the gods, or in a non-Buddhist hermitage, it constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta) in all such cases.
However, there is no offense if one follows a physician’s instructions to fast for the sake of treating an illness.

52. The Training Rule on Touching Fire. The fifty-second training rule concerning touching fire was established when the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. Due to a fire burning trees, a black snake emerged from the smoke; seeing this, the bhikṣus all fled in haste, or some even struck and threw it from afar using the tip of a torch.
Because of the lack of tranquility caused by the practice of using fire, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, for his own sake lights a fire himself or instructs another to light one, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding "without illness": if there is a reason related to illness, touching [fire] is not an offense.
Regarding "for one's own body": it is not for the sake of another.
Regarding "naturally": either blowing so that it emits flames, or turning over firewood.
If one instructs another to light [a fire], it means causing another to kindle a flame.

Whether for the sake of playfulness one brandishes the tip of a flame, or fashions it into the shape of a crescent moon, or the form of a chariot wheel—whenever one touches fire outside of the permitted time, whether lighting or extinguishing it, or through forgetfulness, agitation, blowing with the breath, adding fuel, or moving the wood and charcoal—at the very moment of such movement, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

If one does not understand the local dialect, or if one uses written messages and the like, or if one signals by means of bodily gestures to have a fire lit, in all such cases one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
One may, however, turn over parched grain or husks in the fire, or roast cakes therein for consumption.

Even if one is within the prescribed time limit, if one places hair, body hair, nails, bones, mucus, saliva, blood, or the like into a fire without the intention to maintain them [as relics], one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense if, while within the time limit, one acts with the intention to maintain them.

Regarding the timing: if one performs an action for the sake of the Triple Gem, one's *upādhyāya*, or one's *ācārya*, or for other fellow practitioners of the pure life; or if it is for oneself to temper a bowl, dye robes, or prepare various foods and drinks; or if it is for any activity undertaken due to cold or illness—if one forms the intention to maintain the mindfulness until the task is finished, there is no offense even if one forgets during the interval and touches [the object].
Regarding the "mind of observance": if one wishes to touch fire, one should mentally reflect:
"I now must touch this fire for the sake of performing such-and-such a task," as well as for the sake of my fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin).
When wishing to extinguish [the light], one should say:
"It must be extinguished because there is no purpose [for it to remain].
If one touches a lion or similar creature, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
There are six cases regarding the perception of fire-contact; in the latter two, there is no offense.
If one sets a wild fire, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
One should also not light a fire at will upon a bed of charcoal; rather, one should spread bricks or stones thickly over it before burning.

When lighting a fire in the corridors or the central courtyard of the monastery, do not allow the smoke to blacken the buildings; wait until the smoke has completely dissipated before bringing the wood inside.
One should not burn wood that is required for the construction projects of those engaged in building work.
If one damages it through negligence, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To extinguish a mass of fire, one should use an iron shovel; when reciting sūtras at night, one should light lamps and candles; and the lamp-stands required for this should be made of a single layer.
If it is property belonging to the Saṃgha, it is permitted to make it multi-layered.
