53. The Training Rule on Reversing a Consent Already Given. The fifty-third training rule concerning reversing a consent already given. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the great assembly performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act of suspension) against Upānanda.
Nanda, having realized this, spoke thus to other bhikṣus:
"The *chanda* (consent) I previously gave was not properly given.
Because of this matter of giving consent and the underlying affliction of impatience, this training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established.
"If a bhikṣu, having given his consent (*chanda*) to another, subsequently regrets it and says,
'Give me back my consent; I will not give it to you,' it is a *pāyattika*."

Regarding the phrase "having already granted consent" (*chandadattaka*): it refers to when the Saṃgha has a formal matter that is in accordance with the Dharma, and one has previously given their internal assent.
Regarding "subsequently regretting": it refers to having first granted consent and subsequently giving rise to a mind of remorse.
The phrase "Give us back! expresses a refusal:
"Who would have known that you, having taken me away, would instead act to our disadvantage?"
Regarding the distinction between this precept and the previous violation of the training rules: in the former case, the matter of the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) was already known;
here, it is based on ignorance, serving merely to prohibit the intent.

Regarding the offense herein: if, after having already given one's consent (*chanda*) to another, one subsequently gives rise to regret; and if, once such affliction has arisen, the mind is devoid of shame and dread; and if, regarding the person before one, one perceives them as a *bhikṣu* and speaks to them [of the matter], one immediately incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

54. The Training Rule on Staying Overnight for More Than Two Nights in the Same Room with One Who Has Not Yet Received Full Ordination. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. As the Blessed One had said:
"On the eighth and fifteenth days of every month, the great assembly shall gather together to listen to the Dharma."

Then, at midnight, there was an elderly bhikṣu who lay down to sleep with a lamp lit; he dreamed of his former wife and subsequently engaged in sexual intercourse with her. His delirious words were overheard by others, leading them to give rise to slander.
Therefore, it was established that one should not sleep in the same room as a person who has not yet received full ordination, nor should one lie down while keeping a light burning;
however, there is no offense regarding the light of the sun or moon.

Furthermore, due to the Venerable Rāhula and the sick bhikṣu, it was permitted to stay for two nights; on the third night, those who have not yet received full ordination must be made to sleep outside.
When they are sent outside to sleep, they should not be driven out of the monastery or away from the eaves, but may simply be moved beyond the boundary of the door area of their room.
If one fears that an evil bhikṣu might become a cause for the breaking of the precepts, then by the third night, one should have the śrāmaṇera go to the room of a virtuous friend.
If no such person is available, one should either expel the wicked bhikṣu together with him, or take the śrāmaṇera to another place and sleep there oneself.

If, having entered the rains retreat, one is unable to go elsewhere, one may, with the intention of providing protection, stay overnight with a śrāmaṇera during the three months of the retreat; in this case, there is no offense.
When traveling on a road and reaching the time for lodging, if there is fear or alarm caused by tigers, leopards, and the like, one must remain vigilant until the third watch of the night.
If one is unable to stay awake throughout the entire night, one must certainly not sleep once the dawn light appears;
however, if one is still exhausted, sleeping is permitted and carries no offense.
When permission is granted during times of difficulty, one should not travel when there is no such difficulty.
If there is alarm or fear on the road, one should send [the companion] ahead and remain behind oneself.
If they become exhausted from traveling, one should provide them with a light meal.
At that time, Upānanda had two novices:
one named Tiṇaśūla and the other named Mahallaka.
They stayed together for more than two nights and resided in the same place as laypeople.
Out of concern for the lack of tranquility caused by sleeping and lying down, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu should spend more than two nights sleeping in the same room as a person who has not yet received full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the term "one who has not yet received full ordination," this refers to all human beings other than bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; all such persons violate this training rule.
One should understand it thus: when one stays overnight with a woman until the third night, one commits two *pārājika* offenses.

"Exceeding two nights" means passing through two nights until the third night; from the very first lying down, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing), and when the dawn appears, one incurs a *pācittiya* (offense of expiation).
Regarding the term "the same room," there are four kinds of rooms:
first, those that are completely covered and completely enclosed, such as various houses, guest halls, and multi-storied pavilions, which are fully covered above and have all four walls screened.
2. The *saṃchanna-bahucchidra* (mostly covered with many openings): it has few windows or doors set in its four walls. 3.

The *bahuchanna-saṃvṛta* (mostly covered and fully enclosed): this refers to a house on four sides where walls are erected at the four edges and columns are set in the middle; the four eaves may extend inward, being either low or level.
4. "Much covered and much obstructed" refers to a dwelling with three sides enclosed.

This excludes a dwelling that lacks one side among its four; if it is half-covered and half-obstructed, or mostly covered with little obstruction, or has eaves and so forth, there is no offense in any such case.
If one stays together with a *śaṇḍha*, a *pandaka*, or others for more than two nights during a period of pure residence, and the dawn appears, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.

Regarding the six permutations concerning those who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and the perception that they have not yet received it, four constitute offenses and two do not.
There is no offense if [the bedding] is beneath a precipice or in an empty tree.
If one shares a room with a person undergoing training (śikṣamāṇā), one must likewise purify the lodging.
This person undergoing training must also purify their lodging when staying with those who have not yet received full ordination (anupasampanna).
Whenever one lies down to sleep, if there are circumstances of difficulty and no other bedding available, one should fold the *uttarāsaṅga* into four layers and lie upon it.
One should fold the *saṃghāṭī* and place it beneath the head, or use the *antarvāsaka* as an upper covering, serving as an inner garment.

Whenever one lies down to rest, one should lie on the right side with the feet placed one upon the other, the body unmoving, maintaining the perception of light, abiding in right mindfulness without mental affliction, keeping the robes undisturbed, knowing the proper measure of sleep, and mindful that one shall rise early. Constantly cultivating wholesome qualities during the first and last watches of the night—this is the method for a śramaṇa’s sleeping and resting.
If one is not suffering from illness, one should not lie down during the day.
If one falls asleep while resting and someone causes disturbance, one should move to another place. **The Fifty-fifth Training Rule:

Refusing to Abandon a Wrong View Despite Admonition** When the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Niḥsanimaka developed a sinful and erroneous view. To cause him to abandon it, the Saṃgha performed a formal ritual of fourfold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*). Even when the assembly offered its admonitions, he still refused to relinquish it.
This training rule was established due to unwholesome observation of phenomena, wrong knowledge, and afflictions:
"If a bhikṣu should speak thus:
'I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha that what is an obstacle when indulged in is not an obstacle when practiced.'"
The bhikṣus should say to that bhikṣu: "Do not speak these words:
'I know what was spoken by the Buddha:'"
"To say, 'Sensual desires are things that create obstacles, yet when one practices them, they are not obstacles,' is to misrepresent the Blessed One;
to misrepresent the Blessed One is unwholesome."
The Blessed One does not speak thus; rather, through countless methods, the Blessed One has declared that all sensual desires are obstacles.
You should abandon such a wrong view.
When the bhikṣus have thus admonished him, it is well if he relinquishes [the matter].

If he does not relinquish it, they should admonish him earnestly and correctly up to three times; following their instruction, they should interrogate him so as to cause him to relinquish that matter.
"If you abandon it, that is well;
if you do not abandon it, there is a *pāyattika* offense.

One who speaks these words refers to the teaching of the Blessed One, which states that even those with wives may attain the fruits of the śramaṇa, yet [this monk] subsequently gave rise to a wrong view.
Regarding the teachings spoken by the World-Honored One, there are two types: first, those spoken by the World-Honored One himself;
second, those spoken by his disciples.
Because the Dharma arises in the world through the power of the Great Sage, even when spoken by disciples, it is likewise called the Buddha's teaching.
"Obstructive dharmas" refers to the five classes of offenses.
"Non-obstructive" means that they cannot hinder the noble fruits of a śramaṇa.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu conceives an evil view and, mistaking it for a right view, says:
"My own understanding is the most excellent.
In truth, he has not heard such words from the Buddha, but merely speaks these words and meanings according to his own whims.
Without feeling shame or remorse, he employs false teachings to deceive others.
When other bhikṣus see this, they should offer a private admonition;
if he does not relinquish [the position], he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Next, during the formal ritual of admonition (*karmavācanā*), from the completion of the initial proclamation (*jñapti*) up until the conclusion of the second formal motion, if he still does not relinquish it, he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for each instance.
When the third [recitation] is completed, one incurs the offense of a *pāyattika*.
One should confess this offense before the assembly. The Fifty-sixth Training Rule:

Regarding the One Who Follows a Person Subject to Suspension. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, the Saṃgha had performed the formal act of suspension (*pratisāraṇīya-karman*) against the bhikṣu Niḥsvabhāva, yet Upānanda continued to dwell together with him.
The circumstances and the offense are the same as before; thus this training rule was established:

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a person who speaks in such a manner has not yet acted in accordance with the Dharma and has not abandoned their evil views, should nevertheless engage in conversation with them, dwell together with them, share resources with them, or sleep in the same room as them, it is a pāyattika."

Regarding the statement "not acting in accordance with the Dharma and not relinquishing evil views," although one has obtained the communal rules of the Sangha, one is unwilling to comply with them; as for the evil views expressed, there is no heart of repentance or reform.
If one has not yet conformed to the community, but abandons their evil views, then even if one dwells together with them, there is no offense of falling.
"Engaging in conversation" refers to discussing matters such as good and evil or receiving formal announcements (*jñapti*).
"Living together" means acting as a preceptor (*niśrayācārya*) for one another.
"Receiving [benefits]" refers to accepting provisions.

"Sleeping in the same room" means performing the aforementioned acts within any of the four types of rooms mentioned previously; if one sleeps there until the appearance of dawn, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense, while those who employ the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) incur a light offense.
There is no offense if one does not know that the person has been expelled by the community, or if they are suffering from illness, or if they wish to abandon their wrong views.
The Fifty-Seventh Training Rule on Accepting a Śrāmaṇera with Wrong Views: While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, there were two śrāmaṇeras:
one named Kaṇṭaka and the other named Mahallaka. They committed various evil deeds without any sense of shame.
Seeing an old friend who had attained the fruit of arhatship, he thought to himself:

"That person and I formerly practiced unrighteousness together; yet now he has obtained this supreme, superior fruit. Therefore, we know that committing offenses does not obstruct the attainment of the noble fruits."

This person with such evil views should be exhorted by the assembly; having placed him where he can see but not hear, the community should act in harmony to carry out the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations) to cause him to relinquish his evil views.
Once the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been made, one should go and inform [the assembly]; this applies to each step of the ritual procedure (*karman*) up to the third stage.
If [the offender] does not relinquish [their position] after the third stage is completed, they should immediately be expelled and may no longer dwell together with the community.
Upananda then took him under his care and lived together with him.
As the circumstances of the trouble were the same as before, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu sees a śrāmaṇera making such a statement as this:"
“If one says, ‘I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha such that what is an obstacle when indulged in is not an obstacle,’ the bhikṣus should say to that śrāmaṇera:
‘Do not speak such words.’”
"I know what the Buddha has said:
'Those things which are obstacles, when practiced, are not obstacles.
Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak thus; rather, through countless methods, the Blessed One has declared that all sensual desires are obstacles.
You should abandon such an evil view.
When the bhikṣus speak to that śrāmaṇera, it is well if he relinquishes this matter.
If he does not relinquish it, they should, up to two or three times, admonish him correctly and instruct him correctly, so as to cause him to relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it, that is well.
If he does not relinquish it, the bhikṣus should say to that śrāmaṇera:
"From this day forward, you must not say:..."
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my Great Teacher.
If there are elders or fellow practitioners of the holy life, one should not follow them [in their conduct].
"Just as other śrāmaṇeras are permitted to stay overnight with bhikṣus, you now have no such privilege.
You foolish man, depart at once!
If a bhikṣu, knowing that a śrāmaṇera has been expelled, nevertheless accepts him and provides for his benefit by staying in the same room with him, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Acceptance" refers to providing formal reliance (*niśraya*).
"Benefiting" refers to supplying them with robes and alms bowls, or teaching them their studies and duties; these are also called benefiting.
If one sleeps in the same room, there is one *pāyattika* offense for each of the first two days; by the third day, one incurs two *pāyattika* offenses.
If one provides dependence (*niśraya*) or instructs in reading and recitation, one likewise incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one associates with and shares resources with those who have been suspended for not seeing their offenses and so forth, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) in every instance;

the rest is as previously stated. **The 58th Training Rule: Wearing Garments of Undyed Color** While the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, on the day of the Great Festival at Mount Cālikavata, men and women from distant and nearby towns gathered together; singers, musicians, and performers all assembled like clouds.
At that time, the musicians deliberated thus:
"Our musical compositions are already known to all; they are not yet extraordinary or exquisite. We ought to alter them and create something new and marvelous."
At that time, there was a musician who took the likenesses of the six bhikṣus of the group and incorporated them into his wind and string instruments.

As this was something new and extraordinary, everyone gathered in competition to see it; consequently, no one went to watch the other drummers and musicians, and the performer thus acquired a great deal of precious wealth.
When the six bhikṣus heard of this matter, they said to one another:
"If even ignorant performers who merely imitate our forms for dance and music can obtain so much wealth,
how could we not obtain it ourselves by doing so?"

Since he possessed sufficient robes and alms bowls and had no need for further begging, he eventually dressed in secular clothing during a time when a great assembly was gathered and performed music himself.
All those who came to watch congregated there; all other instrumentalists ceased their singing and playing.
At that time, the musicians said to one another:
"Previously, by performing for him, we obtained much precious wealth; now he performs for himself and we have gained nothing.
We should secretly present our valuables to six of them; seeing our compassion, they will surely comply with our wishes."
At that time, after the group of six bhikṣus had accepted the payment, they remained there to provide musical entertainment.
Bhikṣus should not practice or study singing and dancing, nor go to watch or listen to them.
This training rule was established because of the lack of tranquility caused by the matter of dyed robes and the underlying afflictions.
"If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he must apply one of three types of dye to disfigure it:
blue, mud-color, or madder. Having disfigured it with one of these, he may use it; if he uses it without having applied one of the three types of disfigurement, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding "new robes," this refers to those that are new in substance rather than being newly acquired; such are called "new robes.
There are seven types of robes, as fully described above.

Regarding the term "blue": take *harītakī* fruit, either grind or pound it and mix with water to form a paste. Apply this to an iron vessel and let it sit overnight. Then, using warm water mixed with this paste, dye the material; the resulting color is blue, though not a deep blue.
Regarding "mud," it refers to being dyed with mud.
The text states: "It is red stone."
"Red" refers to tree bark, roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits.
Anything capable of dyeing cloth may be used to achieve the discolored (kāsāya) hue.
Regarding "use," this refers to wearing it; at the very moment one first puts it on the body, one incurs the offense of a *pāyattika*.
All such expedients constitute an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta).

At the very least, items such as the bowl-cloth, the foot-wiping cloth, the bowl-bag, the water-strainer, and the waist-band must all be dyed with a discolored hue and maintained in a state of ritual purity.
If the substance of the robe—whether the warp or the woof—is an impure material, wearing it without first disfiguring it constitutes an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If a previously discolored robe has been seized by a king or a thief, and one later recovers it, it becomes pure once again as an old [robe].
If it is not dyed and one perceives it as not dyed, there are six cases as described above.

If it is a heavy robe or cloak that is the property of the Saṃgha, one is permitted to keep it as it is, with its threads and fringes intact, and use it; furthermore, it need not be dyed, but one must not wear it uncovered when going out into public.
When going out, both the inner and outer layers must be completely covered with red robes so that nothing is visible from the outside.
If even a single thread or hem should be exposed, it must be cut away.
If it is the property of another person, one must employ the method of entrustment (*nikṣepa-dharma*) for its use; one should speak thus to a bhikṣu:
"Venerable one, please attend to me!..."
"This heavy outer robe has been entrusted to me by the donor [Name]; I shall accept and use it with that person in mind.
The second and third times are spoken in the same manner.

59. The Training Rule on Taking Valuables. The fifty-ninth training rule concerning taking valuables. The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha. At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One took up his robe and bowl, with the Venerable Ānanda serving as his attendant, and proceeded from Vulture Peak Mountain to Rājagṛha to beg for food.
Encountering heavy rains from the heavens, the cliffs were washed away and collapsed, revealing a treasure-store deposited by people at the beginning of the eon,
its radiance dazzlingly bright. The World-Honored One said, "Ānanda!"
"You should regard this as a great and harmful poison. Ānanda replied,
"O Bhagavān, Great Virtuous One!"
"This is truly a fearsome poison.
Not far from there, a man gathering roots and fruits heard this and thought to himself:
"In the past, I have only seen poisonous bites, but I have never actually seen a venomous sting; let it not sting and harm me during the night."
"Let us go and observe it to identify its form.
Having arrived, they saw this hidden treasure, its radiance shining forth from within.
They then secretly had this thought:
"May this venomous snake forever bite my parents, my wife and children, and all my kinsmen; I shall not shrink from the pain.
Having said this, he took the leaf-covering and carefully carried it home, where he and his relatives used it as they pleased.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, seeing his great wealth and prosperity, dispatched a messenger to investigate him, who questioned him gently:
"Where did you obtain this royal treasure?"
The man replied, "I truly did not find the royal treasure.
They seized him and sent him to the king.
The king asked himself:
"Can you truly say that you have obtained my hidden treasure? The man replied:
"I truly did not obtain it.
The king asked his ministers:
"What punishment should be accorded for one who violates the king's command?"
He replied, "He deserves death. The king said:
"This violates my command; you must deal with him according to the law, and all his kinsmen shall be cast into prison.
He was then led toward the place of execution. The man wept bitterly as he followed the executioner, crying out in a loud voice: "Ānanda!"
"This is a lethal poison!
This is a lethal poison!
Having spoken these words while being led to execution, the law requires that the report be returned to the throne.
The messenger was sent back with this message to report to the king.
The king said, "These words do not seem consistent; there must be a meaning behind them.
You may summon him here, and I shall question him in person."
That man related the matter in full according to its former circumstances.
As the king had for the first time conceived faith in the Triple Gem, he could not help shedding tears upon hearing these words and said to the man:

"Because of the World-Honored One, you have obtained this precious treasure. Although your crime merits death, I now release you, along with your kinsmen; you should take this object and offer it as alms to the Buddha and the Sangha."

Having received this exemption, he prepared superior offerings and invited the Buddha and the Sangha to his residence. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he, leaping with joy, attained the first fruit of the path.
For this reason, it was decreed that bhikṣus were not permitted to handle precious objects.

Furthermore, when Upānanda went to an archery range and later to a music hall, he intimidated the masters there and forced them to pay for the cost of cakes; he even sold off their bows, arrows, and musical instruments until they were left in poverty—all such items belong to the category of precious things.
Furthermore, Upānanda took the jewelry of another boy in Vaiśālī and claimed it was the property of a yakṣa deity.
Because he accepted impure wealth, this training rule was established to prevent such transgressions and the resulting afflictions of negligence.

"If a bhikṣu should himself take up, or cause another to take up, precious objects or things of a precious nature—except when inside a monastery or in the house of a layperson—he commits a pāyattika offense."
If one sees treasure or things belonging to treasure within a monastery or in the house of a layperson, one should form this thought before taking it:
"If anyone claims this as their own, I shall give it back to them."
"This is the proper time.

As for "treasures," this refers to gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, coral, amber, right-spiraling conch, and *mūśaragalva*, *indranīla*, *mahānīla*, *sūryakānta*, *candrakānta*, and so forth.
Regarding "categories of precious objects," this refers to implements for combat, such as all types of weapons, or various articles and musical instruments required for entertainment.
"To grasp with one's own hand" means to touch them with one's own body.
"Sending another" means instructing another to touch [the object].
"Within the monastery" refers to the dwelling place of bhikṣus; it was because of the mother of Mṛgāra that the rule regarding lifting and seizing was established.
"A layperson's house" refers to the residence of a worldly person.
There is no offense in seizing another's gold purse with the intention of keeping it for them.
Regarding the procedure in this matter: whenever one finds a lost article, if the owner comes to claim it, one should question them in return.
If the identification is correct, the object should be returned to its owner; if there is any discrepancy, it should not be returned.

When one sees another's property outside the monastery, one should cover it securely with leaves, grass, or similar materials and must not treat it with negligence. If the owner comes seeking it, one should take it back to the residence and keep it in private custody for seven or eight days. If no one claims it, it should be deposited in the monastic storehouse. If after five or six months no one still claims it, it should be used for the benefit of the Saṃgha to purchase durable utensils.
If the original owner later demands it back, one should exhort and persuade them to give it as a gift to the Saṃgha;
if they are unwilling to do so, one should repay them the original value.
If they demand interest, one should tell them:
"Since the Buddha has prescribed that one must return such items to their original state, it is improper to seek further profit from them.

Whether it be jeweled necklaces, armlets, or other ornaments for the body; stringed musical instruments; blowable horns or conchs; bows fitted with strings and notches, or arrows equipped with heads; or images containing the *śarīra* relics of the Buddha—if one touches such things oneself or instructs another to do so, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
It should be understood that the offenses of preparatory effort correspond to the results [of the completed act].

If one uses bodily ornaments not adorned with jewels, or various imitation jewels; bows without strings, arrows without points, or musical instruments that have not been set up; a reed flute unfit for blowing; or even necklaces made of knotted grass, images lacking relics, or pearls from the forehead of a dragon-elephant—whether one touches these oneself, instructs others to do so, or has them recorded in writing, or sits upon a jeweled throne—all such acts constitute an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If one touches it while heading toward the heavens, there is no offense.
If it was previously a weapon that has been broken and rendered unusable, there is no offense.
Furthermore, one should not wear various types of necklaces or ornaments.
One must grasp the image containing relics or the image without relics while maintaining the perception of it as the Great Teacher; only then may one grasp it, because it is the Buddha Jewel.
If one does not maintain this mental state, one incurs the fundamental offense upon contact.
If it concerns a moonstone (*candrakānta*) or a sunstone (*sūryakānta*) for the purpose of obtaining water or fire through touch, there is no offense.
One should not point out [the location of] such things if one knows they belong to a band of thieves; however, if they require water or fire, one should provide them.

If one touches the seven treasures of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), one incurs either a light or a heavy offense according to the circumstances: first, an offense requiring communal instruction (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*); second, an offense of transgression (*pāyattika*). One should know that for the remaining four [treasures], there is no offense; however, touching a woman constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, while touching the jewel-treasure constitutes an offense of transgression. Regarding the two evil [beings], the elephant and the horse, one should know there is no offense.

The Sixtieth Training Rule on Bathing at Improper Times: The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha. At that time, the six bhikṣus of the group were at a hot spring, where they engaged in various forms of mockery and harassment toward King Bimbisāra. On account of this incident, bathing was subsequently prohibited.

Because the odor of their bodies was reviled and disparaged by the people of the age, he further permitted bathing once every half-month; furthermore, he allowed it at other times provided there was no fault.
This training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was established because, due to indulging in personal pleasure and exceeding the limit, afflictions arise.
"If a bhikṣu should bathe at intervals of half a month, yet bathes contrary to this rule, except during other times, it is a pāyattika.

'Other times' refers to the heat of summer, the time of illness, the time of labor, the time of travel, the time of wind, the time of rain, and the time of both wind and rain; these are the [permitted] times."
"Intentionally violating" means bathing in violation of the prescribed limit.

"The hot season" refers to the period when one month and a half remains before the commencement of the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat); that is, from the first day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month, as well as the first month of summer, from the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the sixth month. These two and a half months are called the "extreme heat season."
Regarding "when one is ill": if one does not bathe, the body and mind will be uneasy.
Regarding "when performing work," etc., the meaning is as explained above.
Regarding "when there is wind": this refers to when a slight breeze blows, causing the hem of one's robe to flutter.
Regarding "during rain," it refers to even two or three drops of rain falling upon one's body.
Regarding "during wind and rain," it means that both wind and rain are present together.

Initially, bathing was permitted for half a month during periods of extreme heat; subsequently, bathing at will was authorized, and further exceptions were made for those who are ill and so forth—in all these cases, there is no offense.

Regarding the offense herein: whether it be by pouring water over the head, entering a river or pond, using cold water, or using warm water—if one bathes in such places without maintaining the formal intention (*kāla-citta*) for the occasion, and the stream of water poured from above reaches the navel, or if, upon entering a river or pond, the water rises above the navel, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).

If there is an urgent necessity to cross a river or stream; or if one must circumnavigate a sandbank or shoal; or if one falls into the water by tripping at a bridge or embankment; or if one faints and another person sprinkles water on them; or if one is in a pond or river for the purpose of learning to swim; or if one encounters rain—none of these constitute an offense.
If it is necessary to wash frequently during that time, one should bathe while maintaining mindfulness.
The residence of a bhikṣu must always be swept clean; if the area is so vast that it is difficult to maintain throughout, one should sweep and wipe only those places where they are most needed.

If the eighth or fifteenth day arrives, one should strike the *khaṇḍika* drum and the assembly should sweep together. When the assembly has gathered, one should deliver a discourse on the Dharma or remain in noble silence. Once the task is finished, one should bathe; having paid homage to the *caitya*, they should exchange greetings with one another and depart as they please.
When a bhikṣu sees that the ground has been thoroughly sprinkled and swept, or smeared with cow dung, he must recite a gāthā before treading upon it.
Likewise, when passing over the shadow of a Buddha hall, a caitya, or the poles of banners and flags, he must also recite a gāthā.
If there is a location where the ground is subject to much heat, one may bathe at will.
If one comes into contact with a corpse, one should likewise bathe.
When a bhikṣu’s body has died, his corpse should be inspected; if it is free of maggots, it should be cremated by fire.
Those who cannot be cremated should be discarded in water or buried in the ground.

If there are insects or if it rains, they should be carried together to a deserted wilderness or forest, laid down with the head facing north, supported at the head by bamboo or grass, covered over the body with leaves, and facing south. At the place of burial, one should recite the *Anityatā-sūtra* (Sutra on Impermanence) and further have those capable of it recite verses of auspicious benediction.
Once the funeral rites are concluded, one should return to one's original location; those who handled the corpse must bathe their bodies along with their clothes.
Those who did not touch it should wash their hands and feet.
Those who shaved the hair are also included in these requirements.

If one trims the nails, they should be shaped like a razor or an axe blade; they must not be shaped like a grain of rice, a human head, a half-moon, or a crow’s beak. One must not polish them to a shine, but should instead scrape away dust and grime.
Those who shave their hair must do so completely; one should not leave a patch on the crown of the head nor apply vermilion to it, nor should one use scissors to trim the hair.
If there is hair near a sore, one may trim it as needed, but the hair in the three private areas must never be shaved.
If there are parasites or an ulcer, one should inform the Elder before shaving.
If the hair on the calves or shins is near an ulcer, it should be shaved.
When the hair of a forest-dwelling bhikṣu has grown very long, it may be trimmed to the length of two finger-breadths; otherwise, it should not be so.
At the time of shaving the hair, one should not wear the three dharma robes; rather, one should maintain a separate garment specifically for shaving the hair.
If this is unavailable, one may wear the saṃkakṣikā.

If there is no one to shave the hair and a bhikṣu knows how to do it himself, he should shave it in a secluded place; for this reason, the Saṃgha permits the keeping of items such as razors, which those in need may take and use.
If one is in a communal area that has been swept clean, one should not discard hair or nails therein.
However, if one is elderly, ill, or if there is wind and rain, it is permitted to shave wherever one happens to be.

When the shaving of the hair is completed, one should smear the ground with cow dung; next, one should bathe the body. In cases of old age or illness, or when water is scarce, one should wash the five limbs, namely the head, hands, and feet.
When bathing, one should examine whether it is appropriate or not.

As for the one who pours the water, they should wear two robes; one must not allow a lion to bathe a jackal—that is, one must not have a person of broken precepts wash a person who maintains the precepts. However, if these four—parents, ācāryas, and upādhyāyas—are present, even if they are of broken precepts, they should still be served and must not be treated with contempt.
When bathing, one should not allow those who lack faith or those who have only recently begun to believe to enter the bathhouse.
When bathing, one must maintain mindfulness, thinking:
"I now wish to bathe; at what time am I doing so?"
Only after that should one bathe. One must not use bricks, stones, or similar objects to scrub the thighs or calves, nor should one bathe naked.

One may keep a bathing skirt (*snāna-śāṭikā*) four or five cubits long and one and a half cubits wide; it should not be made of double layers, for if it were double-layered, one fears insects might dwell within.
When one is about to bathe, one should observe the water to ensure there are no insects before bathing.
If one has no lower garment, one should shield the body with leaves and bathe in a secluded place. If insects should cling to the body while bathing, one must not bathe in that water.

When one has finished bathing in a river or pond, one should skillfully use the hand to open and lift the bathing skirt while gradually emerging from the water, taking care not to let it cling to the body so as not to bring out small insects.
Upon reaching the bank, one should squat for a moment, then wring out the excess water from one side; one must not put on the *cīvara* while the body is still wet.
One may only don the robe after wiping away the water from the body with a towel or a wash-cloth.
As stated above, those who do not act in accordance with these rules all commit an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The seventh summary verse says:
"Killing animals, intentionally causing distress, poking, and sleeping in the same place as water."
61. The Training Rule on Killing Animals. The sixth and final training rule concerning killing animals:

When the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Udāyin went to an archery hall where he displayed his own skills by performing the "five-arrow method," thereby treating the crowd with contempt and consequently killing a flying bird. **Summary Verses:** Frightening, storing, requisites, and seeking robes; Groundless [accusations], women, and traveling together. 61. **The Sixth and Final Training Rule on Killing Animals.** When the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Udāyin went to an archery hall, where he personally exhibited his skill by performing the "five-arrow method" and treated the assembly with derision, resulting in the injury of a flying bird.
Out of intolerance for the matter of animals and due to a lack of compassion and affliction, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu should intentionally take the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the phrase "intentionally," it means killing with the mind while perceiving the victim as an animal (*tiryagyoni*).
Regarding "animals," this refers to birds, snakes, rats, and so forth.
Regarding "taking life," it means causing the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) to cease its continuity within the body.

Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣu, with his own hand, or by wielding a weapon, or by throwing another object, strikes with the intent to kill, whether the victim dies at that time or later, he incurs the full offense;
if the victim does not die, he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
When one causes a person who is insane to commit a killing, although that person commits no offense, the instructor incurs the fundamental offense.
If one sends a letter or uses hand gestures and the like to command a killing, at the moment life is severed, all such persons incur an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
The six permutations regarding the perception of the object are also as explained above.
Furthermore, there is another passage which states:

"If one actually commits an act against a being that is not an animal, yet perceives it as an animal, one still incurs the fundamental offense; the gravity of the transgression is determined by the intention."
If one intentionally kills that person but mistakenly kills this one instead, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If there was no intention regarding the specific object [of the act], there is no offense.

**The 62nd Training Rule: Intentionally Annoying a Bhikṣu.** When the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Udāyin saw the group of seventeen novices receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*). With a mind intent on causing them distress, he addressed them, saying:
"Although you have received the ritual performance, you have not actually obtained the precepts.
What is the use of exhausting your minds to further seek academic learning?
It was on account of such frivolous behavior and the lack of tranquility due to afflictions that this training rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu intentionally harasses another bhikṣu, even to the extent that it causes him momentary discomfort,
and does so with this as his motive, it is a pāyattika."
"Intentionally causing vexation" means that one's original intention is to produce vexation in another by means of a matter that is a source of remorse.
"Being unhappy for even a short time" means that the arrow of regret pierces the heart.
To say "with this as a condition" means with the intent to cause vexation as the condition. Regarding the offense herein:

when speaking of another's affairs, whether what is said is reasonable or unreasonable, if one acts with a mind of provocation—saying things such as "it is not the right time," "the boundary has or has not been established," "the two teachers have faults and you should receive [ordination] again," or "you stole your preceptor’s robe at such-and-such a place," or "you have committed a grave offense"—at the moment these words are finished, regardless of whether the other person feels vexation, regret, or anger, one incurs a *pāyattika* (falling) offense.
Except for the case of full ordination (*upasampadā*) and the *pārājika* offenses, if one causes disturbance or harassment by other means, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
Likewise, if one intends to cause distress to a person undergoing training (*śikṣamāṇā*) or to someone who does not understand the language, one also incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
If one acts with a mind of benefit, or provides guidance through reason in accordance with the Vinaya teachings, there is no offense in any case.
Regarding the six permutations of the perception of the object (*viṣayasaṃjñā*), two are grave and four are light;
there are likewise six permutations regarding the perception or doubt concerning an act that constitutes a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), which should be considered as explained above.

63. The Training Rule on Tickling Others with Fingers. The sixth and thirteenth training rule concerning tickling others with fingers. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, there was one person among the group of seventeen bhikṣus who was troubled and unhappy.
Those sixteen people came together to offer their apologies with embarrassment; however, by poking him with their fingers and laughing excessively, they caused his death.
As the circumstances of the offense were the same as before, this training rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu, moreover, tickles another with his fingers, it is a pāyattika.
If a bhikṣu tickles another using one, two, or even up to ten fingers, he incurs a downfall (pāyattika) for each instance.
If both persons are paralyzed and one tickles or pokes them, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Regarding the perception of a monk as a monk, there are two heavy and four light cases; the same six permutations apply to the perception of tickling or poking.
If one points with a fingertip to the location of a scar or mole, there is no offense.

The Sixty-fourth Rule: The Training Precept on Sporting in Water. The Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī. At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus were sporting in the river Añjiravatī. King Prasenajit saw this and gave rise to reproach and disdain.
The circumstances and the cause for offense are the same as before;
thus this training rule was established: "If a bhikṣu again plays in water, it is a pāyattika.

Regarding "playing in water," the offense arises from nine matters: namely, taking pleasure oneself or causing others to take pleasure; playing oneself or causing others to play; jumping oneself or causing others to jump; tossing about and sporting with reflections; and striking or clapping one another with the body.

Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: it refers to whether one is emerging or submerging in water, going or coming, splashing the water as if beating a drum, doing so oneself or together with others, or whatever actions are instigated by the three karmas.

If a bhikṣu, with the intention of making sport, first rises from his seat, puts on his lower robe and upper robe, goes to the washing place, puts on his bathing cloth, and enters the water—whether according to its depth or whether it is suitable or not—with the intent to make sport, for each of these acts he incurs an *āpatti duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) by way of preliminary preparation.

If one plays in jest, whether floating or submerging, going out or returning, drifting downstream with the waves, or rowing upstream against the current; or if one strikes the water for amusement, drawing patterns of ripples upon it, or striking with the hand a water jar, a vessel, or a soup bowl to produce sounds like strings or pipes—one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
If one snaps one's fingers to make a sound as a form of playful distraction, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, there is no offense if one stirs up ripples in the water with the intention of seeking coolness, or if one is crossing a river, or practicing swimming.
As the Blessed One said:
"A bhikṣu should practice swimming, for he may encounter circumstances of difficulty where he must cross by swimming.
If one sprinkles water to play with others, one incurs a downfall (pāyattika) according to the number of drops.
If one sprinkles cool water for the purpose of refreshing oneself, there is no offense.
If one drips oil or similar substances onto another person, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
Apart from water, if one uses any other substance to play or tease others, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* in all such cases.
Regarding the six propositions concerning the perception of water as water, some say:
"Even if it is not actually water but one perceives it as water, one still incurs an offense."

65. The Training Rule on Sleeping in the Same Room with a Woman. The sixty-fifth training rule concerning sleeping in the same room with a woman. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Then, the bhikṣu Āniruddha slept in the same room as a woman in a place where no men were present.
A woman conceived a lustful intent and requested that food be prepared at home for her to offer as an act of worship, compelling a bhikṣu to engage in unrighteous conduct.
Due to the scandal and affliction caused by this woman's actions, this training rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu again sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding the term "woman," this refers to a human female who is capable of committing unrighteous acts and whose limbs are proportionate [to those of a man].
Regarding the phrase "the same room," the four types of rooms are as previously described.
In this context, the offense occurs when a bhikṣu sleeps in the same place as a woman until the appearance of the dawn light; he then incurs a *pāyattika* (falling) offense.
If the dawn has not yet appeared, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
This applies whether the woman is on the upper story and the bhikṣu is below, or vice versa;
or if there is a ladder, it must be removed.

If there is a door that must be firmly closed, one should either remove the ladder or install a bolt and lock; alternatively, one may have bhikṣus or others act as guardians. The guardian must not fall asleep, for if one acts otherwise, one incurs a *pāyantika* offense.
Or, although they are in the same room, one may use objects to screen them off so that there is no coming or going.
If a woman is outside the room, one should firmly close the door; or if she is in a cow-pen, a sheepfold, or a solitary hut, the screening is to be done as previously described.
If one surrounds [the area] on all sides with firewood or thorns, there is no offense.
If one does not do so, at the appearance of the dawn light, everyone incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one stays overnight in the same place as a female deity or nāga whose form is visible, or with a female animal, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
There is no offense if the female animal is too small to engage in sexual intercourse.

However, if one stays overnight with a woman in thickets, or within a dense forest, amidst thick bamboo, inside an empty tree, or sheltered by a cliff or the shade of tree branches, in all such cases one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
If one sleeps with a girl who lacks the capacity [for restraint], one also incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
When a house has separate doors for its various rooms, one incurs an offense by sleeping in the same place as where a girl is located.
Regarding the perception of a girl as a girl, there are six permutations: in the first four, one incurs an offense; in the latter two, there is no violation.
If a bhikṣu has already lain down and a woman arrives later, even if the bhikṣu is unaware of her presence, he incurs the fundamental offense.
Some say: "Even if there is no woman present, if one perceives her to be there, one also incurs the fundamental offense."
"If there are parents, a husband, or others acting as guardians, there is no offense in staying overnight together.
**The 66th Precept on Terrifying Bhikṣus** When the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, Udāyin donned a woolen cloak and terrified the group of seventeen monks,
saying, "Gods and ghosts are coming!"
To cause fear to arise.
This training rule was established due to the lack of tranquility resulting from playful laughter and underlying afflictions:
"If a bhikṣu, whether by himself or by instructing another, causes fear in another bhikṣu—even down to doing so in jest—he commits a pāyattika offense."
"Down to those who act in jest": although they may engage in playful mockery, their fundamental intent is to cause mental distress.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu, with the intention of terrifying another bhikṣu, causes them to feel fear and distress by means of loathsome things—namely, using forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tangibles as objects of alarm—and says to that person:
"Piśācas and the like are coming to kill you."
If one complies with that fear and understands the meaning of those words, one incurs the full offense.
If, by means of such things as pleasant forms or sounds, one says, "The king wishes to come and kill you," one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one causes alarm or distress to a person undergoing training (śikṣamāṇā) or to others, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
However, if one speaks of the hells, animals, or hungry ghosts with the intention of transforming and guiding them, there is no offense even if they become frightened.

Regarding the six permutations concerning the perception of a bhikṣu as a bhikṣu, the first two constitute the primary offense (*pārājika*), while the latter four constitute minor offenses (*duṣkṛta*).
There are likewise six permutations for the case where there is actually no cause for fear, yet one forms the perception that there is no fear.
Some say: "Even if one is not a bhikṣu, but perceives them as such, one still incurs a pāyattika offense.

The Sixty-seventh Training Rule on Concealing Another’s Robes and Alms Bowl: When the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the seventeen novices were bathing together with the group of six bhikṣus in the water. At that time, the seventeen novices were playing in the water and remained submerged for too long before emerging.
At that time, the group of six monks took the robe, hid it beneath a thicket of grass, and departed, leaving it behind.
As the circumstances were distressing as before, this training rule was established:

"If a bhikṣu himself hides, or causes another to hide, the bowl, robes, or other requisites of a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī—except in cases of other [legitimate] reasons—it is a pāyattika."

Regarding the term "probationary female practitioner" (śikṣamāṇā): if she is a woman who has previously been married and is twenty years of age, or if she is a maiden and is eighteen years of age, she should be granted the rules for probation; this is to be conferred upon her by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
Regarding what is called the "Dharmas of Training," these refer to the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas.
What are the six dharmas?
First, one must not travel alone on a road.
Second, one must not cross a river alone.
Third, one must not touch the body of a man.
Fourth, one must not sleep in the same place as a male.
Fifth, one must not act as a matchmaker for marriages.
Sixth, one must not conceal the grave offenses of a bhikṣuṇī.
The verse says:
Not traveling alone on a road, not crossing a river alone,
not intentionally touching a man, not lodging with a man,
not acting as a matchmaker for marriage, and not concealing a nun’s grave offense.
What are the six rules of conduct (dharmānudharma)?
First, one must not take hold of gold or silver that belongs to oneself.
Second, one must not shave the hair of the private parts.
Third, one must not dig up or plow uncultivated land.
Fourth, one must not intentionally cut down living plants or trees.
Fifth, one must not eat food that has not been received [with formal permission].
Sixth, one must not eat food that has been touched [by others].
The verse says:
One must not handle gold and such, nor remove the hair from the private parts.
One shall not dig into the earth, nor damage living grass and the like;
one shall not eat food that has not been received, nor food that has been previously touched and is thus unfit for consumption.
The ritual procedures for receiving the precepts by female trainees (*śikṣamāṇā*) and male or female novices (*śrāmaṇera* / *śrāmaṇerī*) are as explained in the extensive text.
"Robes" refers to robes of the proper measure that are subject to formal distribution (*vibhaṅga*).
"Bowl" refers to one fit for formal acceptance and maintenance (*parigraha*).
"Other requisites" refers to the bowl-sack, water vessels, waist-bands, needle-cases, and so forth.
Regarding the term *pātraka*, it refers to a bag for holding the bowl, which may be made of cloth or woven netting.
If one is elderly or infirm, it is permitted to keep a staff and a carrying-net (*daṇḍaka*).
Regarding drinking vessels, these refer to small copper cups.
Regarding waist-bands, it is permitted to keep three types:
first, flat bands; second, round bands;
[and third, square bands].
3. Square Strips.
All types of ropes and cords must not be used; furthermore, any other ornamental strips or sashes are likewise unfit for possession.
Gold and silver ornaments are impure objects and should not be worn.
However, regarding items that a śramaṇa is permitted to possess, one incurs a root offense;
regarding those not permitted to be possessed, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
With the exception of other circumstances—if there is fear of dangers such as kings or thieves and one conceals or stores [the item] for their sake—there is no offense.

Regarding the offense herein: if one knows it is another's property and conceals it with the intent to cause distress, or even in jest, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling) at the moment of concealment, regardless of whether the person previously distressed becomes distressed or not.

If one conceals or takes possession of vessels such as gold or silver; or bowls that have been forfeited due to an offense; or the three robes that are impure; or robes that are deficient in measure; or the property of one undergoing training (*śikṣamāṇa*); or items belonging to this school or another school that have been mutually stored away; or the belongings of other śramaṇas or brahmins—doing so recklessly constitutes an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in all such cases.

68. The Training Rule on Wearing Garments Entrusted by Another Without Asking the Owner. The sixth and eighty-eighth training rule: When the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove in Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, Upānanda gave his own three robes to a disciple under his guidance. Having received them, the disciple finished washing and dyeing them; then, regarding them as his own property, he returned them to his teacher and departed for another region.

At that time, the preceptor took the robe and put it on himself, making it extremely soiled and greasy before returning it to its original place; when the disciple later returned and saw the robe, he was filled with distress.
Due to this act of taking the robe and the resulting affliction of negligence, this training rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu, having received a robe as a trust from another, later wears it himself without asking the owner, it is a pāyattika.
Regarding "robe," this refers to the three robes.
"Without asking" means to put on [a robe] that one has not borrowed from another.
Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣu gives a robe to another bhikṣu, and the latter takes it for himself and puts it on without asking the owner's permission.

If one does not ask, nor has the thought that one has asked, yet suspects [the owner's consent], and takes the robe and puts it on, two cases constitute a grave offense (*duṣkṛta*) and two cases constitute a light offense (*durbhāṣita*); for the latter two cases, there is no offense.
To use the robes of a person under training (*śikṣamāṇā*) or impure robes without borrowing them constitutes an act of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If it is the property of a kinsman or friend, and their mind is joyful when they hear of its use, there is no offense. Some say:
"Even if one actually borrows something but forms the perception that one has not borrowed it, one still incurs a downfall."

**The Sixty-ninth Training Rule: Slandering a Pure Bhikṣu with a Saṃghāvaśeṣa Offense** When the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, Mṛdvīkāpamukhī saw the Venerable Sthiramati’s robe brush against the head of the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā. She then proceeded to slander him, claiming that he had committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Out of intolerance for those who practice the same holy life (*brahmacarya*) and due to unpeaceful afflictions, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu, out of anger, knowing that another bhikṣu is pure and free from offense, should defame him with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*."
"Groundless" means that there is no basis of having seen, heard, or suspected.

Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, among the thirteen [grounds], if one slanders based on any single matter, it is called speaking unreasonably. In the case of an impure person, there is an offense in eleven matters and no offense in six matters;
in the case of a pure person, there is an offense in ten matters and no offense in five matters—this should be understood as explained above.
If one slanders another by means of various teachings, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.

If one slanders by means of a *sthūlātyaya* offense, or if one slanders a person undergoing training (*śikṣādattaka*), or if the person addressed does not understand the words spoken, in all such cases one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one perceives what is pure as pure, or harbors doubt regarding it, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one acts with the thought that it is impure, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense. Some say:

"Even if one does not perceive a person as a bhikṣu, yet slanders them while perceiving them as such, one also incurs a *pāyattika* offense. **The Seventieth Training Rule: Traveling with a Woman on the Same Road** The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, in Śrāvastī. When the bhikṣu saw him, he took him as a companion and traveled with him along the road.
At that time, the weaver followed them and found him; thinking he had been seduced by the monk, he beat him until he died.
Out of concern for the defilement of public censure regarding traveling together on a road, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu travels along a road with a woman and there is no other man present, even for the distance of a single village, it is a pāyattika."
"Regarding the statement 'there are no men,' it means there are only women.
Regarding the statement 'within one village,' it refers to a distance of one *krośa*;
if it is half a *krośa*, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense."
If it extends for a full *krośa*, one incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).
If there is no perception of a male object, there are six cases as previously described; in the latter two, there is no offense.
If a woman is perceived as a woman, there are likewise six cases.

If one travels along the same road with a transformed woman, a celestial maiden, a nāga maiden, a kinnarī, a hermaphrodite, or a woman incapable of sexual intercourse, in all such cases, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
Some say: "If one perceives a woman as not being a woman, or perceives a man as not being a man, one still incurs the fundamental offense.
However, there is no offense if one uses a woman as a guide or protector when crossing dangerous paths, or if a woman points out the way when one has lost it.
The eighth summary verse says:
Robbers, age not yet reached, Digging the earth, invitations, and violating the instructions;
Eavesdropping, departing in silence, Lack of respect, alcohol, and untimely food.

71. The Training Rule on Traveling with Thieves. The seventy-first training rule concerning traveling with thieves: When the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, there were bhikṣus who traveled along the same road as merchants who were stealing customs duties.
The circumstances and the offense are the same as before; thus this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a caravan of thieves, even for the distance of a single village, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding "bandits," this refers to those who commit theft, those who plunder by force, or those who evade taxes by taking detours along winding paths.
Regarding "the same path," this refers to a dangerous road.
The limits regarding the offense should be understood as previously stated.
There is no offense if one abandons the thieves and flees, or if one is afflicted by insanity.
Regarding the thief and the perception of a thief, there are six permutations.
Some say: "Even if one does not perceive a thief as a thief, one still incurs a *pārājika* offense.

72. The Training Rule on Ordaining Those Under Age. The seventy-second training rule concerning the ordination of those under age. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī. Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having conferred full ordination upon a group of seventeen youths, found that they could not endure hunger and consequently began to weep.
Out of the affliction of accepting disciples through the act of conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*), this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a person is less than twenty years of age, should confer full ordination upon them so as to establish them in the state of a bhikṣu, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
"This is not a valid full ordination; all the bhikṣus incur an offense.
Regarding the statement "knowing that the age is less than twenty," it is because, due to their youth, they are unable to endure the pressure of hunger and thirst when such conditions arise.

Regarding "giving and receiving full ordination" (*upasampadā*): this refers to the conduct, deportment, and all ritual procedures for both the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the candidate, which shall be explained in due order.
As for the "preceptor," this refers to the *upādhyāya*, the *ācārya*, and the rest of the Saṃgha.
There are two kinds of upādhyāyas:
first, one who initially grants ordination;
second, one who confers full ordination (upasampadā).
Only after ten years of standing have been fulfilled may one occupy the position of a preceptor; furthermore, one must accomplish five qualities:
first, knowing what constitutes an offense; second, knowing what does not constitute an offense; [and so forth].
Third, knowing what is light;
fourth, knowing what is heavy;

fifth, being extensively able to explain and interpret the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, understanding both the original formulation and subsequent modifications of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), skillfully discerning when there are obstructions or openings due to difficult circumstances, constantly reciting the precepts so as to resolve the doubts of others, benefiting both oneself and others through extensive learning in the precepts and views, and having no deficiency or transgression regarding the methods of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*).
One endowed with such virtues is called an *upādhyāya* (preceptor), because he is able to personally instruct others in the Dharma of renunciation.

Even if a bhikṣu has already received full ordination (*upasampadā*), if he does not recognize the gravity or lightness of the various training rules (*śikṣāpada*), he must continue to rely upon and dwell under the guidance of one of eminent virtue, even after sixty years of seniority.

If the teacher is junior, one should perform all duties except for prostrating; such a person is termed an "elderly or junior bhikṣu," yet they are not permitted to grant others the going-forth or the full ordination.
There are five types of ācāryas:
first, the śrāmaṇerācārya, who bestows the three refuges and the fifty precepts;
second, the rahasyānuśāsakācārya, who inquires regarding obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dharma*) in a private place.
Third, the *karmācārya*, who presides over the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* at the time of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Fourth, the *niśrayācārya*, upon whom one relies for even a single night.
Fifth, the *ācārya* who teaches reading, down to one who imparts even a single four-line verse (*gāthā*) to another;
these five types of persons all occupy the rank of a teacher and are capable of producing a model of conduct, and are thus collectively termed *ācāryas*.
Regarding the term "saṃgha," there are two types:
first, a group of ten persons, which refers to those in the central regions;
second, a group of five persons, which refers to those dwelling in the borderlands.
If ten persons are available at that location, taking only five constitutes a "goodly assembly for full ordination," and one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
If there are only five persons present, this is called a "proper reception."
If the required number of members is insufficient, one may not use the Buddha to complete the quorum, because the Buddha and the Jewel of the Saṃgha are distinct entities.
If those who are insane, deaf, or belong to the faction of Devadatta are used to complete the quorum, the full ordination (upasampadā) is not validly accomplished.

Regarding those who are to be granted [the precepts], there are many types of characteristics: namely, those whose intention is impaired, those whose basis is impaired, those whose personhood is impaired, those whose pure qualities are impaired, those who are dependent on others, and those who possess an ugly and unseemly appearance.
Regarding "corruption of intention," this refers to seeking ordination at the time of death, when threatened by fear, or for the sake of sustaining one's livelihood.
Regarding "corruption of basis," this refers to having an incurable illness and seeking refuge in the Triple Gem in hopes of recovery.
Regarding "one who has damaged the male organ," this refers to a paṇḍaka (eunuch).
There are five distinct types:
first, the *jātipaṇḍaka*, which refers to one who is not a male from birth.
2. The *paṇḍaka* who is a male for half a month and a non-male for half a month;
3. The *paṇḍaka* who is aroused by touch and embrace, whose sexual organ only arises when another embraces and touches him;
4. The *paṇḍaka* who is aroused by jealousy, whose organ arises out of envy upon seeing others engaging in sexual intercourse.
Fifth, the *parājitaka-paṇḍaka* (one who has been castrated), meaning one who has encountered disease and injury or has been cut by a blade.
These five types of eunuchs are all ineligible for the stages of going forth (*pravrajyā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*); as for the last one, it is not fixed.

If one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) has been impaired, if their disposition and conduct have not changed, they shall remain in their former status; if their disposition has changed, they should be expelled. The first type of eunuch is also called a *śaṇḍha*.
Regarding those who damage the white dharmas: this refers to the various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who revere false teachings and lack correct faith.

Among these non-Buddhists, with the exception of those of the Śākya clan and the fire-worshippers, all other non-Buddhists must live together for four months, eat the food of the community, wear the robes of their preceptors, and perform services and duties identical to those of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*).
If they do not abandon their former views, they should be sent away; if they abandon their former views, they should be granted ordination.

Regarding "one who defiles a bhikṣuṇī": this refers to a case where the bhikṣuṇī has not committed any of the eight pārājika offenses. If one defiles such a bhikṣuṇī through unchaste conduct, it does not constitute "defiling a bhikṣuṇī" if both parties possess a defiled mind [only] when first touching the bhikṣuṇī’s body and subsequently performing the unchaste act, because the bhikṣuṇī has already committed the pārājika offense of touching a male.

Regarding those who "dwell as thieves": they have left the household life on their own initiative without relying on a preceptor, and have participated with pure bhikṣus in two or three *poṣadha* ceremonies, even performing the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* together with them.

The *Mānavikā* states that one who has not yet received full ordination (an upasampadā) but participates with a pure assembly in the *jñapti-dvitīya* or *jñapti-caturtha* formal acts, or in the *poṣadha* and *pravāraṇā* ceremonies, as well as those who join the community in appointing the twelve types of officials, is all termed a "thief-dweller" (*steyasaṃvāsika*).

Regarding "returning to external paths": this refers to an externalist who has entered into the Buddha-dharma; although he wears the dharma robes and yet cherishes the views of external paths, he returns to his original place without relinquishing his precepts, and upon removing the dharma robes, the dawn light appears.

Killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an Arhat, maliciously drawing blood from the body of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha—when those who assist these acts know the words of Devadatta and perceive them as unrighteous while forming the thought that they are unrighteous, this also constitutes a schism in the Saṃgha.
Regarding those who have previously violated the precepts: this refers to those who have broken a grave precept among the five trainings or the ten training rules.

If one has previously committed even one of the four *pārājika* offenses, such as a *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) and others, they should not be granted the vows if they have not yet received them; if they have already received them, they should be expelled.
Furthermore, there are two types of persons who live apart:
first, those who have gone from the faction of the Dharma to the faction of non-Dharma;
second, those against whom the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation) has been performed.
If one who has already returned to lay life comes again to receive the precepts, they likewise should not be ordained.
Regarding those "bound to others," this refers to slaves, debtors, and the great generals of a king.
If one's parents do not grant permission, it is not permitted; however, there is no offense if they reside in a distant land.
If a child is abandoned by the biological mother immediately after birth and is subsequently raised by another mother, one should consult that foster mother at the time of ordination.
If one kills the biological mother, one incurs an *ānantarya* (immediate) offense.
Regarding the characteristics of those who are not dignified: this refers to non-humans and animals who have transformed themselves into human form to come and receive the precepts;
or great thieves carrying banners; or those under twenty years of age; or those whose complexions are excessively blue, yellow, red, or white and whose physical forms differ from that of humans;
or those with elephant hair growing on their bodies; or those who are hairless; or those with oversized heads; or those with flattened heads.
Or having many heads, or bulging eyes, or being blind or mute; or having the head of an elephant, an ox, or the like;
or having the form of a horse, a monkey, or a pig; or lacking ears and nose; or having ears and tusks like those of an elephant or a horse; or lacking teeth;
or having a short neck, or one that is too long, or one that is too short; or having hunched shoulders; or...
Those with a hunched back; those lacking the male organ or testicles; those with a prolapsed organ; those whose bodies are excessively coarse or excessively thin;
those whose hands or feet have been severed; those who are lame or paralyzed; those who are deaf or blind; those who move on their knees; those who are wounded by blows;
those who are incapable due to excessive indulgence in sexual intercourse; and those of low birth—these [are excluded].
None of them possessed the appearance of one who has left the household life.
Once they had received full ordination (*upasampadā*), he spoke these two verses for them:
"You have fully received the precepts (*śīla*) Within the most excellent teaching;..."
One should uphold this with a sincere heart; a body free from obstacles is difficult to obtain.
Those who are upright leave the household life; those who are pure receive full ordination.
These are the words spoken by one who speaks truth, known by the Perfectly Awakened One.

Regarding the "dignified deportment of advancing and halting": if there is a layperson who seeks to go forth [into homelessness], one should follow their intention and go to a preceptor; that preceptor may then inquire about obstructing factors (*antarāyika-dharma*).
If they are pure, one should accept them.
Observing their disposition and whether they possess the requisite capacity, one should grant them the three refuges along with the five precepts.
Next, one should request a preceptor.
Furthermore, regarding the request for a bhikṣu to formally announce [the candidate] to the Saṃgha:
once he has accepted the request, he asks his preceptor:
"Have you already inquired of this person concerning the obstructing dharmas?"
If one does not inquire, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If the assembly has gathered, one should inform the *saṃgha*; if they have not gathered, one should go from room to room to notify them.
If one does not inform the assembly, one commits an offense of wrong-doing.
When the proclamation is made, the assembly should all say:
"If he is pure, he should be granted ordination.
If they do not so inquire, all incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Next, have the barber shave the hair; as the shaving is nearly finished, one should leave a top-knot and ask him:
"Shall I remove the *juṭa*? If he says:
"To remain" means to dismiss them so that they may go as they please.
If one says:
Regarding the instruction "remove [hair]," it should be shaved off entirely.

One should bathe him at an appropriate time; once the bathing is finished, one should put on his lower garment for him, carefully examining his body by means of skillful means so that he does not notice, for fear that he might have two sexual organs or none at all.
Next, having put on the *saṃkakṣikā*, one is then given the *antarvāsaka* (inner robe), which one must first place upon the head before donning it.
One should then request a *bhikṣu* to confer the Three Refuges along with the ten precepts (*śikṣāpada*). One must possess an alms bowl; if one lacks a bowl, one should not go forth.
Next, the instructions for the invitation and the formal announcement are the same as those for a *bhikṣu*.
If the candidate has reached twenty years of age, the preceptor should provide the six requisites;
if he lacks them due to poverty, the preceptor should borrow them for him.
One should request a *karmavācanā* master, a private instructor (*raho'nuśāsaka*), and the witnesses for the precepts.

Whether receiving them within the ritual enclosure (*maṇḍala*) or amidst the great assembly, once one has entered the enclosure and set aside one's robes and bowl, the instructor first teaches the candidate to request an *upādhyāya*, and then directs them to perform three rounds of prostrations to each member of the Saṃgha.

Next, he is instructed to hold up the bowl and circumambulate so as to present it to the assembly; once everyone has examined it individually, they all say, "A fine bowl. Anyone who does not speak thus incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
Then, in the presence of the assembly, the preceptor formally accepts and maintains the robes and bowl for him.
