Next, have that person stand with palms joined, facing a place where they can see but not hear, and look up reverently at the assembly. One who desires full ordination should not be sent too far away, nor should they be made to climb high trees, for fear of injury.

In a screened location, once the preceptor-in-charge has questioned him regarding the obstructing factors, he is then summoned into the assembly; finally, having been directed to squat with palms joined, he receives the instruction with single-minded attention before the *karmavācanā* master.

Once the *karmavācanā* has been completed, one should immediately measure the shadow. A tally stick (*śalākā*) bent at four finger-widths (*aṅgula*) is called a *śaṅku*; for every four-finger increment of shadow, it is designated as one person. One should announce the date and time, as well as the distinctions between the five periods of the day.
One should immediately explain to them the four *pārājika* dharmas, followed by the four reliances and the four noble modes of conduct.
If one fails to do so, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*) in each case.
If one were to first explain the four reliances (catur-niśraya), one would incur an offense against the Dharma.
There are five matters that prevent the completion of full ordination (upasampadā):
first, not mentioning the name of the preceptor (upādhyāya); [and so forth].
2. Not mentioning one's own name;
3. Not citing the Saṃgha; 4. Not performing the *karmavācanā*.
5. Regarding the deficiency in the *karmavācanā*: reversing these five improper conditions is termed "properly receiving" [the precepts].
If, at the very moment of the full ordination (*upasampadā*), one's gender changes to female, this still constitutes a valid reception; she should be sent to a nunnery.
If one transforms into a male at the time of full ordination (*upasampadā*), they should be sent to a monastery for monks, where each shall abide by their own respective precepts.

Furthermore, if the two assemblies—the monks and the nuns—perform the *karmavācanā* for one another, it is not a valid full ordination if: the obstructing factors have not been inquired about; there is no preceptor (*upādhyāya*); a preceptor exists but has not been requested; the ten precepts have not been received; or the *karmavācanā* has not been performed. All such cases are not true full ordinations.
If there is no preceptor, and the assembly all transgresses the Dharma, it is still termed "properly received.
If one knows that the preceptor is a violator of the precepts, the full ordination is not accomplished;
if one does not know this, it is termed "received."

If one actually possesses obstructing factors yet claims they do not, or if one actually lacks obstructing factors yet claims they do, in the former case the ordination is not valid and the assembly incurs no offense;
in the latter case, although the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) is accomplished, the assembly incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
At the time of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*),
one says: "I renounce the precepts," or says:
"I do not wish to receive [the precepts]"—
in all such cases, full ordination is not achieved. However,
if one is deaf or a mleccha (barbarian), provided they understand the language, full ordination is successfully conferred.
If this is reversed and not accomplished, the assembly of monks incurs an offense.

If the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or another person who completes the quorum undergoes a change of gender (*mūla-parivṛtti*) during the performance of the rite, or if the change occurs only upon hearing the formal announcement (*jñapti*), then the full ordination (*upasampadā*) is valid; otherwise, it is not accomplished.
If they dwell together in an open space, the reception is likewise not accomplished. He asked:
"To what extent of place and how many persons must be present for the reception of full ordination (*upasampadā*) to be valid?"

He replied: "If three persons in a single boundary receive [the precepts] simultaneously, or even if four boundaries have one, two, or three persons receiving them at the same time, or if there are more boundaries, in all such cases, the full ordination (upasampadā) is successfully accomplished."
In total, there are ten methods for obtaining full ordination (*upasampadā*). What are these ten?
The first is "without a teacher," which refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Second is realized wisdom, referring to the five bhikṣus;
third is inquiry after one's well-being, referring to Udāyin;
fourth is taking refuge, referring to Mahākāśyapa.
Fifth, there are five persons, namely those in a borderland, with the *vinaya*-master as the fifth.
Sixth, there are ten persons, namely those in the central region.
Seventh, there is the receiving of the *gurudharma*, namely Mahāprajāpatī.
Eighth is ordination by dispatching a messenger, referring to Dharmadinnā.
Ninth is ordination by the two assemblies, referring to the gathering of both orders.
Tenth is ordination by "Come hither," referring to the Great Master’s personal summons.
These are called the ten.

Once the World-Honored One had permitted the reception [of ordination] through the ritual of *karmavācanā*, all other methods were discontinued, with the sole exception of the "Come, O Bhikṣu" formula, because that was the final mode of birth.
Once full ordination has been conferred, all the rules of conduct shall be explained below.
Junior bhikṣus should pay homage to their seniors; when first meeting one another, they should inquire about the number of years since ordination and the time of their respective receptions.
At that time, there are five distinct periods:
first, the four months of winter;
second, the four months of spring.
Third, it refers to one month during the rainy season;
fourth, it refers to one day and one night at the end [of the rains];
fifth, it refers to a long period of three months minus one day and one night.
There are four kinds of those who should be paid homage:
first, the Tathāgata, because all humans and devas should pay him respect;
second, those who have left the household life do not pay homage to worldly people, for they are the ones who should be revered by them.

3. All bhikṣus who have already received full ordination (upasampadā) should pay homage to those who received it earlier; however, this excludes the community of bhikṣuṇīs, for their mode of respect is likewise.
4. Those who have not yet received full ordination should pay homage to those who have.
There are ten types of persons who should not be saluted:

those performing the *parivāsa* probation and the other three [categories of] persons; the three kinds of persons under training (*śikṣamāṇā*); persons subject to suspension (*pratisaṃharaṇīya*); all householders; and those who have not yet received full ordination (*upasampadā*). These are called the ten.

If one *karmavācanā* ordains two or three persons simultaneously, there is no distinction of seniority among them; they do not pay homage to one another, and when the assembly’s messengers arrive, they may be dispatched as others see fit.
There are two distinct forms of ritual prostration:
first, the five limbs touching the ground;
second, grasping the calves and feet while reciting:
"Vandana. Some say: "When paying homage to the Great Master, the five wheels [of the body] touch the ground."

If it is for a venerable person or one of similar status, one should place the hands and knees upon the ground, or at times bend the body and lower the head with palms joined, or grasp the calves, or squat with palms joined.
If, toward other fellow practitioners of the holy life, one merely joins the palms, bows the head,

or says "vandana," or if one performs a prostration knowing that the other's body has been defiled by contact with impurities, or performs a prostration while one's own body is defiled by such contact, in both cases one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
There are two kinds of defiled contact:
first, contact when one has finished eating but has not yet rinsed and washed;
second, contact when one has relieved oneself but has not yet performed the cleansing.
A renunciant bhikṣu should not harbor resentment; even if there is a cause for estrangement, when a junior approaches a senior, he must immediately chant "vandate" and perform prostration.
Upon receiving the prostration, the senior shall say:
"May you be free from illness and affliction."
If both parties remain silent, both incur an *dukkaṭa* offense.

If a great bhikṣu dies harboring resentment and is reborn among venomous snakes, when a junior bhikṣu seeks to perform confession, he should maintain mindfulness of his former form and practice the rules of reverence.
If one wears only the lower garment and no upper garment, it is improper to pay respects to others, nor should one accept respect from others.
To act contrary to this rule constitutes an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*) for both parties.
When the elder sneezes, the junior says, "Vandana.
If the junior sneezes, the elder says:
"Āluji. If one does not say this, both incur an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
However, one should not say:
"May I obtain long life.
When a lay elder or a *mahallaka* (an elderly person) expresses a wish for longevity, there is no offense in speaking thus while walking.
When prostrating in the dark, one should not let the body touch the ground; one should simply say:
"Vandana" means to pay homage.

Having already explained the ritual procedures for the veneration associated with the full ordination of those who have left the household life, the method of receiving disciples and their mutual reliance through co-residence shall now be discussed.
Once the full ordination has been completed and ten years have passed, one should remain by the side of the preceptor (upādhyāya) to study the Vinaya-piṭaka as well as other sūtras and śāstras.

If the preceptor has other affairs that prevent him from personally instructing the student, he should appoint another person of eminent virtue who is worthy of being entrusted with the task, and the student should dwell under their guidance.

Next, the method for receiving dependence (*niśraya*) is explained: whenever one wishes to receive dependence, one should observe whether that person’s character and conduct are gentle and respectful, whether they possess a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), whether they are trustworthy, and whether they delight in cultivating all wholesome qualities; if so, one should accept them as a dependent.
When requesting to rely [upon a teacher], one should adjust one’s robe to leave one shoulder bared, perform a prostration, and then place both hands upon the other's feet, saying:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me!"
I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to be my preceptor; may the Venerable One act as my preceptor, so that by relying upon the Venerable One, I may dwell in peace and security.
Thus he spoke three times.
The Master said, “So it is.”
The disciple says, “Excellent,” or says:
"Excellent. If there is no *upādhyāya*, one should not wander among human settlements elsewhere at will.

If one has completed five years of residence (*pañca-varṣa*), clearly understands the five dharmas, recognizes what constitutes an offense and what does not, knows what is grave and what is light, and is well-versed in the points of obstruction and passage within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, one may leave one's original teacher and *upādhyāya* to travel abroad and practice one's studies.
Wherever you arrive, stay and rest for two or three days.
Next, you should observe who might serve as a teacher and should then go to rely upon them for guidance.
If there is no one to rely upon, one should not remain; even an Arhat must have a preceptor to rely on, let alone an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
If, at the place where one has arrived, one seeks a preceptor for five nights or more with an unceasing mind, then one who possesses material goods should share them; otherwise, it is not permitted.
There are five conditions under which one should not grant dependence:
first, a lack of respectful faith;
second, the utterance of coarse and evil speech.
Third, associating with evil friends;
fourth, being chronically indolent by nature;
fifth, lacking a mind of reverence and compliance.
The opposite of this should be granted.
One should know that "abandoning the reliance" and "not abandoning the reliance" apply respectively to the two preceding sets of five.
There are five matters by which one abandons the reliance:
1. Resolutely renouncing [the precepts] and departing beyond the boundary;
2. returning to lay life;
3. the arrival of the preceptor.
4. Departing from this faction to go toward another faction;
5. Abandoning the matter of formal reliance (*niśraya*).
If one sees one’s preceptor (*upādhyāya*), the reliance is immediately lost.
If, while traveling, the preceptor intends to stay behind, the disciple must still attend upon him and provide mutual instructions.

If both the preceptor and the disciple must depart on a journey and return midway, and if after a long time they intend to come back again, they may resume their former positions as preceptor and dependent, because the mental bond has not been severed.
If one establishes a separate dependence upon another person during that interval, one does not lose the status of having previously depended upon the former preceptor.

However, if the preceptor dies at that location, one should not remain there for a second *poṣadha* ceremony without a new preceptor; furthermore, one should not observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) at this place, whether before or after [the death].
If the preceptor passes away during the later retreat (paścimā vārṣikī), one should remain there for two months while guarding the mind; beyond this period, one should no longer remain.
If the residence is at a distance of two and a half yojanas from the ācārya or upādhyāya, one should go to pay respects and inquire after their health every fortnight;
if it is five krośas away, one should go to pay respects and inquire after their health every six or seven days.
If one is five *li* away, one should go there every day;
if one resides within the boundary, one should pay respects and inquire after their well-being three times each day.
Regarding all tasks concerning robes, alms bowls, and other necessities, one should perform them first for the *ācārya* and the *upādhyāya*.
These two teachers, as well as the preceptor, should all be served and attended to in accordance with the Dharma.
If both the resident teacher (niśrayācārya) and the preceptor (avavādācārya) are ill, whom should one attend?
If one has the strength and ability to attend to both places, that is well; if one lacks the strength and ability, one should attend to the *niśraya* (preceptor).
This is because if there is no instruction (*avavāda*), one may remain wherever one is; however, if there is no *niśraya*, one should not stay at all.
If the preceptor has many disciples, they should serve him in rotation.
One should not go to associate with those toward whom the ācārya harbors resentment.

One should serve one's teachers with a respectful mind; unless informed by the teacher, one must not perform tasks such as sweeping, nor attend to robes and alms bowls, nor provide instruction to others.
If a guest arrives whom one has not previously known, one should not immediately provide massage to relieve their fatigue.
To state the essential point: while in the presence of one's preceptor or resident teacher, one should neither ask about nor perform any matter whatsoever, with the sole exception of five things.
What are the five? They are:

drinking water, chewing tooth-sticks, and performing the great and small excretions; within the same boundary, at a distance of no more than forty-nine *vyāmas* from a *caitya*, as previously described.
If one does not follow each and every rule of the ritual procedure for practice, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
For all such offenses, there is also the *pāyattika* offense of disrespecting the instruction, as well as the offense of preliminary effort (*prayoga*).

When requesting instruction or reporting matters, and when inquiring after one’s well-being at dawn, each should present their business individually and not combine them; however, if the matter is urgent, there is no offense in consulting about them together.
Regarding the method of consultation: rising early in the morning, one should first chew a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), then go to the teacher’s room to massage his body.

Once the teacher has arisen, one should provide water for rinsing the mouth and a tooth-stick, arrange a seat, and offer a towel for wiping; then, one should personally pay homage to the sacred image.
Next, one comes before the teacher to perform a single prostration, bows the head with sincere devotion, joins the palms, and makes this declaration: "Upādhyāya!"
"Venerable Ācārya, please bear with me as I now inquire:
I wonder if the noble body of the Upādhyāya has been at ease throughout the night?"
The preceptor should act accordingly.
The teacher may answer such matters as they arise.
If the student is ill, he should inquire what is required and attend to them at all times.
Next, one should personally cultivate wholesome qualities according to one's inclination; when wishing to eat, one must again perform a prostration and address the teacher, saying:
"O Upādhyāya, or Ācārya, please take heed.
I now inform you that I wish to wash my hands, feet, and bowl before eating porridge."
Some say: "I am washing my hands, feet, and bowl, intending to eat my midday meal.

However, regarding all things that are swallowed—whether rice, cakes, fruit, and so forth, down to even a single slice of dried ginger or a single grain of black pepper—as well as drinking non-timely gruel, washing one's feet at dusk, spreading out bedding, sleeping, or resting—all such matters must be announced for their knowledge.
If there is no business to attend to, one must perform prostrations whether it is at noon or in the afternoon.
If one arrives at the hour of *bhu* (the late afternoon) to pay respects at the *caitya*, and when the sun is about to set, one should likewise pay respects to the teacher.
One should constantly perform this practice three times each day.
When wishing to leave the monastery, one must always go to pay respects and state:
"I now have such-and-such a reason and wish to go to such-and-such a place."
The preceptor should appropriately and according to his discretion restrain and dismiss [the disciple]. This is a brief account of the standard ritual procedures.

In all matters, the disciple should diligently inspect himself and must not indulge in arrogance; he should not fail to report his affairs or cultivate wholesome qualities, lest he remain in unrighteousness like a horse without a bridle.
As the Blessed One said:

"O bhikṣus! It would be better for you to be butchers engaged in the work of killing than to allow someone to go forth and receive full ordination, only to abandon them and fail to inquire after them, thereby causing my True Dharma to perish swiftly."

Therefore, bhikṣus must strictly examine their disciples; if they do not comply with the instructions, they should reprimand them according to the circumstances, and if they cannot be instructed, they should be expelled.
Having already discussed other matters, I shall now explain the main text.
Regarding the statement that "the bhikṣus incur an offense," this refers to incurring an *āpatti* of transgressing the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*).
Within this, there are many types of characteristics of such offenses:

If there is a person who is not yet twenty years of age, yet perceives themselves as being less than twenty, or harbors doubts, and when questioned, they answer in accordance with reality, this does not constitute the attainment of full ordination (*upasampadā*). All the bhikṣu-saṃgha incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma (*dharmātikrama*), and this person should not live in communal residence with them.
If there is a person who is under twenty years of age but conceives the thought that they have reached full age, or if they harbor doubts, yet when questioned they speak according to the truth;

or if there is a person who is under twenty years of age but does not know their own age, or harbors doubts, yet when questioned remains silent and does not answer—these two types of individuals do not receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If one undergoes two or three *poṣadha* ceremonies together with pure bhikṣus, one becomes a "thief-dweller" (*steyāśrita*).
If someone, at the time of full ordination (*upasampadā*), actually has not yet reached the required age but conceives the thought that they have, and later a relative informs them:
"You have not reached [the age]."
One should calculate the months of gestation and intercalary months.
If [the time] is complete, this is called "properly received.
If it is incomplete, one shall be demoted to the status of a *śrāmaṇera* and should receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*) once again.
If it were not so, it would be the same as the previous case of "staying like a thief.

Suppose there is a person who is nineteen years old but receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) with the intention that he is twenty; after one year has passed, his relatives come to see him and report:
"He is not [yet] twenty."

Whether one recalls that they were not yet full [twenty years of age], or whether one receives full ordination at eighteen and later, after two years have passed, recalls the same, these cases are all considered valid ordinations; for such an exception is permitted because the True Teaching is difficult to encounter.
If there is someone whose age is complete but whose physical characteristics are not, there should be four permutations.
"Complete in physical characteristics" refers to the overall form, the specific features, and the signs of maturity.
What is meant by "physical form"?
It refers to a physical form and a voice that do not possess the characteristics of a child.
Regarding the signs of maturity: body hair has already grown in places such as the armpits.
Regarding "mature": this refers to one whose intentions and disposition differ from those of a youth.
Among the four cases, there is no offense in the first and third, while there is an offense in the second and fourth.
If there is doubt as to whether one has reached the required age, one must employ skillful means to secretly examine the hidden signs before conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*).
If a person is fifteen years of age, they should be granted the going-forth (*pravrajyā*) and ordained as a novice (*śrāmaṇera*).
If one acts otherwise, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
Furthermore, even those as young as seven years old who are capable of guarding the grain and wheat for the Saṃgha and driving away crows and birds may also be granted ordination.
If one who is eight years old cannot [accomplish what] a six-year-old can, neither should be ordained.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu should not keep two śrāmaṇeras; however, if he knows that a person is capable of following the instructions, he may grant him the going-forth.
Once the ten precepts have been received, they should be entrusted to another person.
The person to whom they are entrusted must not confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) immediately on that basis; rather, they must consult the original teacher before granting full ordination.

73. The Training Rule on Destroying Cultivated Ground. This is the seventy-third training rule. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the group of six bhikṣus personally mixed mud with their own hands and dug up cultivated ground.

Because engaging in base activities obstructs and abandons correct cultivation, and because such base activities and afflictions destroy the integrity of the earth, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hand, or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the term "ground," there are two kinds:
first, natural ground;
second, non-natural ground.
"Native soil" refers to ground that has never been dug.
If it has previously been dug and has been moistened by rain or dampened by other water for a period of three months, this is called native soil.
If there has been no rain or moisture, nor any soaking by water, for a period of six months, it is also called "earth that has not yet been broken" (*ajātā bhūmi*).

Other than this, it is not "earth that has not yet been broken. Regarding the offense herein: if a *bhikṣu*, knowing it to be earth that has not yet been broken—being neither burnt by fire nor previously tilled—digs it himself or instructs another to dig it; or if he drives stakes into it, scrapes it away, breaks the firm surface of the ground, causes banks to collapse, or causes walls to fall; or if he takes hard clay from the ground and lifts it so that it becomes separated [from its base]. This constitutes an offense.
If the soil contains much sand and little earth, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
if the ground is not firm or solid, such as in the case of topsoil or similar areas, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense when scraping it up.
Regarding earth that is earth, one perceives it as earth; regarding earth that is not earth, one perceives it as earth. Each of these has six permutations, all of which are explained as before.

There is no offense if, in a place consisting entirely of sand and stones, or when a *bhikṣu* engaged in construction work obtains an auspicious day but lacks laborers and must therefore fix the foundation of a house by marking lines and driving stakes to a depth of four inches. In such cases, there is no offense.

74. The Training Rule on Soliciting Food After Four Months. This is the seventy-fourth training rule concerning soliciting food after four months. When the Buddha was staying at the city of Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Grove, the six groups of bhikṣus accepted the four-month provision from Mahānāman; after this period had passed, they continued to solicit further offerings from him.
Out of concern for the afflictions arising from the neglect and failure resulting from excessive persistence in accepting invitations, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for four months that requires his presence, he may accept it; if he accepts it beyond that limit, except during other permitted times, it is a pāyattika offense."
"Other times" refers to special invitations, repeated invitations, earnest invitations, and regular invitations; these are the [permissible] times.
This permits [the acceptance of food] for four months; beyond that, one should not accept it.

Regarding "individual invitations," this refers to various individual donors inviting bhikṣus to provide offerings. It was because of the Venerable Pilindavatsa’s allowance for accepting royal invitations that [the bhikṣu] subsequently accepted an invitation to a meal from the king’s brother-in-law.
"Re-invitation" refers to when bhikṣus have arrived at a royal palace and do not dare to accept food; once the king has learned of this, he invites them to eat again.
"Insistent invitation" refers to when one says:
"The affairs of the royal household are many; I shall go to beg for alms."
The king again invited him with a sincere heart to accept his meal.
When the four months of the regular invitation had concluded, the World-Honored One accepted the meal, while the other bhikṣus all went out to beg for food.
The King said, "I invite you to eat at all times, regardless of the season.

Before the four months were completed, he invited them to eat coarse food; if they requested something better, they incurred a *dukkaṭa* offense, and if they ate it, they incurred a *pāyattika* offense.
Having been invited to eat fine food, one further requests coarse food; at the time of requesting it, there is an *duṣkṛta* offense, but at the time of eating, there is no offense.

The Seventy-fifth Training Rule: Prohibiting the Transmission of Teachings. When the Buddha was staying in the Bamboo Grove Monastery at Rājagṛha, the World-Honored One intended to establish a common training rule (*śikṣāpada*). At that time, both divisions of the Saṃgha were required to assemble together; however, when the rule was being established, the nuns who had observed the four-month *pravāraṇā* were not present.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"Let the bhikṣu Upāli go and inform the community of nuns.
Then Upāli, having received these instructions, departed.
At that time, the group of six monks saw this and questioned him; then Upavāna answered them in full detail regarding the matter.
Thereupon, the group of six monks uttered harsh words and collectively obstructed him.
This training rule was established out of concern for the minor matter of the training rules and the minor affliction of contemptuous disparagement: "If a bhikṣu hears other bhikṣus say:
'Venerable one!'"
"You, O virtuous one, should now train yourself in such rules of training. He replies:
"I truly cannot accept and practice the rules of training based on the words spoken by you, who are foolish, lacking in discernment, and unskilled in understanding."
"If I see another who is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, I shall accept and practice according to their words," constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣu truly desires to seek understanding, he should inquire of those versed in the Tripiṭaka; this is the proper occasion.
In this context, the term "fool" refers to one who thinks evil thoughts and speaks evil words.
The "deluded" refers to one who does not uphold the Tripitaka.
The "unclear" refers to one who does not understand its meaning.
One who lacks skillful understanding cannot properly perform a correct discernment;
when speaking of "fools" and so forth, one incurs an offense.
If one speaks the truth, there is no transgression.

76. The Training Rule on Listening in Silence to Criticism. This is the seventy-sixth training rule. When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the group of seventeen monks wished to carry out the formal act of setting aside (*sthāpanīya-karman*) and had something to discuss. The group of six monks then went to a secluded place and listened in silence.
Out of intolerance regarding the act of criticizing others, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu is engaged in criticizing others, seeks out faults and remains involved in agitation and contention."
If one goes there in silence to listen to what is being said, with the thought,
"After I have listened, I shall cause strife and discord," and acts on this motive, it is a *pāyattika*.
Regarding the phrase "the arising of matters for deliberation," it means that upon seeing something disagreeable, one begins to deliberate.
Regarding the phrase "seeking faults and causing turmoil," it means searching for transgressions and engaging in mutual recrimination.

Regarding "contentious dispute" (*adhikaraṇa-śāthya*): it refers to the failure to maintain forbearance in one's disposition, bringing forth a matter by introducing such speech into a formal dispute, thereby forming factions and inciting one another to mutual support.
"Silently going to listen" means to go to a secluded place to eavesdrop on their deliberations.
"Causing strife and discord" means that when a minor matter first arises, one causes it to become a great dispute, leading to incessant turmoil.
If one knows that the bhikṣus are on an upper story engaged in discussion and wishes to go there, it is not an offense provided one snaps one's fingers or makes a sound by clearing one's throat.
If one departs in silence to listen to their discourse, at the moment the sound is first heard, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing);
if one understands its meaning, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
Whether in a middle story, or under the eaves, or on a walking path, if one follows them to listen, one incurs the full offense in each case.
Regarding the six permutations of the offense of criticizing based on the perception that one is criticizing, they are as previously stated. Some say:
"Even if it is not actually a criticism but one perceives it as such, one still incurs a *pāyattika* offense."

"If one has no partiality or prejudice, or if one happens to hear it unexpectedly, or if one listens to their words with the intent to cause them to be extinguished, in all such cases there is no offense.

**The Seventy-seventh Training Rule: Departing in Silence Without Having Granted Consent.** While the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, the group of seventeen monks, having been divided from their faction by the group of six monks, felt resentment in their hearts. They then performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act of suspension) against Upānanda.
At that time, Nanda, reflecting upon his own lack of power and fearing punishment, gathered his woolen cloak and placed it upon his seat, then departed in silence.
As with the previous case, because of such lack of tranquility and affliction, this training rule was established.

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that the Saṃgha is engaged in a formal discussion of affairs according to the Dharma, should rise from his seat and depart in silence without having informed another bhikṣu present—unless there is a compelling reason—it is a pāyattika."
"A legal act" refers to the threefold *karmavācanā*.
"To depart silently" means to rise from one's seat and go to a place beyond the range of hearing.

"Without entrusting another bhikṣu" means that if one is ill, is tending to the sick, is an official (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*), or has other business requiring departure, one should grant one's consent (*chanda*).
If one departs abruptly, if one has not yet left the range of hearing, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense;
if one has left the range of hearing, it is a *pāyattika*.
This applies to the six permutations regarding the legal act and the perception of it as legal.
Some say: "If one actually performs what is not the Dharma while perceiving it as being in accordance with the Dharma, one also incurs a downfall.

However, there is no offense in any of the following cases: if one returns after finishing the business of defecation or urination; if one does not leave the range of hearing; or if one departs in silence when the assembly intends to perform an illegal *karmavācanā*.

78. The Training Rule on Lack of Reverence. The seventy-eighth training rule concerning lack of reverence: When the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, the bhikṣu Citta saw others settling a dispute in accordance with the Dharma within the great assembly; he felt resentment in his heart, or gave rise to anger and indignation, and refused to comply.
This training rule was established due to matters of quarreling and the affliction of disrespect:
"If a bhikṣu is disrespectful, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding what is called "lack of respect," there are two kinds of lack of respect:
first, disrespect toward the Saṃgha, which refers to seeing the great assembly engaged in discourse;
second, disrespect toward individuals, namely the ācāryas and upādhyāyas.

If a bhikṣu, while the Saṃgha is deliberating on a matter, is told by the assembly to stand, or not to sit here, or is sent away, or is forbidden from entering, or is told to take up his mat, or is told not to take it up—if he does not comply with what the assembly has said, he incurs a pāyattika offense.
If one does not act in accordance with the instructions given by an ācārya or an upādhyāya, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
However, there is no offense if one seeks to stop either of these two teachers from speaking in accordance with reason, or if they are elders who speak what is contrary to the Dharma.

Furthermore, there are other accounts regarding matters of disrespect: namely, toward the Dharma, the Buddha, venerable persons, disciples, rulers, or common folk; when one fails to give rise to reverence toward such as these—whether in speech or silence—and does not comply with words that accord with the Dharma; or when, through body, speech, or mind, one acts disrespectfully as the occasion requires—in each such case, one incurs an offense according to the gravity of the act.
Regarding what is called "Dharma-affairs": one must first examine whether one’s own precepts are pure.

If one fails to perform such duties as reciting and teaching, bestowing the meaning of the Dharma upon others, proper mental attention (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as appropriate; if one is constantly indolent and does not cultivate wholesome qualities; if one shows no respect for the precepts and engages in useless talk; or if one listens to, reads, or associates with Lokāyata texts that deny the existence of future lives—all such acts constitute a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding what is called "Buddha-activity": it refers to failing to diligently pay homage to sacred images, not sweeping or cleaning the *caityas* and incense altars at the proper times, seeing them in a state of ruin yet having the power to do so but failing to repair them, and being indolent and negligent toward those tasks that ought to be performed.
Regarding the term "venerable person" (*gurujana*): both those who are venerable and those of a similar status are called venerable persons.

Whenever one arrives in the presence of a venerable person, one’s deportment in walking, standing, or sitting should be neither too high nor too low; one should not wear the robe over both shoulders, nor sit with knees raised and feet crossed, nor lean the body straight and rigid, nor sit with the back turned, nor sit abruptly without having received the venerable person's command. One should not let the body rest in arrogance by placing thigh upon thigh; one should not speak abruptly when told not to speak; one should not interrupt what the venerable person says, nor should one oppose any instruction they give. Rather, one should remain silent and dwell in respectful service, free from envy and anger, having eliminated all evil thoughts, and constantly acting with veneration and support.
If one does not cultivate respect, all such acts constitute a downfall offense.

Regarding the duties toward a disciple: to reprimand them at an improper time or in an inappropriate place; to be unable to tolerate minor transgressions; to fail to provide skillful exhortation and instruction; to fail to eliminate their doubts or regrets; to speak harsh and coarse words without a heart of compassion; to fail to sustain them with the food of the Dharma; and to harbor a mind of affliction or harm instead of seeking to rescue and deliver them—all these constitute downfall offenses.
Regarding those called "rulers," this refers to kings, princes, and their malevolent ministers who come and go; one must not heed their words.
Due to these causes and conditions, feelings of disrespect arise, or they may commit acts of killing and inflict harm.

Regarding "worldly customs": one should not disregard secular people; rather, one should act according to their preferences to avoid being subject to criticism or suspicion. One should not relieve oneself on the road in a manner that would cause reproach from the laity, nor should one engage in conflict or competition with worldly people.
If one acts with a mind of contempt or wishes to annoy others, whatever they do will result in a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).

If, during a formal deliberation by the Saṃgha, one perceives it as a deliberation yet fails to show respect, there are six cases; in the first two, the offense is a *pāyattika* (falling away), and in the remaining four, they are all *duṣkṛta*.

79. The Training Rule on Drinking Alcohol. The seventy-ninth training rule concerning drinking alcohol: The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣu Śāṅkha received non-timely gruel mixed with alcohol from a layperson's house and drank it; he subsequently became so intoxicated that he collapsed, lying prostrate in the middle of the street.
Due to the matter of accepting invitations and the affliction of censure, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu drinks any kind of intoxicating liquor, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding "liquor": it may be made by fermenting rice with yeast, or by steaming rice flour until cooked and then brewing it.
There are also various mixed liquors, meaning those made from roots, bark, leaves, as well as flowers and fruits, to which a small amount of rice yeast is added before fermentation.
"Drinking" refers to swallowing.

Whether one drinks that which possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of wine, or that which lacks one or two of these qualities, if it causes intoxication when swallowed, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
If it does not intoxicate people, drinking it constitutes a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If the substance is not wine but possesses the appearance of wine, drinking it incurs no offense.
Whether one drinks from a vessel, drinks with cupped hands, or even drinks dregs of wine, in all such cases one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If one consumes yeast or eats flowers and fruits that can cause intoxication, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) in all cases.
Regarding the six permutations of the perception of the object (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*), there is no offense in the latter two. Some say:
"Even if one does not perceive it as alcohol, yet perceives it as such, one still incurs a downfall. As the Buddha said:

"O Bhikṣus, those who have gone forth with me as their teacher should not drink alcohol, nor give it to others, nor store it; they should not even place a drop of alcohol on the tip of a blade of grass within their mouths."

There is no offense if the wine has been boiled down so that it does not intoxicate when drunk; or if one has a mouth ailment and a physician orders them to hold wine in the mouth; or if the wine is applied to the body—in all these cases, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣu who was previously addicted to alcohol becomes emaciated and weak when unable to obtain liquor, he may take the ingredients for brewing—yeast, tree bark, and various fragrant medicinal herbs—and grind them into a powder. He should wrap this in a cloth, tie it across with a staff, and suspend it inside a jar of newly fermented liquor, taking care not to let it touch the liquid.
After one or two nights have passed, stir it with water; drinking it then, whether at the proper time or not, constitutes no offense.

Furthermore, there is no offense in the following cases: if the wine has turned into vinegar and drinking it does not intoxicate, or if it is clear enough to see one's reflection, or if it has been diluted with water until it becomes pure; having filtered it through a strainer, it may be drunk at will as a "non-time beverage" (*vikāla-pāna*).

80. The Training Rule on Entering a Village at an Improper Time Without Informing a Bhikṣu. The eighth training rule concerning entering a village at an improper time without informing a bhikṣu: While the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, Udāyin entered a village at an improper time and was killed by bandits.
Regarding the matter of entering a village, as the underlying afflictions were the same as before, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣu, except for other special circumstances, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the term "improper time," there are two boundaries:
first, after midday;
second, before the appearance of the dawn light.
"Village" refers to a place where laypeople reside, provided there are streets and lanes.
Regarding "other bhikṣus," if no other bhikṣus are present, there is no offense.

"Except for other circumstances" means, for instance, when one has an illness, or if one has deposited one's robes and bowl in a village and the house is burned by fire, necessitating entry into the village to check on them.
If there is danger to life or danger to one's pure conduct, there is no offense in either case.
If it is not the proper time and one perceives it as such, or has doubt about it, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is the proper time but one perceives it as not being so, or has doubt about it, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
The latter two cases are without offense.
Regarding the six permutations concerning the perception of a village as a village, they are the same as before.

There is no offense if a bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya must enter a village; or if the path passes through a village; or if the road lies between two villages; or if he enters by traveling through the air; or if there is no other bhikṣu to whom he can entrust his belongings, and he thus instructs a layperson.
The ninth summary verse says:
Food, the appearance of dawn, and present knowledge; The needle case, the measurement of bed-legs, Storing flowers, and the sitting mat; The sore, the rain, and the Master’s robe.

81. The Training Rule on Visiting Other Houses Before or After a Meal. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, a lay follower who was a personal friend of Upānanda had deep faith in the Triple Gem; he prepared an extensive offering in his own home and invited the community of bhikṣus, with Upānanda as their head.
At that time, Upānanda informed his friends, saying, "I have a matter of business that requires me to go to a certain house; you must wait for my arrival before serving the food.
Having gone elsewhere, he did not return for a long time, and consequently, the majority of the assembly was unable to eat.
Because monks visited the homes of laypeople beyond the proper limit, neglecting their duties and falling into affliction, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu, having accepted an invitation to a meal at a layperson's home, visits another house before or after the meal without having informed [the host], it is a pāyattika."
"An invitation to a meal at a house" refers to accepting an invitation for a meal from a layperson, whether a Brahmin or another member of the laity.
"Before the meal" means during the morning period; if one goes beyond two houses without having informed [a fellow monk] before departing, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
"Having finished eating" refers to the period after midday; if one goes to more than three households during this time, one incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).
If one says to the donor:
"Even if I do not come, you should provide food for the Sangha so that it is not neglected."
"If the donor does not designate this person as the primary recipient, there is no offense in departing.

**The Training Rule on Entering the Royal Palace, Number Eighty-Two** The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, in Śrāvastī. At that time, Udāyin had a certain business and needed to go to the residence of Queen Mallikā.

Entering the palace very early, he found the king still lying down and not yet risen; upon hearing that the Venerable One had arrived, the king was suddenly startled awake and put on his usual fine, thin garments for the inner palace to receive him.
The circumstances are the same as before; this training rule was established due to the defilement of causing public censure and depending on specific conditions:

"If a bhikṣu, while the dawn has not yet appeared and before the consecrated Kṣatriya king has hidden his treasures or treasure-like objects, should enter past the threshold of the palace gate, except for other extenuating circumstances, it is a pāyattika."
"A Kṣatriya" refers to one of the Kṣatriya caste; even if one is not of this caste, if they have received the consecration (abhiṣeka), they are also called a Kṣatriya king.
Regarding "before the appearance of the dawn," there are three distinct signs:
the first is the blue sign, meaning that a blue color appears.
Second is the mark of yellow, meaning that a yellow color appears;
third is the mark of red copper, meaning the radiance is like the color of red copper.
"Not yet concealing the treasure" means that the treasure has not yet been hidden within the palace.
Regarding the threshold, there are three kinds: first, the threshold of a city gate;
second, the threshold of a royal palace gate;
[and third, the threshold of a household].
3. Regarding the threshold of the inner palace gates:
entering the first two gates constitutes an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa);
entering the gate of the inner palace constitutes an offense of falling (pācittiya).

Regarding "except for other circumstances": as in the case where the King of the city of Kauśāmbī permitted the house of Ghoṣila to be connected to the royal palace as a single location, there is no offense.
There are five kinds of instructions that must not be transgressed.
What are the five? First, it refers to a king;
second, the Tathāgata, the Great Teacher.
Third, the senior monk (sthavira) among the assembly;
fourth, the ācārya; fifth, the upādhyāya.
The six phrases beginning with "not having understood" and "the perception of not having understood," etc., are as explained above.
If one enters the gates of the Four Heavenly Kings or the palaces of the Garuḍas, one also incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
There are ten faults in entering a royal palace:
first, if a queen smiles upon seeing a bhikṣu, the king will give rise to suspicion;
second, if a woman of the palace becomes pregnant, he will immediately suspect the bhikṣu.
Third, precious objects are lost within the palace.
Fourth, the king’s secret words are heard outside.
Fifth, the crown prince suffers harm.
Sixth, the king’s person will suffer injury;
seventh, the state chancellor will be dismissed;
eighth, a great minister will be promoted.
Ninth, frequent military expeditions.
Tenth, when the king seizes back for himself what was obtained through those expeditions.
Because such matters as these all lead to suspicion that the bhikṣu is directing them, one should not go.

83. The Training Rule on Not Listening with Attentive Ears and Speaking as if One Does Not Know. The eighth and final training rule: When the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, the group of six bhikṣus did not listen attentively during the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month, but instead spoke thus:
"Only now do we know that this dharma was spoken by the Sugata."
This training rule was established due to the affliction of arrogance regarding the Dharma, arising from treating the matter of the training rules lightly.
"If a bhikṣu, when the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is recited every half-month, should speak thus:
'Venerable one!'"
"I have only now learned that this dharma is taught in the *Śīla-vinaya-sūtra*.
When the bhikṣus learn that this bhikṣu has performed the *poṣadha* together with them two or three times, let alone more than that.
One should say to him:
"Venerable one! You cannot escape this offense simply because you were unaware."
"You must confess and repent for the offense you have committed according to the Dharma.
One should then exhort them, saying:
"Venerable one!..."

This Dharma is rare and difficult to encounter; yet when you recited the precepts, you were without reverence, lacked a settled mind, were not earnest or attentive, did not maintain focused thought, and did not lend your ear.
"To listen to the Dharma without applying mindfulness constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
"Without respect" is the general heading;
"not abiding in the mind," etc., are the specific explanatory phrases that reveal six faults:

That is to say, the loss of faith, the loss of respect, the loss of aspiration, the loss of focusing on external objects, the loss of mental lethargy, and the loss of giving rise to weariness; these are to be assigned respectively [to the six causes].
If a bhikṣu has already heard the Prātimokṣa Sūtra being recited two or three times previously, yet at the time of the Poṣadha ceremony makes a claim of ignorance—
whether due to afflictions, forgetfulness, sleep, or a distracted mind— and fails to listen to any single precept, he incurs a pāyattika offense for each instance.
If one hears the unique training rules for bhikṣuṇīs and speaks in such a manner, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense;
if it concerns the common training rules, one incurs the primary offense.
If one is elderly and infirm, lacking the capacity for discernment, there is no offense in speaking according to the facts.
At the time of the *poṣadha*, one who is proficient and well-versed in reciting the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* should be appointed to recite it for the assembly.
When the time for the morning announcement has arrived, the bhikṣus should each recall their own offenses and confess them according to the Dharma before proceeding to the assembly.

The Eighty-fourth Rule: Regarding the Use of Ivory or Bone to Make Needle Cases. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī. There was a skilled craftsman named Dharma who was expert in working with ivory and bone.
Using his own craftsmanship, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "If there is a need for anything made of ivory or bone, I shall provide it for you to make.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know moderation; they employed him all day long to have needle cases made, without a moment's rest, until finally his household affairs were brought to ruin.
Due to the excessive use of needle cases, their neglect, and the resulting reproach and affliction, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu makes a needle case out of bone, ivory, or horn, it shall be smashed; it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the needle case, there are two types that should be kept:
first, a cylinder; second, a tube.
Regarding "making," it means either making it oneself or having another make it.
Regarding the term "breaking and smashing": this refers to when an item has been completed and come into one's possession; it should be broken and discarded.
If it has been made but not yet finished, it should likewise be abandoned.
If one completes the work but does not accept it for oneself, or if one makes it for another, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one has already obtained [a permissible substitute], there is no offense in using it.
When confessing the transgression before a bhikṣu, he should ask:
"Have you already smashed the needle case?"
If one does not ask when it is not the proper time, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There are four kinds of needle cases that should be kept:
those made of copper, iron, brass, and red copper.
One should not use gold, silver, lapis lazuli, or crystal to make a needle case, nor should it be fashioned from a sharp point or variegated with various colors.
One who keeps a needle case should store it away in a concealed place.
If a monk who lacks shame or one who is not fully ordained borrows [an item], it should not be given; however, it should be given to one who is capable of lovingly protecting it.
Fearing that iron will develop rust when needles and knives are stored, they should be wrapped in waxed cloth.

Just as one should not use a needle case that has been made for the purpose of being smashed, so too should it be understood that other requisites made in violation of the rules are likewise forbidden.
A monk should possess a knife and a small seal.
There are three kinds of knives:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
Their shapes are like the curved feathers of a chicken, or like the curved wings of a crow.

The superior [type] is six finger-widths long and one finger-width wide; the inferior is four finger-widths; those between these two are called medium. These are all attached to an iron hilt; if they have a wooden hilt, it must be straight and pointed, and in all such cases, they are not permitted to be kept.
There are four kinds of seals:
namely, white copper, red copper, brass, and wood.

As for the inscription on the Saṃgha seal, it should bear the name of the monastery founder; above it, there should be an image of the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, serving as a mark of identification according to its size.

If it is a seal for an individual, it may be made in the form of a chain of bones or in the form of a skull; when seeing it, one should give rise to the thought of practicing the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). In all such cases, one must not use precious materials to make them.
The six permutations regarding the perception of the object may be understood as before.
**The 85th Training Rule: On Making a Bed Exceeding the Proper Size** The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

As the Blessed One had said: “One should not wash one’s feet at the head of the bed. However, if one is old, ill, or exhausted from traveling, one may wash them at either end of the bed. Furthermore, one should not sleep on a bed whose legs are excessively short.”
At that time, the group of six monks constructed large bedsteads with legs twelve cubits long, using ladders for ascending and descending.
Due to the matter of the bed's dimensions and the afflictions being the same as before, this training rule was established.
"If a bhikṣu makes a large or small bed, the legs should be no higher than eight finger-breadths of the Buddha's measure, excluding the portion inserted into the frame.
If they exceed this, they must be cut down; [the offense is] a pāyattika."
This matter of causing distress applies equally to all the lower precepts.
Regarding the phrase "making a bed," it means either making it oneself or having another person make it.
"The Buddha’s eight fingers" refers to one cubit (*hasta*) of a person of medium height.
"Except for the wood inserted into the frame" means except for the wood inserted into the frame of the bed legs.
"That which should be cut off" means that if it exceeds [the proper length], one must cut it away before confessing the offense.
If it is adorned with jewels, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) offense.

The legs of all beds should be cut flat; if one fears they might damage the floor, one should place supports beneath them, such as bags of grain husks, bricks, or wood. That which is said to be "one cubit for a person of medium height" measures one chi and five cun by the long *hu* scale; anything exceeding this is the measure of a high bed, and using such a bed constitutes an offense.

86. The Training Rule on Storing Cotton from Grass and Trees in Beds. The eighty-sixth training rule concerning the storage of cotton from grass and trees in beds: While the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, Upānanda stuffed cotton from grass and trees into a monastic bed. When other bhikṣus lay down upon it, their entire bodies became white.
Regarding the matter of bedding and the afflictions involved, they are the same as before; thus this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu should store cotton from grasses or trees and the like within a monk’s bed or seat, it must be removed; [otherwise] it is a pāyattika."
Regarding what are called "grass and wood cotton," there are five kinds:
first, grass cotton;
second, wood cotton; [and so forth].
Third, cotton; fourth, wool; fifth, various types of stuffing and the like.
Regarding the term "storing" (*nicaya*): it refers to spreading cotton down upon a bed or mattress and then covering it with a cloth sheet at appropriate times.
If one uses pure cotton or pure cloth, at the time of first making it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; once it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
Using impure cotton cloth constitutes an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
Generally, that which is suitable for a bhikṣu to use is termed "pure," while that which is unsuitable is termed "impure.

**The 87th Training Rule: On Making a Niṣīdana of Excessive Size** The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, various bhikṣus were making *niṣīdana* (seating mats), but they did not follow the prescribed measurements.
Regarding the matter of the dimensions of the robe, as the afflictions were the same as before, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu makes a niṣīdana, he should make it according to the prescribed measurements."
Regarding the measurements therein: the length shall be two spans of the Buddha’s hands, and the width one and a half spans; within that length, one may further increase it by one span.
If one makes it exceed these dimensions, it must be cut down; this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the statement "two spans longer than the Buddha’s [robe]," this refers to a measurement of three *cubit* (*hasta*) for an average person.
"Adding one further span" refers to half a *cubit*.
With a total length of four and a half cubits and a width of one and a half spans— the total width being two cubits plus six finger-breadths—
one should construct a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) by cutting it into pieces and arranging them in patches; it is to be used as a liner for bedding, as detailed in the extensive text.

88. The Training Rule on Making Oversized Covering Cloths for Sores. The eighty-eighth training rule concerning making covering cloths for sores that exceed the prescribed dimensions. When the Buddha was staying at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in Śrāvastī, many bhikṣus suffered from skin diseases such as sores and scabs; consequently, the World-Honored One permitted them to keep covering cloths for sores.
Because the bhikṣus made [the garments] in excess of the proper measure, and as the circumstances causing distress were the same as before, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu makes a garment for covering sores, he should make it according to the prescribed measure."
Regarding the measurements herein: the length shall be four spans of the Buddha’s hands, and the width two spans.
If one makes it exceeding these dimensions, it should be cut down; this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
"Making" refers to making it oneself or instructing another to make it.
A length of four spans of the Buddha’s hand is equivalent to six cubits of a medium-sized person;
a width of two spans is equivalent to three cubits.
To exceed these measurements constitutes an offense of transgression (pāyattika).
If one makes [a garment] smaller than the prescribed measure while observing the rule, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense. If one makes it for another person, one also incurs an *dukkaṭa*.

The Eighty-ninth Training Rule on Making a Rain-Bathing Garment Exceeding the Proper Measure: While the Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park in Śrāvastī, the bhikṣus were bathing with their bodies exposed. Consequently, Vimalakīrti Mṛgāramātṛ permitted the keeping of rain-bathing garments.
Because the bhikṣus made them in excess of the proper measure, the resulting distress was the same as before; thus, this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bathing robe, he should make it according to the prescribed measurement."
Regarding the measurements therein: the length shall be six spans of the Buddha’s hand, and the width two and a half spans.
If one makes it exceeding these dimensions, it should be cut down; [otherwise] it is an *pāyattika* offense.
As for the maker, it may be made by oneself or caused to be made by another.
The measurement is three times that of a person of medium stature.
To maintain [the robe] when it is less than this measurement constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

90. The Training Rule on Making Robes Exceeding the Measure Equal to the Buddha’s. The ninety-first training rule: Making robes exceeding the measure equal to the Buddha’s. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, Upānanda had finished sewing a large *cīvara* (robe); he put on only one side of it, gathering the rest upon his shoulder, and went to another residence.
The circumstances and the grievance are the same as before; thus this training rule was established:
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe according to the measurement of the Buddha’s robes, or one that exceeds it, it is a pāyattika."
Regarding the measurement of a Buddha’s robe among these, it is ten spans long and six spans wide; this is the measurement of a Buddha’s robe.
As for the phrase "of the same measurement as a Buddha’s robe," this refers to the measurement of the robe being derived from the measurement of a Buddha’s robe, which constitutes an offense.
"Divided garment" refers to that which is fit to be maintained as one's own.
A length of ten *hasta*s of the Buddha is equivalent to fifteen *cubit*s (*hasta*) of a person of medium height;
a width of six *hasta*s is equivalent to nine *cubit*s of such a person.
If one makes a robe with a measurement less than this, one does not incur the primary offense (*maulāpatti*).
If it exceeds five *hasta* or more, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*) in all such cases.
